Neural networks have become a standard approach for solving tabular data problems, yet they often exhibit significant biases against protected groups, leading to unfair decisions. While recent studies have introduced various fairness-aware algorithms for tabular data, most rely on preprocessed labels and fail to incorporate structural context, limiting their applicability to complex scenarios like social network analysis. To address this, we propose fairness-aware Graph Neural Networks (f-GNNs), which enable the consideration of structural information during the learning process. Our method introduces a fairness-aware message-passing mechanism that adjusts message content based on both the source node's protection status and the relationship between the source and target nodes. Additionally, we present a fairness-aware aggregation module that modifies the aggregation function to reflect the protection status of neighboring nodes. We also provide a node-level fairness-aware loss function to guide the network toward learning fair patterns. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms baseline methods in terms of both accuracy and fairness. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi1997/f-GNN.

We examine the kinetic equation governing reversible enzyme reactions, which features a piecewise linear right-hand side. This nonlinear equation is approximated by linear equations, and the corresponding probability density functions are solved using two distinct methods: (1) the Fourier method, yielding solutions in the form of infinite series of Bessel functions; and (2) the finite Legendre polynomial method, which utilizes the Legendre polynomial expansion of the solution. The equation solutions derived from these two approaches are compared, and second-order approximate solutions are computed for each. Finally, the stationary solutions of the various approximations are analyzed. It is demonstrated that the number of terms in the series solutions required to achieve a specific level of accuracy is of the same order as the number of terms in the Legendre polynomial expansion. Furthermore, the kinetic equations and their respective stationary solutions for the first-order approximations are compared across both methods. Notably, the first-order approximate solutions for the probability density function are identical in both cases, whereas the stationary solutions differ. These differences are also illustrated through their respective Laplace transforms. The findings indicate that while the kinetic equation solutions are equivalent, the stationary solutions are not. Consequently, we conclude that the two approximation methods are not entirely interchangeable. To address this discrepancy, we propose a modification to the series solution. Using this adjusted approach, the stationary solutions are recalculated and compared with those from the Legendre polynomial expansion. The results show that the relative error between the two modified stationary solutions is approximately 10%. Finally, the Laplace transforms of these modified stationary solutions are compared. Based on these findings, we recommend that future research utilize the modified series solution rather than the original one. Additionally, we suggest that when applying the Legendre polynomial expansion method, the first two terms of the expansion should be included to ensure higher accuracy. This paper presents the initial application of the Legendre polynomial expansion method to enzyme reaction kinetics. Future studies could explore higher-order approximations and investigate alternative solution methods, such as the finite element method. Furthermore, extending these analyses to more complex reaction models, such as those involving multiple enzymes, would be a valuable direction for subsequent research. We have also prepared to apply the Legendre polynomial expansion method to other reversible reaction models, including reversible Michaelis-Menten reactions and reversible enzyme reactions with competitive inhibition. Finally, we intend to explore the application of the Legendre polynomial expansion method to irreversible reaction models. To facilitate these future efforts, we have developed a computational program based on this method, which will be made available to the scientific community.

This study investigates supersymmetry (SUSY) within final states characterized by jets and missing transverse momentum. The analysis examines two distinct SUSY scenarios: natural SUSY, characterized by a compressed mass spectrum of light states, and split SUSY, defined by heavy electroweak bosons. The search utilizes proton-proton collision data from the CMS experiment at the LHC, collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$. For the natural SUSY search, results are derived from events featuring at least one energetic jet and missing transverse momentum. In the split SUSY search, the selection criteria require at least one very energetic jet and missing transverse momentum. No significant signal was detected in either analysis. Consequently, various sparticle masses were excluded at 95% confidence level; for the natural SUSY search, gluino masses up to 2.1 TeV and top squark masses up to 1.6 TeV are ruled out. For the split SUSY search, gluino masses exceeding 1.9 TeV are excluded. Additionally, limits are established for the neutralino lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) mass under both scenarios. The most stringent exclusion corresponds to a LSP mass of 1.1 TeV in the natural SUSY search and 2.5 TeV in the split SUSY search. This latter limit represents the most stringent exclusion of LSP masses in split SUSY scenarios to date. Furthermore, this search sets the highest exclusion limit for gluino masses at 13 TeV. The study concludes by outlining improvements achieved through machine learning techniques. This work is based on the doctoral thesis of Dr. J. Lazo-Fernandez. We simulated the time evolution of a quantum harmonic oscillator driven by a sinusoidal force, performing path integral calculations via both Green's function and Metropolis methods. Initially, we computed the system without driving forces to validate our code, confirming that the wave function oscillates between the ground and first excited states. Subsequently, we applied a sinusoidally driven force to the initial ground state. Our results demonstrate that when the driving frequency matches the system's natural frequency, the system transitions to the first excited state; conversely, when the driving frequency is twice the natural frequency, it transitions to the first excited state. These simulations successfully illustrate quantum resonance phenomena. Additionally, we determined the Rabi frequency by analyzing the probability of finding the system in the first excited state. Finally, we compared our numerical findings with analytical solutions, observing strong agreement. This study confirms the effectiveness of both the Green's function and Metropolis methods for simulating quantum systems. Furthermore, the path integral approach, particularly through Green's function calculations, offers a straightforward method for simulating quantum systems without the need for sampling. However, we also note that the path integral method can be computationally expensive when utilizing Green's function techniques. To address this limitation, we also employed the Metropolis algorithm to simulate the system. Our findings indicate that while the Metropolis method yields accurate results, it requires a large number of sampling points to achieve convergence, making it a more computationally demanding approach. Nevertheless, the Metropolis algorithm holds significant potential for simulating more complex quantum systems. Overall, this paper aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the path integral approach to quantum simulations and to establish a foundation for future investigations into driven quantum systems. Finally, we propose several avenues for further research, including the simulation of anharmonic oscillators, multi-mode systems, and higher-dimensional systems. By extending the current methodology, these approaches could offer deeper insights into the behavior of quantum systems. By leveraging machine learning, researchers could develop more sophisticated algorithms for simulating complex quantum systems. In recent years, Item-anchored Fusion Networks (SIFN) have gained significant attention for their superior performance in review-based recommendation tasks. However, existing SIFN architectures face a critical limitation: they rely on average pooling to aggregate item reviews, which fails to capture the diverse perspectives of individual reviewers. This limitation leads to a loss of valuable information and prevents the model from effectively identifying reviews most relevant to a specific user. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that incorporates a user-specific attention mechanism to fuse item reviews. This mechanism enables the model to extract reviews pertinent to a given user by leveraging both review text and user profile data. Furthermore, we present the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SiFiN), which further enhances SiFiN's capabilities. SiFiN employs a two-stage interactive sentiment analysis process to extract fine-grained sentiment features from reviews, thereby enriching the model's sentiment awareness. Experimental results demonstrate that SiFiN significantly outperforms the baseline SIFN model. Additionally, an ablation study confirms that the proposed sentiment-aware sentiment analysis module is a key driver of SiFiN's success. Finally, case studies illustrate how SiFiN effectively captures user preferences through sentiment analysis. Overall, this paper demonstrates that integrating user-specific attention and fine-grained sentiment analysis into the fusion network substantially improves review-based item recommendation performance. This paper explores data augmentation techniques for Arabic-English code-switched (CS) text, which is prevalent in informal communication and often absent from standard corpora. We investigate two approaches: back-translation and lexical replacements. Our findings indicate that combining these methods yields the best results, producing CS sentences that are more diverse and of higher quality than those generated by using either method alone. This superior quality is particularly evident in lexical replacements, which generate significantly higher counts of out-of-vocabulary words for training data, thereby enhancing model training. Additionally, the integration of back-translation allows for the generation of multiple augmented sentences from a single original sentence. The effectiveness of our proposed pipeline is validated through its application in the widely adopted text classification task. The code for our work is accessible at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan123/CS-DataAugmentation. Given the success of our approach, it is expected to be beneficial for other natural language processing tasks involving Arabic-English code-switching. Future research will focus on developing better metrics for evaluating the quality of augmented CS data. We also plan to extend this work to other languages, such as Hindi-English CS, which is also under-represented in public datasets. Finally, we intend to explore the impact of data augmentation on cross-lingual tasks involving multilingual CS data. To our knowledge, this is the first paper to propose a data augmentation pipeline for Arabic-English code-switching. We hope this work will inspire further research in this area. We introduce a metric-based regularity condition for reinforcement learning, which encompasses and extends Lippel et al.'s (2015) L2 smoothness concept. This work presents a novel, more general framework that enables the analysis of Lippel et al.'s Lp smoothness for p > 2. The findings demonstrate that, under this metric-based regularity, the Lp smoothness property of a Q-function is both necessary and sufficient to guarantee sublinear regret. Furthermore, we present a regret bound that explicitly incorporates Pseudohyperdiameter, a metric-dependent parameter that generalizes the state space dimension. These insights facilitate the development of new reinforcement learning algorithms tailored for this metric-based regularity within fixed horizon, finite horizon, and infinite horizon Markov Decision Processes. Notably, in fixed horizon finite horizon MDPs, we introduce Coarse-Grained Smooth Dimension (CGSD), a metric-based parameter that generalizes state space dimension. We show that our algorithms achieve regret bounds dependent on the square of the CGSD rather than the state space dimension, thereby improving upon prior results. Additionally, we establish that our proposed algorithms are minimax optimal with respect to the Pseudohyperdiameter and CGSD. Finally, we extend these findings to continuous state space MDPs by introducing Metric-based Coarse-Grained Smoothness, a property that allows for the design of algorithms achieving logarithmic regret. Our approach relies on a metric-based covering technique that is applicable to any metric space. Empirical evaluations on the MuJoCo continuous control benchmark confirm that our methods outperform existing techniques. The animacy category is a fundamental aspect of object knowledge, yet its neural underpinnings remain poorly understood. While fMRI research has linked animacy to the ventral temporal cortex (VTC), the specific nature of this relationship is still unclear. This study employed representational similarity analysis (RSA) to investigate how animacy ratings correlate with neural representations. We examined the relationship between animacy and neural dissimilarity using both parametric modulation and RSA. Our findings indicate that animacy ratings are not strongly predictive of neural dissimilarity within VTC. Furthermore, we determined that the animacy organization in VTC is dynamic and temporal, characterized by fluctuations in strength and spatial extent across time. Finally, we explored the link between animacy and object selectivity in VTC, revealing that high animacy stimuli tend to be less selective for specific categories. Collectively, these results suggest that animacy is not a distinct, separable category representation within the ventral temporal cortex. Instead, the animacy organization appears to be an emergent property of the visual system's response to naturalistic image sequences. This study introduces a general framework for developing a structure-preserving filter (SPF) tailored for finite element simulations across various spatial dimensions. The approach relies on solving a specific convex optimization problem that minimizes the $L_2$ norm of filtered quantities while utilizing a weighted graph Laplacian as the objective function's matrix. We demonstrate that this solution effectively smooths simulation data, yielding results comparable to those of a diffusion filter, yet it also maintains key physical properties such as the maximum principle and specific geometric attributes like area and volume. Furthermore, we present a method to adaptively weight graph edges based on gradients, enabling area- and volume-preserving filters for 2D and 3D simulations. The paper concludes with numerical examples that illustrate the diverse capabilities of the proposed structure-preserving filter. The implementation is accessible via the PySPF Python package. Additionally, we acknowledge that the filter is not fully scale-invariant, as its parameters depend on the mesh size, and we outline potential future research directions for enhancing its robustness. Finally, we demonstrate how the filter can be integrated with meshless methods, specifically the finite pointset method, to smooth and preserve physical properties in 2D and 3D simulations. Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in black hole X-ray transients are typically observed during the hard-intermediate state, a phase characterized by a transition from hard to intermediate spectral states. This study employs the high-resolution hard X-ray data from the Insight-HXMT mission to investigate the evolution of the corona in the black hole X-ray transient MAXI J1535-571, as traced by type-C QPOs. The analysis reveals that the energy centroid of the type-C QPOs shifts from 1.8 to 2.0 keV as the soft X-ray flux declines from 0.3 to 0.1 mCrab. Furthermore, we observe a strong correlation between type-C QPO power and both soft X-ray flux and hard X-ray flux, with a notably steeper dependence on soft X-ray flux. Additionally, a significant anti-correlation exists between type-C QPO power and the hardness ratio. These findings suggest that the type-C QPO is linked to a compact, rapidly moving region located near the inner edge of the accretion disc. Finally, we propose that the evolution of the type-C QPO in MAXI J1535-571 can be explained by a model combining a variable disc radius with a superposition of two thermal components. These results are consistent with the scenario describing the evolution of type-C QPOs across different hard X-ray flux levels. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the evolution of type-C QPOs in MAXI J1535-571 aligns with the correlations previously reported for other black hole X-ray transients.

This study investigates cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) within the context of multi-agent coordination games, specifically examining how agents can reliably react to their partners' behaviors. We introduce a method that leverages a transferable reward signal to effectively learn a robust response to the actions of a chosen team member. Our approach employs an auxiliary reward known as "transfer empowerment," which quantifies the influence an agent holds over the received reward by simulating the behavior of that specific team member. We demonstrate that this auxiliary reward induces a social intrinsic motivation to exert influence over the simulated partner, thereby enabling a reliable reaction to their actual actions during joint tasks. Furthermore, we show that incorporating this transfer empowerment into the credit assignment process facilitates effective coordination among multiple agents. Experimental results indicate that our method performs competitively against established MARL techniques across various influence-based multi-agent coordination games. Additionally, we demonstrate the approach's applicability in a real-world setting by having a group of small robots coordinate to follow a leader. We begin by revisiting the definition of strict Lie 2-algebras, which are equivalent to idempotent $L_{\infty}$-algebras, and review various categorical and geometric perspectives. Subsequently, we present the definition of weak Lie 2-algebras, offering an alternative formulation through pentagons. This conceptual framework paves the way for a comprehensive and unified understanding of the homotopy theory inherent to the category of Lie 2-algebras. Furthermore, by connecting Lie 2-algebras to 2-plectic geometry, we outline the definition of Courant 2-plectic structures. Ultimately, we sketch the definition of Lie n-algebras, serving as the natural generalization of Lie algebras to higher dimensions. In doing so, we highlight the intricate and fascinating homotopy theory of Lie n-algebras. We anticipate that this review will contribute to a deeper comprehension of the homotopy theory surrounding higher-dimensional Lie algebras. Additionally, we provide an appendix detailing the definition of multilinear curvatures. We introduce a new approach for local image feature matching that bypasses the traditional sequential steps of detection, description, and matching. Instead, our method first establishes coarse, pixel-level correspondences and subsequently refines them independently for each image. This strategy eliminates the need to locate or refine individual interest points, allowing for direct matching of new views even when key points are absent. To achieve this, we employ a hybrid architecture combining coarse-to-fine feature extraction with a transformer-based matching module. The former generates corresponding image patches, while the latter generates cross-attention maps to identify precise pixel-level matches. Additionally, we incorporate a learning-based refinement network to enhance the robustness of these attention maps. This study examines the impact of instrumental bias in line-of-sight (LOS) measurements on the accuracy of vector magnetic field data derived from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory's (SDO) mission. We analyze 10 years of HMI data to identify systematic biases in LOS measurements, which are primarily caused by pointing errors and variations in instrument sensitivity across the detector. By comparing these LOS measurements with field-of-view-averaged synoptic maps generated by the Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG), we quantify the biases present in HMI-derived vector magnetic field data. Our results indicate that, on average, HMI data overestimates the magnetic field strength in the GONG south polar region by approximately 100 G. Furthermore, we introduce a method to correct these biases, which successfully reduces the discrepancy between HMI and GONG synoptic maps. This correction is particularly significant in the southern polar region, where HMI magnetic field strengths are reduced by roughly 50%, bringing them into closer alignment with GONG observations. Additionally, we explore the potential for applying this correction to other data sources, such as the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) and the Interface Region Eclipse Spectrograph (IRES). Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for coronal models that utilize HMI vector magnetic field data as boundary conditions. Correcting the bias in HMI magnetic field data is essential for accurately modeling the Sun's magnetic field and its associated energy. Within this framework, consumers utilize scheduling algorithms to reduce their individual expenses, while simultaneously reporting instantaneous power consumption to the supplier for the duration of the agreement. The supplier, in turn, allocates instantaneous load to each consumer based on usage data. Consequently, the consumer optimization problem becomes an aggregative game, while the supplier's cost minimization task is modeled as an aggregative best response game. This paper demonstrates the existence of the solution to the supplier's problem and establishes the conditions under which the consumer aggregative game possesses a unique solution. Furthermore, we introduce an alternating algorithm to address the joint problem and provide theoretical and numerical evidence of its convergence. This study examines the Hawking radiation of charged black strings within Rastall theory using the Euclidean action method. The analysis demonstrates that gravitational effects influence the temperature, entropy, and mass of these systems. Specifically, the research establishes that both the mass and entropy decrease as the Rastall parameter increases, whereas the temperature rises under the same condition. These findings indicate that Rastall gravity can account for the observed evolution of black strings. Additionally, the study confirms that charged black strings exhibit a constant surface gravity, a characteristic consistent with the weak equivalence principle. Finally, the results show that when the Rastall parameter equals one, the black string reverts to the standard Einstein gravity scenario. We demonstrate that the power-law decay exponents in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems correspond to the pointwise scaling exponents of a spectral measure at the spectral value $1$. Furthermore, we establish that, assuming mild conditions, the convergence rates in the weak ergodic theorem are determined by the scaling exponents of the spectral measure at $-1$. The paper also explores implications for ergodicity in systems with quasi-compact spectra. Additionally, we present an example of a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space where the convergence rate of a power-law type arises from the behavior of a spectral measure at $0$. Finally, we examine an instance where the rate type is mixed, resulting from the superposition of two or more spectral measures with distinct scaling behaviors. This research was motivated by a recent study [1] linking the convergence rates of a stochastically stable Markov chain to the singularity exponents of its spectral measure at $1$. The search for extremely metal-poor stars serves as a primary method for investigating the early Universe and the characteristics of Population III stars. However, detecting these rare objects is challenging due to their scarcity and the difficulty of obtaining high-resolution spectra, which are required to measure precise metallicities. This study introduces a novel approach to identify metal-poor stars by utilizing the low-resolution blue and photometric red spectra from the Gaia mission. We developed a machine learning algorithm that leverages the relationship between spectral features and stellar parameters to predict the log[Fe/H] of individual stars. Our results indicate that this method can effectively distinguish between metal-poor stars and the majority of the stellar population, offering a straightforward and efficient means to select candidates for follow-up high-resolution spectroscopy. We successfully identified 12 previously known metal-poor stars using our technique, achieving a median log[Fe/H] prediction of -1.92 ± 0.11 dex. Furthermore, we detected 1,000 new candidates with log[Fe/H] < -1.5 dex; among these, 100 exhibit log[Fe/H] < -2.0 dex. These candidates are expected to provide valuable insights into the chemical evolution of the Galaxy. We have made the Gaia Data Release 3 (Gaia DR3) catalog of these new candidates publicly available to facilitate future high-resolution spectroscopic observations. Our findings suggest that this selection method is highly effective for identifying metal-poor stars, significantly advancing our understanding of the early Universe. This study introduces a new dataset for predicting global fire seasons, encompassing over 20 years of observations from 1997 to 2019. We define fire season severity as the daily maximum 850-hPa potential temperature anomaly during a season, which shows a strong correlation with the season's peak temperature anomaly. Our analysis reveals a statistically significant trend of increasing fire season severity across 40% of the Earth's land surface. We attribute this rise to a combination of rising global temperatures and a growing frequency of extreme heat events. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fire season severity can be forecast using a straightforward linear model driven by the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and global mean surface temperature. This model proves statistically significant and accurately predicts interannual variability in fire severity for regions including the Amazon, Australia, and the western United States. These findings suggest that as global temperatures continue to climb, fire seasons will become increasingly severe, posing greater risks to ecosystems and human populations. Additionally, the research indicates that long-term climate change may be altering the relationship between ENSO and fire severity in some areas, a dynamic that could be monitored in the future to detect early warning signs of ecosystem shifts. Finally, we highlight the potential for utilizing this forecast model to enhance fire risk assessment and management strategies. We conclude by discussing the limitations of our approach and outlining future research directions. The data and code utilized in this study are accessible at https://github.com/andrews2000/gfss. We investigate the reliability of various corpus-based metrics for assessing morphological complexity. To investigate whether these measures capture a single underlying dimension, we computed ten syntagmatic and paradigmatic metrics from morphologically rich corpora covering German, Hungarian, Italian, Korean, Macedonian, and Russian. We evaluated their intercorrelations using both parametric and robust statistical approaches. Results indicate that while some measures align closely with others, others diverge significantly. Through simulation studies, we determined that these discrepancies arise because the measures respond differently to variations in agreement morphology versus nominal inflection. Finally, we demonstrate that a statistical model grounded in information theory, specifically entropy, effectively predicts morphological complexity based on a limited set of features. Consequently, we argue that entropy serves as a robust and interpretable metric for this purpose. Our findings offer a foundation for future research into quantifying morphological complexity. To facilitate this, we have made our code and measures accessible via a web interface, which can be found at https://inferrus.github.io/inferrus/. This interface also provides access to the original corpus data and a suite of pre-computed measures. We invite researchers to utilize these resources to explore the relationship between complexity measures and grammatical typology. Furthermore, we encourage the community to extend our analysis to additional languages and measures, thereby strengthening the validity of these complexity measures across a broader spectrum of languages. We investigate gravitational lensing within galaxy clusters, focusing on the substructure signal in the galaxy cluster A521. Our analysis of the convergence power spectrum in the outer regions reveals a distinct peak at angular scales of approximately 1 arcminute, a feature that cannot be explained by a $\Lambda$CDM model with a standard cold dark matter (CDM) halo. Instead, this observation is well-reproduced by a self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) halo. We further examine the potential of gravitational lensing to constrain dark matter self-interaction cross sections in galaxy clusters. By employing a semi-analytic framework, we demonstrate that the SIDM model can account for the observed lensing signal in A521 without contradicting other existing data. Our results indicate that SIDM models with self-interaction cross sections of $\sigma/m \sim 0.1-10~\mathrm{cm^2/g}$ are favored by lensing data in cluster outskirts. We conclude that future high-resolution lensing studies will significantly enhance our ability to constrain dark matter self-interactions in cluster substructures. Additionally, we show that the projected substructure mass in SIDM models is lower than in CDM models, suggesting that dynamical mass estimates derived from galaxy kinematics can also serve as a constraint on self-interactions. However, we note that the projected mass in cluster outskirts remains largely insensitive to the presence of self-interactions. Finally, we demonstrate that the projected mass of substructures in A521 is consistent with both a CDM model featuring a cored density profile and an SIDM model. This paper introduces a model reduction framework capable of handling systems with incomplete state observability. The approach begins by constructing a complete balanced grammian for the original system, utilizing both local and global methods to estimate the Gramians necessary for Gramian completion. Subsequently, a balanced truncation reduction is executed on this synthesized system. To evaluate the accuracy of the resulting reduced model, an approximation of the simulation error is employed to estimate the discrepancy between the original and reduced models across all possible initial conditions. Finally, a balanced realization is computed for the identified reduced model with a finite state dimension, which is then validated against a random system through numerical simulation. The study demonstrates that the proposed algorithm effectively generates high-quality linear reduced models for random systems under partial state observations. Furthermore, the methodology is noted for its ability to provide accurate estimates of the Gramians of the reduced model, thereby eliminating the need for iterative estimation. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Keywords: Model Reduction, Linear Systems, Gramian Completion, Balanced Truncation, Random Systems, Simulation Error.

This paper introduces the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm, a novel method for solving the m-Arithmetic-Kurtosis-based Fast Independent Component Analysis problem. This specific optimization task involves maximizing the multivariate arithmetic kurtosis of the projected data from a linear mixing matrix. The proposed algorithm is an improved version of the previously published M-ar-Fast algorithm, which relied on multivariate geometric kurtosis to resolve a different problem. The primary innovation of the M-ar-Fast approach lies in its utilization of a new gradient ascent step, designed to accelerate the convergence of the algorithm. We provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's fixed points and demonstrate that the updated gradient ascent step achieves a quadratic rate of convergence in the vicinity of these fixed points. Additionally, we incorporate a new step to enhance numerical stability, ensuring the algorithm's robustness when applied to real-world data. Extensive simulations were conducted to evaluate the proposed method's performance against state-of-the-art algorithms. These results indicate that the proposed approach achieves a significantly faster convergence rate compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we present experimental findings that extend the algorithm's applicability to real-world scenarios, including color image processing and electrocardiogram signal recovery. These experiments confirm that M-ar-Fast outperforms competing algorithms in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. This study employs evolutionary search to identify cobalt-abundant materials within the Y-Co-B system, a process that also discovers numerous promising superconducting candidates. A total of 1,022 stable compounds containing at least 20% cobalt were found, with 210 of these featuring an average magnetic moment of 1.0 $\mu_B$/f.u. or higher. The most frequently occurring structure among the top 100 magnet compounds is the AuCu3-type (Pm-3m) structure, observed in 31 instances. Among the 210 magnetic materials, 111 exhibit Heisenberg exchange interactions, while 91 display single-ion anisotropy. The average total magnetic moment for these compounds is 2.8 $\mu_B$/f.u., with a maximum of 6.0 $\mu_B$/f.u. achieved in YCo2. Furthermore, 105 superconducting candidates were identified, with YCo2Yb emerging as a particularly promising new high-Tc system. Additionally, 102 Heisenberg exchange-interaction compounds were detected, characterized by an average magnetic moment of 1.0 $\mu_B$/f.u. and a maximum of 2.0 $\mu_B$/f.u. Real-time bidding (RTB) has emerged as a dominant model for digital display advertising, enabling advertisers to bid for impressions on a transactional basis. This process involves two primary participants: the Demand Side Platform (DSP), which represents the advertiser, and the Supply Side Platform (SSP), which represents the ad publisher. During the RTB process, the advertiser submits a bid to the exchange for a specific impression, while the publisher, via the SSP, indicates its asking price. Subsequently, the exchange facilitates a second-price auction where the advertiser determines the bid price, and the publisher receives payment only if the ad is served. However, if the bid exceeds the advertiser's budget, only a subset of the requested impressions can be fulfilled. Consequently, an advertiser must strategically balance bid pricing against budget limitations to maximize Return on Investment (ROI). This paper introduces a new adaptive risk-aware bidding (ARAB) framework that integrates risk awareness, budget constraints, and ROI optimization into a unified system. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world data demonstrate that ARAB surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in maximizing ROI. Furthermore, the ARAB framework is now deployed in production environments. Our approach effectively learns an adaptive bidding strategy that accounts for both risk and budget considerations, ensuring high ROI even when facing budget restrictions. Additionally, ARAB employs a novel deep reinforcement learning method that utilizes an actor-critic model to jointly optimize the bidding price and participation decision. This innovative solution enables ARAB to explore a broader range of strategies, thereby enhancing its ability to maximize ROI. Specifically, ARAB learns a value function that evaluates the potential ROI of an impression, incorporating a risk assessment to determine bid amounts. This risk evaluation considers the likelihood of a bid winning and the potential loss if it results in wasted budget. By combining these features, ARAB achieves a significant improvement over existing state-of-the-art bidding strategies. Our method is now live in production, and we have released an open-source library to facilitate further research and development in this area. This work offers valuable insights for practitioners and researchers aiming to enhance bidding strategies within the display advertising industry. Wigner negativity serves as a necessary and practically beneficial indicator of quantum magic. This note demonstrates that for a broad class of channels, local operations combined with these channels are capable of steering a quantum state into a quantum state with negative Wigner functions, thereby establishing the existence of magic. Consequently, the strength of Wigner negativity in the steering scenario imposes an upper limit on the strength of nonlocality in Bell scenarios. We derive this constraint for several popular Wigner functions and construct specific sets of measurements to achieve nonlocality in these cases. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the Wigner angles of two quantum states and the strength of steering, which also helps explain the derived bounds. Finally, we explore the potential of this framework for future research. Additionally, we present a rigorous proof of the equivalence between Wigner negativity and PPT distillability for two-mode Gaussian states, a result that had previously been supported only by numerical evidence. This finding suggests that the strength of steering may be quantified by the Wigner angles. Our approach also yields a new proof of the separability condition for two-mode squeezed thermal states. Finally, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the connections between Wigner negativity, distillability, and steering. These findings may prove valuable for advancing the understanding of non-classicality across different quantum frameworks. In quantum key distribution (QKD) systems employing random seed randomness extraction via privacy amplification, the security bound is typically determined using a uniform random seed. However, this approach is often impractical for field deployments due to the high computational costs associated with finding optimal extractors for uniformization. To address this, we introduce a security analysis based on a non-uniform random seed. Our findings demonstrate that the secure key rate can be efficiently calculated by solving a semidefinite program. We validate our theoretical framework through numerical simulations, which show that the secure key rate analysis for non-uniform random seeds yields essentially identical results to the uniform case. Consequently, this method offers a viable solution for achieving efficient and secure QKD. Additionally, we present a security analysis for phase-encoding twin-beam QKD utilizing a non-uniform random seed for randomness extraction. In this scenario, we prove that the secure key rate can be determined by solving a convex optimization problem. We confirm this theoretical result with numerical examples, indicating that this scheme is also applicable to other practical QKD protocols. Furthermore, we illustrate that the secure key rate in this scheme can be approximated by solving a convex optimization problem, thereby enabling a fast estimation of secure key rates. These results hold significant value for the practical implementation of QKD. Our proposed security analysis methods are implemented in the open-source Python package `qkdsecurity`. We provide a user-friendly interface within this package to facilitate the rapid calculation of secure key rates for various QKD schemes. This study examines the sample distributions of Brownian motions on $[0,1]$ governed by the Feller diffusion (also known as the $\frac12-\frac12X^2$ process), which exhibit random coalescence points. We present and validate a novel family of orthogonal polynomials, termed the "coalescing monic orthogonal polynomials" (CMOP), and calculate their explicit forms for the first few degrees. Utilizing these CMOP, we derive expressions for the coalescence time and coalescence point of the sampled trajectories. Furthermore, we analyze the sampling distribution of the process at the terminal time $t=1$, demonstrating that it adheres to a determinantal point process structure. Notably, the kernel associated with this process is identified as the reciprocal of the CMOP evaluated at coalescence points, revealing an unexpected connection to random matrices. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Our methodology is also applicable to other Feller diffusions, such as those on the real line following the $\frac12\sigma^2X^{\prime\prime}+\sigma X^{\prime}-\frac{\nu}{2}X$ dynamics. In this broader context, the CMOP correspond to the eigenfunctions of the Jacobi ensemble. This paper serves as an extended abstract for a more comprehensive research report. Additional details regarding the coalescence time and point, the sampling distribution, and the connection to the Jacobi ensemble can be found in the author's PhD thesis, which includes a more extensive proof of the determinantal point process property. Specifically, the full version of the CMOP definition is provided in Chapter 2, while the complete proof of the determinantal structure is located in Chapter 3. The version of the coalescence time distribution presented in this paper is a simplified variant of the one found in the thesis. Finally, the proof of the reciprocal relationship between the CMOP and the sampling distribution is also omitted here; it is included in the thesis under the title of the "eigenfunction kernel." Boosted Dark Matter offers a promising framework for investigating Dark Matter with masses exceeding the TeV scale. In this scenario, Dark Matter particles scatter off nuclei within the galactic halo, transferring momentum to the produced momentum-boosted states. These boosted states subsequently escape the halo and interact with nuclei in terrestrial detectors, generating signals that are significantly distinct from those of standard Dark Matter. This paper examines the scattering of spin-dependent DM off hydrogen, focusing on the production of semi-leptonic and jet final states. We analyze the scattering cross-sections for these channels across various theoretical models, including scalar, vector, axial-vector, and fermion mediators, as well as contact interactions. Our findings indicate that mediators coupling to the spin of the DM or the target nucleus yield suppressed cross-sections in the boosted regime. Consequently, signals arising from mediators that do not couple to spin offer a more potent means of constraining boosted Dark Matter. We further illustrate how signals from these specific mediators can be constrained by existing searches, such as those conducted by LHCb. Finally, we present exclusion contours in the cross-section versus DM mass parameter space, demonstrating that boosted Dark Matter can be probed up to approximately 10 TeV. This range extends beyond the sensitivity of traditional direct detection experiments, which are limited to about 1 TeV. Additionally, we note that boosted semi-leptonic signals can be directly detected using LEP data. Our results underscore the necessity of incorporating boosted Dark Matter into direct search analyses and emphasize the value of leveraging LEP and LHCb data to constrain this parameter space. Within the framework of noncommutative space-time, this study examines nucleon structure functions at fixed $x_{bj}$ using the $^*TPiC$ model, which incorporates a modified tensor hadron-tensor hadron interaction. The findings indicate that structures below 1 GeV$^2$ are highly sensitive to the noncommutative parameter, whereas at higher energies, the deviations from standard commutative space-time become negligible. These results can be contrasted with commutative spacetime predictions, where the influence of the noncommutative parameter is considered. Furthermore, the study explores the impact of the $\theta$-term in the Lagrangian on the nucleon tensor interaction. Finally, the effects of varying noncommutative scenarios are compared with data from HERMES and COMPASS experiments. The research concludes that the $\theta$-term's contribution is minimal, and the influence of the noncommutative parameter is more pronounced in the COMPASS experiment than in HERMES. Additionally, the paper suggests that future experiments could provide more precise measurements of the noncommutative parameter. Finally, the study proposes that the $\lambda$ parameter in the Lagrangian can be determined through the ratio of longitudinal to transverse cross-sections. This study investigates topological line excitations within frustrated Toric code models. In the standard Toric code, these lines are classified into two types: open lines and closed lines (loops). This work demonstrates that, in frustrated Toric code variants, each spin-1/2 is effectively split into two distinct $\sigma$ variables. Consequently, the physical open lines correspond to configurations where the $\sigma$ values along the line differ from those outside the line by a specific sign. Furthermore, open lines in these models exhibit a finite lifetime, decaying exponentially over a timescale determined by the model's parameters. In contrast, closed lines behave identically to those in the non-frustrated Toric code. These findings offer a theoretical basis for interpreting recent experimental results. Specifically, time-resolved muon spin rotation experiments on the frustrated quantum spin ice material YbMn$_{12}$O$_{19}$ observed the disappearance of muons after a brief interval. This observation is interpreted as the decay of open lines, which are hypothesized to be created by local flips of muon spins. Additionally, the experiments detected a topological loop effect, consistent with the presence of closed lines. Finally, the results indicate that the open line decay timescale is governed by a critical exponent, which can be adjusted by varying the model's parameters. This provides a potential experimental method for detecting topological lines. The proposed model and its predictions can be realized in both quantum simulators and actual quantum materials. To achieve this, one must either introduce frustration into existing topological materials or engineer frustration into quantum simulators. The characteristic timescale for open line decay can be tuned via model parameters, and its topological nature can be verified by observing the nonlocal entanglement between spins at the line endpoints. Overall, this research establishes a new framework for exploring frustrated topological quantum spin models. It offers a pathway to experimentally observe open lines, investigate their properties, and develop quantum technologies utilizing these lines. Topological lines are expected to find diverse applications, including quantum computing, quantum memory, and quantum sensors. Topological quantum computation, for instance, relies on the braiding of excitations to perform quantum operations. By extending braiding to include open lines, this work expands the scope of topological quantum computation. Moreover, topological lines may offer a solution to the critical problem of quantum error correction, a key challenge in quantum computing. We investigate the statistical behavior of eigenvalues in random Hermitian $N \times N$ band matrices, where non-zero entries are confined to a band of width $W$ along the diagonal. To these random band matrices, we add a complex deformation $V$ composed of a Hermitian matrix of finite rank $q \ll N$. In the limit where $N, W, and q$ all tend to infinity while maintaining $q/W \to 0$, we demonstrate that the deformation $V$ can be approximated by a weak coupling to a non-Hermitian Gaussian random matrix. This approach relies on the approximation of a suitable sigma-model. Furthermore, we establish that this weak-coupling approximation remains valid even when $q$ scales as $o(W)$. This finding is essential for extending the weak-coupling framework to scenarios involving multiple deformations, thereby enabling an analysis of the phase diagram of random band matrices coupled to a non-Hermitian matrix, a topic of significant interest in the study of non-Hermitian Anderson localization transitions. Unsupervised anomaly detection is a critical task across numerous domains, including security, finance, and healthcare. While deep learning methods have become prevalent, they are often resource-intensive and ineffective for the Tiny ML era, where tasks must run on edge devices with severe memory and computational constraints. Furthermore, the necessity of extensive labeled data hinders practical deployment in real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we introduce TiWS-iForest, a novel anomaly detection approach that merges weak supervision with unsupervised learning. This method leverages class activation maps (CAMs) to generate sample-level weights, enabling TiWS-iForest to identify anomalies even when only class labels are available. Additionally, TiWS-iForest is designed for tiny machine learning, ensuring it remains effective across various model architectures and optimized for deployment on edge hardware. Evaluated on the CIFAR-10 dataset, TiWS-iForest demonstrates superior performance in anomaly detection tasks compared to existing methods, achieving a lower FPR@90TPR of 1.1% versus 1.4% for the baseline iForest, and 2.1% versus 3.1% compared to the state-of-the-art WS-iForest. These results confirm that TiWS-iForest outperforms current solutions in weakly supervised settings and establishes itself as a robust baseline for tiny machine learning environments. This paper outlines our system for the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 shared task, which focuses on establishing a bridge between symbolic commonsense knowledge (CST) and natural language. The organization of our system is detailed in the first section, where we explain the rationale behind our decisions and how CST can facilitate large-scale semantic parsing. The second section details the three tasks addressed: Task 1 involves generating a set of ATOMIC-K670 facts from a sentence, Task 2 entails retrieving a specific fact using a set of candidate facts, and Task 3 requires identifying the semantic role of a specific argument within a fact. Our system is the leading entry for all three tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance on tasks 1 and 2, and significantly outperforming existing methods on task 3. The system comprises a hybrid architecture featuring a neural component for learning distributional properties of words and a symbolic module for integrating precise commonsense knowledge. Evaluation results and a discussion on the strengths and limitations of our system are presented at the end of the paper. This study outlines the data reduction pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey, which maps the 160 and 250 $\mu$m bands of the Galactic plane using the Herschel Space Observatory's SPIRE instrument. The pipeline is designed to be adaptable for other SPIRE extragalactic and all-sky mapping initiatives. It incorporates a series of tasks to execute the initial stages of Hi-GAL data processing, including absolute and relative radiometric calibration, map creation, and image quality assessment. Additionally, a new tool is introduced to facilitate the generation of metadata describing the SPIRE imaging process. This metadata is utilized to produce a comprehensive set of calibration maps, which are subsequently applied to correct the observed data. Finally, all reduced Hi-GAL data are made publicly accessible via the Hi-GAL archive at http://www.higal.org. The data reduction procedures detailed here will be released as a standalone software package to ensure uniformity and reproducibility across the survey. This approach will enable other researchers to replicate the reduction process for their own data and allow Hi-GAL team members to apply consistent corrections to future datasets. Furthermore, this methodology can be extended to other SPIRE extragalactic and all-sky mapping projects, such as the Goksu et al. We have conducted high-resolution spectroscopic observations of five blue horizontal branch stars in the globular cluster NGC 2808 to determine their iron abundances. By utilizing a novel model atmosphere code, we derived precise abundances for the first time. Our findings reveal a metallicity spread of approximately 0.1 dex among these stars, which aligns with earlier studies that employed the traditional method. This result supports the hypothesis that multiple distinct populations exist within NGC 2808. Additionally, we determined the surface helium abundance for one of the observed stars. We also present the surface abundances of C, N, O, and Mg for this star, which were derived using a grid of 3D MHD models. The derived parameters are consistent with those obtained using the 1D model. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results regarding the existence of multiple populations in globular clusters. Quantum mechanics has historically faced the challenge of applying classical Bayesian inference to measurement results due to non-classical state representations. This work demonstrates that non-classical states can be interpreted as probability amplitudes, enabling the direct application of quantum Bayes' rule to update inferences derived from measurement outcomes. Consequently, consistency is maintained between pre- and post-measurement inferences. The paper illustrates this framework using a spin measurement example and concludes by presenting potential applications of these methods. Notably, an extension of the example shows that quantum Bayes' rule facilitates the analysis of measurement results without requiring a complete specification of the pre-measurement state. Furthermore, the study confirms that quantum mechanics remains consistent even when only partial information is extracted during a measurement. Finally, the authors propose that this approach to quantum measurement is essential for the development of quantum information processing. In quantum information theory, the non-classical nature of state representations is often viewed as a hindrance to inference, but this paper argues that it is actually a vital resource for inference tasks. Additionally, the work addresses the issue of non-uniqueness in measurement results, a topic that has generated significant debate within the quantum mechanics community. The analysis reveals that this debate stems from a misunderstanding of what constitutes a measurement result, leading to the conclusion that the current debate is unnecessary. To achieve this, the paper clarifies the relationship between measurement operators and observables, a relationship that is frequently misunderstood. Finally, the paper underscores the critical role of quantum measurement in quantum information theory, emphasizing that this role is currently underappreciated. Specifically, it is shown that quantum information theory achieves greater efficiency in measurement-based information processing by fully exploiting the non-classical characteristics of state representations. These findings are expected to contribute to advancing quantum information theory. This study reports initial findings regarding finite volume corrections to thermodynamic quantities of the QCD plasma, calculated using Monte Carlo methods within a $2+1$-flavor continuum QCD framework. These findings are crucial for understanding the statistical nature of the hadron gas that transitions into the QCD plasma. Our results indicate that these corrections are substantial and must be accounted for when analyzing the physics of small systems, such as those produced in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. Consequently, the statistical nature of the hadron gas may evolve as a function of event multiplicity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that finite volume effects can be significantly reduced by employing the "twisted boundary condition" approach. This technique has already proven effective in other lattice QCD contexts, such as the axion mass calculation, and is now essential for generating precise thermodynamic data. Finally, we outline an ongoing effort to incorporate dynamical quarks into this computational setup. This represents a critical step toward a comprehensive and accurate description of high-energy heavy-ion collision phenomena. Specifically, we aim to investigate the formation of a critical-like state in small systems, a hypothesis that has previously been tested in large systems. Our preliminary observations suggest that the critical-like state may be accessible in small systems, potentially offering a new pathway to explore the critical region of the QCD phase diagram. This could be achieved by utilizing the extensive experimental data available from the LHC. We conclude by discussing the potential for experiments to vary event multiplicity, thereby enabling the systematic exploration of the QCD phase diagram in small systems. This approach could provide a unique and valuable method for mapping the low-temperature, high-density region of the QCD phase diagram. Theoretical predictions regarding the existence of a critical endpoint in the QCD phase diagram have been available for some time, yet experimental confirmation remains pending. Our research aims to address this gap. We anticipate that the high-quality thermodynamic data we are generating will soon be available for the community to utilize. The Steenrod algebra's cohomology forms a graded, commutative algebra over a field of characteristic 2. Its non-trivial elements are generated by the Milnor primitives $\Q_{i}$ and the dual Steenrod operations $\Psi^{k}$. This note demonstrates that, up to a degree shift, the Q-duals of the $\Q_{i}$ operations are also generating elements. Furthermore, we present a diagrammatic interpretation for a specific formula linking these Q-duals to $\Psi^{k}$, which holds significant utility in the (diagrammatic) calculation of Steenrod cohomology. The paper's primary motivation stems from a diagrammatic approach to the isomorphism $\Q_{i}\cong\Psi^{2^{i}-1}\Q_{1}\Psi^{2^{i}-1}$ proposed by the first author in [arXiv:2101.01002]. Ultimately, this work contributes to the ongoing quest to identify diagrammatic generators for the Steenrod algebra. Additionally, we offer a diagrammatic characterization of the Milner duals $\Q_{i}$, which may prove valuable in deriving diagrammatic presentations of the Steenrod algebra. Finally, this note includes a diagrammatic proof of a formula regarding the Q-duals of $\Q_{i}$, originally due to the second author in [arXiv:2101.01002]. Specifically, we establish that $\Q_{i}\cong\Psi^{2^{i}-1}\Q_{1}\Psi^{2^{i}-1}$ by demonstrating that the duals of $\Q_{i}$ are isomorphic to $\Q_{i}^{*}\cong\Psi^{2^{i}-1}\Q_{1}^{*}\Psi^{2^{i}-1}$. This result confirms the conjecture proposed by the second author in [arXiv:2009.01002]. We also provide an alternative proof of this fact using the methods introduced by the first author in [arXiv:2101.01002]. Finally, we outline a diagrammatic approach to the Q-duals of $\Q_{i}$, which may aid in deriving diagrammatic presentations of the Steenrod algebra. The Lyman-alpha emission line at 1216 Å serves as a critical tool for studying the formation and evolution of the first galaxies. Although this line is easily observable in high-redshift spectra, isolating the line flux from the continuum requires the use of narrow-band and broad-band filters. While numerous narrow-band Lyman-alpha filters exist for laboratory-based spectroscopy, there is currently no space-compatible narrow-band filter capable of isolating Lyman-alpha in space telescopes. This paper introduces a prototype Lyman-alpha filter designed for space use, featuring a 3.0 Å full width at half maximum (FWHM) centered at 1216 Å. We evaluated this prototype's transmission and out-of-band rejection characteristics using an integrating sphere and an optical power meter. Additionally, we conducted an astronomical test by observing the galaxy at redshift z=0.293, SDSS J0942+0037, using a laboratory spectrometer. Our results indicate that the filter's performance aligns with its design specifications, demonstrating its potential for future space-based Lyman-alpha filters. This technology could enable Lyman-alpha photometry in the Lyman-alpha forest, thereby facilitating new investigations into the reionization of the intergalactic medium. Furthermore, it may support new missions dedicated to Lyman-alpha surveys of high-redshift galaxies. We conclude that this filter technology is ready for deployment in upcoming space missions. The filters are accessible at http://www.spectroscopicfilter.com. The spectral data is available at https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ac022b. The source code can be found at https://github.com/ChenYi1990/Lyman-alpha-filter-3.0A.

This paper introduces a distributed algorithm designed to solve graph symmetric control problems within multi-agent systems. To achieve graph symmetry, such problems typically require calculating the gradient of a global cost function dependent on all agent states. However, in many practical scenarios, this gradient computation is either infeasible or prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose leveraging graph filters to estimate these gradients in a distributed fashion. We demonstrate that such estimates can be generated through simple and efficient communication protocols. Furthermore, we establish that under specific conditions, these estimates converge to the true gradient values in a distributed setting. Finally, numerical simulations are provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The results indicate that, compared to existing methods, our protocol enables multi-agent systems to solve graph symmetric problems with significantly reduced computational and communication costs. Additionally, our approach demonstrates superior performance in addressing graph symmetric problems involving complex functions. The methodology is also shown to be applicable to distributed optimal power flow problems. In this application, our algorithm allows for the decentralized calculation of the gradient of the global cost function with respect to injected powers, a task that is typically impossible to perform in a distributed manner. Consequently, the resulting power distribution is nearly identical to that obtained through centralized gradient calculations. This represents a substantial advancement over current distributed solutions for optimal power flow. Moreover, our method achieves a significantly higher power quality than existing distributed techniques. The core innovation of this work is the development of a general protocol for distributed gradient estimation using graph filters, which can be extended to various graph symmetric problems. Notably, our results suggest that these protocols can be utilized in distributed machine learning applications. In this context, the agent state vector corresponds to the local model, and the gradient of the global cost function corresponds to the gradient of the local loss function. This finding is particularly significant given the growing interest in distributed machine learning. Our approach enables the distributed estimation of gradients for local loss functions, a task that is generally infeasible to perform centrally. Image retrieval is a fundamental challenge in modern information retrieval, yet it remains difficult due to the vast volume of digital images and the need for users to rapidly identify and locate images containing specific content. While active learning has been widely adopted across numerous domains to enhance machine learning efficiency, its application in image retrieval has been limited. This paper introduces an active learning approach designed to reduce the time required for users to find relevant images. The proposed method employs a multi-armed bandit algorithm to strategically select images for user feedback, thereby accelerating the initial retrieval phase. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly cuts down the time users need to identify desired images compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the study investigates the impact of user response latency on performance, revealing that long response times can hinder retrieval performance. Consequently, a user study was conducted to assess image quality and gather insights into user behavior. The findings indicate that the system performs well in identifying image content, though users often struggle to understand the rationale behind the system's recommendations. These results highlight a need for improved user feedback mechanisms to enhance the overall user experience. Overall, the paper suggests that integrating active learning into image retrieval can substantially boost performance, while also underscoring the necessity for more intuitive user interaction strategies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1234/ActiveImageIndexing. Future research will explore advanced user modeling techniques and more sophisticated feedback mechanisms to further refine the system. This study investigates keyless authentication for the discrete scalar Gaussian channel with keys at both the transmitter and receiver. In this keyless framework, the common secret key is eliminated, allowing authentication performance to be evaluated based solely on the public channel. We introduce a new authentication scheme utilizing a deterministic encoder paired with a random decoder, demonstrating that it achieves superior error exponent compared to random coding. We define the secret exponent—the rate at which error exponents scale with secret message power—and determine the secret exponent region for this proposed random decode scheme. Furthermore, we establish that this region is sufficient for keyless authentication in the discrete scalar Gaussian channel. Finally, we propose an open research question regarding the characterization of the complete secret exponent region for this channel. Our findings are grounded in a unified framework that links secret message power in authentication to error tolerance in coding. This framework enables the translation of existing channel coding results into corresponding secret exponent regions for authentication, facilitating a direct comparison between our proposed scheme and random coding. Additionally, we demonstrate that this approach yields optimal security-latency tradeoffs for keyless authentication over the discrete memoryless channel. The proposed unified framework represents a significant advancement in the theory of secret messaging. It also holds potential for applications in other areas, such as keyless source coding and keyless channel coding. We have developed a comprehensive theory for these topics, which will be detailed in a separate paper. This study examines the dispersionless transport of particles within washboard potentials, offering a comprehensive theoretical framework that encompasses both quantum and classical regimes alongside various dispersionless approximations. It is demonstrated that the dispersion of the transported particle flow vanishes up to any order of perturbation theory, yet it emerges at first order when utilizing the multiple-scale method. Consequently, this results in a complete description of particle transport in both classical and quantum scenarios, covering the diffusion-limited, tunneling-limited, and coherent switching-limited regimes. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to a wide range of systems, including the diffusion and tunneling of particles in tilted periodic potentials, the motion of domain walls in magnetic media, flux in superconducting loops, and the tunneling and diffusion of charges in Josephson junction arrays. The methodology also extends to the transport of quantum entities such as photons and excitons. Ultimately, the paper addresses the limitations of dispersionless approximations and their validity ranges across different temperature scales. A key finding is the discovery of a novel quantum effect: quantum interference in tunneling, which occurs in systems with smooth disorder and leads to a reduction in conductivity. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the coherent transport of particles in tilted Josephson junction arrays can be accurately described by a one-dimensional model, even though the system is inherently higher-dimensional. Finally, the issue of current conservation is explored, with results indicating that the continuity equation is satisfied only when the system is not driven by external sources. The proposed theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations. Finally, the work examines the impact of phase diffusion on quantum transport in Josephson junction arrays, demonstrating that phase diffusion can be viewed as a quantum analogue to thermalization. This insight helps explain the transition from coherent to diffusive transport in quantum systems. The findings are illustrated through examples of quantum transport in Josephson junction arrays, which hold significant potential for developing quantum information devices. These examples highlight the critical role of quantum interference in tunneling and the existence of a quantum Hall effect in quantum phase slips. The latter manifests as a plateau in the current-voltage characteristic, where the current remains independent of voltage over a finite range. This plateau arises from the quantum interference between different tunneling channels, leading to a non-uniform distribution of tunneling probabilities across the system. Ultimately, the paper underscores the intricate interplay between quantum interference, interference length, and system size, which are essential factors in understanding and manipulating quantum transport phenomena. This paper presents a flexible local projection method designed to estimate impulse responses of dynamic variables following structural shocks. The approach accommodates arbitrary vector moving average orders of varying lengths and allows for time-varying volatility and covariances. Furthermore, the method extends to time-varying impulse responses, enabling the analysis of how varying policy reaction functions influence these responses. Estimation relies on a nonparametric regression technique utilizing orthogonal polynomials, which are selected based on a data-driven criterion that balances model fit with penalization for excessive complexity. The study derives the asymptotic properties of the estimator and provides a bootstrap procedure to calculate standard errors and confidence intervals. Empirical applications are applied to various economic shocks, including monetary policy shocks, fiscal shocks, and oil price shocks. The paper begins with an introduction followed by a review of existing literature. Section 2 outlines the proposed flexible local projection framework, while Section 3 presents the theoretical results. Section 4 details the estimation strategy, and Section 5 reports the empirical findings. Finally, the paper concludes with a summary and suggestions for future research directions. Introduction This paper introduces a novel framework for estimating impulse responses to structural shocks. We begin by reviewing the literature on this topic. The standard approach involves two stages: first, identifying structural shocks via structural vector autoregressions (SVARs), and second, simulating their impulse responses. However, this traditional method faces two significant challenges. First, the vector autoregressive model assumes a time-invariant vector moving average (VMA) order, which may not hold in reality. Second, the identification of structural shocks relies on the assumption of time-invariant volatility and covariance, which is often unrealistic. These limitations motivate the development of a more robust framework for estimating impulse responses. To address these issues, we propose a flexible local projection method for estimating impulse responses. This framework offers several advantages. First, it permits time-varying VMA orders, providing a more accurate representation of dynamic relationships. Second, it allows for time-varying volatility and covariances, enhancing the robustness of the estimates. Additionally, the method can be extended to account for time-varying impulse responses, which is crucial for understanding the impact of changing policy reactions. We examine the angular momentum of a charge $q$ rotating within a uniform magnetic field, investigating the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum. The orbital angular momentum of the charge, defined as the integral of $\vec r\times\vec j$ over space, consists of classical and quantum components. The classical part adheres to standard mechanical principles, whereas the quantum contribution arises from the interference of a Landau-Klein-Gingerberger electron with plane waves. This phenomenon represents a manifestation of angular Casimir momentum in a dynamical setting. The energy momentum tensor of the electromagnetic field, derived from the charge's current, also yields a torque that aligns with the angular momentum of the charge. This result demonstrates that the quantum field exerts a force on the particle, and the corresponding angular momentum is conserved. Furthermore, the electromagnetic field carries an energy that varies periodically with the charge's revolution period, and this energy flux across any closed surface surrounding the charge is non-zero. This outcome highlights the intricate interplay between quantum fields and charged particles. The derived expressions for angular momentum and energy are valid for all values of the cyclotron frequency $\omega_c$. In the limit where $\omega_c\rightarrow 0$, the magnetic field vanishes, and the cyclotron charge transitions into a Klein-Gingerberger charge. This specific charge, moving in a quantum vacuum without a magnetic field, generates angular momentum, confirming that the quantum vacuum itself possesses angular momentum. Consequently, the quantum vacuum functions as a reservoir of angular momentum, capable of transferring it to the charge. This conclusion is supported by the electromagnetic torque, which opposes the charge's rotational motion and draws energy from the quantum field. Finally, we demonstrate that the electromagnetic torque exerted on a charge by the quantum field is non-zero. These findings underscore the intricate and fascinating relationship between quantum fields and charged particles. Our results are applicable to any charge, including electrons, within a uniform magnetic field. The cyclotron charge's angular momentum has been experimentally verified in the absence of a magnetic field. Additionally, we show that the angular momentum of a charge in a uniform magnetic field is independent of its electromagnetic mass. This conclusion holds true for any quantum state of the charge within the magnetic field. The angular momentum of a photon in a uniform magnetic field has also been calculated. The electromagnetic torque exerted by the quantum field on a charge is non-zero, indicating that the quantum field performs work on the charge. Fine-grained named entity typing (FNET) involves classifying entities into specific subtypes within a predefined schema. Unlike coarse-grained methods that rely on classification, FNET treats schema subtypes as a hierarchy, enabling the use of a hyperboloid as a manifold to represent both subtypes and the geometric characteristics of textual data. This manuscript introduces FGNET-RH, a method designed to leverage the inherent properties of the Poincaré ball model to encode entity attributes within an FNET framework. By utilizing word embeddings trained on the target text, FGNET-RH establishes a Fine-Grained Entity Representation Knowledge Base (FGRKB) to capture semantic relationships between subtypes and fine-grained entities. Furthermore, the model incorporates a regularization term that aligns predicted entity centroids with their representations in the FGRKB. Experimental results demonstrate that FGNET-RH surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches, achieving an F1 score of 81.02 on the F100 dataset. Additionally, the model exhibits robustness against data perturbations, including variations in segmentation strategies and the use of smaller pre-trained language models. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/leehyuklee/FGNET-RH. Our findings indicate that the FGRKB enhances the understanding of semantic relationships between subtypes and fine-grained entities, thereby boosting the model's performance. This concept of a FGRKB is also applicable to other NLP tasks that necessitate the encoding of relationships among specific entities. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into leveraging FGRKBs for various domains of named entity recognition. Finally, we hope this research will encourage the creation of more comprehensive fine-grained schemas to support future advancements in the field.
