As the demand for cloud computing grows, so does the need for more efficient resource allocation. This paper introduces Prepartition, a novel load balancing strategy designed to minimize the time required for virtual machine reservations in cloud data centers. By distributing VMs across data center nodes based on their specific resource requirements, Prepartition achieves a 20% reduction in execution time compared to the existing OpenNBI load balancing method. Additionally, we developed a new cloud-based load testing tool to evaluate and compare the performance of these two approaches. Experimental results demonstrate that Prepartition outperforms OpenNBI in terms of efficiency and speed. Future research will explore the Prepartition method using various VM configurations and data center sizes to further validate its effectiveness. This study is particularly relevant to cloud computing researchers and practitioners focused on load balancing applications. To support this work, we have made the source code for the Prepartition method available online. Our code repository includes the prepartition method, a prepartition class, and a prepartition test class. We also provide a prepartition execution file, which is a bash script that compiles the code, runs the execution, and saves the output to a file named "prepartition.txt". Furthermore, we have included a prepartition test file that contains various VM sizes for comparison with OpenNBI. The repository also features an opennbi execution file, an opennbi class, an opennbi method, and an opennbi test class, which can be compiled and executed in the same manner as the prepartition code. This study addresses the challenge of forecasting Nash equilibria in extensive-form games, a critical yet difficult task with significant implications for economics and evolutionary biology. We introduce the Fixed Point Network (FPT-Net), a novel, interpretable, and efficient architecture designed to predict Nash equilibria. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on extensive computational effort to calculate these equilibria, our method learns a functional mapping from extensive-form game representations to their equilibrium payoffs. To ensure the model adheres to the theoretical constraints of the Nash equilibrium, we incorporate an inductive bias based on the fixed-point property. Empirical results demonstrate that FPT-Net achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines while offering superior interpretability and reduced computational requirements. Furthermore, we validate the model's effectiveness through a large-scale experiment on evolutionary stable strategies within the Prisoner's Dilemma. The associated code and data will be made publicly available. This work represents a collaboration between the fields of representation learning and extensive-form games. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashwinbalsubramani/FPT-Net. This research was conducted while the first author was a PhD student at the University of Washington. This study addresses the challenge of estimating causal effects when adjustment variables required by the back-door or front-door criteria are only partially observed. To resolve this, we introduce methods that leverage bounds on unobserved variables derived from posited constraints, such as positivity or UNIVALE, to achieve precise causal effect estimates. We develop two distinct approaches: one utilizing linear programming for cases where unobserved variables are discrete, and another employing Gaussian process regression to generate non-parametric causal bounds applicable when unobserved variables are continuous. Furthermore, we extend these techniques to high-dimensional settings by developing efficient algorithms for both discrete and continuous scenarios. Our computational strategy relies on identifying a minimal sufficient statistic for the discrete case and applying the Lasso for the continuous case. We validate the performance of these methods through simulations and demonstrate their utility with real-world data from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study. Finally, we discuss how these techniques can be extended to causal effect estimation involving multiple treatment variables. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1992/CausalEffectBounds.

This paper presents a predictive monitoring framework designed to identify stealthy attacks on linear time-invariant systems. Specifically, the study focuses on sparse switching attacks that evade both static and dynamic residual generators. Leveraging the system's known dynamics, the proposed method constructs a finite-horizon input-output model to forecast future outputs. It then monitors these predictions for deviations caused by potential attacks. The resulting optimization problem is cast as a mixed-integer linear program, which is solved efficiently using the sparse nature of the attacks. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the method's properties, including conditions guaranteeing attack detection and an assessment of its computational complexity. Finally, the approach is demonstrated through two simulation examples. Notably, this work marks the first application of sparsity-driven sparsity methods to attack detection, offering a significant advancement over existing techniques. Text summarization remains a challenging task, particularly for low-resource languages where resources are scarce and infrastructure is often lacking. To address this, we introduce GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised model designed for Indian languages. This approach employs a graph autoencoder to capture both local and global contextual information, utilizing a novel aggregation strategy. Experimental results across five Indian languages demonstrate that the model achieves state-of-the-art performance in summarization. Additionally, we present a comprehensive dataset for summarization, which includes 100,000 article-summary pairs spanning five languages. The resource can be accessed at https://github.com/aryan-agarwal-21/GAE-ISumm. Our source code is available at https://github.com/aryan-agarwal-21/GAE-ISumm. We hope this model and dataset prove valuable to the community. The paper is scheduled for presentation at the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2022).

This work defines S-rings of Krull type and outlines their fundamental properties and characterizations. Furthermore, for an independent S-ring of Krull type A, we establish the dimension of the spectrum of multiplicative linear functionals on A, denoted as Spec(A), and the rank of the class group of A, GC(A), which corresponds to the divisor class group of A. Additionally, the free S-rings over finite sets are examined, their properties are analyzed, and it is demonstrated that they are of Krull type. The paper also investigates S-rings of Krull type arising from multiplicative semigroups of matrices. Finally, the authors extend the concept of Krull type to Boolean algebras of sets, proving that the lattice of sets constituting any finite S-ring of Krull type is always atomic. **Aims.** The goal of this study is to constrain the masses and orbital separations of potential unseen companions to five accelerating nearby stars. **Methods.** We conducted a thorough search for these hidden companions using high-resolution imaging data from the VLT/SPHERE and Keck/NIRC2 instruments. **Results.** Our findings reveal no evidence of companions within the expected separation range for all targets. **Conclusions.** The absence of these unseen companions suggests that the observed orbital accelerations are likely caused by low-mass stellar spots rather than by unseen objects. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the measured accelerations align with the shifts in active regions identified in archival spectra of the targets. Consequently, this indicates that stellar surface activity can generate quasi-Keplerian proper motion anomalies in nearby stars. These results reinforce the hypothesis that such activity-induced accelerations may explain the "n-body problem" regarding the unexpectedly high frequency of accelerating stars in the nearby field. Furthermore, our results suggest that the hypothesis of a "dark companion hypothesis" (DC), which posits that surface activity cannot produce these accelerations, is incorrect. This is because the DC predicts that accelerations should be detectable in high-resolution imaging data, whereas our observations show no such evidence. **Discussion.** Our findings also suggest that the DC predicts a higher likelihood of detecting a companion around HD 162967, as this star has the largest measured acceleration. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are a type of generative model that create data by learning a latent representation using an autoencoder architecture. While standard VAEs rely on a fixed KL-divergence kernel for regularization, this paper introduces a regularized least-squares VAE. The objective is to minimize a cost function composed of an encoder's output KL-divergence, a decoder's least-squares reconstruction error, and an additional regularization term. This modified cost function is equivalent to a standard VAE cost function augmented with a specific regularization component. The study demonstrates that incorporating this extra regularization term can significantly enhance the model's generative capabilities. Furthermore, the paper provides numerical experiments comparing the performance of standard and least-squares VAEs on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results indicate that the proposed approach is effective and can generate higher-quality data. Additionally, the method exhibits robustness when dealing with incomplete datasets. Finally, the paper explores potential extensions of this approach for generative adversarial networks. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ahmed-ibrahim1999/Ls-VAE. The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has significantly increased the number of connected devices, leading to heightened security and privacy risks. This study introduces a private blockchain framework designed to securely manage and monitor IoT devices within a residence. By integrating private blockchain with the Weighted Euclidean Distance (WED) localization algorithm, the system monitors device activity and determines their physical locations. The framework successfully transmits raw sensor data to the blockchain, enabling the recording and tracking of all device operations. Additionally, a smart contract was developed to facilitate monitoring and localization via the blockchain network. Testing across both simulated and real-world environments demonstrated that the proposed system effectively monitors and localizes IoT devices at home. Furthermore, the system's security was validated through various attacks, including replay, read, and write operations. Ultimately, this approach offers a more secure and efficient solution for IoT monitoring and localization compared to existing methods. The proposed framework is expected to enhance security and privacy, thereby encouraging broader adoption of IoT technologies. Future research will focus on optimizing the system for greater scalability and efficiency. This paper introduces a deep learning-based approach to quantize Likelihood statistics ($L$-values) for generic higher-order Gray-coded modulation schemes. The proposed method utilizes a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) network designed to perform the quantization of these $L$-values. A key advantage of this proposed deep learning-based quantizer (DLBQ) is its ability to support any $M$-ary modulation scheme, regardless of whether the order is fixed or variable. The effectiveness of the DLBQ is validated through simulations using 16-QAM and 64-QAM schemes. Results demonstrate that the DLBQ achieves near-optimal performance with significantly lower complexity compared to traditional methods. This study examines the classical problem of determining if a directed acyclic graph can be embedded in the plane such that all edges align with a specific coordinate direction, alongside related challenges. While the standard upward planarity test operates efficiently in linear time, we demonstrate that testing for horizontal upward planarity is NP-complete. Furthermore, we identify other variants, including cases where vertices are fixed in position or have restricted degrees of freedom, that are also NP-hard. We explore parameterized formulations of these problems, proving that they are W[1]-hard when parameterized by the number of movable vertices. However, under a fixed coordinate direction, we present a polynomial-time algorithm capable of simultaneously testing for UPWARD PLANARITY, SERIES-PARALLELITY, and OUTERPLANARITY. Additionally, we illustrate that for SERIES-PARALLELICITY, checking for OUTERPLANARITY is unnecessary, as the former implies the latter. Finally, we introduce a polynomial-time method to verify the simultaneous existence of UPWARD PLANARITY and PLANARITY WITH SEPARATORS. Our findings are supported by illustrative examples and animations. The code is accessible at https://github.com/andrewjg/UpwardPlanarity. This research investigates algorithms and complexity regarding the conditions under which Directed Acyclic Graphs can be simultaneously embedded in an upward planar manner while satisfying various other properties. Crowdsourced data, characterized by inherent noise and uncertainty, is frequently utilized in machine learning. This study examines ensemble modeling applied to noisy, crowdsourced datasets, introducing a novel method that combines maximum likelihood estimations, a "Human Softmax" distribution representing human uncertainty, and uncertainty metrics like entropy. A strength-$t$ covering array, denoted $\mathrm{OA}(N,t,q)$, is an $N \times t$ matrix with entries from a set of size $q$ such that every $N \times t \times q^t$ hypercube in the associated $N$-dimensional grid over $\{0,\ldots,t\} \times q$ contains at least one point from the matrix. Covering arrays are extensively utilized in software testing, where $N$ represents the number of tests, $t$ the number of parameters, and $q$ the number of parameter values. The goal is to minimize $N$ for fixed $t$ and $q$. The strength of the array can be interpreted as ensuring that for any combination of parameter values, there exists at least one test (row) that assumes that specific combination. While optimal covering arrays for small $t$ and $q$ are well-documented, the focus of this paper is on small covering arrays with strength 2. We demonstrate that for $q \le 7$, every non-optimal strength-2 covering array can be constructed from an optimal one using four elementary operations. These operations involve duplicating rows, swapping entries within a row, inserting new values into a row, and creating new rows. Consequently, we can determine the count of distinct non-isomorphic strength-2 covering arrays for $q \le 7$ based on the number of their optimal counterparts. Furthermore, we establish that for $q \le 7$, the number of covering arrays of a given size is independent of the specific value of $q$. This insight enables us to compute the number of covering arrays for any $q$ by referencing the counts for arrays with $t=q+1$. We also provide a method to convert covering arrays into graphs, which aids in understanding their structural properties. Leveraging this graph representation, we derive several structural results, including the number of rows containing exactly two distinct values and the number of rows that can be altered without compromising the covering array property. Finally, we present a series of conjectures grounded in structural arguments. We examine ferromagnetic (FM) and antiferromagnetic (AFM) interactions on triangular and kagome lattices, deriving the ground state for every possible combination. Our analysis reveals that in the kagome case, non-ordered states emerge only within specific intervals of the interaction ratio, whereas on the triangular lattice, non-ordered phases appear exclusively at discrete points. We further characterize these configurations as linearly stable, locally stable, metastable, or unstable. Additionally, we calculate the energy per site for the resulting ground state phases. Finally, we present a general framework applicable to any regular magnetic ordering on any lattice, with a dedicated appendix dedicated to these observations. This study is particularly relevant for systems featuring low and frustrated symmetries, such as triangular and kagome lattices. We anticipate that these findings will be valuable for investigating various quantum magnets, including organic salts, quantum spin liquids, van der Waals magnets, and quantum materials. Notably, this work addresses a fundamental question in statistical mechanics: determining the set of ground states for a given classical spin model. This inquiry is frequently overlooked in the literature, where researchers often assume a single ground state and subsequently explore whether it remains stable at finite temperatures. In contrast, our approach explicitly accounts for the existence of multiple ground states. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these multiple ground states for finite-temperature phases, a topic that has received limited attention. We demonstrate that the presence of multiple ground states can significantly influence the finite-temperature phase diagram. We introduce a new statistical approach for identifying causal treatment effects within large-scale experiments, specifically designed to control the false discovery rate (FDR) while accounting for arbitrary dependence among the resulting p-values. This method is particularly suited to large-scale settings where the number of p-values far exceeds the sample size. Our primary application involves detecting treatment effects across numerous subgroups in large-scale online experiments, utilizing readily available user-level observational data. By leveraging this auxiliary data, we develop a screening procedure to isolate p-values likely to reflect genuine treatment effects. We then derive theoretical guarantees ensuring controlled FDR under a weak null distribution assumption, even in high-dimensional scenarios. Furthermore, we propose a practical implementation of the recently developed knockoff procedure to achieve FDR control under a strong null distribution assumption. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that our proposed procedures maintain rigorous FDR control and exhibit superior power compared to conventional alternatives. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenchenWang1992/TEDE. Additionally, we have released a user-friendly R package, TEDER, available at: https://github.com/ChenchenWang1992/TEDE. This package enables researchers to easily conduct treatment effect detection with FDR control under both strong and weak assumptions. The fundamental concepts of cosmological inflation are examined. We derive the equations of motion governing the inflaton field, define the slow-roll parameters, and outline the calculation of inflationary perturbations along with their relationship to the temperature anisotropies observed in the cosmic microwave background. Additionally, we present a brief overview of chaotic, hybrid, and line-inflation models, which may be suitable for inclusion as optional topics. Temporal action segmentation is a critical task for learning-based systems, yet it demands substantial manual annotation, resulting in high costs. While recent years have seen significant advancements in temporal action localization through the utilization of large-scale video datasets, progress in temporal action segmentation has been comparatively slower. This paper introduces an unsupervised approach for temporal action segmentation that relies on the co-occurrence of actions within videos. We propose an unsupervised training framework capable of generating high-quality segmentation masks from unlabeled videos without requiring any video annotations. Our method employs a novel Self-Supervised Co-occurrence Action Parsing (SSCAP) technique, which leverages the correlation between actions and video segments to learn a robust segmentation model. SSCAP utilizes a multi-task learning framework to simultaneously train for action recognition and segmentation, thereby enhancing temporal coherence and improving overall segmentation performance. Extensive experiments on the HMDB51 and UCF101 datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results in both accuracy and computational efficiency. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenShi1997/SSCAP.

Using the framework of current algebra, we investigate the formation and decay of hidden-charm pentaquark states. Within this approach, pentaquarks are represented as bound states of diquark-antiquark-diquark triples, where the diquark-antidiquark pairs emerge from the strong interaction between two quarks. The production of these states is modeled by the matrix element of the relevant seven-quark operator, with the antidiquark acting as the "spectator." This method successfully reproduces the experimental data regarding the production of $P_s(3842)$ and $P_c(4312)$ states in $J/\psi+p$ collisions, as well as the decay of $P_z(4440)$ into $J/\psi+p$. This study investigates the impact of a pedagogical approach to software testing education that utilizes inquiry-based learning (IBL) to foster critical thinking. Software testing education is vital for computer science curricula, yet it is often overlooked because students typically lack exposure to programming and are unfamiliar with the concept of testing. The primary challenge lies in motivating students to understand testing as a mechanism for identifying defects before release. This research evaluates the efficacy of an IBL-driven, inquiry-based learning (IBL) framework utilizing a web-based game for teaching testing concepts, comparing it against a traditional detailed feedback method. The IBL approach focuses on guiding students to formulate testing strategies and apply them within the game environment. To ensure a rigorous comparison, the same game was used in both conditions, with the only variable being the type of feedback provided. The IBL method offered conceptual feedback that prompted students to reflect on and construct their own testing strategies, whereas the traditional method provided detailed, prescriptive instructions. The study involved 100 undergraduate students divided into two groups, with post-experiment surveys assessing the effectiveness of each feedback type. Results indicated that the IBL approach yielded higher scores on a 10-point scale for measuring the development of effective testing strategies. Furthermore, open-ended responses revealed that participants in the IBL group demonstrated a deeper understanding of the game's objectives and the rationale behind their testing approaches. These findings suggest that IBL offers a more effective mechanism for teaching software testing concepts, thereby enhancing students' ability to create testing strategies prior to release. The paper concludes by outlining the benefits of this approach and discussing its implications for software testing education. Additionally, the authors provide a link to the game and testing materials used in the study, which are available for adaptation in computer science curricula. The research also addresses the limitations of the IBL method, such as the extended time required for students to develop their own strategies, and suggests that instructors can mitigate this by offering examples of effective testing approaches. Ultimately, the IBL method serves as a valuable tool for improving the quality of testing strategies, and its successful application in a game-based learning environment underscores the potential of such environments for software testing education. The authors recommend that IBL be adopted in computer science curricula to enhance the quality of testing strategies among software engineers. Future work will explore the application of IBL to other programming concepts, including unit testing, integration testing, and security testing. Domain adaptation is a widely adopted strategy for addressing domain shift issues in image recognition. However, most existing methods rely on sharing source and target feature spaces through a fixed teacher network, a requirement that limits their practicality in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a novel approach that eliminates the need for a teacher network by adapting features within a single network. Specifically, we propose a domain-invariant feature extractor and a domain-specific feature adapter. The adapter dynamically adjusts feature representations to align with a semi-supervised hypothesis transfer network, which is trained solely on domain-invariant features. This hypothesis transfer mechanism effectively bridges the domain gap between source and target datasets. Furthermore, we integrate a multi-scale discriminator to capture features at various levels and a domain-adversarial discriminator to minimize distribution discrepancies across scales. Experimental results on person re-identification and image classification demonstrate the superiority of our method. The code is accessible at https://github.com/cheny1997/SHS-TANet. This paper outlines the design of a gas-core nuclear reactor intended for deep space propulsion. Unlike its liquid-core counterpart, the gas-core design avoids the complexities associated with two-phase flow. We demonstrate that this reactor can achieve the high power output and specific impulse necessary for deep space travel by operating at extremely high temperatures and utilizing a light molecular fuel such as hydrogen. The analysis covers fuel circulation, the impact of centrifugal forces on core structure, and methods for removing fission products like krypton and xenon. Additionally, we examine a propulsion system variant that incorporates a nozzle to accelerate an oxidizer, thereby enhancing the overall system's specific impulse. A three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics simulation of such a nozzle is currently in progress. Finally, the paper discusses potential engineering challenges and proposes a roadmap for future research. This proposal aims to stimulate discussion regarding the viability of gas-core reactors for deep space propulsion and to outline a path forward for their development. The results indicate that domain-informed networks are essential for reliable interaction reconstruction, particularly in scenarios involving detector failures. Atmospheric models for brown dwarfs and exoplanets are typically constrained by database limitations, which restrict the range of temperatures, pressures, and abundances for species like water, methane, CO, and TiO. This constraint arises because most existing studies rely on models developed for stellar atmospheres. We introduce a new database designed specifically for substellar and exoplanetary atmospheres, expanding the parameter space for H$_2$O, CH$_4$, and CO to include temperatures from 200 K to 10,000 K, pressures up to 300 bar, and electron abundances between 0 and 10$^{-3}$. This work presents the inaugural release of the EXOPLINES database, featuring 1,000 H$_2$O cross-sections, 1,000 CH$_4$ cross-sections, 1,000 CO cross-sections, and 1,000 H$^-$ cross-sections. Additionally, we provide 10,000 molecular line lists for H$_2$O, CH$_4$, CO, and H$^-$, each covering a specific atmospheric condition. These resources are accessible via our online repository at http://exoelines.org. Our findings indicate that EXOPLINES enables broader parameter space exploration, thereby enhancing the accuracy of atmospheric retrievals. We demonstrate this by calculating the atmospheric properties of the brown dwarf WISE 1426$-$2227 using the new database. Furthermore, we highlight that EXOPLINES offers significant computational efficiency, requiring approximately 10 times less time than the existing PHOENIX stellar atmosphere code. The inclusion of H$^-$ cross-sections in EXOPLINES is particularly valuable for modeling the atmospheres of L-type brown dwarfs and hot Jupiters. Ultimately, the EXOPLINES database facilitates the investigation of atmospheric conditions that were previously inaccessible, while simultaneously improving computational efficiency. We anticipate that the EXOPLINES team will continue to expand this database in future releases. This work offers a foundational exploration of grounding within Answer Set Programming (ASP). It examines various grounding techniques for rule-based knowledge representations, with a specific focus on the grounding method employed by the ASP solver, ASPCAS. The paper highlights the knowledge flow characteristics of different approaches and introduces alternative grounding strategies for ASPCAS. Furthermore, it investigates the computational complexity of the resulting rule sets and provides a theoretical analysis of grounding complexity for the most prevalent methods. Additionally, a complexity analysis is conducted for the co-occurrence graph used in ASPCAS's iterative grounding algorithm. Finally, the study addresses limiting factors of ASPCAS's current grounding algorithm and proposes solutions to mitigate them.

This work establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for monotonicity and additivity within generic quantum resource theories. These criteria are expressed as quantum relative entropy inequalities involving the resource-depleted states of the underlying theory. Consequently, this framework generalizes recent findings from quantum thermodynamics and generalizes the first law of physics to diverse quantum resource theories. Furthermore, we demonstrate the broad utility of these new resource of transformations. Specifically, we derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for the monotonicity of thermality, thermality relative to a bath, coherence, and coherence relative to a shift. Additionally, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for the monotonicity of thermodynamic work, thermal work, coherence, and coherence distillation. Finally, we extend the second law of thermodynamics to general quantum resource theories. To achieve this, we introduce a generalization of the second law for thermal states relative to a bath, a concept that may hold independent significance. These results are derived using a resource of operations approach, which is both conceptually straightforward and mathematically rigorous. We also examine the relationship between this approach and the more conventional methods found in the literature. Our primary findings are applicable to any operation that leaves the free states of a theory invariant. As a practical application, we derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for the unitary generation of coherence and thermality. These findings may inspire future research into general quantum resource theories and their resource theories of transformations. Moreover, our derived necessary and sufficient conditions for the monotonicity of generic quantum resources can be directly applied to construct resource theories for various operational tasks. Finally, we illustrate this application by deriving the necessary and sufficient conditions for the success of generic discrimination tasks. This work introduces a framework for measuring information flow within dynamical systems. We define information current as a multivariate function that captures the transfer of information from one variable to another. We demonstrate that for Gaussian processes, this measure can be derived from the dynamical system's linear response function, establishing a unique method to infer information transfer from observable data. Furthermore, we prove that the information current is intrinsically linked to information entropy production, offering a data-driven approach to quantify entropy production in nonequilibrium systems. Finally, we validate this framework by calculating information flow in a stochastic model of a cell cycle and in a simple case of information transfer between two neurons. These findings suggest that this metric holds significant potential for measuring information transfer in various biological systems. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python package implementing this framework, which can be accessed at https://github.com/alexei-blok/IMM. The associated code for all examples is available at https://github.com/alexei-blok/IMM/tree/main/examples. This paper investigates inference regarding the parameters of a non-linear, non-stationary time series model featuring heavy tails, with applications focused on estimating risk measures in financial time series. We introduce a non-linear autoregressive model with exogenous variables (NARX) that incorporates a time-varying location and a time-varying scale, the latter designed to capture evolving tail behavior. To facilitate efficient Bayesian parameter estimation, we develop a novel class of models termed "tractably approximated heavy-tailed non-linear time series" (TAHT). This framework facilitates straightforward likelihood computation, enabling the use of standard Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques. Furthermore, we propose a new Bayesian model selection criterion for identifying the appropriate scale model, which accounts for both tail thickness and temporal variation. Extensive simulations and real-world applications demonstrate the superior performance of our approach compared to existing methods. We introduce a novel class of good quantum low-density parity-check codes equipped with linear-time decoders. Specifically, for a block length $n$, these codes feature a relative distance $\Omega(1/n)$, a rate $\Omega(1/n)$, and can be sampled in linear time. The associated decoding algorithm operates within $O(n \log^2(n))$ time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, assuming the Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis, no family of quantum LDPC codes can simultaneously achieve constant rate, constant relative distance, and linear-time decoding. This finding underscores that current quantum LDPC code designs, which typically sacrifice constant rate and distance to maintain good distance and efficient decoding, fundamentally cannot achieve all three properties at once. Our codes retain the advantageous decoder architecture of existing quantum LDPC codes, utilizing only local checks and syndrome measurements on four wires. Additionally, we establish that any quantum LDPC code family with constant rate and constant relative distance necessarily possesses a decoder requiring super-linear time. Finally, we prove that no quantum LDPC code can simultaneously maintain constant rate, constant relative distance, and linear check size. Our findings also clarify the inherent tradeoffs among rate, relative distance, and check size in quantum LDPC code design. To our knowledge, this work marks the first instance of good quantum LDPC codes achieving constant-time decoders. Our approach builds upon recent constructions by Kovalev and Yehudayoff, which we modify to produce a code with a relative distance of $\Omega(1/n)$. We also propose a conjecture that, under the Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis, our construction yields codes with rate and relative distance both scaling as $\Omega(1/\sqrt{n})$. Additionally, we present a conjecture that our construction achieves constant rate and relative distance when using super-linear check sizes, a claim that likely holds without relying on the Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis. Our proofs rely on a novel, self-contained argument that establishes a tradeoff between rate, relative distance, and check size for quantum LDPC codes. This argument also implies that any quantum LDPC code with rate and relative distance of $\Omega(1/n^c)$ for some $c > 0$ must employ a decoder with time complexity exceeding $O(n^{1+\epsilon})$ for any $\epsilon > 0$. We anticipate that this argument will find applications in other research areas. Our proof technique is inspired by recent classical results by Dinur, which also demonstrate that no classical code can achieve constant rate

This study examines the distributed complexity of the Distance-$r$ Dominating Set problem on sparse graphs with high girth within the BSS model. Graph properties are provided as oracles, and all runtime measurements include queries to these oracles. We demonstrate that for any fixed $r$ and $\epsilon$, the problem is solvable in $O(n^{1+\epsilon})$ time when given oracles for both sparsity and girth. Furthermore, assuming the graph class lacks a constant-degree clique minor, we establish that the problem is solvable in $O(n^{2-\delta})$ time for some $\delta > 0$ using oracles for the number of vertices at each distance up to $r$. Additionally, we prove that if the Maximum Independent Set problem can be solved in $O(n^{2-\delta'})$ time with distance-1 count oracles, then the Distance-$r$ Dominator number can be computed in $O(n^{1+\delta'})$ time using oracles for the vertex and edge counts at every distance up to $r$. Finally, we present a conditional lower bound: if the Distance-$r$ Dominator number is computable in $O(n^{2-\delta})$ time with distance-1 count oracles for all graphs with girth exceeding $cn^{\alpha}$ (where $c, \alpha > 0$ are constants), then $P=NP$. The proofs for our upper bounds rely on a recent structural result by Abboud, Grandoni, and Vassilevska (SODA 2020). To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first polynomial-time algorithm for Distance-$r$ Dominator on sparse high-girth graphs and the first subquadratic algorithm for this problem on such graphs when girth is not constrained. Additionally, our findings imply a conditional lower bound for the Independent Dominator problem, a recently introduced problem by Abboud, Grandoni, and Vassilevska (SODA 2020). We show that if Independent Dominator is solvable in $O(n^{2-\delta})$ time with oracles for the number of neighbors at each distance up to $r$ on $n$-vertex graphs with girth at least $cn^{\alpha}$ (for constants $c, \alpha > 0$), then $P=NP$. Our lower bound construction utilizes a reduction from 3SAT.

This study investigates the bulk-boundary correspondence in the one-dimensional disordered higher-order topological insulator (HOTTI) model. The pristine HOI model, characterized by a bulk quadrupole moment and quadrupolar boundary states, transitions into a disordered phase where the bulk quadrupole vanishes. We demonstrate that while the disordered system retains quadrupolar boundary states, the bulk spectrum becomes completely delocalized. Furthermore, we show that the bulk quadrupole defined on a hypercube does not capture the topological nature of the system, as its value fluctuates randomly with system size. In contrast, the real-space Z₂ invariant, calculated via the real-space Green's function, remains constant regardless of disorder or system size. Additionally, we find that the real-space index is equivalent to the real-space winding number, which is also topologically invariant under disorder. Finally, we confirm the stability of bulk-boundary correspondence in the disordered HOTTI model by analyzing the energy level statistics of the boundary spectrum. These findings offer a comprehensive framework for investigating bulk-boundary correspondence in higher-order topological models subject to disorder. Finally, we note that the disorder-robustness of the bulk quadrupole in 1D can be enhanced by incorporating a second-neighbor term into the Hamiltonian. However, this modification necessitates a more complex definition of the real-space index, which must be adjusted to account for the additional term. We also observe that the real-space index for this generalized model differs from the winding number. Through numerical analysis, we establish that the real-space index continues to characterize the disorder-free bulk spectrum and boundary states, whereas the winding number specifically targets the boundary states. Finally, we show that both the bulk and boundary spectra exhibit topological protection against disorder. These results provide a robust numerical method for analyzing bulk-boundary correspondence in disordered HOTTI models. Overall, our work offers a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between bulk and boundary topological invariants in disordered HOTTI systems. These findings are also applicable to other one-dimensional topological insulators, such as the disordered SSH model. Our analysis reveals that the winding number serves as the effective bulk topological invariant for the SSH model, while the real-space index identifies the presence of boundary zero modes. We further show that the bulk and boundary spectra of the disordered SSH model exhibit topological protection, and the real-space index remains independent of system size. These insights contribute to a deeper comprehension of the relationship between bulk and boundary topological

This contribution outlines the experimental strategies employed by the CMS experiment to investigate the Standard Model's potential extension into supersymmetry. Specifically, it details searches for gluino and top squark pair production conducted during 2015 and 2016, which yielded the most stringent limits on supersymmetry to date. Additionally, the text presents a novel search for chargino-neutralino pair production, designed to explore the lightest supersymmetric scenarios undetected by prior analyses. The discussion concludes by addressing the challenges and opportunities associated with searching for the Higgs boson within supersymmetric frameworks. The presentation is based on the work of the CMS Higgs Working Group, a specialized group dedicated to analyzing Higgs boson properties through the lens of supersymmetry. We introduce a new framework for rendering scenes using 2D and extended light fields within neural networks. In 2020, the speckle interferometry instrument on the Southern Astrophysical Research Telescope (SOAR) achieved a total exposure time of 12.5 hours, yielding 1,000 images with a median seeing of 0.12 arcsec. A new data reduction pipeline was introduced, which successfully corrected for atmospheric turbulence and detector readout noise, delivering 95% of the anticipated scientific output. The analysis of this new data revealed 1,000 binary systems, including 100 new discoveries, bringing the total catalog to 1,900 binaries. The average separation of these newly detected binaries is 0.18 arcsec, and the average flux ratio is 0.12. Additionally, 100 previously known binaries were observed, allowing for the measurement of changes in their separations and position angles. The study also reports on 10 triple systems, with variations in their relative positions and orientations. Finally, the paper discusses the current status of the speckle interferometry program at SOAR and outlines its future prospects.

We investigate celestial chiral algebras within celestial holography, with a specific focus on the holomorphic components of two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) and their applications to $(3+1)$-dimensional self-dual Yang-Mills theory and self-dual gravity. These gravitational theories are both integrable and governed by a single function, $w_{03}(z)$, representing the stress tensor of the CFT. We demonstrate that the structure of the chiral algebra is entirely determined by $w_{03}(z)$. In standard CFTs, the positive-mode generators of the stress tensor constitute the complete set of chiral algebra generators. Furthermore, we establish that the non-stress tensor generators can be expressed as integrals of the stress tensor modes, implying that all local operators in the CFT emerge from the Fourier-transformed positive-mode sector. Consequently, the full celestial chiral algebra is built exclusively from the stress tensor and its descendants. This finding suggests that the chiral algebras of (2+1)- and (4+1)-dimensionself-dual gravity may also be generated solely by the stress tensor. Additionally, we examine a novel set of colour-kinematics duality relations applicable to self-dual Yang-Mills theory, which could have significant implications for the development of an amplitude programme in celestial holography. Finally, we explore the connection between the conformal weights of CFT operators and the scaling dimensions of their corresponding operators in self-dual Yang-Mills theory. This link is derived from the Ward identities associated with the chiral algebra, revealing that the operator spectrum in self-dual Yang-Mills theory is encoded within the chiral algebra. We also examine the colour-kinematics duality in self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its relationship to the chiral algebra. Finally, we extend our analysis to self-dual gravity, showing that its operator spectrum is likewise captured by the chiral algebra. We further examine the role of a conformal Ward identity that arises in the gravitational context but has no counterpart in the CFT. Collectively, these findings indicate that the operator spectrum in self-dual Yang-Mills theory and self-dual gravity is fully represented by the chiral algebra. We conclude by discussing the potential for a non-linear positive-mode stress tensor that could generate an even richer class of theories. Solar eruptions frequently produce jets that drive shocks through the corona, generating shocks and waves observable across various wavelengths. However, a comprehensive analysis of these shock-driven waves remains absent from the literature. This study addresses that gap by examining a solar eruption observed on 2018 May 10, utilizing a multi-wavelength dataset from the WISPR and STIX instruments on the Solar Orbiter spacecraft, alongside LoWiSo and SDO/K-AIA images. LoWiSo's unique capability to detect plasma at 1.6 R$_\odot$ allowed for the identification of a jet-driven piston shock, which was subsequently tracked using LoWiSo, STIX, and WISPR. The observed trajectory of the shock front aligns with the trajectory of the jet's leading edge, confirming the shock's driving mechanism. Furthermore, LoWiSo and STIX detected a brightening region on the far side of the jet, suggesting the presence of a loop connecting the jet to the far side of the eruption. We examine fermion couplings within the general two Higgs doublet model, where the Yukawa interaction structure is defined by arbitrary $3\times 3$ real matrices. By analyzing the flavour anomalies and the standard model muon anomalous magnetic moment, we derive constraints on these couplings. Our findings indicate that while the hierarchical nature of fermion masses necessitates specific couplings, the model can also account for the observed flavour anomalies through couplings that are significantly larger. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a broad spectrum of new physics scales can be accommodated, provided that the Higgs boson couplings to gauge bosons and the Higgs sector mass spectrum exhibit significant deviations from standard model predictions. Finally, we identify that the model's viability relies on the alignment of the two Higgs doublets, which occurs when their mass eigenstates are aligned with the vacuum expectation values. This condition is necessary to maintain tree-level unitarity in elastic scattering amplitudes involving initial and final state fermions. Additionally, we show that this alignment requirement can be derived from an analysis of the unitarity of elastic scattering amplititudes involving initial and final state fermions. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for collider searches. Our conclusions suggest that the most promising search channels are those involving the production of new heavy Higgs bosons in association with fermion pairs, a process that could be observable even at the LHC. We also note that the search sensitivity is not heavily dependent on the specific fermion pair produced. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the search strategy for Higgs pair production via vector boson fusion can be enhanced by considering final states with three bottom quarks. In this specific scenario, we estimate that the Higgs pair invariant mass spectrum could provide a significant new physics signal. We introduce a new functional stochastic differential equation (FSDI) designed to model the random dynamics of vortices and vortex rings. This FSDIE operates within a functional stochastic differential equation framework, where the diffusion coefficient relies on a functional variable that encompasses both the system's positional and orientational characteristics. Specifically, for vortex pairs, this descriptor is a relative quaternion representing their orientation, whereas for random vortex dynamics, it involves the system quaternion defined by the velocity vector and a specific observation direction. We demonstrate that the generated FSDIE system adheres to a Fokker-Planck equation, which describes a Fokker-Planck probability density dependent on position, orientation, time, and a specific observation direction. Furthermore, we show that the FSDIE system can be decomposed into a set of Itô stochastic differential equations. The proposed FSDIE system successfully replicates key characteristics of vortex pair dynamics, including short-range attraction, long-range repulsion, and a dipolar moment. Additionally, we illustrate that this model can account for the random behavior of vortex pairs in random turbulence, as well as the random dynamics of random vortex rings and ring pairs. We also provide examples of trajectories and path ensembles derived from the new FSDIE system. Finally, we present results from particle simulations based on this novel FSDIE system. These simulations indicate that the new model can reproduce fundamental properties of vortex rings, such as their persistence length, lifetime, and radius, as well as properties of ring pairs, such as their linkage length, lifetime, and relative distance. The paper concludes with a discussion of the new FSDIE system and its potential applications. Additionally, we provide a Fortran code implementing this new model for simulating random vortex pair dynamics. This code is available at: https://github.com/alexei-fedorov/vortex-dynamics. The Fortran code can be easily adapted to simulate other scenarios, such as the dynamics of vortex rings or ring pairs. We have also prepared a Python version of the code for users who prefer Python over Fortran. This version is available at: https://github.com/alexei-fedorov/vortex-dynamics/tree/main/python. Users are encouraged to review the Python code to understand the implementation details of our new FSDIE system. We have also prepared a Python version of the code that includes a Jupyter notebook to facilitate the simulation process. This version is available at: https://github.com/alexei-fedorov/vortex-dynamics/tree/main/python

Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to be difficult for classical computers to replicate. While the average entanglement within this framework has been previously examined, this study investigates the entanglement structure of the complete output probability distribution. We evaluate the entanglement of every possible output state using negativity as a metric. Our findings indicate that most outputs possess high entanglement entropy, with the proportion of low entanglement outputs remaining nearly constant regardless of the number of photons or modes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the distribution of these low entanglement outputs adheres to a Dyson-Skew-Wigner-Sato distribution, which governs time-reversal invariant systems with broken symmetry. Additionally, we prove that the entanglement of individual outputs in boson sampling can be characterized as a Schur-Weydinger duality between the Weyl and Schur representations of the symmetric group. Finally, we provide an efficient algorithm to calculate the entanglement of any arbitrary output. These results offer a quantitative assessment of entanglement in boson sampling, deepening our understanding of the quantum nature of this model. Additionally, we have made our code available to facilitate the investigation of entanglement in other quantum models. High-dimensional time-series data are prevalent in life sciences, yet analyzing them remains difficult. While supervised learning offers a solution, it is often hindered by the complex temporal dependencies inherent in such data. This study introduces a method to enhance the performance of supervised learning models when applied to short, high-dimensional temporal sequences. We demonstrate that these sequences can be effectively represented as weighted graphs, where nodes signify time points and edges denote the strength of temporal relationships. Consequently, we developed a graph-based model that utilizes these graphs as features for supervised learning. Our approach is evaluated on two real-world datasets: one concerning treatment responses in acute myeloid leukemia patients and another regarding treatment responses in ovarian cancer patients. The results indicate that our model can learn to predict treatment responses from high-dimensional time-series data, outperforming baseline methods. Furthermore, the identified features offer potential biological insights. Overall, this study highlights the potential of our graph-based approach for supervised learning in short, high-dimensional temporal sequences. These representations may serve as a new data format for deep learning applications in temporal sequence analysis, with applications extending to treatment response prediction in oncology and drug discovery within chemical biology. Reinforcement learning (RL) focuses on agents interacting with environments to maximize long-term rewards. However, many real-world scenarios involve partial observability, where agents lack complete knowledge of their surroundings. This paper demonstrates that deep recurrent networks, when trained via policy gradient methods in such partial settings, internally construct a dynamic representation of the environment. Specifically, we show that the hidden states of these networks function as "beliefs" regarding environmental states, consistent with Bayesian inference, and can explicitly predict those states. Consequently, this reveals an interpretable internal mechanism within a black-box architecture, offering valuable insights into how agents navigate uncertain worlds. Our findings are based on experiments using a deep recurrent policy network trained on a standard RL benchmark. Additionally, we explore the potential of this internal representation to enhance the agent's performance. We conclude by discussing broader implications for understanding internal representations in artificial neural networks. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexschneuer/RL-internal-structure. Keywords: Reinforcement learning, internal representations, partial observability, interpretability. This paper addresses weakly-supervised action detection, where training data consists solely of video-level labels. While recent methods have focused on generating and leveraging discriminative class-specific features, they often overlook the importance of contextual information within untrimmed video segments. We introduce an approach that automatically identifies and utilizes relevant context for action detection. Specifically, we employ a novel video graph model that captures contextual relationships between adjacent segments and integrates this into a graph convolutional network to extract context-aware features. Furthermore, we develop a new action detection framework that combines these context-aware features with class-specific features to distinguish relevant context from irrelevant one. Experimental results on two standard action detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we present a visualized training process that highlights the relevance of context in action detection. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/leeyang1225/SpotWhatMatters. The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge (ISC2021) introduced a new dataset designed to evaluate the visual similarity of 3D objects. This dataset encompasses 100 source 3D models, each rendered into 100 images featuring variations in viewpoint, lighting, and texture color. The task required systems to identify the single image most similar to a given query, which was randomly selected from the 100 options. The challenge was divided into two tracks: a texture-only track and a real-world track, the latter involving 2D images corrupted by noise, illumination changes, viewpoint shifts, and occlusions. This paper presents the results of top-performing teams across both tracks and analyzes the dataset and evaluation metrics to offer insights for future research. Additionally, the authors release a benchmarking tool to facilitate future evaluations on this dataset. The dataset and tools are accessible at https://github.com/3D-Shape-Watermarking/ISC2021. This study examines diffusion processes within domains featuring moving or oscillating boundaries within a degenerate medium modeled by a weighted $p$-Laplace operator. The analysis addresses small perturbations subject to both Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, deriving asymptotic formulas that capture the metastable dynamics of principal eigenfunctions and eigenvalues. This study investigates the properties of nuclear matter at zero temperature under strong magnetic fields using the lowest-order constraint variational (LOCV) method with a finite-range Urbana force derived from the one-pion-exchange (OPE) model. The UR14, UR16, and UR18 parameter sets are analyzed to determine the energy per nucleon, symmetry energy, and momentum of the most stable configuration. Results indicate that magnetic fields influence these quantities, with the symmetry energy showing greater sensitivity to field strength than the energy per nucleon. Specifically, the symmetry energy decreases at magnetic field strengths below $10^{19}$ G but rises significantly when the field exceeds this threshold. Furthermore, the calculated energy per nucleon and symmetry energy align well with existing literature values. Finally, the symmetry energy is observed to be more sensitive to magnetic field strength in the UR14 case compared to the UR16 and UR18 cases. These findings demonstrate that magnetic fields can substantially alter the equation of state for nuclear matter. Additionally, the momentum of the most stable configuration is found to be non-zero, suggesting that matter may form paired states under these conditions. These conclusions are supported by various theoretical frameworks. This study addresses privacy and communication challenges in federated learning (FL) by introducing a novel framework called DP-REC. This approach integrates federated early stopping with a new privacy mechanism known as the Random Erasure Channel (REC). We provide a theoretical analysis of REC's privacy guarantees, demonstrating that it achieves the same level of protection as traditional DP-SE mechanisms. Furthermore, we prove that the combination of REC and early stopping constitutes a post-processing operation that preserves privacy, thereby establishing the overall security of DP-REC. Theoretical findings are supported by experimental results. Our contributions offer a more efficient and privacy-preserving alternative for FL, with potential applications in various domains. Additionally, we propose a new communication efficiency metric for FL, which is expected to be valuable for future research in this field. We conducted far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the Taurus-Perseus-Auriga complex using the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph on the Hubble Space Telescope. These observations successfully captured FUV emission from both the Taurus and Perseus star-forming regions, marking the first time FUV data has been obtained from these areas. The FUV emission in Taurus originates from a compact nebula situated near the center of the Ophiuchus cluster, while in Perseus, it arises from a large, extended nebula covering approximately 10 square degrees. Notably, the FUV emission in Perseus is not uniform; it exhibits a strong concentration toward the center of the nebula, accompanied by several distinct patches of enhanced emission. This pattern indicates that the illumination of the diffuse nebula is driven by a few bright O-type stars, while the bright patches are likely caused by the presence of additional O-type stars or early B-type stars. Furthermore, we identified several previously unknown emission-line nebulae in the FUV emission of both regions. The spectral energy distribution of the FUV emission in Taurus aligns with the spectral characteristics of O-type stars, whereas the emission in Perseus is primarily dominated by H$\beta$ emission. Additionally, we detected FUV emission from a few diffuse molecular clouds in Taurus that lack any associated H$\beta$ emission. These findings suggest that the H$\beta$ emission in Taurus is confined to the central compact nebula, whereas the H$\beta$ emission in Perseus is distributed more broadly across the region. Finally, we observed FUV emission from several diffuse molecular clouds in the Auriga region that are illuminated by a newly discovered O-type star. Overall, this study provides a comprehensive survey of the FUV emission within the Taurus-Perseus-Auriga complex. These observations offer valuable insights into the physical conditions of the regions and the characteristics of their stellar populations. Tables are a common feature in documents, where the spatial arrangement of cells conveys semantic meaning. However, existing methods often overlook the unique spatial structure of these tables during extraction. This paper introduces an approach that first encodes the table by representing each cell as a node within a graph, capturing both the cell and its relationships. Subsequently, a Graph Neural Network (GNN) is employed to extract features from an input image, treating the cell nodes as an embedding space. The GNN then processes these nodes to identify the table's structure and locate the table within the document. Experiments conducted on the PubLayNet dataset demonstrate that this method achieves a table extraction F1 score of 80.2, outperforming the second-best result by 2.2 points. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi-1996/ICDAR2021-PublicationPaper-TableExtraction. The paper can be found at https://chenyi1996.github.io/publications/ICDAR2021-TableExtraction.pdf. Keywords: Table Extraction, Document Understanding, Information Retrieval, Information Extraction, Graph Neural Networks.

We introduce a cognitive hierarchy model tailored for multi-stage games of incomplete information, wherein agents sequentially undertake decision tasks under uncertainty regarding others' actions and private information. This framework enables agents to form beliefs about future outcomes and adjust their cognitive depth based on these expectations. We provide general existence results for a equilibrium where the cognitive hierarchy remains stable over time, illustrating the model with cases that produce time-varying rationalizability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that calibrating the degree of rationality to the size of an agent's information set can resolve the issue of infinite rational agents. Our findings suggest that cognitive hierarchy dynamics can be viewed as an extension of traditional one-shot models to multi-stage settings, where the anticipation of future events influences both information acquisition and cognitive investment. Additionally, this framework offers a unified approach to analyzing dynamic rationalizability, potentially explaining why agents exhibit higher rationality in the present than in hypothetical future scenarios. Finally, we propose that this model can help interpret the mixed results from experiments on multi-period public good games, where some evidence points to time-invariant rationality while other evidence suggests it varies over time. The proposed solution lies at the intersection of these two extremes. We also outline avenues for future research, including the potential for agents to learn the appropriate level of rationality for a given information set size. Our results indicate that, under certain conditions, agents can indeed learn to adapt their rationality to their information set size. These contributions advance our understanding of how rationality functions in complex, evolving environments. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the model and its solution concepts; Section 3 discusses existence results; and Section 4 applies these findings to experimental data. Given the paper's length, we have omitted several technical proofs, which can be found in an online appendix available at https://www.econ.ucsb.edu/faculty/cheny/Files/CH_Comp.pdf. Accurate population estimates are essential for formulating evidence-based policies and allocating resources effectively. This study introduces a technique for estimating population counts by integrating the geometry of Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) road networks with data from the most recent national censuses. We trained a machine learning model to predict population numbers based on census-derived features, specifically focusing on road network characteristics. We then applied this model to other recent census datasets to generate population predictions. Finally, we evaluated the durability of these predictions by contrasting them with subsequent national census figures. Our findings indicate that a linear regression model utilizing road network features yields a robust population estimate with a 5.2% margin of error. Furthermore, we demonstrate that leveraging accessible GNSS road data allows for accurate population estimation without relying on census inputs. This approach offers a sustainable solution for maintaining precise population estimates in developing nations where monitoring infrastructure is limited and census data may be inaccessible. This technique was developed and validated using data from Mozambique. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekdatta100/estimating_population. Given the growing availability of GNSS road data, we anticipate that this method will soon be applicable to other countries. We have also published an open-source Python package to facilitate the implementation of this framework. This work was conducted while the first author was a visiting researcher at the University of Oxford. Additional details can be found in our white paper, which is also available online. In scenarios where a small set of objects must be rapidly checked for presence, traditional hash tables are often inefficient due to their optimization for dynamic insertion and deletion. Conversely, static approximate filters offer constant-time checks with minimal extra space, though they inevitably allow some objects to be filtered out. This paper introduces a novel class of static filters capable of identifying all members of a specific set while filtering out non-members, except for a designated small set known as the "free set." We present a new family of filters termed "all-but-one" (AbO) filters, which exclude exactly one element from the free set. We demonstrate that AbO filters are equivalent to standard Bloom filters augmented with a single additional bit. Furthermore, we outline a method for constructing these filters directly and prove their equivalence to the standard Bloom-plus-bit approach. Finally, we extend the AbO filter concept to create "almost all-but-one" (AObO) filters, which exclude a random element from the union of the target and free sets. Experimental results indicate that AObO filters outperform standard Bloom filters in terms of space efficiency. The source code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/robertklemm/aboo-filters. Our implementation is integrated into the Julia DataStructures package. Additionally, we have developed a package containing various filters, including AbO and AObO variants for different hash families, which can be installed via `Pkg.add("DynamicFilters")`. We invite researchers to explore this package and contribute new filters. Contributions should be submitted via email to robert.klemm@ist.ac.at. This work investigates the spinor atom-molecule conversion process occurring in a degenerate Fermi gas of $^{40}$K. It demonstrates that laser-induced three-body recombination can transform two free atoms into a molecule alongside a single electron. The study outlines the design of an experimental apparatus to detect the resulting electron and analyzes the reaction rate within a trapped, degenerate Fermi gas. Results indicate that even with modest trap sizes and confinement strengths, the atom-molecule conversion rate can reach values comparable to those observed in atomic systems. Furthermore, by adjusting the trap size and magnetic field, researchers can manipulate the relative rates of Fermi and Pauli allowed reactions. Finally, the work explores potential applications of this mechanism for cooling molecules and generating entangled electron-positron pairs. Additionally, the proposed setup can be adapted to study other reactions, such as electron-positron pair creation, thereby extending current research into the realm of relativistic physics. This paper begins with a review of P. M. Robins' seminal 1990 discussion on the relationship between frequentist and Bayesian reasoning in statistical inference. It subsequently examines the p-value controversy surrounding Benjamin's "five sigma" rule and connects it to Robins' insights. The discussion then shifts to a straightforward linear regression scenario, followed by an exploration of a more complex hierarchical regression context. This latter section demonstrates how Bayesian methods can be applied to resolve issues arising in frequentist approaches within regression analysis. The paper concludes by suggesting that the Bayesian perspective offers significant advantages over the frequentist approach for addressing fundamental statistical problems. Accordingly, it proposes that researchers and graduate students in the field consider adopting Bayesian techniques to address the various challenges currently facing classical regression analysis. Finally, this introduction aims to serve as an accessible entry point for graduate students and researchers interested in learning more about Bayesian regression analysis.

Mafia is a well-known social party game that functions as a simple yet fundamental example of a social dilemma. This paper introduces a straightforward mathematical model of the game to analyze the strategic choices players face. We begin by examining a scenario where players are unaware of their roles, followed by a more complex version incorporating player heterogeneity. In both instances, we calculate the probability that the player assuming the role of "Cop" will succeed in exposing the "Mafia" members. Additionally, we consider a variant where participants can vote to eliminate a player each round; in this case, we determine the likelihood that good players will win. Our findings indicate that voter heterogeneity significantly impacts the chance of the good player prevailing. Specifically, if the Cop holds a strong position, a composition of aggressive voters maximizes their winning probability, whereas a mix of voters is optimal when the Cop's position is weak. These insights are validated through an experimental study. Finally, we discuss how these results can be extended to broader social contexts. This model represents the initial step toward a more comprehensive analysis of multi-player games, and it can be readily adapted to study other games with analogous structures. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to real-world scenarios involving heterogeneous groups, such as political elections, corporate board meetings, and international negotiations. This study investigates the simultaneous accretion of a gas accretion cavity within a protoplanetary disk by two giant planets, a process that significantly influences their ultimate masses and the disk's structural evolution. We conducted 2D hydrodynamical simulations of a single gas accretion hole formed by a pair of planets with fixed orbital separation, varying their initial masses to assess the impact of sequential versus simultaneous accretion. Our findings indicate that simultaneous accretion results in a final mass ratio ($q_{\rm fin}$) approximately 20% greater than accretion occurring sequentially. Furthermore, we examined how the initial mass ratio ($q_{\rm ini}$) influences the gas accretion cavity; higher $q_{\rm ini}$ values produce deeper and wider cavities, leading to more massive disks beyond the outer edge of the cavity. Consequently, these objects are predicted to have longer gas disk lifetimes and a higher probability of becoming massive binary systems. We also explored the impact of migration on the final mass ratio, observing that planets with different migration rates can result in $q_{\rm fin}$ values differing by up to 50%. Finally, we compared our simulation results with observed binary exoplanet populations, finding that the $q_{\rm fin}$ distribution from our simulations aligns well with the observed distribution of known exoplanet binaries. Overall, our results suggest that the simultaneous accretion of a gas accretion cavity by two giant planets can explain the formation of binary exoplanet systems. This model also accounts for the fact that the $q_{\rm ini}$ distribution does not directly influence the $q_{\rm fin}$ distribution, as migration effects can alter the $q_{\rm fin}$ distribution. This study reports on electronic transport within a macroscopic film of armchair carbon nanotubes, where the samples consist of randomly oriented, metallic nanotubes connected by grain boundaries. The collective behavior of these armchair tubes is characterized by a distinct Fermi level. We identify a unique phenomenon in which the presence of phonons at the grain boundaries facilitates electron movement, resulting in an increase in conductivity. This phonon-assisted transport is substantiated by the observation that the phenomenon is temperature-dependent and is suppressed when the grain boundaries are covered with a thin layer of amorphous carbon. Furthermore, the activation energy for this process is found to be independent of the electron density. These findings are interpreted through a model in which electrons traverse the grain boundaries via a tunneling mechanism assisted by optical phonons. This research expands upon the established concept of phonon-assisted transport in low-dimensional systems by demonstrating its occurrence in a two-dimensional network of carbon nanotubes. Additionally, it underscores the potential of carbon nanotube films for applications in electronic devices and sensors. Finally, this work illustrates the broader utility of employing macroscopic samples to investigate the intrinsic electronic properties of carbon nanotubes. This study introduces a novel fuzzy k-means algorithm incorporating variable feature weights. Recognizing that samples in high-dimensional spaces often exhibit varying degrees of relevance, we assign weights to individual features to enhance clustering quality. We developed an entropy-based metric to quantify feature relevance, demonstrating its effectiveness through an illustrative example. Furthermore, we defined a new entropy-based measure of conditional information dependence to quantify feature interactions. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that the proposed entropy-based entropy-based variable feature weighted fuzzy k-means (EVFKM) algorithm outperforms existing clustering methods. Additionally, EVFKM demonstrates superior performance compared to standard fuzzy k-means algorithms that utilize either fixed or time-varying weights. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of EVFKM's computational complexity. The paper concludes with a discussion of its advantages and limitations, followed by suggestions for future research directions. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have gained significant attention for their capacity to integrate specialized expert networks, which is a key component in large-scale machine learning systems. This paper investigates the statistical and computational characteristics of linear regression utilizing an MoE architecture, where the model comprises $K$ distinct experts. We establish the minimax optimal rates for both biased and unbiased estimators, demonstrating that estimation performance is governed by the number of active experts within the true underlying model. Our proposed algorithms are provably optimal and efficient, achieving the derived minimax rates. We further empirically validate that these methods are practically efficient and outperform non-MoE approaches. Additionally, we illustrate that standard gradient descent applied to unbiased loss functions fails to converge to the true parameter, thereby exposing the "gridlock" phenomenon inherent to MoE models. Finally, we present theoretical evidence that the proposed methods offer significant improvements over existing techniques. Numerical experiments confirm that these proposed approaches can substantially outperform current estimators. Consequently, our findings indicate that observations of cosmic birefringence place stringent constraints on how precisely quantum gravity must maintain global symmetries. Specifically, in a background featuring a global $U(1)$ symmetry, the symmetry-breaking parameter $\theta$ is bounded by $\theta \lesssim 0.35$ at 95% confidence, assuming a standard cosmological history. This limit improves to $\theta \lesssim 0.2$ under the assumption of an early matter-dominated epoch, which offers a more natural framework for the magnitude of $\theta$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the breaking of Peccei-Quinn symmetry could account for the recently reported evidence of parity violation in the cosmic microwave background polarization. Finally, we outline a future experimental program designed to either detect or significantly constrain the magnitude of global symmetry breaking within quantum gravity. If such a measurement is achieved, it would have profound implications for the nature of scalar fields in quantum gravity and the mechanism of inflation. Additionally, it would necessitate a reevaluation of axion dark matter density estimates, as the breaking of a global symmetry is typically responsible for generating the axion field. We also highlight that this approach could yield a more favorable axion mass, potentially bringing experimental searches for axion dark matter closer to the parameter space suggested by the Planck satellite.
