We present a chiral effective field theory analysis of low-energy pion-nucleon interactions, utilizing the most precise dataset available. Our results yield values for the low-energy constants $c_1$, $c_2$, and $c_3$, which are critical for modeling low-energy pion-nucleon interactions and solving the many-body problem within the pion sector. Additionally, we determine the isoscalar isovector scalar resonance $P_{00}$, a quantity that is difficult to measure experimentally. Finally, we compare our calculated resonance with findings from lattice QCD simulations. Our derived low-energy constants align with recent lattice QCD results, thereby supporting the validity of the chiral effective Lagrangian framework used in those studies. This agreement suggests that the pion-nucleon sigma term can now be extracted from lattice QCD with high precision. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the recent pion-nucleon scattering data can be accurately described by the low-energy constants obtained from the lattice calculations. This consistency between our effective field theory analysis and lattice QCD results confirms the validity of the pion-nucleon chi-PT Lagrangian employed in the lattice approach. Consequently, our findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for the recent lattice QCD determination of the pion-nucleon sigma term. We anticipate that the most recent lattice QCD calculations will soon provide a precise value for this term. Additionally, we have established the first low-energy constants using the pion-nucleon scattering data from the Pion-Nucleon Interaction Experiment (PNI) at the Paul Scherrer Institute. These values are comparable to those derived from the IUCF dataset, despite the PNI data being based on a different experimental method. This suggests that the PNI data is of high quality and can be effectively utilized in chiral effective field theory calculations. Finally, we have established the first values for the low-energy constants using the PNI data, thereby providing a basis for future PNI data analyses. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) underwent a full upgrade between 2017 and 2021, including the replacement of the innermost pixel detector with Phase-1 pixels. These new sensors are mounted on innovative telescopes and modules connected via flexible printed circuit boards (FPCs) to front-end electronics. The LHC's 2021 shutdown marked the conclusion of the upgrade, allowing for the commissioning of the upgraded CMS in 2022. This paper examines the reconstruction of the pilot pixel blade, which was operational during the testing phase. The blade's data was utilized to reconstruct tracks and vertices from proton-proton collisions, demonstrating the efficacy of the new reconstruction software. Additionally, vertex and track performance were evaluated across various trigger configurations. The results indicate that the Phase-1 pixel upgrade has been successfully commissioned. Furthermore, the track reconstruction efficiency is comparable to that of the original CMS, while the expected improvement in impact point resolution is approximately 1.5 times. These findings confirm the success of the CMS pixel upgrade, paving the way for the detector's performance in the high-luminosity LHC era. This achievement is expected to significantly enhance the LHC's discovery potential for the Standard Model and enable the exploration of new physics. This study utilizes Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide (HSC-W) imaging to investigate the morphologies of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) with redshifts $z<1$. We identified 1,000 X-ray point sources from the Chandra Deep Field South (CDFS) catalog, cross-matched with the Pan-STARRS1 30 Megaparsec (30MC) catalog, to serve as our AGN sample. By analyzing the HSC-W images, we classified each source as either a spiral or an elliptical galaxy. To validate our image analysis, we compared our results with the morphologies of 100 sources determined by the Galaxy Zoo 2 (GZ2) community, finding strong agreement. Subsequently, we applied a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to the same images to independently verify the classifications. We then trained a Random Forest (RF) classifier using source properties—such as color, magnitude, and position within the color-magnitude diagram—to predict spiral versus elliptical categories. Finally, we compared our HSC-W derived classifications with those from GZ2, revealing that the majority of sources share similar morphologies across both datasets. These findings suggest that our image analysis methods are effective for determining AGN host galaxy types. Furthermore, we examined the relationships between source properties and their morphologies, concluding that AGN host galaxies do not occupy a distinct region in the color-magnitude diagram or exhibit unique colors compared to other galaxies. This research provides a foundation for analyzing AGN host galaxies in the HSC-W imaging survey. Nuclear short-range correlations (SRC) are investigated using high-energy electron scattering. By measuring the relative event rates of knocked-out protons and neutrons, the two-body correlation functions can be reconstructed. This study reports the first three-dimensional reconstruction of nuclear SRC phase-space distributions, achieved by combining knockout spectra data from E15-10100 and ELN15-10102 experiments. The resulting 3D distribution aligns with recent SRC counting ratio measurements, offering new insights into the spatial and momentum configurations of correlated nucleons. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the fraction of correlated nucleons residing outside the conventional nuclear radius ($r \gtrsim 2.5$ fm) may be comparable to that inside this radius. These results also indicate a potential need to adjust the magnitude of the SRC contribution to the isospin-symmetry-violating (ISV) neutron skin thickness in heavy nuclei. Additionally, the data reveal that the one-body distribution of the "spectator" nucleon is significantly broader than the one-body distribution of the ejected nucleon. Finally, the 3D SRC correlation function derived in this work is utilized to forecast the event rates for correlated proton and neutron knockout spectra in the sea level cosmic ray flux, which is crucial for neutrino detectors aiming to detect SRC in the near future. These predictions suggest that approximately 10% of SRC events in deuterium and roughly 20% in oxygen will occur outside the conventional nuclear radius. The 3D SRC correlation function is also expected to be valuable for future studies examining the nuclear medium modification of the SRC correlation function in light nuclei. This study investigates symmetry within the deep learning framework, focusing specifically on the co-domain symmetry of finite layers. We demonstrate that Swapping Symmetry (SS) arises naturally from the linearity of affine layers, whereas Complex Conjugate Symmetry (CCS) is produced by the complex-valued nature of weight initialization. Through extensive experiments, we find that layers exhibiting both SS and CCS exhibit significantly enhanced numerical stability and outperform standard real-valued networks across various classification tasks. Furthermore, in certain scenarios, these layers achieve performance comparable to established complex-valued activation functions. Finally, we explore the relationship between SS and CCS in multi-layer networks and highlight the critical roles these symmetries play specifically within Electrocardiogram (ECG) denoising and classification tasks. The saturation of the gluon distribution within the nucleon is a fundamental concept in nuclear physics, which can be investigated through the scale-dependent behavior of the gluon distribution function. This study examines the transition from the linear to the saturated regime of gluon distribution using deep inelastic $ep$ scattering data. Furthermore, it explores the relationship between gluon distribution and nuclear matter density across various collision systems, demonstrating that the same data can be described using a universal function of $Q^2$ and $\tau = x_0 / x$, where $x_0$ represents the value of $x$ at which the gluon distribution reaches saturation. Additionally, we show that the nuclear matter density, $\rho$, of the participating nuclei can be derived from the same data set. Finally, the paper investigates the impact of gluon distribution function saturation on heavy ion collisions and its connection to geometrical scaling observed in particle production. The proposed method for studying gluon distribution function saturation offers a straightforward approach to analyzing both small-$x$ and high-energy physics phenomena. A key advantage of this technique is that it relies on a single universal function dependent on $Q^2$ and $\tau = x_0 / x$. The universality of the resulting function is evident in the analysis of both deep inelastic scattering and heavy ion collision data. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that gluon distribution functions can be derived from either deep inelastic scattering or heavy ion collision data without any prior assumptions. Consequently, this work provides a valuable tool for analyzing small-$x$ and high-energy physics. The paper is structured into two sections: the first focuses on gluon distribution function saturation in nucleons and nuclei, while the second addresses geometrical scaling in high-energy heavy ion collisions. Additionally, we have developed a computer program to facilitate the analysis of gluon distribution function saturation. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of high-resolution spectra from 100 stars with metallicities below $Z = -1.0$, utilizing a new generation of stellar models to investigate abundance dispersion. Our results indicate that stellar rotation is the primary driver of abundance scatter, which is largely caused by the rotation-induced mixing of inner- and outer-zone material. This effect is especially pronounced in the $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ ratio, where the rapid evolution of $\alpha$-elements in low-mass stars causes them to originate from different stellar regions compared to iron. Consequently, the observed scatter in $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ is typically 2 to 3 times greater than that of iron. We demonstrate that this impact is most significant for stars with masses between $1.0$ and $1.5\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, which are prevalent in the sample. Additionally, we find that the scatter in $[\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{Fe}]$ is primarily caused by rotation, whereas the scatter in $[\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{Fe}]$ arises from a combination of rotation and the initial carbon and nitrogen content of the stars. Finally, we show that the observed scatter in $[\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{Fe}]$ is generally 2 to 3 times larger than in $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$, a fact that must be accounted for when interpreting the chemical signatures of low-mass stars in dwarf galaxies. These findings are crucial for understanding the chemical enrichment history of dwarf galaxies, particularly during their early stages. We conclude that the significant abundance scatter seen in low-mass stars is a natural outcome of stellar evolution, implying that the need for multiple stellar populations to explain chemical enrichment patterns is less critical than previously assumed. This conclusion is especially relevant for the Sculptor dwarf galaxy, where a large abundance scatter in low-mass stars has been reported. Our study underscores the necessity of accounting for rotation-induced mixing when analyzing chemical enrichment in dwarf galaxies. Finally, we demonstrate that our methodology can be applied to investigate the abundance scatter in globular clusters. Our findings suggest that the abundance dispersion observed in NGC 6752 and 47 Tuc is primarily driven by stellar rotation, with a minor contribution from the initial chemical composition of the stars. This implies that the previously proposed multiple population scenario for these globular clusters may be unnecessary. We apply this methodology to a new index measuring financial literacy within machine learning frameworks. Using the novel R tool, we analyze how financial literacy scores respond to fluctuations in various explanatory variables. Our findings indicate that for both low and high income groups, financial literacy scores are highly sensitive to changes in financial knowledge, whereas they are not significantly affected by changes in financial behavior. Furthermore, we observe that this index performs more robustly in classifying individuals into distinct groups rather than predicting specific probability levels. These results underscore the robustness of the index and its potential to enhance the interpretability of machine learning models in financial contexts. This study introduces SQUID, an open-source framework designed for Quantum Machine Learning (QML) applications. The framework encompasses end-to-end solutions for data pre-processing, feature engineering, model training, and post-processing. Additionally, it provides a unified interface supporting various back-ends, including hardware-based systems like IBM's cloud-based superconducting quantum processors and simulators, as well as the Qiskit Aer state vector simulator. By offering a single entry point for these different back-ends, the work aims to streamline QML development and enhance portability across various configurations. Furthermore, the paper illustrates the framework's utility by implementing a single-layer perceptron and comparing its performance against an existing implementation in the Python library QMLpy. The study concludes that the QML ecosystem requires further standardization to ensure the portability of algorithms and data structures across diverse back-ends. Finally, the paper outlines the development roadmap for the SQUID framework. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ISRO-ML-SQUID/SQUID. Building on the research of B.-Y. Chen and A. Lina [1], this study investigates the geometry of pointwise semi-slant submanifolds within almost contact manifolds. We demonstrate that no such non-trivial submanifolds exist in real codimension one. Furthermore, we establish that the only non-trivial pointwise semi-slant warped product submanifolds in almost contact manifolds are those composed of anti-invariant and slant submanifolds. Consequently, our primary objective is to examine warped product pointwise semi-slant submanifolds. We derive several key results and theorems, supported by illustrative examples. Additionally, we prove that pointwise semi-slant warped product submanifolds cannot exist when the Weyl tensor is null. Finally, we present a specific example of a pointwise semi-slant warped product submanifold that is both semi conformal flat and anti-invariant.

The PALEOCCENE concept enables the development of passive, room-temperature detectors capable of identifying low-energy nuclear recoil events. This approach leverages the robust and stable nature of color centers in diamond, which can maintain stored information for thousands of years. The initiative aims to advance fundamental research into the physics of defects within the van der Waals crystal diamond. Additionally, it seeks to advance technologies essential for diamond color center arrays, with the ultimate goal of creating detectors that could observe dark matter, supernova neutrinos, and potentially new physics beyond the Standard Model. Furthermore, PALEOCCENE will foster new collaborations between industry and academia and facilitate the transfer of specialized technologies to industry. To achieve this, a dedicated R&D program will be established to design, build, and test functional diamond sensors based on color centers. The program will also establish a comprehensive quality assurance framework to ensure the reliability of the detectors. Additionally, efforts will be made to identify, characterize, and mitigate noise sources that could mask the extremely faint signals expected from these detectors. Finally, the initiative will conduct a thorough analysis of the complete value chain to identify potential bottlenecks and implement strategies to address them. This comprehensive approach ensures the successful realization of PALEOCCENE as a novel detector technology with the potential to achieve discovery-level sensitivity. To support this, a dedicated diamond production facility will be established to supply high-quality material for the sensors. The program will also establish a specialized color center engineering facility to facilitate the precise and reproducible initialization and readout of the quantum systems embedded in the diamond. The resulting devices will be deployed in various applications, including fundamental research, space-based space weather monitoring, and industrial sensing. The PALEOCCENE project is scheduled to run for five years, from 2022 to 2027. It is a collaborative effort involving industry partners such as Element Six, TNO, and Delft University of Technology, alongside academic institutions including the University of Geneva, the University of Oxford, the University of Vienna, and the Austrian Academy of Sciences. We investigate a rigid pair of active Brownian particles, constituting an active colloidal dimer, subjected to spatially varying activity fields. Our analysis examines both translational and rotational collective dynamics, alongside the system's statistical properties. We demonstrate that asymmetries in the chemical potential profile of the dimer's components can be quantified through the local activity field. Furthermore, the Brownian dimer exhibits a bias in its drift velocity, which stems from the combined effects of rotational diffusion and the asymmetry in activity. Additionally, we find that the dimer's residence time within observation windows is governed by the local activity field. Finally, our findings indicate that the local activity field influences the system's entropy production rate. These insights are corroborated by numerical simulations. This study revisits the fractional quantum Hall effect within the low-density Fermi liquid framework, demonstrating that roton behavior can be characterized by sum rules involving sound velocity, the effective mass, and energy gaps between Landau levels. This approach enables the identification of multiple magnetorotons, a concept previously suggested by Liang et al. [Phys. Rev. B 104, 045120 (2021)]. We apply this methodology to investigate the energy spectrum of Landau levels in two-dimensional electron systems, revealing that the magnetoroton possessing the third-largest group velocity is associated with the emergence of an additional Landau level. Furthermore, we establish a link between this phenomenon and the quantum Hall effect in bilayer systems. These findings underscore the utility of the low-density Fermi liquid theory in elucidating the fractional quantum Hall effect. Finally, we outline a potential experimental procedure for detecting multiple magnetorotons. These results offer a novel perspective on velocity gaps and provide a new avenue for exploring magnetoroton excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems. Additionally, they suggest a means to detect the formation of new Landau levels. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenChunYuan1992/MultipleMagnetorotons. This study examines the epidemic spread of the Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) model across various networks, analyzing how different transmission probabilities influence propagation dynamics. The objective is to identify networks that exhibit similar spreading behaviors. To achieve this, we propose a geometric approach utilizing the concept of geodesics within metric spaces. We demonstrate that clustering networks based on epidemic spreading properties can be reduced to clustering points within a metric space defined by geodesic distances. Furthermore, we introduce a straightforward network measurement to quantify network geometry, which aligns with existing measurements in the literature. Finally, we apply this methodology to the Internet, showing how to identify networks with analogous epidemic characteristics. These findings hold significant implications for epidemiology, particularly in the context of viral marketing. Additionally, the methodology is versatile and can be adapted to other models, such as the Susceptible-Exposed-Infected-Recovered (SEIR) model. The code required to replicate these results is publicly accessible at [1].

This study investigates the origin of X-shaped artifacts that may form during the deconvolution of temperature maps derived from optimal deconvolution (OD) and maximum likelihood (ML) methods. We demonstrate that these X-shapes arise because the ML reconstruction of a compact, unresolved point source mimics the convolution of a Gaussian with the instrumental beam, creating a pseudo-extended structure. While the ML estimator is unbiased, this creates a bias in the data model that leads to spurious signal reconstruction. To mitigate this, we propose a straightforward modification to the standard data model, which eliminates the artificial extension of point sources and significantly reduces associated noise. This solution involves adding a Dirac delta function to the map model, thereby treating point sources as pseudo-extended structures. We validate this approach using both simulations and real observations from the 2018 BICEP3 experiment. Furthermore, we show that the same method effectively mitigates these X-shapes in ML reconstructions of Planck 2018 frequency maps. We also briefly address potential applications for point source reconstruction. Finally, we examine the relationship between these X-shapes and the "ringing" phenomenon previously reported in ML reconstructions. Our analysis indicates that X-shapes are more prevalent in small, localized regions, whereas ringing is more widespread; consequently, the proposed solution offers significant improvements in reducing both features. We conclude that implementing this simple modification to the map model is essential for unbiased ML map reconstruction. Additionally, we note that the current Planck 2018 ML maps already incorporate this solution. However, we observe that the resulting "ringing" in the 2018 ML maps is more pronounced than in the 2013 and 2015 versions, suggesting that further research is needed to understand the causes and origins of this ringing. We also explore the link between ringing and the statistical properties of the ML estimator. Ultimately, we argue that the solution to the ringing problem lies in developing a new estimator that is both unbiased and consistent. We outline the necessary mathematical properties for such an estimator and propose a specific candidate. Finally, we show that this new estimator produces reconstructions nearly identical to standard ML results, offering a promising avenue for future research.

Training agents to learn from natural language is a fundamental requirement for building intelligent systems capable of interacting with their surroundings. While prior research has primarily concentrated on immediate instructions, this study investigates learning guided by high-level statements containing subject-predicate objects that can map to multiple entities. We examine the challenges posed by this referential ambiguity and introduce a task framework that allows agents to ask questions to resolve uncertainty. Our findings demonstrate that this approach yields significant performance gains over methods that simply sample potential referents for ambiguous terms. Additionally, we show that the learned policies can be reused in similar future tasks, thereby enhancing overall sample efficiency. We validate the efficacy of our task by having both humans and GPT-3 solve it, revealing that human solutions are more sample-efficient than those of the language model. Finally, we explore how various components of a task-oriented language interface influence sample efficiency and the complexity of the resulting policies. The code and models are accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/ambiguity-aware-tac-towers.

This approach leverages the fact that certain channel classes remain closed under concatenation with specific channels, meaning the process matrix of the resulting composed channel exhibits the same characteristic. We demonstrate that our proposed shadow process matrix-based protocol is equivalent to a method originally developed by Haah et al. for concatenating unitary shadows, but with an enhanced measurement efficiency. This outcome is significant because it indicates that the channel class derived from such interactions is closed under composition with certain specific channels. These findings suggest that our proposal is well-suited for modeling and simulating open quantum systems. Our goal is to establish precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using various geometric measures, including area $|\cdot|$, perimeter $P$, inradius $r$, circumradius $R$, minimal width $w$, and diameter $d$. Specifically, we introduce novel sharp inequalities relating these quantities for planar convex bodies and propose new conjectures derived from numerical simulations. While many of our findings align with or extend existing literature, certain aspects represent original contributions. Additionally, we provide sharp inequalities and conjectures regarding the relationship between the Cheeger constant and geometric parameters for convex polygons with an odd number of vertices $n$, as well as for triangles. Finally, we present several conjectures and open problems concerning the interplay between the Cheeger constant and geometric parameters for convex polygons with an even number of vertices $n$, as well as general convex bodies. Throughout, all inequalities are formulated as isoperimetric-type statements, with equality holding if and only if the body is a disk. We also examine the implications of our results for the isoperimetric quotient $PI=\frac{P}{\sqrt{||}}$. Our proofs primarily rely on numerical methods, numerical optimization, and computer algebra, with simulations conducted using Mathematica. We believe this computational approach offers a valuable alternative to traditional techniques in modern geometric analysis. This work serves as a natural extension of our recent study in \cite{CJ2021}, where we utilized the same computer-assisted methodology to derive sharp inequalities for the inradius and circumradius of planar convex bodies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that all results in \cite{CJ2021} can be recovered as direct corollaries of our current inequalities. Finally, we outline potential applications of these inequalities to problems in convex geometry and mathematical physics. Coulomb-interacting graphene and the broader class of two-dimensional systems with a linear dispersion relation are examined using renormalization group (RG) analysis. The study demonstrates that these systems exhibit a many-body instability at low energies, where the RG flow drives the Fermi velocity to zero. This phenomenon is interpreted as a Fermi-liquid instability, a conclusion supported by the successful calculation of the Landau quasiparticle weight within the RG framework. Furthermore, the results indicate that the zero Fermi velocity arises from a first-order RG transition, a finding corroborated by the emergence of a discontinuity in the renormalized Fermi velocity across the transition. Finally, the implications of this instability for the low-energy properties of a finite density of interacting electrons in bilayer graphene are explored. Specifically, the RG approach predicts a first-order transition between a metallic state and an insulating state, a prediction that aligns with recent experimental findings. Additionally, the calculated critical exponent for this transition, $\beta = 0.5$, matches the experimental value. Finally, Section 9 offers a discussion of the results, followed by conclusions in Section 10. Appendices A and B provide supplementary material, including the second-order RG equation for the Fermi velocity and the derivation of the Landau quasiparticle residue. The methodology employed in this work is also utilized in a companion study \cite{Korshunov2021}, which investigates the electronic properties of a single layer of graphene. The structural and electronic characteristics of endohedral fullerenes are significantly influenced by the nature of their metallic atoms. This study employed X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and density functional theory to investigate the behavior of the Sc2TbN@C80 molecule adsorbed on an h-BN monolayer supported by a Ni(111) substrate. Results indicate that heating the sample from 10 K to 300 K triggers a conformational change within the molecule. This transition is attributed to the C2-symmetric Sc2TbN@C80 molecule overcoming an energy barrier to switch between two equivalent orientations, a process facilitated by temperature. Furthermore, analysis reveals that the molecule's interaction with the substrate is primarily driven by electronic coupling between the LUMO of the C80 cage and the d-band of the Ni(111) substrate. This coupling creates a potential barrier between the two equivalent positions, a feature that is influenced by the specific occupation of the C80 molecular orbitals. These findings offer valuable insights into the interaction between fullerene molecules and metal surfaces. Additionally, the study demonstrates that temperature can be utilized to manipulate the orientation of such molecules, a capability that holds promise for developing molecular devices. Finally, the research underscores the necessity of conducting experiments at low temperatures to achieve a precise understanding of the properties of molecules adsorbed on metal surfaces. This approach is particularly critical for endohedral fullerenes, as their unique features are heavily dependent on the specific electronic configuration of their atoms inside the cage. Furthermore, the study highlights the necessity of performing experiments at temperatures below 100 K to prevent unwanted conformational changes. These conclusions are applicable to other endohedral fullerenes, such as Sc3N@C80. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for future studies aimed at developing endohedral fullerenes as qubits. Such applications require precise control over molecular orientation and a thorough understanding of the interactions between the molecule and the substrate, both of which are addressed in this work. The findings also offer insights into the impact of temperature on the properties of endohedral fullerenes, a factor that is often overlooked in existing literature. The Internet of Things (IoT) encompasses a vast network of interconnected devices capable of communication, including those that are low-power and low-bandwidth. While security is a primary concern for IoT, traditional encryption methods are often too computationally intensive for resource-constrained devices. Consequently, there is a growing demand for lightweight encryption algorithms. This paper reviews existing lightweight solutions, evaluates their performance, and compares them against one another. It also addresses current challenges and proposes future research directions. Ultimately, the study aims to assist IoT device manufacturers in selecting the most appropriate and efficient encryption algorithm for their specific applications. The paper is structured into six sections: an introduction, a survey of existing lightweight algorithms, performance analysis, a comparison of these algorithms, discussions on challenges and future research, and the concluding remarks. Keywords include security, encryption, IoT, and lightweight algorithms.

The Ramsey sequence is a fundamental quantum technique used to measure frequency intervals, such as atomic transitions, by analyzing the phase evolution of superposed states. While traditional Ramsey measurements rely on fixed experimental parameters, adaptive approaches dynamically adjust these parameters to optimize specific metrics like estimation precision or data acquisition speed. This work introduces a sequential Bayesian experiment design method for adaptively controlling phase accumulation during Ramsey measurements. The results demonstrate that this Bayesian design achieves high estimation precision at rapid rates, surpassing both nonadaptive strategies and common adaptive algorithms. Furthermore, this experiment design framework is applicable to a wide range of quantum measurements. Additionally, the fast acquisition of high precision is achieved without requiring prior knowledge of the target frequency, as it only necessitates an initial estimate to initiate the experiment design. This capability is particularly valuable in scenarios where precise frequency knowledge is unavailable, such as during the initial calibration phases of atomic clocks. The proposed experiment design is implemented in a Ramsey measurement on a trapped ion. In this implementation, we achieve an estimation precision of $10^{-11}$ over a $1\,\mathrm{s}$ integration time, utilizing just $10$ ions with a $40\,\mathrm{kHz}$ trapping frequency. This performance exceeds that of nonadaptive algorithms and aligns with the precision of state-of-the-art trapped-ion clocks. All calculations are provided in open-source Python code. The results indicate that sequential Bayesian experiment design is a versatile tool for quantum measurements, capable of enabling high-precision experiments across diverse platforms. This approach is especially pertinent in emerging quantum technologies, including quantum computing and sensing, where quantum algorithms are increasingly being employed to solve complex problems. By applying sequential Bayesian experiment design to the control of quantum experiments, these emerging technologies can achieve high performance at rapid speeds. This capability is crucial for addressing the growing demand for quantum solutions in real-world applications. Additionally, sequential Bayesian experiment design can be readily adapted for use in quantum machine learning tasks. In such applications, the target frequency functions as a parameter within a quantum machine learning model, allowing sequential Bayesian design to optimize training protocols for enhanced learning efficiency. This optimization can occur in real time, facilitating rapid convergence to optimal solutions. Furthermore, this approach can be utilized to determine optimal training sets and hyperparameters, thereby improving quantum machine learning performance. Ultimately, sequential Bayesian experiment design is poised to play a pivotal role in advancing quantum technologies and addressing the complexities of emerging quantum applications. Centrality measures are widely used to identify key nodes within networks, with applications ranging from locating hubs in biological networks to determining the most influential individuals in social groups. These metrics typically rely on pairwise distances, which are often defined as the length of the shortest path between nodes. However, in networks characterized by negative edge weights, the length of the shortest path can paradoxically increase as more edges are incorporated. To address this, we propose a metric that inverts this behavior: Gromov centrality. This approach leverages the Gromov triangle inequality, which remains valid for networks with negative edge weights. Furthermore, Gromov centrality offers a multi-scale perspective on node importance, enabling the analysis of centrality changes across various length scales. This capability is particularly valuable for detecting hub nodes within local network regions. We validate the efficacy of Gromov centrality through a case study of a social network, demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying hubs. Additionally, we show that this metric is effective for hub detection in both synthetic and real-world networks. The Gromov centrality method is implemented in an open-source Python package, which is available at https://github.com/robertkelly/GromovCentrality. Source code for all examples can be found at https://github.com/robertkelly/GromovCentrality/tree/main/GromovCentrality_examples. The implementation is also accessible via Binder at https://mybinder.org/v/gh/robertkelly/GromovCentrality/HEAD. Furthermore, the package includes a tutorial available at https://gromovcentrality.readthedocs.io/en/latest/gromov_centrality.html. The Gromov centrality method is featured in the upcoming book, *Networks with Negative Edge Weights*, edited by Robert Kelly, published by Cambridge University Press in 2024, which is accessible at https://www.cambridge.org/core/publications/gromov-centrality-a-multi-scale-measure-of-network-centrality-using-triangle-inequality-excess/2552D722122255212522522222222222. The book is also available on Amazon at https://www.amazon.com/Networks-Negative-Edge-Weights-Gromov/dp/1108960003. We introduce a new theory of gravitation, designated as AZ (for Azimuthally Symmetric), which relies on the principle of azymuthal symmetry. This principle asserts that, at any given point in space-time, physical laws maintain the same form under rotations around an arbitrarily selected axis. The AZ framework is built upon four postulates: the azymuthal symmetry of the world, uniform linear motion, the equivalence of physical systems, and the local validity of special relativity. These postulates imply that all possible physical systems exist within the theory. We demonstrate that this theoretical structure necessitates equations governing the evolution of the gravitational field and matter. Furthermore, we outline the equations applicable to matter in its most basic configuration. The Azimuthally Symmetric theory adheres to the principle of equivalence alongside the conservation laws of energy, momentum, and angular momentum. Additionally, it incorporates the conservation of a novel quantity termed the "azimuthal moment," which arises from enforcing azymuthal symmetry. This theory offers a resolution to the problem of dark energy and predicts a specific type of dark matter. We also establish a link between the Azimuthal Symmetric theory and General Relativity. We provide a topological field theory interpretation of T-duality on a torus that incorporates discrete twists. Our approach relies on the free field realization of non-Abelian anyons found on a standard torus. By employing a specific basis of anyons, we demonstrate that twists arising from discrete gauge theories can be viewed as anyons with a trivial Chern-Simons coupling. This framework enables us to derive the general T-duality rule for twisted tori and offers a topological understanding of how discrete gauge theory twists interact with conventional T-duality observables. Additionally, we present a field-theoretic interpretation of the duality between anyon bases. We find that one basis corresponds to the standard toric code, while the alternative basis aligns with a theory of anyons that are topologically neutral. Furthermore, we show that the anyon representation of the toric code can be constructed by applying a Chern-Simons coupling to the standard T-duality free field theory. This construction facilitates a field-theoretic comprehension of fractional fluxes and how they transform under T-duality. Finally, we briefly connect these findings to the quantum double of a finite group and its relationship with discrete gauge theories. This work extends our earlier study of T-duality on a torus without discrete twists. (arXiv:2101.03302 [hep-th])

This algorithm is pivotal for advancing research into minor-excluded classes and graphs with restricted treewidth. Furthermore, we demonstrate that numerous dynamic graph algorithms, which are currently restricted to minor-closed classes with constant degeneracy, can be broadened to encompass broader minor-closed classes and graphs with limited treewidth. This finding holds significant relevance for numerous minor-closed classes and treewidth-bounded graphs, as they are often naturally represented as subgraphs of planar graphs augmented with a linear number of edges. Variational algorithms represent a primary method for utilizing near-term quantum hardware to investigate chemical and material systems. Nevertheless, their practicality is restricted by the necessity for extensive qubit counts and the computational complexity of state preparation. This study introduces a general approach to mitigate these constraints within adaptive variational eigensolvers. By employing qubit-excitation-based state preparation, we demonstrate that the energy convergence issues typically associated with adaptive variants can be eliminated. We validate this algorithmic advantage through simulations on small molecules, revealing superior convergence characteristics. Furthermore, we outline a viable path toward implementing this method on current hardware using mid-circuit reset and readout techniques. Ultimately, our work establishes a robust foundation for advancing adaptive variational eigensolvers on near-term quantum devices. Deep generative models are recognized for their ability to represent data efficiently, yet their performance is often constrained by the limitations of their stochastic nature. This paper introduces a new algorithm that incorporates a deterministic component into training, specifically by utilizing a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of the representation alongside the standard stochastic gradient. We demonstrate this method through two distinct approaches: a variation of variational autoencoders employing a Gaussian mixture prior, and a new technique called latent autoencoders. Experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets indicate that these proposed models can achieve superior performance compared to their purely stochastic counterparts. Furthermore, we show that these approaches are particularly effective for tasks involving multiple instances of similar data, such as contact states in robotics or image patches within natural images. Finally, we outline future observational tests that could confirm or rule out this hypothesis. The PanSTARRS comet C/2015 ER61 (also known as PanSTARRS) was observed using the Atacama Compact Array, a compact configuration of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. This interferometric survey targeted the cometary coma for emission lines of CS, HCS+, and CS2 at 3 mm wavelengths. The observations revealed a diffuse source of CS with a flux density of 0.14 ± 0.02 Jy, which was subsequently subtracted from the dataset. This residual CS emission was then modeled as originating from a distributed source, such as a diffuse coma, rather than a point source. The resulting CS column density, derived from the integrated flux density, is estimated at 1.1 ± 0.2 × 10^11 cm^-2. Additionally, upper limits were established for HCS+ and CS2. These findings suggest that CS is a significant component of the cometary coma, with its production likely driven by the photodissociation of more complex molecules like methyl mercaptan (CH3SH) and dimethyl disulfide (CH3-S-S-CH3). The study concludes that the Atacama Compact Array is highly effective for observing diffuse molecular emission from comets, with the capability to detect CS column densities as low as 10^10 cm^-2. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that interferometric surveys can be utilized to derive column densities for molecules distributed throughout the coma. The PanSTARRS comet is proposed as a valuable target for future observations to investigate the chemical complexity of cometary atmospheres. These results are expected to enhance our understanding of the comet's chemical composition and its role in the early solar system. The data will be accessible via the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA) database. The paper also includes a discussion on the potential for using the Atacama Compact Array to search for prebiotic molecules in other cometary objects. The study underscores the necessity for a dedicated survey of the solar system's comets to investigate the origins of prebiotic molecules. Such a survey would enable the detection of diffuse molecular emission from comets, thereby advancing our knowledge of the chemical complexity within the cometary environment. The architecture first generates an undercomplete codebook for a Gaussian noise input using a sequence-to-code model, which is subsequently transformed into the target output via a diffusion-based decoder. Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in various real-world scenarios, yet their complexity often prevents most existing algorithms from delivering high-quality solutions within a reasonable timeframe. This paper introduces a hybrid approach that integrates Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) with a Branch and Bound (B&B) solver. The method utilizes the continuous variables from a B&B solution to guide the NSGA-II search process, thereby enhancing the generation of high-quality, diverse solutions. Additionally, the NSGA-II derived solutions inform the B&B search, increasing the likelihood of identifying feasible points that dominate current bests. The study validates this algorithm's effectiveness by applying it to multi-period energy hub optimization problems. Results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid algorithm significantly outperforms the standard NSGA-II in terms of both solution quality and computational time. Furthermore, it surpasses the commercial MO-MINLP solver BARON, achieving superior results in reduced time or providing feasible solutions when barons fails to converge. Finally, the paper confirms the method's robustness by testing it on problems from existing literature. (This research was conducted while the first author was a visiting scholar at the University of Queensland, Australia.) We generalize core concepts from the established extension of Lie theory involving Lie groupoids by recasting them within a well-adapted synthetic differential geometry model. Specifically, we introduce internal versions of source path and source simply connected groupoid definitions, as well as the integration of $A$-paths. Our primary findings demonstrate that when a classical Lie groupoid adheres to these internal source path and simply connected conditions, it guarantees the existence of corresponding classical groupoid versions. Furthermore, we show that integrating source simply connected Lie groupoids via source $A$-paths ensures the internal completeness of the Lie algebra-to-Lie algebra exponential map. These results underscore how synthetic differential geometry facilitates the unification of Lie theory for both Lie algebras and Lie groupoids. Additionally, we provide a sketch of a functor that connects synthetic differential geometry with topos theory, which allows us to extend our findings to any topos capable of supporting smooth manifolds and smooth maps. To support these developments, we also present a comprehensive collection of definitions and theorems essential for this generalized framework, many of which are novel. Finally, we have formulated several conjectures and posed open questions regarding this generalization of Lie theory using synthetic differential geometry. Our work includes numerous examples and counterexamples to clarify these theoretical extensions. To our knowledge, this research represents a significant contribution to the field. For accessibility, we have also provided a version of our results that remains within standard set theory. We anticipate that these findings will inspire further research into generalizing Lie theory through synthetic differential geometry. The growing demand for large-scale data and computational resources in healthcare and biomedical research has created a critical need for a secure, interoperable, and scalable data-sharing infrastructure. This paper outlines a strategy to facilitate secure, high-performance, and effective collaboration among distributed communities by utilizing Cyberinfrastructure (CI) services and Gateways. Specifically, we propose a data-sharing model that allows communities to interact with federated resources as if they were local. Leveraging concepts from Virtual Organizations and Data Spaces, our approach enables communities to define their specific requirements and access services via Gateways, which act as intermediaries between these groups and the distributed CI. These Gateways provide secure, high-performance computing and data services tailored to the needs of their respective communities. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach through a proof-of-concept implementation, which has already been successfully tested in a real-world biomedical data-sharing scenario. This work was supported by the NSF Cyberinfrastructure for Discovery (CyberX) program. Additional details are available at http://www.biomed-gateway.org. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment polarity of specific aspects within product reviews. Pre-trained language models have proven highly effective for this task, yet they typically struggle to capture the nuancedness of human opinion expressions. To address this, we introduce a pre-training approach that leverages implicit sentiment expressions to enhance the models' ability to comprehend such nuances. Our method employs a supervised contrastive learning algorithm that utilizes labeled data from an implicit sentiment corpus. This approach enables the model to cluster sentences sharing similar implicit sentiment expressions into the same cluster while maintaining distinct groups for sentences with different implicit sentiments. We validated this method on the LCA-ABSA benchmark, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/Supervised-Contrastive-Pre-training-ABSA. Given its reliance solely on labeled data, the method is easily adaptable to other domains. Furthermore, the authors will soon release the Chinese implicit sentiment corpus, which contains over 100,000 samples, to support this pre-training strategy. This corpus can be retrieved from the authors' GitHub repository. We anticipate that this methodology will prove effective for enhancing the pre-training of language models in other applications. This study examines mediation analysis within case-control designs involving a binary outcome, a binary exposure, and a binary mediator. We demonstrate that under the assumption of no unmeasured confounding, the natural direct effect is identifiable. However, identifying the natural indirect effect requires an additional constraint on the conditional probability of the mediator. Leveraging this identifiability result, we introduce a weighted logistic regression approach that yields a consistent estimator for the natural direct effect, even when the mediator's probability remains unspecified. Furthermore, we propose a method to estimate the natural indirect effect under the assumed probability constraint and prove that this estimator achieves the $\sqrt{n}$-consistency property. Simulation results indicate that the proposed weighted regression estimator performs competitively against existing methods. Additionally, we apply this methodology to a case-control study investigating the link between oral contraceptive use, current age, and oral cancer. The resulting estimates suggest that the biological mechanism responsible for the association between exposure and outcome operates partially through the mediator. Finally, we discuss how our approach can be extended to scenarios with multiple mediators. Keywords: Binary outcome, Binary exposure, Binary mediator, Case-control sampling, Mediation analysis.

We introduce a new resampling and relabeling technique for offline reinforcement learning that functions as a contrastive value policy, which we term the Contrastive Value Function (CVF). The CVF functions similarly to a generative model, producing samples from the most likely hindsight summary of the dataset. By treating the observation space as continuous, we employ a VAE-based approach to learn the CVF. This method enables the relabeling of both states and actions, facilitating experience replay via on-policy policies. We have implemented this experience replay using both a policy gradient algorithm and a value function that relies on a fixed policy. Our approach demonstrates significant improvements over baseline methods on several test environments. Additionally, we have validated the method on a complex, real-world task involving the control of a 3D printed robotic arm. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/aleksandar-nikolic/Executive-Function.

The energy budget of the heliosphere is fundamentally anchored to the Sun, where the solar wind energy flux serves as the primary driver for the interplanetary environment. This study presents initial findings from the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) regarding energy fluxes across kinetic scales, spanning from ion gyroradii down to the electron inertial scale. Utilizing data from the FIELDS and SDC instruments aboard PSP, we analyze energy budgets at the in-situ locations of the two spacecraft. Our results indicate that PSP energy fluxes align with in-situ measurements from the Ulysses and ACE missions, which operated at distances of 1.2 AU and 0.3 AU, respectively. Furthermore, we compare these in-situ energy flux estimates with those derived from a hybrid simulation of the inner heliosphere. The Parker Solar Probe has now sampled heliospheric energy fluxes at the closest distance to the Sun ever achieved by a spacecraft, offering a unique vantage point for investigating energy transfer processes at heliospheric scales. These findings are critical for understanding the energy budget of the inner heliosphere and for modeling the interaction between the solar wind and the heliosphere. Ultimately, this research supports the Parker Solar Probe mission's objective of identifying the sources of solar wind energy. We demonstrate the existence of a natural extension of the original action on a new unital C*-algebra B, such that any free and minimal action of a locally compact quantum group, free and transitive actions of locally compact topological groups, or free and numerable principal bundles of quantum groups originating from a C*-tensor category with a global faithful state can be realized as actions on B. Furthermore, we establish that any free and minimal action of a locally compact amenable quantum group, along with any free and numerable principal bundles of quantum groups constructed from a C*-tensor category possessing a faithful state, are automatically numerable. Additionally, we characterize the specifically defined cohomology of quantum principal bundles and the associated transgression map, proving that this map is an isomorphism for free and numerable cases. Finally, we highlight that the recently developed noncommutative Iwasawa manifolds serve as natural examples of free and numerable quantum principal bundles. These bundles are generated by quantum group actions on noncommutative tori featuring a faithful state, where the associated cohomology is computed to be one-dimensional. This result confirms that the quantum Chern character is non-trivial. The numerical aspect of this finding is supported by computations using our dedicated computer program, which is made available to the community. This program is derived from the one utilized in the author's thesis. The package features a user-friendly interface and includes a collection of pre-defined free and minimal principal bundles of quantum groups, alongside a set of free quantum groups. Users can select a principal bundle and a free quantum group, after which the program calculates the associated cohomology. The output includes the cohomology and a representation of a basis. Users may also input their own quantum principal bundles, though the program will not compute the cohomology for them. The Unruh effect, which posits that uniform acceleration induces entanglement between future and past light cones, is notoriously difficult to observe due to the need to manipulate massive numbers of particles. This study demonstrates that an accelerated observer can detect this entanglement through the Berry phase acquired by their system. Specifically, we introduce a detector capable of measuring the entanglement within the Unruh effect and establish a protocol to execute this measurement. Furthermore, we validate that the entanglement observed by the accelerated user aligns with the entanglement perceived by an inertial observer, thereby confirming the consistency of Unruh effect entanglement across different reference frames. Our findings suggest that this approach may facilitate experimental verification of Unruh effect entanglement using existing technology. Additionally, we discuss the potential to enhance the detectability of this entanglement by leveraging quantum correlations in both the field and the detector. Finally, our results offer a promising pathway for conducting experiments to verify the entanglement characteristic of the Unruh effect. The interaction between a compact object's accretion flow and the wind from a companion star is a critical component of binary X-ray systems. This study investigates the impact of a companion's wind on the X-ray spectral-timing characteristics of a compact object in the Cyg X-1 binary. We developed a model that integrates an advective accretion flow with a companion wind to analyze this interaction. Our results indicate that the wind significantly influences both the spectral and timing properties of the hard state in Cyg X-1. Specifically, the model predicts that the soft component in the hard state originates from the inner edge of the accretion flow, while the soft X-ray excess in low/hard state systems arises from the outer regions of the accretion flow. Furthermore, the soft X-ray flux exhibits a strong correlation with the mass accretion rate, which aligns with observations. Additionally, the power density spectrum of the soft component in Cyg X-1 displays a broken power-law shape, with the break frequency showing a positive correlation with the mass accretion rate. These findings suggest that the accretion flow within the companion wind constitutes the primary source of soft X-rays in the hard state of Cyg X-1. We also propose that the wind can serve as a diagnostic tool for understanding the accretion flow's structure and the physical mechanisms driving its variability. Finally, our predictions offer a potential explanation for the observed correlation between the soft X-ray flux and the root mean square of the soft X-ray light curve in low/hard state X-ray binaries. These insights may facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of the physical processes governing accretion flows in binary systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the non-abelian nature of the term introduces a screening effect for the velocity, which diminishes as the coupling constant grows. We investigate the formation of jets and their impact on post-merger outflows from magnetized neutrino-cooled accretion disks, a scenario occurring in binary neutron star (BNS) mergers. Our analysis examines how the rotation rate of the central compact object (CCO) and the accretion disk's mass influence the production of non-thermal and thermal radiation. Our results indicate that a rapidly rotating black hole (CCO mass $<0.95\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$) facilitates the formation of a jet, whereas a neutron star (NS) remnant does not. When a jet is present, we observe a luminous, long-lived jet-driven wind with a mass loss rate of $\sim 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and a spectrum dominated by thermal emission. Conversely, in the absence of a jet, a disk-driven wind is generated. This disk wind is characterized by a mass loss rate of $\sim 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and a spectrum dominated by non-thermal emission. Our findings suggest that the properties of BNS merger post-merger outflows can serve as an indicator of whether a black hole or neutron star remnant is formed. Additionally, we explore the potential for using these post-merger outflows to constrain the equation of state of nuclear matter. Specifically, we propose that the non-thermal emission from BNS mergers can help determine the mass-radius relationship of an NS, with a precision of approximately 10%. This level of precision is comparable to that achievable through the tidal deformability measured by the GW170817 event. Furthermore, we highlight that the non-thermal emission from BNS mergers can help constrain the mass of the NS, with a precision of $\sim 0.1\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$. This is comparable to the precision derived from the gravitational wave signal from GW170817. Finally, we note that the non-thermal emission from BNS mergers can also constrain the NS mass maximum, with a precision of $\sim 0.2\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$. We analyze 100 early-type galaxies (ETGs) with stellar masses exceeding $10^{11} M_{\odot}$, identified within the 1.5 square degree HSC-SSP Wide Area Shallow Survey. Using high-resolution imaging from the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam, we isolate tidal features and quantify their flux fractions. Our findings indicate that the average flux fraction for these features is 0.011, with a notable distinction between smooth tidal features (mean fraction: 0.008) and prominent ones (mean fraction: 0.024). We establish a correlation between the flux fraction of smooth tidal features and the fractional radial size of ETGs, observing that galaxies with larger radii tend to possess more pronounced smooth features. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between tidal feature flux fractions and galaxy morphology, discovering that irregular ETGs exhibit a higher mean flux fraction (0.015) compared to elliptical ETGs (0.010). Finally, we estimate the merger rate for these 100 galaxies by modeling the evolution of tidal feature flux fractions over time, yielding a mean merger rate of 0.001 per year. These results align with previous studies on similar galaxies, supporting the hypothesis that tidal features in ETGs are primarily the outcome of minor mergers. Additionally, we note that minor mergers result in smaller flux fractions and lower merger rates compared to major mergers. The flux fraction of smooth tidal features serves as a valuable tool for investigating the impact of minor mergers on ETG evolution. This study revises the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), a previously introduced framework, to incorporate magnetic fields and their interaction with gravitation. This revised approach offers a resolution to the longstanding enigma of how young stars generate bipolar outflows. The new theory posits that the gravitational force between two magnetic dipoles can be repulsive under specific conditions. By applying this repulsive force to molecular clouds, the theory successfully explains the formation of bipolar outflows. Furthermore, it provides a novel perspective on the attractive nature of gravity. The proposed mechanism for creating repulsive gravitational force is also applicable to other astrophysical contexts. This paper serves as the sequel to the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (I), which originally established the theory and demonstrated how magnetic fields interact with it.

This study examines the optical characteristics of four well-localized fast radio bursts (FRBs) that occurred in 2020, which were localized to less than one square arcsecond. We report that none of these bursts were detected in optical follow-up observations, despite their radio signals being exceptionally bright. Our results impose stringent limits on any optical emission occurring simultaneously with the radio bursts, with upper limits reaching as low as 10 mags in the r-band. Additionally, we analyzed high-cadence optical data from the Zwicky Transient Facility and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time to search for delayed optical emission associated with these bursts. No such emission was detected, placing tight constraints on the energy of any delayed radio-to-optical emission, which we limit to less than 10% of the radio burst energy. These findings suggest that FRBs are not powered by a mechanism that produces bright optical emission either concurrently with or shortly after the radio burst. Consequently, our findings argue against a magnetar origin for FRB 20201124A and restrict the class of viable FRB progenitors. High-power laser systems are extensively utilized across numerous scientific and industrial fields. This review examines three core computational disciplines essential for their advancement: laser system design, performance optimization, and reverse engineering. We highlight specific algorithms and software tools that facilitate these processes, alongside a discussion of current challenges and future opportunities within the field. The review is intended for researchers and engineers engaged in the design, development, and application of high-power lasers. A collection of freely accessible software packages is also provided to support readers in conducting research on laser system design, optimization, and reverse engineering. Furthermore, several open-source projects are introduced to assist in reverse engineering and performance prediction. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these tools by analyzing existing literature on high-power laser systems, offering readers a practical example of how to apply these methodologies. A user-friendly website has been created to host these software tools and enable readers to easily replicate the case studies. To our knowledge, this represents the first comprehensive review to address these specific topics and to offer accessible software for such research. We anticipate that this work will inspire further developments in computational laser technology and its application to the design and optimization of high-power laser systems. Although current language models are trained exclusively on textual data, they are typically deployed to generate unstructured plain text. This paper introduces a framework that integrates visual controls into text generation using GPT-2. By fine-tuning the model's final classification head with visual annotations, we enable the model to produce text that aligns with guidance from ground-truth visual features. We successfully implemented generators for text associated with object detection bounding boxes, image segmentation masks, and image captioning. Our results demonstrate that these systems can operate without the need for fine-tuning when dealing with text generated from bounding boxes and segmentation masks. Furthermore, we show that text-conditional visual feedback can significantly enhance the accuracy of generated visual controls. Finally, we explore the application of this approach to image editing and introduce the concept of in-the-wild visual controls, which are derived from generic datasets rather than specific task labels. This research holds significant potential for developing more versatile and accessible generative AI models. Our code and data can be found at https://github.com/alexsandru/visual-gpt2.

We introduce a new variant of the widely used RingCT protocol, designed to enable the rapid verification of anonymous transactions. Our method achieves this by incorporating two key improvements: first, we utilize a novel proof system that significantly reduces computational costs; second, we propose a mechanism that streamlines verification by eliminating the need to validate a specific property across all elements within a ring. We have thoroughly analyzed the security of our approach and integrated it into the Decred blockchain to benchmark its performance against other RingCT implementations. The experimental results demonstrate that our solution is faster than existing alternatives, achieving a 30% reduction in both signing and verification times. Additionally, we have made the source code available on GitHub to facilitate easier comparison with other protocols. Given that our method maintains compatibility with the Decred blockchain, it can be directly employed to enhance verification speed without necessitating any modifications to the blockchain itself. Furthermore, we have developed a Python-based tool to aid in verifying anonymous transactions. This tool not only simplifies verification for users but also allows them to confirm the authenticity of a ring, thereby mitigating certain risks. We believe these contributions will advance the field of privacy-preserving technologies. The source code and related materials can be accessed at https://github.com/eduardo-garcia/delegated-ringct. Driven by the growing demand for interpretable and robust models, cooperative data-driven modeling has emerged as a solution that integrates the complementary strengths of physics-based and data-driven techniques. This survey begins by outlining the primary challenges in current data-driven modeling, followed by a systematic review of existing cooperative methods categorized into four types: hybrid, linking, augmented, and deep physics-informed neural networks. Each type is paired with its corresponding mathematical framework and illustrative examples. Finally, we identify key open issues and potential future research directions. This paper introduces AskewSGD, a novel algorithm designed to train low-precision neural networks by incorporating an interval constraint that permits weights to be shifted. We provide a theoretical proof demonstrating that this training approach can match the accuracy achieved with full precision floating-point arithmetic. Additionally, network parameters are represented using quantized low-precision binary values, enabling the training of models that exhibit superior quantization robustness. Theoretical findings are validated through experiments on various datasets, which confirm the method's enhanced resilience to quantization. AskewSGD holds the potential to significantly advance the development of more robust low-precision neural networks. Furthermore, we have made the associated code available at https://github.com/askewsgd/askewsgd. The results presented in this study support the viability of training binary neural networks on edge devices, as demonstrated by our results on the CIFAR10 dataset. Soft robots are defined by their ability to undergo large, nonlinear deformations, which complicates the development of accurate models and the design of effective control strategies. Despite this, control techniques grounded in these models are essential for achieving precise and robust performance. This article offers a comprehensive review of model-based control approaches for soft robots, examining both the current landscape and future challenges. It begins by outlining the primary modeling methods for soft robots, followed by an in-depth analysis of the principal control techniques derived from these models. The discussion highlights how model-based control can be integrated with other methodologies, such as learning-based and hybrid control, to address specific operational requirements. Finally, the paper identifies key open challenges and proposes potential solutions to advance the field. By synthesizing existing research and proposing new directions, this survey aims to foster deeper comprehension of model-based control within soft robotics and guide future investigations. The content is structured to be accessible to researchers and engineers across various disciplines, including mechanical engineering, mechatronics, mechatronic systems, and mechatronic system design. Additionally, the article serves as a foundational reference for those seeking to apply model-based control techniques to soft robot applications. The survey covers the following specific topics: (1) continuum robots, (2) pneumatic artificial muscles, (3) soft grippers, (4) soft actuators, (5) soft robots, and (6) mechatronic systems. Its target audience encompasses researchers and engineers in mechanical engineering, mechatronics, mechatronic systems, and soft robotics. The review examines the current state of the art and identifies open challenges, providing a solid foundation for applying model-based control in advanced soft robot research and development. The article concludes by outlining promising future research directions and their implications for the advancement of mechatronic systems. Furthermore, it addresses the application of model-based control in the design and control of soft grippers, offering insights into optimizing their performance for tasks such as object manipulation and assembly. The discussion also explores continuum robots, detailing their actuation mechanisms, sensing capabilities, and control strategies, while emphasizing the need for more robust and adaptive control techniques to handle uncertainties and disturbances. This study examines the real Jacobi group, focusing on its Lie algebra, Bloom and Jacobi differential operators, and Jost functions. We demonstrate that, up to unitary equivalence, every irreducible unitary representation of the real Jacobi group arises from an induced representation of the affine group beginning at a specific parameter value. Furthermore, we provide a complete classification of these representations and their associated Jost functions. Finally, we apply these findings to Jost solutions and the spectral theory of the bloom-Jacobi differential operator. As an application, we derive the spectral theorem for the bloom-Jacobi differential operator and establish the limiting absorption principle. These outcomes extend prior research by J. Anantharaman, which concentrated exclusively on the constant coefficient case. Additionally, our work offers novel results regarding the spectral analysis of the bloom-Jacobi differential operator. Verifying facts using structured data is crucial for numerous downstream applications. While recent studies have introduced various neural architectures to address this challenge, they predominantly depend on complex logic programs for natural language-to-logic programming and struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution data. We contend that the primary obstacles in current methods stem from distribution shifts between training and test data, as well as between text and SQL queries. To mitigate these issues, we introduce a novel pipeline that decomposes fact verification into two sequential tasks: first, identifying the queries relevant to each hypothesis, and second, verifying those queries. This decomposition alleviates distribution biases and enhances performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art performance on both AG News and FEVER-WF-SQL benchmarks. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) generate synthetic data by learning a complex mapping from a low-dimensional latent space to a high-dimensional output space. While the latent space is known to be semantically interpretable, allowing controlled generation through minor perturbations, the specific encoded information remains unclear. This study investigates a method for incorporating auxiliary information into a GAN's generated output by conditioning the network on this data. We demonstrate that a GAN conditioned in this manner outperforms an unconstrained GAN in both quantitative and qualitative metrics. Furthermore, we show that this approach enables the recovery of an image from an incomplete sketch. Our experiments reveal that the technique successfully reconstructs the GAN's output to match the provided sketch. Additionally, we explore how varying the amount of sketch information impacts reconstruction quality and examine the method's effectiveness in completing sketches. GANs trained with this conditioning approach produce more realistic images and higher-quality reconstructions compared to those trained without it. Finally, we demonstrate the method's utility in generating images based on color information. The code and models are available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1992/LATENT-CONDITIONING. Bayesian nested sampling serves as a method for calculating evidence and performing model comparison. It utilizes importance sampling to navigate high-dimensional, highly constrained posterior distributions. This study evaluates different samplers employed within nested sampling, specifically comparing deterministic versus random walk samplers. We analyze their performance regarding mixing properties, evidence estimation, and model comparison. Furthermore, we introduce a new "nested Metropolis" algorithm designed for nested sampling and compare it against existing methods. Finally, our findings are illustrated through the estimation of a simple model and a more complex hierarchical model. This research is supported by the EPSRC grant EP/R003040/1.
