The distance labeling problem involves assigning labels to graph vertices such that the distance between any two vertices $u$ and $v$ can be determined solely from their labels, $\lambda(u)$ and $\lambda(v)$. While research has primarily focused on minimizing the label set size for a fixed maximum label, this study prioritizes minimizing the label set size for a fixed maximum label length. We introduce a novel labeling scheme for planar graphs that tolerates a specific number of faulty labels. This scheme guarantees a maximum label size of $O(n^{2/3})$ and a maximum label length of $O(n^{1/3})$ when up to $O(n^{1/4})$ labels are faulty. Furthermore, for any fixed number of faulty labels, the maximum label length is reduced to $O(1)$. Additionally, we demonstrate that this bound is tight by presenting a family of planar graphs where any scheme tolerating a constant number of faulty labels requires a label size of $\Omega(n)$. Finally, we extend these results to graphs within the class of $k$-degenerate graphs. Our scheme achieves a maximum label size of $O(n^{2/(k+1)})$ and a maximum label length of $O(n^{1/(k+1)})$ to handle $O(n^{1/(k+2)})$ faulty labels. For a fixed number of faulty labels, the maximum label length remains $O(1)$. Similar to planar graphs, we prove that for a constant number of faulty labels, no scheme can achieve a label size better than $\Omega(n)$. Our findings also apply to simple $k$-degenerate graphs, yielding a label size of $O(n^{(k-1)/(k+1)})$ and a label length of $O(n^{1/(k+1)})$ to tolerate $O(n^{1/(k+2)})$ faulty labels. In this context as well, the scheme achieves a maximum label length of $O(1)$ for a fixed number of faulty labels. Moreover, we show that for a constant number of faulty labels, any scheme requires a label size of $\Omega(n^{(k-1)/(k+1)})$. To our knowledge, this represents the first scheme to address the issue of faulty labels in distance labeling. Additionally, our proposed scheme for planar graphs improves upon the best existing scheme for the general problem. We also establish that no scheme can utilize labels smaller than $O(n^{2/3})

We investigate two-particle correlation functions within a driven, dissipative Bose-Hubbard model using quantum trajectory methods. These correlations are categorized into two distinct types: incoherent, which depend on the instantaneous density distribution, and coherent, which involve field operators. By analyzing both types in the time and frequency domains, we identify two dissipative regimes: a single-particle regime characterized by linear response and a non-linear regime defined by non-linear susceptibility. Furthermore, we distinguish between dissipative and dephasing mechanisms, demonstrating that the latter can be effectively suppressed through two-particle correlations. These findings are substantiated by exact numerical calculations. Additionally, we establish a link between the system's response functions and those of the non-dissipative model derived from time-dependent perturbation theory. This model is analyzed using both exact diagonalization and the density-matrix renormalization group approach. Our results indicate that the proposed model is viable for experimental realization on quantum simulators. Finally, we suggest that this theoretical framework can be extended to investigate non-equilibrium systems with complex driving and dissipation. This extension could facilitate a deeper understanding of dissipative quantum phase transitions and non-linear transport phenomena in driven quantum systems. Finally, we highlight the potential of this model for developing quantum technologies, such as quantum memories. Specifically, we show that the system can store information in a frequency band that remains isolated from the driving field and experiences minimal dissipation. The effectiveness of this storage mechanism is evaluated through entanglement measures. These insights regarding dissipation and coherence are expected to contribute to the advancement of quantum technologies. In conclusion, the responses of driven, dissipative quantum systems can be quantified by two-particle correlation functions, which are computable in quantum simulations and measurable in quantum experiments. This approach may facilitate a more profound understanding of the fundamental physics governing driven and dissipative quantum systems. Moreover, the identified characteristics of these correlations could aid in the development of new quantum technologies. Recent studies indicate that standard Gaussian Processes (GPs) often underperform compared to deep learning models when tasked with identifying out-of-distribution (OOD) data. This paper introduces and theoretically examines Distributional Gaussian Processes (DGN), a new Bayesian layer designed for neural networks that enhances in-domain classification accuracy while maintaining or improving OOD detection capabilities. By relaxing the traditional GP constraint of a finite input set, DGN allows for an infinite number of inputs, enabling seamless integration into deep architectures. Furthermore, DGN offers a straightforward method for calculating the theoretical relationship between DGN networks and their deep GPs (DGNs) equivalents. This relationship reveals that DGNs can be viewed as a special subset of deep networks where OOD detection is guaranteed, and it also establishes a link between DGNs and DGN architectures, demonstrating that DGN architectures can achieve equivalent OOD detection performance to DGNs without requiring retraining. Finally, we provide empirical evidence supporting the theoretical claim that DGNs can be embedded into neural networks for OOD detection. Experimental results confirm that DGNs can match the performance of various existing DGN architectures in terms of both in-domain and OOD performance. Additionally, we show that while multiple DGN architectures can detect OOD data, their specific learned functions may result in false positives. In contrast, we find that architectures utilizing a Gaussian kernel tend to produce fewer false positives. Overall, this work provides both theoretical and empirical support for the assertion that DGNs can effectively detect OOD data. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChenchenWang1993/DGN. This Letter investigates how dissipation influences condensation within an open, driven optical-lattice system interacting with a reservoir. We demonstrate that, in the presence of dissipation, a system-mode Floquet heating mechanism triggers a sudden surge in the occupation number of a protected "scar-like" mode, ultimately leading to Bose condensation. This finding underscores the intricate relationship between heating and condensation, offering a distinct pathway to achieve Bose-Einstein condensation. Furthermore, we outline potential experimental applications of this phenomenon. Specifically, we propose a feasible two-dimensional scheme that leveraging this heating-driven condensation to generate entangled states in open, driven lattices. These proposals establish a novel method for both generating and harnessing Bose-Einstein condensation. Additionally, we highlight that, under certain conditions, the system exhibits a dynamical phase transition from an incoherent to a coherent state, a feature that may hold significant implications for quantum information processing. Finally, we suggest that the proposed scheme could be experimentally realized using ultracold atoms within optical-cavity setups. Our results demonstrate that this mechanism is broadly applicable to various driven and dissipative Bose-Hubbard models. The study investigates several variants of the Alexandrov maximum principle applicable to the complex Monge–Ampère equation. Within the open bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$, consider a function $\psi$ that is bounded from below and upper semi-continuous, along with a bounded function $f$ defined on $\Omega$. Let $u$ be a bounded, upper semi-continuous, and $\psi$-plurisubharmonic solution to the complex Monge–Ampère equation given by $\det(D^2u) = f$ within $\Omega$. The primary objective is to establish a uniform Hölder continuity estimate for the solution $u$ in terms of $\psi$ and $f$. This result is demonstrated in two distinct scenarios: first, when $\psi$ satisfies a specific convexity condition; and second, when $\psi$ is merely bounded from below. In both instances, the Alexandrov maximum principle is derived as a direct consequence. Furthermore, the paper provides an explicit Hölder exponent as a function of the specific parameters involved. The authors also present an alternative proof of the Hölder continuity of quasi-plurisubharmonic solutions to the complex Monge–Ampère equation, originally established by D. S. Kim. Additionally, the paper offers a novel proof of the regularity theorem regarding the Hölder continuity of bounded plurisubharmonic solutions to the complex Monge–Ampère equation, a result previously proven by L. Caffarelli, M. J. Kolodziej, and A. Viaclovsky. Finally, the work examines the Alexandrov maximum principle and its application to the Hölder continuity of plurisubharmonic solutions in a more general context. This broader framework encompasses various well-known regularity theorems as special cases, including those by L. Caffarelli, M. J. Kolodziej, and A. Viaclovsky, as well as the corresponding result for the real Monge–Ampère equation. The paper concludes with a detailed examination of specific instances where the Alexandrov maximum principle yields quantitative estimates. These examples cover the classical Alexandrov maximum principle, the Alexandrov maximum principle for the complex Monge–Ampère equation, the local Alexandrov maximum principle, and the Alexandrov maximum principle for the real Monge–Ampère equation. The analysis covers various forms of convexity, including strongly convex functions, convex functions with a modulus of convexity, and convex functions with a linear modulus

Defining time involves two distinct components: a continuous, continuously differentiable magnitude known as the instantaneous value, and a discrete set of reference points called "clock readings." While classical clocking theory has historically concentrated on analyzing the statistical properties of these clock readings, this paper introduces and investigates statistical methods for clocking the instantaneous value. We examine two types of instruments used for this purpose: discrete detectors that capture energy at specific instants, and continuous detectors that integrate energy over a finite duration. Both are modeled as "non-periodic optical clocks," representing devices that measure the instantaneous value using a discrete mechanism with an optical integration time. We develop statistical techniques to estimate the mean and variance of the instantaneous value based on observed clock readings, deriving estimators that are unbiased, consistent, and computationally efficient. Furthermore, we establish a statistical framework to characterize the performance of non-periodic optical clocks, enabling a comparison between them and periodic optical clocks. Finally, we apply this theory to the emerging field of quantum metrology, specifically the measurement of the fine structure constant. This theory is essential for analyzing experimental data from an apparatus that combines an atom interferometer with a non-periodic optical clock. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, our analysis yields a consistent estimator for the fine structure constant that is unbiased and possesses the minimum possible variance. Additionally, we show that our analysis outperforms the method proposed by Jeffery et al. (Nature 531, 359, 2016). The theory developed in this work is applicable to any non-periodic optical clock, regardless of the physical quantity it measures. Consequently, it is expected to be valuable in quantum metrology, where such instruments are increasingly utilized to measure various fundamental constants. This includes, for instance, recent efforts to measure the speed of light and the Planck constant. The latter is particularly relevant given the 2019 redefinition of the kilogram, which now relies on measurements of a non-periodic optical clock's frequency. This approach is currently being tested in experiments conducted by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and the National Research Council of Canada (NRCan). The theory is also pertinent to the emerging field of quantum optical clocks, which may soon surpass existing optical lattice clocks in precision. These future devices will likely operate as non-periodic clocks, necessitating the application of the analysis methods presented here. This study introduces a fog-supported Software Defined Network (SDN) designed to enhance the efficiency of Service Function Chains (SFCs). The primary goal is to minimize SFC provisioning costs, power consumption, and failure recovery times. To achieve this, we propose an optimal resource allocation strategy that jointly optimizes SFC routing, failure recovery, fault prevention, and power-efficient resource allocation. This strategy utilizes fog computing to enable real-time, dynamic resource adjustments, thereby ensuring SFCs meet Quality of Service (QoS) requirements. Additionally, we develop an online algorithm to reduce the time complexity of the optimization problem. Simulation results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves SFC provisioning costs, power usage, and failure recovery times compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the online algorithm performs nearly as effectively as the optimal solution while requiring substantially less time to compute. This online algorithm is recommended for practical deployment due to its efficiency. Finally, we outline key challenges and future research directions for SFCs within a fog-supported SDN environment. The proposed solution is expected to be valuable for researchers and practitioners in the field. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first work to jointly optimize SFC routing, fault prevention, failure recovery, and power-aware resource allocation in a fog-supported SDN setting. The remaining task is to implement this solution in a real-world scenario. We have made our code available on GitHub to assist researchers in this endeavor. We hope this contribution will inspire further research and innovation in the area. Section IV details the proposed solution, while Section V provides a detailed analysis. Section VI concludes the study and suggests future research directions. Although various loss functions are employed to train deep neural networks, their specific influences remain poorly understood. This study investigates those impacts by analyzing how gradients propagate from the loss to the parameters across varying network depths and architectures. We demonstrate that standard gradient analysis is insufficient for this purpose, as it fails to capture the dynamics of backpropagation through composite loss functions. To address this limitation, we introduce a numerical method for computing gradients of parametric losses. Furthermore, we propose applying the ReIm transformation to parameters, which enables the efficient calculation of both real and imaginary components of the gradient for parametric complex losses. Our findings indicate that reparameterizing losses and utilizing gradient analysis via the Im transformation can reveal previously unknown characteristics of deep learning training processes. Additionally, we present a numerical case study on a deep convolutional network trained with different losses to illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods. This work offers a novel perspective on understanding how different losses affect training, with potential applications in hyperparameter optimization and loss design. We introduce a new holographic error correction code inspired by the AdS/CFT correspondence. This code utilizes a binary tree structure where each edge is assigned a specific bond dimension. By modifying the edge and triangle edges through random unitary operations, we create a hyper-invariant MEERA (hYMERA) that supports a continuous family of codes. This design enables the construction of an approximate holographic error correction code, facilitating the emergence of power-law correlations within bulk operators expressed in boundary operators. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the minimum distance of these codes and propose a method to calculate the distance between two trees. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to verify these theoretical predictions. This work represents a significant advancement toward constructing more realistic holographic error correction codes. Additionally, the code construction methodology may hold potential applications in quantum error correction for various machine learning algorithms. This study continues an investigation into the statistical characteristics of the Galactic Center (GC) X-ray filaments, focusing on the spacing between them. We analyzed the two-point spacing distribution of these filaments within the GC region. The data indicates that the mean spacing between adjacent filaments is approximately 0.25 pc, with a distribution that closely follows an exponential pattern. Furthermore, we examined the mean spacing across various subregions of the GC, revealing that the eastern portion exhibits the shortest average separation. These findings align with the presence of a more turbulent environment in that area, as suggested by our prior research. Additionally, the observed mean spacing is comparable to the typical interstellar medium (ISM) density in the GC, supporting the hypothesis that these filaments consist of dense gas. Finally, we compared our results with prior studies, noting that the average spacing between the GC filaments is roughly ten times greater than the mean distance between stars in the GC. This significant disparity suggests that the filaments are unlikely to be composed of stars. Overall, our results reinforce the conclusion that the GC filaments are primarily made of gas. These conclusions are consistent with the hypothesis that the filaments form through the interaction of the ISM with the outflows generated by the central black hole. This hypothesis is further supported by the fact that the mean filament spacing matches the typical ISM mean free path in the GC. Consequently, the filaments likely represent shocked regions created by the accretion of the ISM onto the central black hole. This process is also consistent with the observed morphology of the filaments, which resembles the Parker spiral structure. These observations are also in line with the mean density of the GC filaments, which is approximately 1000 times the mean hydrogen density in the Galaxy. This high density is comparable to the critical density required for the transition from a molecular cloud to a filament. Furthermore, the mean density of the GC filaments is similar to that of the molecular cloud G0.25-0.01, which is also approximately ten times the mean Galactic hydrogen density. These density measurements are also consistent with the mean temperature of the GC filaments, which is roughly 1000 K. This temperature is also approximately ten times the mean Galactic hydrogen temperature. The mean temperature of the GC filaments is also consistent with the mean temperature of the X-ray plasma in the GC region, which is approximately 1 keV. This study introduces a distributed control strategy designed to implement Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) across both primary and secondary distribution networks. The approach utilizes voltage telemetry data from primary substations and transformer tap positions, alongside local voltage measurements taken at representative loads within secondary networks. By accounting for the non-linear CVR characteristics of aggregate loads, the proposed method aims to lower distribution network voltages to curb real-time energy losses, utilizing step-size limits to ensure stable convergence. Results from a 96-bus test system demonstrate that the distributed controller successfully achieves optimal CVR with high accuracy, closely matching centralized solutions while eliminating the need for secondary network voltage measurements and reducing computational complexity. Furthermore, a robustness analysis reveals that the distributed controller maintains satisfactory performance even under communication link failures. Ultimately, the efficiency of this distributed CVR implementation is validated through a scalability analysis. Overall, the findings indicate that the distributed controller delivers high-performance CVR control, effectively balancing network energy losses against customer power consumption. Additionally, the strategy ensures stable convergence, avoids unnecessary tap changes, and minimizes the number of required voltage measurements. These outcomes are achieved without requiring detailed network parameter knowledge, thereby simplifying the overall control problem. Finally, the proposed solution demonstrates robustness against telemetry measurement errors and significant fluctuations in CVR parameters. This enhances the controller's adaptability to varying load types and reduces sensitivity to model parameter variations. Consequently, the distributed CVR controller exhibits resilience to nonlinear CVR parameter variations, ensuring stable convergence and preventing excessive tap changes. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Specifically, the integration of distributed CVR with automated voltage control schemes is suggested to further optimize network voltage levels and minimize real-time losses. Additionally, the application of distributed CVR to distribution networks with high renewable energy penetration is proposed to improve the overall efficiency of power distribution. Finally, the implementation of distributed CVR in radial distribution networks featuring distributed energy storage systems is recommended to further optimize power distribution efficiency. These future research avenues aim to leverage the benefits of distributed CVR in addressing critical power system challenges, such as energy loss reduction, improved voltage regulation, and enhanced power system resilience. By integrating distributed CVR with advanced technologies like automated voltage control, renewable energy integration, and distributed energy storage, power system operators can achieve significant improvements in operational efficiency, reliability, and sustainability. Ultimately, the proposed research directions aim to advance the field of power system control and optimization, ultimately benefiting the broader electricity grid. Specifically, the integration of distributed CVR with automated voltage control schemes is suggested to further optimize network voltages

This research investigates nonstochastic bandits and experts within a delayed framework where delays vary based on both the arm and the specific round. We introduce a straightforward algorithm achieving a regret bound that accounts for every delayed bandit and expert variant considering only fully arm-independent delays. Furthermore, we develop a nontrivial bound for the EXP3.D algorithm, originally proposed by Seldin and Shapira, in this arm-dependent setting. Our approach leverages the information gain derived from observing delayed rewards, a concept introduced by Seldin and Shapira that we extend to this new context. Notably, our analysis demonstrates that the expected count of underestimated underestimates remains bounded, a critical step in proving the algorithm's performance. We establish a regret bound that generalizes arm-independent findings to the arm-dependent scenario, showing that delayed losses occasionally underestimate an arm's potential but rarely do so to such an extent that it significantly impacts performance. We conclude by demonstrating that this essentially tight bound cannot be improved without assuming arm-independent delays. Finally, we present numerical results comparing our results to existing lower bounds and other algorithms. In this numerical analysis, we observe that our method performs comparably to other algorithms when delays are arm-independent, while it significantly surpasses them in cases of arm-dependent delays. To our knowledge, this work represents the first application of the information gain technique to the bandits and experts setting under arm-dependent delay conditions. Additionally, it marks the first instance of a non-trivial upper bound for a delayed expert algorithm in a setting involving arm-dependent delays. Finally, we prove that the upper bound established for a specific expert algorithm is optimal in this arm-dependent environment. Optimal algorithms for arm-independent delays were previously established by Seldin and Shapira; however, we demonstrate that their upper bound does not hold in our arm-dependent setting. Furthermore, we show that their lower bound remains valid even when arm-dependent delays are present. This work was conducted in collaboration with Yuval Seldin, who also contributed to the numerical results. His contributions were instrumental in establishing the optimality of our upper bound and in demonstrating the tightness of the lower bound for arm-dependent delays. We believe these contributions are of independent significance. The code for this work is available at: https://github.com/rodrigoar/Nonstochastic-Bandits-and-Experts-with-Arm-Dependent-Delays. Yuval Seldin's code can be found at: https://github.com/yuseldin/delayed-bandits-and-experts

Text generation in dialogue remains a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing. While current state-of-the-art methods rely on deep learning, they often produce outputs that lack human-like fluency and coherence. To address this, we introduce LEATHER (Learning to EnAbLe As human as possible resp. Text-generation via Reinforcement), a framework designed to mimic human dialogue through a combination of language models and reinforcement learning. LEATHER was evaluated on the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) and the Commonsense Conversations (COCO) dataset. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on both datasets. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the generated text, including an evaluation of human ratings for fluency and coherence. This paper reviews recent lattice QCD findings on the quark-gluon plasma at non-zero temperature and density, with a specific focus on light quarks. It covers the pure QCD phase diagram, the transition from hadronic matter to a deconfined state of quarks and gluons, the formation of a dense quark matter phase at non-zero chemical potential, and the mixing of quark flavors. The review begins with an overview of the fundamental challenges in lattice QCD at non-zero chemical potential, followed by a discussion of recent numerical advancements and their implications for the nonperturbative strong interaction regime under these conditions. Key topics include the finite baryon density phase transition, the emergence of a critical endpoint, the baryon momentum spectrum, and the mixing of quark flavors. The paper concludes by outlining future directions aimed at advancing our understanding of QCD at non-zero temperature and chemical potential. This review is based on a talk delivered at the International School of Advanced Studies (School of Physics) in Erice, Italy, during August 2019. This study employs a multi-fidelity modeling strategy to simulate structural loads on offshore wind turbines. A multi-fidelity approach utilizes two distinct modeling techniques to generate datasets with varying levels of detail and computational cost. The high-fidelity data, derived from physics-based simulations, is sparse due to its computational expense. In contrast, the low-fidelity data is sourced from a physics-informed surrogate that incorporates both aerodynamic and structural simplifications, yielding a denser dataset at a reduced computational price. By combining these data sources, the research aims to create an efficient and precise probabilistic model for wind-turbine loads. The study applies this methodology to an 8 MW semi-submersible wind turbine located in the North Sea. Results indicate that the proposed modeling framework can accurately predict tower base moments using data from a significantly smaller simulation size compared to traditional single-fidelity methods. Furthermore, the framework demonstrates the potential to accelerate probabilistic load assessments for wind-turbine design. Additionally, the research investigates the impact of specific data sources on the probabilistic characterization of these loads.

The Izmir Earthquake occurred on October 30, 2010, at 02:17 local time, measuring a magnitude of 5.7. This event triggered significant interest across various social media platforms, prompting data collection from Twitter, Facebook, and Orkun. This study specifically examines the analysis of Twitter data regarding the Izmir Earthquake. The objective is to determine the most active Twitter users, the event's spread velocity, the primary topics discussed, the frequency of mentions for each topic, and the total volume of tweets. To achieve this, we developed a Python-based application that integrates both the Twitter API and a custom application programming interface. The analysis was conducted using data from October 30, 2010. We identified 1,000 of the most active Turkish Twitter users, calculated the spread velocity of the earthquake information, and extracted the main subjects from the tweets. Furthermore, we counted the tweet volume for each topic and generated visualizations of the collected information. The results indicate that the earthquake spread at a velocity of 5.7 within 30 minutes. The most active users were primarily journalists, politicians, and celebrities. The topics discussed, in descending order of frequency, were: "deprem" (earthquake), "izmir" (Izmir), "deneyim" (experience), "yaralı" (injured), "ev" (house), "deprem" (quake), "yaralı" (injured), "deneyim" (experience), "izmir" (Izmir), and "deprem" (quake). Time-resolved spectroscopy is a powerful method for monitoring the evolution of chemical systems, yet reconstructing the underlying trajectories of observables from experimental data is challenging due to noise and other experimental inaccuracies. This work introduces an inversion technique based on forward optimization within a trajectory basis. The process begins by defining a model space using a fixed set of time-evolving basis functions. By optimizing weights for this basis through a forward design—specifically, minimizing the discrepancy between model predictions and noisy experimental data—the method yields an accurate representation of the system's time-dependent behavior. We demonstrate that this approach is robust against noisy data, outperforms conventional least-squares fitting, and remains effective even when the assumed model is imperfect. Furthermore, the technique is flexible enough to be adapted for use with time-dependent basis sets. Applications are explored through examples involving noisy data, incorrect model assumptions, and both continuous and discrete measurement time points. The inversion is applied to fit time-resolved data obtained from ultrafast pump-probe experiments on the NaI molecule and a complex protein. In the protein case, we successfully identified the most relevant molecular properties driving the dynamics and derived a compact, efficient set of time-evolving basis functions. These findings suggest that the proposed method is a versatile tool for analyzing time-resolved data in chemistry and physics. The implementation is accessible via the PyBOC Python package. The relevant code and data required to replicate the results presented here can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7090000. Additionally, a Jupyter notebook providing a step-by-step guide to the method is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7090000.1. The PyBOC package also includes a suite of example datasets for testing and evaluating the method. Finally, we have developed a set of example problems to assess the method's performance, which are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7090000.2. These problems are integrated into the PyBOC package and can be easily accessed and solved. We encourage readers to utilize these example problems to explore the method's capabilities. The code for these example problems is also included in the PyBOC package. This paper introduces SceNDD, a scenario-based naturalistic driving dataset collected in the United States. The data comprises 1,000 hours of 30fps video recordings from dashcams, alongside synchronized records of driving contexts, events, and EDR measurements. Driving contexts were derived from GPS and inertial sensor data, while event logging and EDR information were gathered via an in-vehicle system. The dataset was annotated by domain experts to facilitate the development of driving behavior analysis and understanding systems. We demonstrate its utility by implementing three representative tasks: driving behavior recognition, event detection, and event feature extraction. Boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) and interface conformal field theory (ICFT) have garnered significant interest due to their connections with holography, quantum criticality, and the g-theorem. These frameworks are also essential for investigating boundary entropy within quantum information theory. In this work, we demonstrate that the reflected entropy—a recently introduced entanglement measure—can be computed via double-trace deformations in the BCFT/ICFT. Furthermore, we examine the behavior of reflected entropy across various entanglement regions to explore its relationship with the monotonicity of mutual information. We further extend these results to ICFTs by applying a similar methodology. Our findings offer new insights into the characteristics of reflected entropy and its relevance to boundary and interface conformal field theories. Additionally, we calculate the reflected entropy for a free fermion system, a model that exhibits specific characteristics of ICFT. This study investigates users' comprehension of Signal's PIN security mechanism. We surveyed 100 Signal account holders to assess their knowledge of the PIN, finding that only 20% possessed a correct understanding. To explore why this gap exists, we conducted in-depth interviews with 20 participants. Through thematic analysis, we identified three key user mindsets that hinder a proper grasp of the PIN: (1) a perception of Signal as an open-source, transparent application; (2) a preference for simplicity and ease of use; and (3) a sense of mastery over the app's features. These findings highlight the challenges end-users face in understanding Signal's security architecture and suggest a need for the platform to improve its security communications. We conclude by offering design implications for Signal based on our research results. (Video summary available at https://youtu.be/4222222222).

This paper introduces a parameterization for curvature access derived from the generalized Gauss-Newton (gGN) matrix, leveraging its inherent low-rank structure. This approach, termed ViViT, is designed to be integrated into existing models, such as the Vision Transformer, to enable efficient access to both parameters and curvature while maintaining a minimal increase in the model's rank. ViViT offers a more efficient alternative to gGN-based curvature representations found in other research. We demonstrate that ViViT can be embedded within current deep learning architectures without significantly increasing rank or computational cost, thereby facilitating the use of second-order optimization techniques. Furthermore, we show that incorporating second-order methods with ViViT allows for the achievement of state-of-the-art results on various computer vision tasks. Experimental results confirm that ViViT enhances both training and inference efficiency for curvature access compared to alternative second-order methods. Additionally, second-order optimization utilizing ViViT has surpassed existing state-of-the-art performance on several computer vision benchmarks. Finally, we illustrate that the superior performance of second-order optimization with ViViT stems from its ability to identify a sharper local minimum. Leveraging this result, we establish that any torsion-free hyperbolic group $G$ possessing a non-trivial abelian subgroup is charmable within a product of $p$-groups for various primes $p$. Furthermore, we introduce a new invariant, stiffness, which extends virtual charm; we show that torsion-free hyperbolic groups possess this property. As applications, we prove that any torsion-free hyperbolic group with a non-trivial abelian subgroup admits a faithful representation as a wreath product of $p$-groups for any prime $p$, and that such groups are residually finite $p$ for every prime $p$. Finally, we examine torsion-free hyperbolic groups with stiffness and charm as $p$-groups, noting that while torsion-free hyperbolic groups are charmable as $p$-groups, they are not necessarily stiff as such. Object pose estimation is a critical area within 3D vision, yet it is difficult due to the vast diversity of object poses. While most current research relies on annotated datasets, obtaining labels for every possible pose is often impractical. To address this, we introduce a novel approach for recognizing the category and predicting the pose of objects that have never been seen before. Our method leverages a pre-trained contrastive self-supervised model to learn a common representation across different views of various categories. By utilizing cross-modal contrastive learning between 2D and 3D data, the model learns a category-specific representation that supports pose estimation through a subsequent regression module. We evaluated our approach on the CUB-357 dataset for bird category recognition and pose estimation, achieving state-of-the-art results in both tasks. Additionally, we assessed our model on the Planes dataset, where it successfully estimated the pose of all 13 plane categories, outperforming other methods in both recognition accuracy and pose estimation. Accurate short-term traffic prediction is essential for intelligent transportation systems, yet it remains difficult due to the scarcity of historical data and the complex nature of traffic dynamics. To address this, we introduce a similarity-based deep learning approach designed for large-scale, sparse traffic forecasting. This method leverages trip attributes and temporal patterns to identify similar trips, utilizing a graph neural network to extract significant features for prediction. Our experimental results demonstrate that the features derived from these similarity-based trips substantially enhance forecasting accuracy. Furthermore, the model's simplicity and efficiency make it well-suited for deployment within real-time transportation systems. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/leeyang1223/STP. The source code and pre-trained models can be found at https://drive.google.

This paper introduces VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders designed for causal inference. VACA enables the approximation of interventional and counterfactual distributions for specific causal models, facilitating the response to various interventional and counterfactual queries. Unlike most existing variational autoencoders that rely on latent variables, VACA utilizes auxiliary variables. We provide theoretical guarantees demonstrating that VACA achieves consistent interpolation between causal variables. Furthermore, we validate VACA's effectiveness through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. These results illustrate VACA's ability to accurately estimate interventional and counterfactual distributions and answer relevant queries, while also outperforming current methods in this regard. The Irish LOFAR station, situated in the west of Ireland, functions as a dedicated small array optimized for rapid data transmission and processing. Its backend, known as REALTA, delivers real-time information regarding both individual sources and the entire sky, while also transmitting calibrated data to the LOFAR Data Archive. This paper details the REALTA backend and array, presents initial results on source variability and sky evolution, and outlines the array's future prospects. The system is currently being upgraded to enhance its capabilities for time-domain astronomy. Additionally, the station is being augmented with a new low-frequency receiver, which will expand the field of view and significantly improve sensitivity. These upgrades will further strengthen the array's role in the broader LOFAR strategy for time-domain observations. Over the past few decades, metaphotonics has emerged as a rapidly evolving field dedicated to controlling light within confined volumes using confined states of charge, distinct from conventional electromagnetism which governs light propagation via electric charges and currents. This advancement has unlocked new pathways for designing high-performance optoelectronic devices and integrated systems. Concurrently, machine learning has become a transformative methodology for deciphering intricate data-driven relationships, offering intelligent solutions to complex challenges. This review examines the intersection of metaphotonics and machine learning, highlighting how this combination is driving the next generation of metaphotonics. We outline the fundamental principles of machine learning, its applications within metaphotonics, and the future prospects of this interdisciplinary domain. Specifically, we address the underlying rationale for applying machine learning to metaphotonics, explore current use cases, and discuss future opportunities, aiming to foster interdisciplinary collaboration and propel the continued advancement of intelligent metaphotonics. Keywords: Intelligent metaphotonics, machine learning, optoelectronics, optoelectronic systems.

This study examines secondary frequency control (SFC) implementation in high-inverter penetration grids, focusing on its ability to stabilize voltage dynamics. High inverter counts introduce nonlinearities that make analytical solutions difficult, so the work employs both simulation and analytical methods. We propose a local droop-based linear control strategy for frequency and power, which is typically modeled as a perturbation. However, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, inverter power can be accurately approximated by an analytical expression even for large deviations. Using this approximation, we derive stability criteria for power and voltage. These findings are validated through simulations of real-world data, specifically a 2017 Australian day-time snapshot. The results indicate that while secondary frequency control can stabilize power dynamics, it may simultaneously destabilize power and voltage dynamics. Consequently, voltage stability must be evaluated within the context of power dynamics, and we provide a method to determine a stabilizing voltage region. Notably, this region is influenced by the grid's equivalent damping coefficient, prompting an investigation into adaptive damping. We present a local adaptive damping scheme that utilizes secondary frequency control to achieve a stable, high-inverter penetration grid. This scheme is shown to be stabilizing via a Lyapunov stability analysis. Finally, the proposed schemes are tested on a real-world grid using actual inverter data. Results demonstrate that adaptive damping effectively stabilizes power and voltage dynamics, even under large disturbances. Furthermore, the stability of these systems is linked to the average frequency error, which is minimized by a distributed algorithm. Simulations confirm that this algorithm achieves convergence in a realistic high-inverter penetration grid. Overall, this work offers a new framework for analyzing the stability of nonlinear inverter-based power grids. The analysis relies on a novel stability criterion for nonlinear systems, which is validated through numerical simulations. This criterion is particularly effective for analyzing the stability of nonlinear systems with periodic equilibria. Finally, we discuss the potential application of these results to other nonlinear systems. Keywords: Stability analysis, nonlinear systems, inverter-based power grids, secondary frequency control, distributed algorithm.

Cyber-physical systems (CPS) are anticipated to become increasingly widespread in the coming years, with their deployment significantly influenced by the level of intelligence they possess. This intelligence enables a single CPS to independently acquire knowledge, adapt to dynamic environments, and make decisions. However, within the context of Cyber-Physical Systems of Systems (CPSoS), intelligence is not confined to individual units; it can also emerge from the collaboration between multiple CPS and between a CPS and an autonomous agent. This phenomenon is termed "collaborative intelligence." The primary objective of this paper is to define collaborative intelligence, explore the advantages it offers to a CPS, and outline the essential characteristics a CPS must exhibit to harness this intelligence. Furthermore, we propose the Cyber-Physical Intelligence (CPI) framework, which integrates established CPS concepts with intelligence, and provide an initial exploration of this framework. Finally, the paper concludes by identifying key research challenges that must be addressed in the future to advance the study of collaborative intelligence within cyber-physical systems. (For more information, visit: http://www.123science.net/cpi/) Keywords: Cyber-Physical Systems, Intelligence, Cyber-Physical Intelligence.

This study utilizes MAPPIES, the successor to the previously published MCESCAL, to investigate the origin of ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excesses in blazar spectra. The model incorporates a relativistic jet with electron populations divided into thermal and non-thermal components. These electrons upscatter external photons via inverse Compton scattering, while the non-thermal electrons simultaneously emit X-rays through synchrotron radiation. We applied this framework to analyze the spectra of Mrk 403 and Mrk 501 during their flaring states. The model successfully reproduces the observed spectra, indicating that the UV and soft X-ray excesses in these sources can be attributed to a combination of non-thermal and thermal Compton components. Furthermore, we find that a two-component electron population is essential to account for the spectral characteristics of flaring blazars. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the proposed jet-based mechanism of X-ray emission in active galactic nuclei. We present a quantum algorithm that employs online learning to ID pure states exhibiting symmetries among a class of possible states. This approach extends the original ID algorithm, which was designed for arbitrary pure states. By leveraging symmetries, the method reduces the number of required queries and enhances the efficiency of state identification. The resulting circuit depth is $O(\log^2(N))$, where $N$ represents the dimension of the target state space. This circuit depth remains independent of the size of the target state's support, thereby outperforming the online learning algorithm for arbitrary pure states, which has a circuit depth of $O(N)$. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm surpasses the online learning circuit for symmetric quantum states, which also achieves $O(\log^2(N))$ depth but requires support for multiple control Toffoli gates. Our algorithm utilizes exclusively two-control Toffoli gates and single-control NOT gates. We also examine the method's robustness against bit-flip errors in queries. These findings are particularly relevant for applications involving symmetric quantum states, such as symmetric quantum circuit synthesis and quantum machine learning. Additionally, we outline potential extensions of this work to online learning with classical inputs and to identifying mixed states with symmetries. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta123456789/Online-Identification-of-Symmetric-Pure-States. Baryon production is analyzed using the quantized fragmentation model of a QCD string with helical boundary motion. In this framework, baryon formation corresponds to a string world-sheet that wraps the space-time cylinder an odd number of times. By approximating the QCD string as a classical bosonic string with a moving endpoint, we calculate the density of baryon production. This density is shown to depend on the eikonal parameter, the boundary helix angle, and the classical string length. Furthermore, baryon momentum distributions are derived from this density. When integrated over momentum to yield the total yield, the resulting baryon-to-meson ratio aligns with experimental data from the STAR collaboration for $p_{T} < 2$ GeV. Additionally, the derived baryon momentum distributions are consistent with recent STAR measurements. These findings suggest that the quantized fragmentation of a QCD string offers a viable mechanism for explaining baryon anomalous enhancement in small systems. The subsequent paper will address baryon production in a QCD string with kink boundary motion, which is relevant to the formation of baryons in large multiplicity small systems. This scenario, where the string endpoint velocity approaches the speed of light, necessitates corrections to the baryon density and momentum distributions due to the non-linear Dirichlet boundary condition of the QCD string. This approach also enables the investigation of the influence of varying initial string configurations on baryon production. **Context.** The global travel-time measurements of acoustic waves exhibit a distinct north-south asymmetry, with travel times toward the south being shorter. **Aims.** This study investigates the contribution of flows surrounding active regions to this observed asymmetry. **Methods.** We analyzed the travel-time variations relative to the solar rotation phase for 1,000 active regions identified in the Sun1000 catalog, which were tracked over periods of 1–2 solar rotations. Using a weighted average, we calculated the mean travel-time difference between the northern and southern hemispheres. **Results.** The solar rotation phase shows a clear correlation with the travel-time variations of active regions, with flows around these regions causing travel-time changes of approximately 10 $\mu$s. The weighted average of these variations yields a travel-time difference of 1.5 $\mu$s, which is insufficient to account for the global north-south asymmetry. **Conclusions.** This finding suggests that the global north-south asymmetry in travel times is not primarily driven by flows around active regions. Additionally, we observed that travel times are shorter in the southern hemisphere for regions with larger magnetic flux. **Discussion.** We propose that this correlation may be attributed to the north-south asymmetry in helioseismic travel times themselves. Furthermore, we suggest that the flows around active regions could be linked to the global north-south asymmetry in helioseismic travel times. Finally, we note that the travel-time variations induced by active regions are comparable in magnitude to those caused by solar activity cycles. This implies that the time-averaged travel-time maps, which are commonly used to study solar-cycle variations, may not be entirely free from the influence of active-region flows. **Conclusions.** The primary conclusion of this paper is that the contribution of active-region flows to the global north-south asymmetry in helioseismic travel times is negligible. This conclusion is based on the analysis of 1,000 active regions, a sample size that is likely sufficient to support this finding. However, it is important to acknowledge that this analysis is limited to active regions with lifespans of 1–2 solar rotations, meaning it does not encompass all such regions. Consequently, the conclusion is subject to the constraint that the contribution of long-lived active regions to this asymmetry is minimal. Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments are currently searching for a stochastic gravitational wave background within the nanohertz frequency range. This study examines how a stochastic gravitational wave background generated by a decaying primordial magnetic field could be detected by PTA networks using pulsar frequency data. The analysis covers two specific PTA collaborations, NANOGrav and EPTA, incorporating their recent findings. Our results indicate that if the decay parameter $\alpha$ falls between $10^{-1}$ and $10^{1}$, the PTA data could be interpreted as evidence for a stochastic gravitational wave background. Furthermore, the peak amplitude of this signal would be approximately $10^{-10}$ times greater than the gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes. Additionally, the PTA could constrain the upper limit of $\alpha$ to be less than or equal to $10^{1}$. Consequently, PTA observations offer a valuable method for investigating the properties of primordial magnetic fields. Finally, we explore the potential for detecting this background via PTA and discuss the implications of this detection for cosmology. Light field (LF) images capture substantial 3D environmental details, making them highly valuable for applications like virtual reality and autonomous driving. However, the high resolution of these images often renders them unsuitable for bandwidth-limited systems. To address this, we introduce a disparity-aware LF compression model that leverages a generative adversarial network (GAN) to enhance compression performance. By utilizing disparity information, our approach enables the compressor to generate high-quality down-sampled LF images. Furthermore, a discriminator within the model is trained to identify artifacts in compressed images, thereby facilitating the learning of more effective compression strategies. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art compression techniques across various benchmarks. Additionally, we have implemented the proposed model in a web-based interface to support bandwidth-constrained scenarios for virtual reality applications. This study investigates a generalized quantum version of the classic Kelly betting problem, inspired by recent proposals for quantum single- and double-oracle gambling. In this framework, a trader allocates a fixed capital across a set of bets on quantum observables, aiming to maximize the quantum analog of the Kelly criterion: the von Neumann entropy of the final state, denoted as $S_1(N)$ for an initial state $S_0(N)$. We investigate the evolution of the difference $\Delta S = S_1(N) - S_0(N)$ as a function of the betting multiplier $\mu$, specifically within the continuous variable context using position and momentum observables. Our findings indicate that the quantum Kelly criterion can be interpreted as the maximum relative entropy production achievable through optimal betting on position or momentum. Furthermore, we observe that the multiplier $\mu$ functions as a temperature parameter for the von Neumann entropy of the final state. Finally, we demonstrate that the quantum Kelly criterion can be derived from the classical version by applying a suitable unitary transformation to the payoffs. These outcomes offer a novel and fundamental perspective on quantum gambling. Additionally, we show that the quantum doubling strategy introduced by Biham and Brodutch can be recovered from our method by selecting a specific set of observables and measurement bases. The quasiparticle band alignment and stacking-independent exciton in MA$_2$Z$_4$ (where M = Mo, W, Ti; A = Si, Ge; Z = N, P, As) were investigated using density functional theory. This study demonstrates that these materials can be categorized into two groups based on their quasiparticle band alignments. Furthermore, excitons in these compounds remain stacking-independent, exhibiting strong binding energies that make them detectable via photoluminescence spectroscopy. The analysis of quasiparticle band alignments is crucial for understanding charge transfer mechanisms in heterostructures, while the identification of stacking-independent excitons is significant for advancing optoelectronic device applications. These findings provide a foundation for the rational design of low-dimensional optoelectronic devices. Additionally, the study offers a comprehensive overview of the electronic structures of MA$_2$Z$_4$ materials, which is essential for developing new two-dimensional materials. This work is part of a broader initiative aimed at constructing a complete database of two-dimensional materials. To achieve this, we have developed a high-throughput computational framework capable of calculating the quasiparticle band alignment and stacking-independent exciton for any given two-dimensional material. This code is now publicly available. The methodology employed is also applicable to investigating other low-dimensional materials. The LHCb experiment analyzed $pp$ collision data collected at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 3 fb$^{-1}$ to search for the rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$. No significant local excess was detected near the signal region. Consequently, upper limits on the branching fraction were established as $\mathcal{B}(\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-) < 1.2 \times 10^{-8}$ and $< 1.0 \times 10^{-8}$ for the 7 TeV and 8 TeV datasets, respectively. Additionally, a combined limit of $< 7.5 \times 10^{-8}$ was derived from the combined dataset. These findings are the most precise results to date. Furthermore, the experiment reported the first observation of the decay $\Lambda \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, achieving a significance of 5.2 standard deviations. The combined branching fraction for this process is determined to be $(7.4 \pm 1.2) \times 10^{-8}$. The resulting inclusive and differential spectra for both $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $\Lambda \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ are presented and compared against various theoretical predictions. All measured results align with standard model expectations. However, the inclusive branching fraction for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ exceeds the lower bounds predicted by QCD sum rules. Moreover, the differential branching fraction for $\Lambda \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ deviates from QCD sum rule predictions in the low-$q^2$ region. These discrepancies suggest the potential existence of new physics. The inclusive branching fraction for $\Sigma^+ \to p e^+ e^-$ is also discussed. We present a novel hydrodynamic simulation tracking the collapse of a prestellar core to form a protostar, from which a protoplanetary disk emerges. This simulation incorporates a comprehensive suite of physical processes, including self-gravity, radiative transfer, and the evolution of dust grains. The prestellar core, characterized by a mass of 0.5 solar masses and a radius of 0.03 parsecs, collapses over a timescale of 1.5×10^5 years. The resulting protostar has a mass of 0.5 solar masses and a radius of 2.2×10^-3 solar radii, while the disk contains 0.03 solar masses and extends to 0.03 parsecs. The simulation's high physical fidelity stems from advanced modeling of radiative transfer and dust evolution. Specifically, the inclusion of dust growth in the inner disk regions facilitates more efficient radiative cooling, which in turn enhances the formation of a circumstellar disk. Furthermore, the evolution of dust grains plays a critical role in regulating the cooling rate of the collapsing gas. These findings underscore the necessity of modeling dust evolution and radiative transfer with high fidelity to accurately capture the physical conditions within the inner regions of a star-forming disk. Our results indicate that the final stellar mass is highly sensitive to the initial mass of the prestellar core, with a strong correlation observed between the two. Additionally, we demonstrate that the stellar mass correlates with the disk mass, suggesting that more massive stars are accompanied by more massive disks. These insights are valuable for interpreting observations of young stellar objects and for understanding the link between stellar and disk masses. Our analysis also reveals that the disk is not in Keplerian rotation, a conclusion supported by recent observational data. Finally, we show that the stellar wind is driven by the accretion process, with a mass ejection rate of 1.5×10^-8 solar masses per year, which is comparable to observed values. Overall, this study provides a detailed examination of disk formation from the collapse of a prestellar core, offering valuable insights for researchers in the field. Our methodology can be applied to a wide range of prestellar core masses to investigate the relationship between stellar and disk masses. The simulation code is publicly available for the research community to facilitate further research in this area. We hope this work will contribute to a deeper understanding of disk formation from the collapse of a prestellar core. Atmospheric dispersion correctors (ADCs) are essential instruments in modern ground-based telescopes, designed to counteract wavelength-dependent refraction in the atmosphere. However, these optical devices rely on precise models of atmospheric refraction to function effectively. This study presents a detailed analysis of dispersion measurements taken across the 360–900 nm wavelength range using the spectrograph mounted on the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT). By analyzing these on-sky data, we develop and evaluate various refraction models to determine their accuracy and identify the optimal model for ADC control systems. We characterize the observed refraction curves by examining their linearity, asymmetry, and dispersion rate. Furthermore, we measure the temporal stability of atmospheric refraction and analyze its statistical properties. Based on these findings, we compare multiple refraction models, including the Saemundsson, Bennett, Bennett II, and Bennett/Davies models, as well as a new empirical approach. Our results indicate that the empirical model offers the highest accuracy, followed by the modified Bennett/Davies model. Additionally, we observe that refraction remains stable over timescales of a few minutes, with fluctuations of a few milli-arcseconds. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for ADC control systems. These findings are particularly relevant for future optical systems, such as the LBT Integral Field Unit (LBTI), which lack access to external atmospheric refraction models. We conclude that an ADC designed for such a system should be optimized using on-sky refraction measurements. Specifically, for LBTI, we recommend an ADC configuration featuring a flat field corrector, a horizontal tilt plate, and a vertical tilt plate. We also outline the necessary steps to achieve the required refraction compensation for LBTI. This research was conducted under the LBT Summer Student Program. This paper introduces a Bayesian Variational approach designed to address multi-period time series modeling. The proposed method models the time series using a multi-period dynamic linear model (DLM), which incorporates multiple regression components to capture various temporal patterns. These components are linked via a common covariance matrix, and a sparsity prior is applied to their coefficient vectors to eliminate redundant components. The Bayesian Variational procedure approximates the intractable joint posterior of these shared covariance matrices and coefficient vectors. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through simulation studies and apply it to two real-world datasets: daily closing prices for the S&P500 index (2007–2019) and monthly unemployment rates (1948–2019). The approach is compared against several benchmark methods, including quasi-maximum likelihood estimation, variational Bayesian inference, the dynamic factor model, and principal component analysis. Results indicate that the proposed Bayesian Variational method outperforms all benchmarks in terms of forecasting accuracy. Furthermore, because the method does not require the strong assumption of Gaussianity, it is particularly well-suited for financial time series, which often exhibit non-Gaussian characteristics. Finally, the method is computationally efficient, as the Bayesian Variational procedure avoids the high computational costs associated with Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling. The implementation is available at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenWang1992/Multi-period-DLM}. Keywords: Dynamic factor model, Dynamic linear model, Financial time series, Multi-period dynamic linear model, Principal component analysis. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 62M10, 62P12.

We present a Pontryagin-style representation theorem for the uniform algebra of continuous Bohr-type almost periodic functions on an abelian Polish group, tailored for representation in continuous logic. This work addresses a query raised by Gideon Samet regarding nearly almost periodic functions. A natural extension of our findings to non-abelian Polish groups is briefly discussed. Additionally, we provide a continuous logic formulation of Todorov's theorem by establishing an embedding of the almost periodic function algebra into an algebra of shifts within continuous logic. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the uniform algebra of continuous almost periodic functions on an abelian Polish group can be defined as a logic symbol within a specific language of continuous logic. Our approach to proving the embedding involves utilizing the shift representation of almost periodic functions, which was developed by our collaborator, the late Professor Todorov. We also provide a continuous logic version of Todorov's theorem. The primary tool employed is a novel application of the continuous Gelfand-Naimark theorem within continuous logic. We anticipate that these methods will find applications in other areas of research. This note serves as a contribution to the memory of Professor Todorov. Any errors are solely my responsibility. This study examines privacy and fairness challenges within federated learning (FL), focusing on differential privacy (DP) and robust stochastic gradient descent (RSGD). We introduce a novel RPSD RPSD combination of these methods, which integrates RPSD with differential privacy. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that this proposed algorithm achieves RPSD with a specific epsilon, running time, and memory usage. Furthermore, we apply this algorithm to two classification tasks involving non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data, calculating the optimal global parameters and assessing both fairness and privacy. Finally, we compare our algorithm's performance against two baseline approaches. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method surpasses one of the baselines in achieving both privacy and fairness objectives, while also offering greater computational efficiency. However, compared to the second baseline, our approach is less efficient in terms of runtime and memory consumption. Overall, our findings suggest that the algorithm effectively balances privacy and fairness, though future work should explore strategies to optimize its runtime and memory usage. We introduce a supersymmetric framework extending the Standard Model with a $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry, where the gauge boson acquires mass through the vacuum expectation value of a specific linear combination of the charges associated with right-handed up-type quarks and right-handed neutrinos. Within this model, we investigate the possibility of generating neutrino masses via a combination of the seesaw and Weinberg mechanisms. Furthermore, we examine the viability of a heavy neutralino state, composed primarily of right-handed neutrinos, serving as dark matter. We analyze the constraints imposed by experimental data on the parameter space and identify a region consistent with all observational limits, featuring a gauge boson mass near 1 TeV and a neutrino mixing parameter $\epsilon \sim 10^{-3}$. In this scenario, neutrino masses arise from both the seesaw and Weinberg mechanisms. Additionally, we investigate the production and detection of dark matter at the Large Hadron Collider. Our findings indicate that while direct detection experiments set stringent lower bounds on the neutrino mass scale $M_N$, the large mixing parameter $\epsilon$ allows the model to remain viable in the region where the dark matter candidate mass $M_N \sim 1$ TeV. Furthermore, we demonstrate that dark matter can be directly produced at the LHC through $Z'$ boson fusion. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting this dark matter at the High-Luminosity LHC and future electron-proton colliders such as the Electron-Ion Collider. This study examines an IRS-assisted Wireless Powered Communication Network (WPCN) subject to interference, proposing a deep unsupervised learning (USL) approach to optimize the system's throughput. The USL framework is designed to resolve the joint optimization challenge of energy harvesting (EH) time allocation and IRS phase shifting. To ensure practicality, the model incorporates an IRS phase constraint, allowing the IRS to switch between two configurations: a fully active state for signal amplification and a passive state for interference neutralization. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the USL approach yields superior performance compared to existing benchmark methods. Furthermore, the findings indicate that utilizing the IRS in a passive mode to neutralize interference results in higher throughput gains than employing it actively to amplify signals. Finally, the analysis reveals that implementing IRS-assisted neutralization is particularly advantageous when the interference time fraction is low. These results offer valuable insights for future WPCN designs. Additionally, the proposed USL method is applicable to a broader range of WPCN scenarios, such as optimizing specific KQoS metrics or addressing problems with intractable solutions. The paper concludes with a discussion on the generalizability of these results. The associated code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/IRS_WPCN}. This study examines the relationship between dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified framework extending the standard model with three right-handed neutrinos and a complex scalar singlet. The singlet interacts with standard model fields and possesses a cubic coupling to the right-handed neutrinos. In this scenario, leptogenesis occurs via decays of the right-handed neutrinos during the early universe, while dark matter is generated through the coannihilation of the singlet with these same neutrinos. We analyze the correlation between the baryon asymmetry and dark matter relic density, demonstrating that for a fixed baryon asymmetry, the relic density can be either enhanced or suppressed depending on the specific parameter values. Furthermore, we explore the implications of current baryon asymmetry and dark matter relic density measurements for the model's parameter space. Finally, we assess the viability of future dark matter direct detection experiments in constraining this framework. Our findings indicate that while direct detection offers a promising avenue for testing the model, the resulting constraints are relatively weak. However, if dark matter is identified as a mixed state of the singlet and right-handed neutrinos, it may evade stringent limits from both relic density calculations and direct detection searches. Additionally, we note that the decay of the right-handed neutrinos in the early universe could have significantly altered dark matter properties, a factor that must be incorporated into any direct detection analysis. Consequently, we recommend that future research incorporate this decay history when analyzing direct detection results. Overall, this work establishes a foundation for investigating the connection between dark matter and baryon asymmetry, a topic that remains underexplored in the literature. We anticipate that our findings will facilitate further investigations into this interplay. Our analysis utilized the publicly available package \texttt{CosmoRec} for relic density calculations and \texttt{IlcPOTGen} for direct detection computations. We conclude that this framework is viable, with further research required to explore its parameter space in greater detail. We have made our numerical code public to facilitate these future investigations. Finally, we emphasize that this model is highly testable through direct detection experiments, offering a unique opportunity to explore the dark matter sector. We have also made our numerical code public to support this experimental investigation. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a machine learning approach where an agent interacts with an environment to maximize long-term rewards. However, this interaction-driven method is impractical for real-world applications due to safety risks and the high sample counts required for convergence. To address this, we introduce a data-driven learning framework that utilizes prior knowledge of system dynamics to accelerate learning and ensure safety. Specifically, our approach employs a novel control technique that projects the ideal control signal—derived from an offline RL model—into the actual control input by leveraging system invariants. We validate the efficacy of this proposed control method through a series of simulations on real-world robotic platforms, including robots designed for walking, swimming, flying, and reaching tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves task success with fewer than 10 trials, significantly outperforming baseline models that require over 100 trials. Furthermore, we confirm the method's safety by verifying constraint satisfaction across all experiments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/DDC. Conformal field theories that are invariant under conformal transformations form a special category within conformal field theory, distinguished by an algebra of infinitely many conserved charges. This paper investigates such a theory in $d=2$ dimensions, specifically the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. We demonstrate that local charges correspond to integrals of local operators, which are descendants of primary operators. By utilizing conformal invariance, we derive a novel set of Ward identities applicable to correlation functions. These identities express $n$-point functions of descendants in terms of primary operator correlation functions and can be interpreted as descendant-recombination relations. Furthermore, we establish that correlation functions of primary operators remain invariant under the addition of specific linearly independent linear combinations. We analyze how these findings constrain correlation functions and their associated Ward identities, offering a framework for the systematic construction of Ward identities and the derivation of correlation functions. Additionally, we identify a related set of "dual" Ward identities and examine their relationship to the standard ones. Finally, we explore the connection to integrability by calculating conserved charges and examining their two-point functions. Our results indicate that correlation functions are subject to non-trivial constraints, which may facilitate the construction of specific charges. We also provide a comprehensive list of conserved charges for the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This work serves as a precursor to our subsequent study, where we will further investigate these constraints and correlation functions, ultimately deriving exact results for specific four-point functions. This approach will also enable the construction of non-trivial charges, thereby advancing our understanding of the connection between conformal field theory and integrability. Furthermore, we will examine how Ward identities influence the spectrum of the theory. Our findings can be readily extended to the general $d$-dimensional case. This article serves as a precursor to [arXiv:2109.00020]. Keywords: Conformal Field Theories, Integrable Models, Sigma Models.

Relation networks have recently gained significant attention for their ability to model interactions between objects within an image, demonstrating superior performance in nearest neighbor retrieval and ranking compared to other relation-based methods. However, current approaches typically rely on pre-trained networks for feature extraction, which restricts their generalization to unseen data. This paper introduces a novel method that integrates relation networks with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to extract features directly from latent space. By incorporating triplet loss, the model learns highly discriminative representations. Unlike prior work, this approach does not depend on pre-trained generators or discriminators. We validate the method's efficacy through retrieval experiments on the SWIM and MIT67 datasets, where our results surpass those of existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, qualitative analysis of the generated images reveals that the model successfully captures semantic information. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/RelationGANs.

Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) has recently become a promising solution for long-distance fiber-based quantum communication. However, TF-QKD typically relies on precise phase locking between transmitted pulses and the local reference phase at each end, demanding complex hardware. We introduce a modified twin-field QKD protocol that eliminates the need for phase locking by utilizing a single coherent pulse with a very low mean photon number. This approach simplifies the equipment required to generate the twin fields. We demonstrate that the key rate of our protocol remains comparable to the standard TF-QKD protocol under identical channel conditions. Furthermore, we show that our method can achieve a secret key even without ideal detectors, offering additional advantages. Experimental validation is also provided. We anticipate that this simplified version of the twin-field protocol will facilitate the deployment of TF-QKD in real-world applications. Additionally, the technique for generating the two-mode field may find broader applications in quantum communication.
