For a complex Drinfeld vertex algebra $A$, we define $T(A)$ as the Toeplitz algebra generated by compactly supported holomorphic $L^2$-representations of $A$. This construction encompasses both classical Toeplitz algebras and novel examples arising from Drinfeld vertex algebras associated with the general linear group. By leveraging the connection between Drinfeld vertex algebras and conformal block spaces, we derive a specific structural description of $T(A)$ and elucidate its representation theory. Furthermore, we extend the definition to Toeplitz algebras $B(A)$ over Fock spaces and $S(A)$ over Bergman spaces, providing explicit descriptions for these variants and highlighting their interrelations. Finally, we apply these general findings to Bergman spaces linked to the $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ and $SL(3, \mathbb{R})$ coherent state Berezin transforms. These applications yield novel Toeplitz algebras, clarify the structure of their quotient algebras, and offer a partial classification of their representations. Notably, the classification of representations for the $SL(3, \mathbb{R})$ case represents a new result. Additionally, our methodology extends to Drinfeld vertex algebras derived from holomorphic principal $G$-bundles. Although object detection has advanced significantly, most current approaches are restricted to a limited set of predefined classes. To address this, the concept of open-vocabulary detection has emerged, aiming to identify visual content from a broad range of categories. However, existing open-vocabulary methods are hindered by a scarcity of pseudo-labels and fail to utilize the inherent visual information within category names. This paper introduces a novel method that generates pseudo bounding-box labels by training a classifier on category-specific visual embeddings. These visual embeddings are then mapped to natural language descriptions of categories using a pre-trained text encoder. Finally, an objectness classifier is trained on these embedding pairs to predict visual instances for novel categories based on their names. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach effectively leverages visual semantics derived from category names, achieving state-of-the-art performance on COCO and DBL benchmarks. We conducted a survey of the Rho Oph A region using the IRAM 30m and NRO 45m radio telescopes to map the distribution of ionized gas, atomic hydrogen, and molecular regions surrounding the young stellar object S1. Our findings reveal a compact core of ionized gas with a radius of 100 AU, which is more than ten times larger than the ionization radius predicted by photoionization models. This excess of ionized gas is likely caused by the leakage of X-rays from S1. The atomic hydrogen component exhibits a size comparable to the ionized gas but is shifted approximately 100 AU away from the source. This offset is interpreted as a result of the interaction between the ionized gas and the ambient magnetic field. Additionally, we identified PDRs with sizes similar to the atomic hydrogen component, which are spatially separated from the ionized gas by a distance of about 100 AU. We propose that this separation is driven by the interaction between the ionized gas and the magnetic field. Furthermore, the PDRs show a clear asymmetry, with a size roughly twice that of the HII region, which we attribute to the presence of a nearby dense molecular cloudlet. Our results indicate that the ionized gas influences the distribution of atomic and PDR gas, while the magnetic field shapes the morphology of the ionized gas. These observations suggest that the interaction between stellar radiation and the magnetic field is a critical factor in the evolution of PDRs. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the evolution of PDRs in star-forming regions. The data are accessible via the MIRCA archive (http://www.mpia.de/~hennemann/MIRCA/). The remarkable success of transformers within natural language processing has spurred extensive research into extending this architecture to computer vision. This paper offers a comprehensive survey and survey-on-wheels (rew) of transformers in vision. We begin by examining the primary motivations for adopting transformers in vision and reviewing the foundational components that power current vision-based applications. Subsequently, we categorize and analyze various vision tasks executed by transformers, covering both low-level and high-level domains. Following this, we present a systematic comparison of transformers against other vision architectures. Finally, we outline key challenges and future research directions for transformers in computer vision. Given the rapid evolution of this field, we have curated and open-sourced a collection of code resources at https://github.com/robinlontoo/CodeResources_Transformer_in_Vision. To our knowledge, this represents the most extensive survey on transformers in computer vision to date. Furthermore, recognizing the potential for multi-modal applications, we have prepared an accompanying survey on transformers in multi-modal tasks, available at https://github.com/robinlontoo/Survey_Transformers_in_Multi-Modal_Task. We anticipate that this work will serve as a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners operating in various vision tasks. Our aim is to foster collaboration and accelerate future advancements in transformer-based computer vision. Source code will be released upon acceptance. Please cite this article if you use our survey: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12633.

This study evaluates two structural factor models designed to forecast mortality rates: a standard time-invariant factor model where factor loadings remain constant over time, and a proposed time-varying factor model where loadings can shift dynamically. The latter is implemented using a dynamic factor model with time-varying parameters. Both approaches are applied to predict all-cause mortality rates across 14 countries, utilizing data from the Human Mortality Database. The analysis covers two distinct forecasting horizons: one to one-year-ahead (short-term) and two to five-year-ahead (long-term). Results indicate that time-varying factor loadings significantly enhance forecast accuracy for the one-to-five-year-ahead period. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the potential of these models to predict age-specific mortality rates. Finally, the paper outlines how the estimated factor models can be utilized to determine life expectancy. Available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.01015. Keywords: mortality forecasting, dynamic factor model, time-varying parameter model, life expectancy.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has demonstrated that well-optimized architectures can match the performance of state-of-the-art models while requiring fewer parameters. However, the high computational cost of NAS remains a significant barrier. To address this, researchers have developed various techniques to reduce search expenses, including reducing training iterations, lowering model precision, and implementing early stopping. This paper investigates a different approach by reducing interference among candidate architectures. We analyze the sources of this interference and propose a novel method that minimizes it by training multiple architectures simultaneously within a single network. Our results demonstrate that this strategy significantly outperforms existing cost-reduction methods, achieving comparable accuracy with a 3.2x decrease in computational cost on ResNet-50 and E2E-DL benchmarks. Additionally, we introduce an architecture search metric to quantify inter-architecture interference, which can guide the co-training of multiple architectures to mitigate interference. The code is available at https://github.com/ChenchenShen/CoNAS.

Time series analysis serves as a critical method for comprehending temporal patterns and forecasting future outcomes. This tutorial demonstrates how to compute a broad spectrum of feature-based indicators for univariate and multivariate sequences using the theft package in R. These included metrics cover summary statistics, frequency domain features, stationarity, and others. Additionally, theft provides forecasting capabilities for various time series models, including ARIMA, SARIMA, ETS, and structural time series. The tutorial begins with an introduction to theft and its data structures, followed by an overview of available analysis methods. It then presents a case study applying theft to analyze and forecast monthly sales data. The goal is to equip users with the knowledge to select appropriate methods for their specific cases and to build a robust foundation for future research. All code used in this tutorial is available on GitHub.

We provide specific, "infinitesimal" criteria ensuring that a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space possesses a semistable fundamental group at infinity. These conditions are met by a wide range of spaces arising from geometric group theory, including proper actions of hyperbolic groups, Coxeter groups, and SL groups. Additionally, we demonstrate that assuming a semistable fundamental group at infinity allows for the extension of several techniques developed by Cornulier and Rieffel. This enables us to derive properties of asymptotic cones and invariants for specific classes of CAT(0) spaces, such as graph manifolds. As an application, we establish that the fundamental group at infinity of a geodesically complete proper CAT(0) space is coarsely connected whenever the space contains a geodesic triangle with three infinite sides. This result offers a partial resolution to a question posed by Cornulier and Rieffel. Our approach relies on a novel lemma that generalizes Gromov's filling lemma to the CAT(0) setting. We illustrate the broad applicability of this lemma by applying it to geodesic spaces and metric graphs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this lemma facilitates a straightforward inductive proof of the local cohomological dimension of any CAT(0) space being at most its covering dimension. Finally, we generalize our findings to geodesic spaces satisfying a local version of the CAT(0) inequality. In this broader context, we prove that the local 1-Lipschitz extension property holds for any geodesic space with non-positive local curvature. This property is instrumental in extending geodesics from compact subsets into unbounded rays and serves as a key tool in our arguments. Our findings also have significant implications for the study of asymptotic cones within the category of metric spaces. Zhukov. Moreover, we show that any geodesic space exhibiting non-positive local curvature and possessing a geodesic triangle filling property must be weakly CAT(0). This conclusion follows from an alternative characterization of weakly CAT(0) spaces originally presented by M. D. Chepoi. We demonstrate that in time-independent scattering systems, nearly all depolarizing processes occur through a minimal set of eigenchannels associated with energy deposition, which are independent of incident polarization. This finding is illustrated through examples involving both electromagnetic waves and cold atoms interacting with matter. These results hold significant implications for the study of wave and atomic scattering, particularly regarding material characterization and the design of polarizing devices. Additionally, we introduce a new metric for measuring the minimum eigenchannel count, which is particularly sensitive to nonreciprocal scattering effects. Finally, this theoretical framework is applied to investigate how nonreciprocity influences polarization maintenance across various wave frequencies. Specifically, we examine microwave scattering from ferrite materials and demonstrate, via numerical simulations, how nonreciprocity enhances the polarization-maintaining capabilities of ferrite slabs at microwave frequencies. These insights are valuable for both fundamental research and the development of ferrite components for microwave applications. Furthermore, our theoretical approach is applied to analyze the polarization-maintaining properties of silicon at optical frequencies. We show that silicon exhibits significant nonreciprocity due to the breaking of inversion symmetry in its crystal structure, resulting in a low number of polarization-maintaining eigenchannels at certain incident polarizations and wavelengths. This characteristic distinguishes silicon from other common materials, such as aluminum, and may be advantageous for specific device applications. Ultimately, this work establishes a framework for identifying and characterizing polarization-maintaining scattering systems, offering a pathway to design new devices and materials with tailored nonreciprocal scattering properties. Additionally, the study provides a method for quantifying the degree of nonreciprocity in scattering systems. These tools are expected to advance both fundamental understanding and technological applications of nonreciprocal scattering phenomena. Supplementary material is available at [1]. Pruning techniques have been utilized to enhance the efficiency of deep neural networks. Recently, research has demonstrated that extremely sparsely pruned deep networks can retain accuracy comparable to their dense counterparts. This study investigates the characteristics of such pruned, accurate subnetworks. These findings suggest that existing pruning methods can improve the efficiency of deep neural networks without compromising performance. This study examines maximizing the expected return of a Sports Lotto ticket by strategically choosing when to purchase and which numbers to select. While standard approaches typically focus on selecting an optimal set of numbers, this work introduces a novel framework that simultaneously accounts for price fluctuations. We analyze the optimal strategies within a discrete-time stochastic process, demonstrating that the problem can be effectively approximated using the continuous time-utility framework of Merton's portfolio optimization. Consequently, we develop a practical numerical algorithm to solve the discrete version and validate its outcomes against Merton's continuous solution. Our methodology allows us to evaluate the impact of various market factors on a player's expected value. Furthermore, we show that a player can significantly enhance their expected value by timing the purchase to the optimal moment, rather than simply identifying the best numbers. Finally, numerical simulations illustrate the potential gains achievable through this combined strategic approach. The paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and suggests directions for future research. These computations were achieved using the Feynman integral method, employing both sector decomposition and differential equations to resolve the integrals to the required precision. The necessary order-$\varepsilon^6$ accuracy corresponds to solving the model up to four-loop order. Our findings provide fresh data points for testing the asymptotic freedom of the $O(N)$ model as a function of $Q$. Additionally, we determine the four-loop beta function for the $O(N)$ model, which may have independent applications. Finally, we derive the leading-order anom dimensions for the $\phi^5$ operator in the Wilson-Fisher fixed point of the $O(2)$ and $O(3)$ models, along with their two-loop counterparts. The valley Hall effect in two-dimensional materials is influenced by both electron-phonon coupling and lattice anharmonicity. This study employs first-principles methods to investigate how these phenomena interact in hexagonal boron nitride. We demonstrate that lattice anharmonicity substantially alters the valley Hall effect by modifying the band structure and introducing additional valley points. Furthermore, we identify a novel electron-phonon coupling mechanism that arises from the valley-dependent warping of the Fermi surface, which can be observed through valley-resolved Raman spectroscopy. Our findings indicate that this mechanism can induce significant lattice distortions and shifts in vibrational modes, offering a potential route to detect defects in two-dimensional materials. Additionally, we propose a Raman spectroscopy technique to identify these lattice distortions. Ultimately, our results highlight the critical role of electron-phonon coupling in valley physics and underscore the necessity of incorporating these effects into future theoretical models. This work paves the way for exploring electron-phonon interactions in other two-dimensional materials. To facilitate these investigations, we have provided a Python code for valley Hall calculations, which is available at https://github.com/valleyphysics. The code includes a demonstration using hexagonal boron nitride. We also provide a Python script for calculating Raman spectra from first-principles, available at https://github.com/valleyphysics/raman_spectra. This paper presents our approach to the Visual Domain Adaptation (VDA) challenge, which addresses three tasks: (i) developing a domain-agnostic model for object detection, (ii) deriving insights from adaptation results to enhance model performance, and (iii) evaluating the impact of specific data augmentation techniques on adaptation outcomes. Regarding the first task, we developed a novel method leveraging pseudo-labeling and a multi-task learning strategy that combines detection with classification and instance-level image-to-image translation. For the second task, we analyzed evaluation metrics to identify performance trends and explored the effects of data augmentation, domain shift, and model capacity. Specifically, regarding data augmentation, we demonstrated that hard augmentation methods like Mixup and CutMix outperform easy methods such as random cropping and horizontal flipping. We also examined domain shift impacts, finding that adaptation from ImageNet-C to Cityscapes yields superior results compared to adapting from ImageNet to Cityscapes. Finally, we investigated model capacity effects, observing that larger models like Faster-RCNN-XL improve adaptation performance, though they are more susceptible to overfitting. t-SNE is a widely adopted method for visualizing high-dimensional data in lower dimensions. It operates by representing data points as a high-dimensional probability distribution using a Gaussian kernel, while simultaneously projecting them into an embedding space defined by a different probability distribution generated via a non-Gaussian kernel. However, these two distributions often fail to align perfectly, leading to significant information loss. This paper introduces VMF-SNE, a novel algorithm that projects spherical data into a spherical embedding space governed by a von Mises-Fisher distribution. Theoretically, the distance metric employed in VMF-SNE provides a more accurate representation than the approaches of t-SNE and sphere-SNE. Experimental results demonstrate that VMF-SNE surpasses t-SNE and sphere-SNE in visualizing spherical data, effectively preserving both local and global data structures. Furthermore, VMF-SNE exhibits superior performance in terms of running time and memory consumption. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1998/VMFSNE. We establish a log-convexity property for a novel sequence of invariants $\mathcal{I}_k(G)$ associated with simple graphs $G$. These invariants represent the coefficients of the polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^{2n} \mathcal{I}_k(G) t^k = \det(I - tA + t^2(I - D))$, where $A$ and $D$ denote the adjacency and degree matrices of $G$, respectively. We further propose the conjecture that the characteristic polynomial of the Laplacian, $\det(I - t^2(I-D))$, exhibits the same property, while also outlining potential applications of these invariants to other graph-theoretic concepts. Additionally, we present a conjecture regarding the reciprocal of this function, which is supported by numerical evidence for graphs with maximum degree $\Delta \leq 3$. Finally, we demonstrate that this conjecture holds true when $\mathcal{I}_k(G)$ is substituted with the corresponding coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of $L = D + A$. In this specific case, our findings align with and extend the work of Bapat and Li [Linear Algebra Appl. 439 (2014) 2000–2008]. We conclude by providing several examples of graphs with $\Delta \leq 3$ that verify this conjecture. Notably, the only graph with $\Delta = 3$ that fails to satisfy it is $K_{2,2,2}$, which corresponds to the complement of a perfect matching. This result is consistent with the work of Bapat and Li [Linear Algebra Appl. 439 (2014) 2000–2008]. Furthermore, we observe that the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial for $A$ are also conjectured to satisfy the log-convexity property. We provide a proof of this conjecture for graphs with $\Delta \leq 2$ and offer numerical evidence for the case $\Delta = 3$. The primary tool employed in our approach is the Cauchy-Binet formula. Our work also draws upon the recent findings of Bapat and Li [Linear Algebra Appl. 439 (2014) 2000–2008]. Finally, we note that the coefficients of the reciprocal of the function are conjectured to also satisfy the log-convexity property, and we verify this conjecture

This work provides an explicit formula for the pullback of the Hitchin connection from the moduli space of genus two curves to a ten-fold cover of a Teichmüller curve identified by Veech. Furthermore, we derive an expression using iterated integrals for the monodromy representation associated with this connection. As a consequence, we establish quantum representations for infinitely many pseudo-Anosov elements within the genus two mapping class group. Additionally, we provide explicit formulas for iterating vector fields linked to Hitchin's connection and for iterated integrals related to Hitchin's isomonodromy system on the Teichmüller curve. Our approach is explicit, enabling the calculation of pullbacks of Hitchin's connection, quantum representations, and monodromy representations for specific vector fields and paths on the moduli space of genus two curves. We also present explicit formulas for iterating vector fields and computing monodromy representations through path integration. This work marks the initial instance of applying the theory of iterated integrals to explore moduli spaces and Teichmüller spaces. Finally, we offer a self-contained exposition of Hitchin's connection and its application to the KZ connection, alongside an explicit construction of the relevant flat connection. These methods are expected to be applicable in various other contexts. Finally, we demonstrate how to apply our explicit formulas to investigate quantum cohomology on the moduli space of genus two curves. The concept of the Gau–Wu number was originally developed to characterize arrowhead matrices that are both gauge equivalent and unitary. This paper investigates certain classes of arrowhead matrices to determine their respective Gau–Wu numbers. Specifically, we provide the numerical value for the Gau–Wu number corresponding to a particular category of4x4 matrices. These findings may have practical applications in the fields of control theory and signal processing. Furthermore, our results contribute to the broader objective of identifying sufficient conditions under which unitary arrowhead matrices are gauge equivalent. The study relies on diagonal gauge transformations and permutation matrices. Additionally, we examine the spectral properties of these matrices and explore the relationship between their gauge factors and permutation matrices. Our work also addresses the existence and uniqueness of gauge factors, offering several theorems and examples that highlight the challenges inherent in this area. Finally, we analyze the numerical stability of various algorithms used to compute the Gau–Wu number for arrowhead matrices. To achieve this, we evaluate the computational complexity and numerical stability of different approaches, including the Gauss–Jordan elimination method, the QR decomposition method, and the Givens rotation method. We conclude by providing a comprehensive comparison of these algorithms to assist researchers in selecting the most appropriate method for specific applications. The paper includes numerical examples to validate our findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms. Overall, this study aims to provide a solid foundation for future research on arrowhead matrices and their gauge factors. By understanding the spectral properties and computational complexity of these matrices, researchers can develop more efficient algorithms for computing the Gau–Wu number, which has significant applications in various fields. Additionally, our findings can be extended to other types of matrices, further advancing the field of matrix theory. Through this research, we hope to contribute to the broader goal of advancing our understanding of the mathematical structures underlying modern technology. By developing more efficient algorithms for computing the Gau–Wu number, we can help solve some of the most pressing challenges facing modern society, from optimizing power grids to designing more efficient communication systems. Ultimately, our work seeks to advance the field of matrix theory and contribute to the development of more effective solutions to the complex problems we face every day. Our findings can be applied to various fields, including the study of matrix factorization, the development of more efficient numerical methods for solving linear systems, and the design of more effective algorithms for machine learning and data analysis. This report presents measurements of the elliptic flow ($v_2$) for electrons originating from the semi-leptonic decays of beauty hadrons, derived from Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV. The analysis utilizes a dataset of 44.4 $\mu$b$^{-1}$ collected by the ALICE detector at the LHC. The study examines $v_2$ across transverse momenta ($p_{\rm T}$) ranging from 1 to 10 GeV/$c$, covering centralities from 0--80%. The observed $v_2$ values are compared against results from light hadrons and those predicted by hydrodynamic and transport model simulations. The experimental data align well with hydrodynamic model predictions. Furthermore, the $p_{\rm T}$ dependence of $v_2$ for electrons from beauty hadron decays is found to be harder than that of light hadrons, a trend consistent with both hydrodynamic and transport model calculations. Additionally, the $p_{\rm T}$ dependence of $v_2$ for electrons is compared with that of muons from charm hadron decays, revealing a harder $v_2$ dependence for electrons. These findings are also interpreted within the framework of hydrodynamic and transport models. The measurements demonstrate that electrons from beauty hadron decays exhibit similar hydrodynamic-like behavior to both light and charm hadrons. This indicates that, despite their significantly higher $p_{\rm T}$, beauty hadrons are not fully quenched and still participate in the collective flow of the medium. These results provide valuable insights into the interaction of heavy quarks with the quark-gluon plasma. The study also includes a measurement of the nuclear modification factor ($R_{\rm AA}$) for $v_2$ as a function of $p_{\rm T}$, which reveals a strong $p_{\rm T}$ dependence. Finally, the paper concludes with an outline of future prospects for this topic. The presented results were obtained during ALICE Run 2 Pb-Pb collisions and are published in Phys. Rev. We present an algorithm grounded in persistent homology to analyze the chromatic mixtures of quasicrystals, a task that extends beyond decoding the actual atomic positions within the crystal. By examining a collection of chromatic quasicrystalline structures, our method offers both a quantitative and qualitative perspective on how varying color schemes influence the overall geometry of the resulting complex. Specifically, our approach calculates and displays key metrics, including higher-order persistence diagrams, entropy, and persistence entropy, to evaluate the stability of topological features across different chromatic configurations. Furthermore, the method is equipped with visualization tools that employ heat maps to illustrate how distinct chromatic setups impact the persistence of geometric structures. Finally, we validate this technique using the Bernal-Herrmann quasicrystal dataset. This work represents the first application of persistent homology to the study of chromatic quasicrystals. The proposed method is implemented in Python and is publicly accessible. The accompanying code includes examples of chromatic and multicolor q12 and Bernal-Herrmann quasicrystals, featuring a Jupyter notebook with visualization code for chromatic analysis. Additionally, the code provides a chromatic analyzer tool for conducting chromatic analysis on any quasicrystal structure. This study examines the Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) performance improvement achieved by optimal power control (OPC) compared to binary power control (BPC) in a $K$-user interference network. In this setting, each user's transmitter operates under a power budget of $P$, selecting either to transmit with power $P$ or not at all. We demonstrate that the maximum extremal GDoF gain of OPC over BPC scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This finding indicates that, in the asymptotic regime, a substantial number of transmitters must utilize power to significantly impact the network's GDoF, a result that contrasts with scenarios involving point-to-point links. Additionally, we present a simplified lower bound for the extremal GDoF gain that relies on the difference between the number of active links and isolated links within the interference graph. Finally, we explore the application of our findings to wireless cellular networks. Specifically, we show that the lower bound derived in this work is tight for regular cellular topologies, such as hexagonal grids. For a hexagonal grid with $K$ users, the extremal GDoF gain is given by $\frac{1}{2}\log_2(K+3) + O(1)$. This result is achieved by an OPC scheme where transmitters adjust their power levels to either dominate or be dominated by their neighbors. Furthermore, we prove that the power levels required by this scheme are minimal, thereby establishing its optimality. These conclusions hold true for the specific case of a 3-user cluster. However, for larger clusters, the specific OPC scheme remains an open question. We also investigate the GDoF performance gain of joint GDoF optimization versus BPC in hexagonal grids and establish a lower bound for the extremal GDoF gain of joint optimization over BPC. This bound is derived from the difference between the total number of links and the total number of isolated links in the interference graph. For large $K$, this lower bound approximates to $\frac{1}{2}\log_2(K+3) + O(1)$. We also note that this bound is tight for hexagonal grids with 4 users. However, it remains an open question whether this lower bound is tight for larger clusters. Our results are based on the GDoF model, which is widely recognized as the most effective tool for characterizing the asymptotic performance of interference networks. The growing adoption of blockchain technology has enabled the decentralized recording of financial transactions, including those involving illegal drugs. This transparency allows for the detection of suspicious activities, such as money laundering, by analyzing transaction graphs. However, a significant challenge remains: many transactions lack labels, rendering them useless for data mining tasks like categorization. This paper introduces a novel categorization method designed to process unlabeled transactions. The proposed algorithm leverages formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer theory to flexibly assign categories to individual transactions. We successfully applied this approach to a real-world case study involving illicit drug transactions on the blockchain. The results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms traditional categorization techniques. Furthermore, we confirm that categorization is feasible for these transactions and that the new method offers the added benefit of uncertainty representation. Finally, we conclude that the method is effective for unlabeled transaction categorization and suggest several directions for future research. Specifically, future work should explore the method's performance in preventing money laundering and in categorizing transactions within other industries. Additionally, we intend to extend the method to handle cyclic transaction graphs and to develop a mechanism for automatically generating transaction attributes. Finally, we plan to investigate techniques for reducing the computational complexity of the proposed approach. Keywords: Blockchain, Categorization, Money Laundering, Audit, Uncertainty.

The STrauss process is a point process defined by an unnormalized density relative to a Poisson point process, where any pair of points separated by a distance $r$ contributes a factor $\lambda \exp(\beta r^{-\gamma})$ to the total weight $\lambda$. This paper presents an algorithm for sampling from the Strauss process on $[0,1]$ with density proportional to $\lambda \exp(\beta |x-y|)$, corresponding to the case $\gamma=1$. Our method is a stitching algorithm grounded in dynamic programming, which we demonstrate is significantly faster than current alternatives. We extend this approach to handle pairs of points at fixed distances in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and discuss its application to related point processes. Additionally, we provide a Python implementation of the method within the `stlattice` package. Our implementation achieves speeds orders of magnitude faster than the `kerneldensity` package's `random_delaunay_triangulation` function and more than two orders of magnitude faster than `spatstat`'s `runifstraw` function. Furthermore, we show that our method is over four times faster than `spatstat`'s `strattpoint` function when generating 1000 samples. These results are based on experiments using parameters derived from a real-world dataset. The accompanying code is available in our GitHub repository, `https://github.com/alexbeyene/stlattice`. The `stlattice` package can be installed via `pip install stlattice`. We also demonstrate how to utilize `stlattice` to generate Strauss point patterns in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with isotropic pairwise interactions. The `stlattice` package is released under the MIT license. Multitasking scheduling involves determining the execution order for multiple tasks, where each task may require processing in several modes, or "slices," to achieve completion. While traditional scheduling assumes a single mode per task, this paper addresses a more complex variant where mode selection is flexible. In this context, a scheduler can choose to process one slice at a time or concurrently execute multiple slices using shared processing resources. The study focuses on minimizing the total time required to finish all tasks. We present both positive results and complexity findings regarding this multitasking scheduling problem. Specifically, we analyze a scenario with unit-length slices and variable numbers of modes per task, introducing a new parallel slice execution model that generalizes the parallel machine model. For this case, we demonstrate that a simple list scheduling algorithm achieves an optimal approximation ratio of 2, provided no task has more than two slices. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to the scenario where slice lengths are not uniform. Finally, we examine a case with a uniform number of slices per task, showing that when slice lengths are unrestricted, the problem becomes NP-hard even if each task has only two slices. Consequently, we propose a list scheduling algorithm and establish its performance bounds. Additionally, we derive a performance bound for the case where each task possesses only one slice. Internet of Things (IoT) systems are expanding rapidly, yet their firmware update mechanisms often suffer from significant security and reliability vulnerabilities. This paper examines the performance characteristics of a production IoT firmware update system deployed across the San Francisco Bay Area. Our findings indicate that the region's mesh network topology, combined with the specific design of the update system, creates substantial challenges for large-scale deployments. We identify the primary bottlenecks within the system and provide recommendations for future improvements. Additionally, we explore the trade-offs between various architectural designs and outline potential directions for enhancing both security and reliability. Ultimately, this study offers critical insights for the development of next-generation IoT firmware update architectures.

Specifically, we calculate the fractal dimension as a continuous function of the non-uniformity parameter. We further examine the scaling of the one-step propagator in the Fock-space basis, demonstrating that its scaling behavior mirrors the entanglement entropy of a single spin. These findings are derived from a numerical study of the disordered transverse-field Ising model. We conclude that the Fock-space basis proves effective for characterizing the continuous transition to many-body localization, offering a framework that avoids the computational costs associated with time evolution. This approach involves partitioning the Hilbert space into subspaces defined by energy eigenvalues and analyzing the spectral properties of the corresponding sub-Hamiltonians. We anticipate that these techniques will prove valuable for studying many-body quantum systems in the presence of disorder. Finally, we outline potential avenues for future research. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the scaling of the return probability in the Fock-space basis can be related to the entanglement entropy of a single spin, a connection that may extend to even more complex systems. Interactive search for multiple targets is a critical task in real-world scenarios, where the primary goal is to efficiently identify all target objects while minimizing the budget of issued queries. This paper addresses the challenge of constructing optimal query sets under a limited budget to confirm the presence of all targets. We introduce a novel target confirmation model that prioritizes confirming every target, even if this requires sacrificing some retrieval performance. We provide a formal description of the model and develop the first optimal algorithm for this custom target confirmation query model. Additionally, we propose a new algorithm designed for practical deployment, demonstrating that it achieves performance nearly equivalent to the optimal approach. Finally, we evaluate our proposed algorithms against existing methods on three real-world datasets, showing that our approach outperforms current solutions. This study examines Steklov eigenvalues for three-dimensional domains that are nearly spherical. Building on prior research demonstrating that these eigenvalues are analytic functions of the domain perturbation parameter, this paper derives an explicit formula for the first derivative of a Steklov eigenvalue. This derivative is expressed as the inner product of two modes, evaluated in the direction of the specific perturbation. As a practical application, we utilize numerical methods to assess Steklov eigenvalues across various perturbation directions, aiming to identify those that minimize eigenvalue sensitivity. Our findings indicate significant variations in the eigenmodes associated with the lowest eigenvalues, suggesting that future inverse problems utilizing Steklov data should prioritize modes other than the first. Additionally, we explore the analytic properties of Steklov eigenvalues within the context of nearly spherical domains and conclude by addressing an open question regarding the existence of a positive lower bound for these eigenvalues. Specifically, we present a counterexample to such a bound in two dimensions, whereas we conjecture that a positive lower bound does exist for three-dimensional cases. However, these alignments often fail to capture the complete set of deviations present in a single fragment. To ensure all deviations are accounted for, we introduce postfix alignments, a novel method for comparing process models with trace fragments. This approach is the first of its kind, offering a theoretical foundation comparable to that of infix alignments. Our study provides the first formal analysis of post, infix, and suffix alignments, demonstrating their relationships and establishing their computational complexities. Furthermore, we develop a sound and complete algorithm for discovering deviations within trace fragments using postfix alignments. Experimental evaluations confirm that our method is practically viable and outperforms the use of infix and prefix alignments. In summary, we provide the first formal analysis of postfix alignments and the first method for discovering trace fragment deviations, which are essential for understanding fragment behavior and enhancing conformance checking techniques. Additionally, our proposed technique is the first to identify all deviations in trace fragments. The source code is available at https://github.com/ProcessMiningGroup/postfix-alignments. Power system expansion planning (PSEP) models are essential for determining future generation, transmission, and storage investments. However, their outcomes are highly sensitive to input parameters, including future costs, loads, and emissions constraints. This study examines the robustness of PSEP results by analyzing how variations in these parameters influence outcomes. It further explores the impact of such sensitivities on future policy decisions, specifically focusing on carbon dioxide emission limits. The analysis employs a deterministic, multi-period, linear optimization model to project the power systems of Brazil, China, India, and the United States through to 2050. Results indicate that PSEP outcomes can be highly sensitive to parameter inputs, with uncertainties in future costs and loads driving most of this sensitivity. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that current policy decisions regarding emission limits are strongly influenced by cost and load uncertainties. Consequently, policymakers should consider alternative scenarios that relax or exceed current emission constraints to better inform decision-making. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of conducting sensitivity analyses to ensure that policy outcomes are not overly dependent on specific parameter values. This paper serves as a foundation for future work aimed at quantifying and mitigating these sensitivities. Additionally, the model and associated data will be made publicly available to facilitate replication and enable other researchers to conduct their own sensitivity analyses. Colloidal gels formed by Brownian particles suspended in a liquid exhibit a unique dual nature: they function as both solids and fluids. Their solid-like structure consists of a percolating network of particle aggregates, while their fluid properties are maintained by the liquid phase. This study demonstrates that applying ultrasonic vibrations to a Brownian colloidal gel during gelation allows for the control of its solid-like characteristics. We show that incorporating acoustic energy shifts the gel's structure toward the glass transition, thereby enhancing its solid-like behavior. Furthermore, we prove that these properties can be adjusted across a broad spectrum by varying the intensity and frequency of the applied acoustic energy. These rheo-acoustic gels hold promise for applications requiring both solid and fluid attributes, such as drug delivery systems, smart materials, and advanced sensors. Additionally, they offer a novel method for exploring the transition between the gel and glass states in colloidal systems. Our findings provide a foundation for further research into the fundamental physics governing the gel-to-glass transition and establish a versatile platform for developing new materials with tunable properties. The resulting acoustic gels demonstrate enhanced mechanical robustness, greater elasticity, and improved reversibility. These results pave the way for future investigations into the fundamental physics of acoustic gels and their potential use in next-generation materials and technologies. Our findings have broad implications for fields ranging from materials science to biophysics, as they provide a new tool for manipulating the properties of colloidal gels. These results could lead to the creation of new materials with improved performance and functionality, as well as advancements in understanding the behavior of complex fluids and soft matter systems. Overall, this work represents a significant step forward in the study of colloidal gels and their applications. This analysis reveals that the resulting self-focusing thermal profile deviates from the anticipated coexistence of two-dimensional self-heating at early stages and three-dimensional diffusion at later stages. The final thermal parameter is determined by a specific material-dependent crossover time, which marks the shift from early to late regimes. Utilizing this numerical description of the thermal lens, we successfully explain the formation of diffraction patterns in standing wave configurations, specifically addressing the emergence of diffraction orders beyond the central spot and the mechanism behind pattern fading. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the fading of the central spot in moving single-beam setups can be attributed to the same phenomenon. Finally, we outline a straightforward method to estimate the thermal profile based on the beam's power and residence time in the liquid. These findings hold significant implications for applications involving thermal self-focusing in liquids, such as thermal lensing, high-harmonic generation, and laser propulsion. Additionally, our results offer a means to assess the validity of various approximations and models concerning laser-induced thermal profiles in liquids. Software design discussions are frequently documented in source code comments, commit messages, and pull request descriptions. By automatically extracting design decisions from these records, developers can generate design diagrams and retrieve prior decisions for new requests. However, this process is inherently complex because natural language is diverse and design decisions are often implicit. Consequently, researchers have developed various mining methods, yet their results frequently diverge, leading to inconsistent outcomes. This paper introduces Conclusion Stability to quantify such inconsistencies and demonstrates that existing mining methods lack stability. We identify four specific sources of this instability and propose four corresponding countermeasures to enhance stability. An experimental evaluation confirms that these countermeasures significantly improve stability. Furthermore, we show that mining design decisions using the proposed approach can reduce manual annotation effort by 80% while maintaining high precision and recall. This indicates that the method is viable for practical application. The paper's conclusion is that stability serves as a critical metric for assessing and comparing software design discussion mining techniques. Code for this paper is accessible at https://github.com/DesignMining/DecisionMining. Additional resources, including data and supplementary materials, can be found at https://github.com/DesignMining/DecisionMining/tree/master/Experiment/stability. Finally, this work was conducted in collaboration with the University of Oxford.

This paper introduces H-STREAM, a novel big data processing pipeline designed for querying massive data streams and their historical records. We also present the stream analytics platform built upon H-STREAM, which integrates stream processing capabilities with data visualization tools. The study demonstrates the platform's scalability and usability through a real-world application: a real-time air quality monitoring system deployed in the city of Ljubljana. Stream analytics is increasingly vital for decision-making across various sectors, including weather forecasting, traffic management, and energy control. These systems typically rely on data streams from sensors, GPS devices, and other IoT hardware. This work focuses on the implementation of the H-STREAM pipeline and the development of Ljubljana's air quality monitoring system. We also outline the platform's user interface and its specific application to Ljubljana. Finally, we discuss the challenges encountered during implementation and how they were addressed. The paper concludes by summarizing the benefits of H-STREAM and suggesting future research directions. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has emerged as a leading method for Knowledge Base (KB) to Natural Language generation, specifically for producing SPARQL. However, as a sequence-to-sequence neural network, it struggles with modeling long-distance dependencies, which are crucial for generating syntactically correct SPARQL. This paper introduces a copy mechanism designed to address these challenges by directly copying pre-defined KB elements during translation. The proposed model was evaluated on a real-world dataset comprising triplets from the DBpedia KB. Experimental results demonstrate that the model effectively handles long-distance dependencies and surpasses state-of-the-art neural models in translation performance. Furthermore, the model was tested on query generation tasks involving subgraph matching and database annotation, with experimental outcomes confirming its superiority over existing state-of-the-art systems. Finally, the paper discusses the model's application in natural language question answering. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/leeyu1012/SPARQLCopyNet. Rather than evaluating individual papers or researchers, our method assigns quality scores to specific venues. This study addresses safety verification for neural network (NN) controllers within safety-critical systems, such as autonomous vehicles and UAVs. Since NN controllers are typically "black-box" models lacking explicit control law formulations, their behavior is difficult to predict, and their non-convex nature renders exact verification intractable. Consequently, we present a review of existing approximation techniques for NN verification and evaluate their performance across standard benchmarks. Our findings indicate that current methods are either too computationally intensive for real-time applications or suffer from low accuracy. Finally, we propose that a hybrid approach combining multiple techniques could enhance both accuracy and efficiency. To support this, we introduce a new verification method that leverages the specific structure of ReLU NNs to achieve superior accuracy and efficiency compared to current state-of-the-art approaches. Experimental results demonstrate that our method yields an average accuracy gain of 10% over the best existing solution across several benchmarks. Furthermore, our method achieves real-time performance, completing verification for ReLU controllers with up to 100 hidden units in under 10 milliseconds. The comprehensive benchmark suite, including implementation code for all reviewed methods, is made publicly available to foster future advancements in NN verification. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/NNVerif. Our findings suggest that integrating multiple verification techniques is essential for the safe deployment of NN controllers in critical applications. We introduce a novel method for clustering data points into overlapping groups, with special attention to identifying when multiple valid clusterings exist. This approach leverages functoriality to establish a many-to-one map, or edge, within synthetic data trajectories. By utilizing edge overlaps, we generate clusters and provide a mechanism to determine if an ensemble of functorial clusterings can be reduced to a single functorial clustering. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this framework offers an alternative perspective on traditional hierarchical clustering, enabling the recovery of existing clusterings while also revealing new groupings. Tensor completion leverages low-rank structures to reconstruct missing data in incomplete tensors. While streaming tensor methods are computationally efficient for this task, they struggle with large-scale data due to a limited buffer size that restricts the range of available information. To address this limitation, we introduce a patch tracking-based streaming approach for visual tensor completion. This method enhances effective information gain by utilizing local patch correlations to refine the state estimates of visual tensors. Additionally, a novel patch tracking strategy is developed to adaptively adjust the visual tensor's mean and covariance, thereby improving estimation accuracy. The proposed algorithm was evaluated on two datasets of varying scales, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenZhang1997/PSTRTC. Furthermore, the methodology is implemented within the OpenCV library, allowing users to test the algorithm using the command: opencv_demo CVDTCA_demo.mp4. This implementation can recover corrupted regions in input videos, such as those affected by occlusion or occlusion-like cloud cover in remote sensing imagery. We present numerical simulations of three-dimensional isotropic turbulence within a rotating, inviscid, incompressible fluid subject to stochastic forcing. Our results offer compelling evidence supporting the validity of the inverse energy cascade and the Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) spectrum for energy transfer at small scales. Specifically, we observe energy transfers consistent with both the inverse energy cascade and the Zakharov-Kolmogorov inverse energy flux. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ZK spectrum accurately characterizes the small-scale structure of the simulated flow. These findings suggest that the ZK spectrum represents the small-scale limit of energy-critical rotating incompressible fluids driven by stochastic forces. Additionally, our study confirms the existence of an energy cascade to zero frequency at large scales, although the associated exponent differs from the inverse five-halves power law predicted by weak wave turbulence theory. Finally, we show that the large-scale dynamics of the simulated flow are governed by a single large-scale vortex. These latter two observations align with previous studies on two-dimensional turbulence and two-dimensional turbulence driven by a stochastic advection-diffusion equation. Collectively, these results indicate that large-scale dynamics in rotating incompressible fluids are influenced by large-scale rotation, large-scale stretching, and large-scale dissipation. The latter two mechanisms are analogous to those found in the advection-diffusion equation. Consequently, our findings suggest that large-scale dynamics in rotating incompressible fluids are governed by large-scale stretching, large-scale dissipation, and large-scale geostrophic balance. This conclusion is supported by numerical simulations of three-dimensional incompressible fluids, as well as geophysical and astrophysical observations. This paper introduces a class of iterative graph normalization techniques, offering a unified framework that encompasses well-known approaches such as degree normalization and bias normalization. For each algorithm, we establish corresponding linear operators and analyze the properties of their limit points. Furthermore, we demonstrate the equivalence between these normalization processes and iterative projection methods aimed at identifying the independent sets with the highest total weight. Finally, we present experimental results that substantiate our theoretical findings. The theoretical insights and numerical evidence suggest that graph normalization can serve as a valuable tool for addressing graph optimization challenges. Additionally, we have made our code accessible to facilitate future research. Our code repository can be found at: https://github.com/ChenYi1999/GNN_normalization.git.

This study investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of monolayer graphene subjected to electric field modulation. By applying a semi-classical approach, we derive expressions for specific heat, compressibility, thermal conductivity, and electronic viscosity across various electric field intensities. Our findings indicate that both specific heat and compressibility vary with the random electric field, exhibiting peaks at certain field strengths. Furthermore, we observe that the thermal conductivity of a modulated graphene sheet is significantly lower than that of an unmodulated one, while the electronic viscosity is correspondingly higher. These results suggest that such modulation could facilitate tunable thermal and viscous properties in graphene, thereby advancing its potential applications in thermal management. Additionally, the methodology employed is extensible to other two-dimensional materials. Finally, the numerical codes utilized in this research will be made available to the scientific community. These codes are written in Python and can be accessed at: https://github.com/abhishekdatta123/Graphene. Our hope is that this work will inspire further research into the thermal properties of two-dimensional materials.

This study details a low-frequency monitoring campaign of the M1.5 star binary system CR Draconis, conducted between 2017 and 2019 using the LOFAR radio telescope. The campaign targeted the detection of electron-cyclotron maser (ECM) emission, a mechanism known to produce radio bursts from active M dwarfs. We identified 12 new ECM events, with a notable one occurring on 2017-08-18 that lasted 11.5 hours. This is the longest-duration ECM event linked to an M dwarf reported to date. Additionally, we detected a radio continuum source during this period, which we attribute to thermal emission from the chromosphere. Our findings indicate that ECM emission in M dwarfs is a frequent phenomenon, with a potential recurrence rate of 10–20% per flare. We propose that the sustained nature of the emission results from a continuous supply of electrons to the chromosphere, likely driven by a steady outflow from the stellar photosphere. Furthermore, the presence of a radio continuum source suggests that the rate of ECM emission may be regulated by the rate of chromospheric evaporation. These insights are crucial for understanding the fundamental processes governing M dwarf flares. Our results also suggest that low-frequency monitoring is a highly effective method for identifying ECM emission, thereby enhancing our ability to study these events and their impact on exoplanet atmospheres. Finally, we demonstrate that LOFAR can successfully detect ECM emission from M dwarfs at distances of approximately 10 pc. This capability is particularly promising for upcoming large-scale surveys of the nearby solar neighborhood, such as the Low-Frequency Array Flare Survey (LOFARFS). Such surveys could significantly advance our understanding of M dwarf flares and their effects on the habitability of exoplanets. The data presented in this study will be made available to the scientific community via the LOFAR Data Archive. To address this limitation, we introduce a new system designed to produce high-fidelity virtual avatars. Our approach leverages a pre-trained model to map real-time skeletal data into detailed facial geometry and texture. We investigate how human and machine classifiers respond to extreme image transformations, specifically focusing on rotation and color shifts. Our results indicate that human performance declines significantly when colors are inverted or images are rotated 180 degrees, yet remains largely unaffected by minor color adjustments or small rotations. In contrast, machines exhibit high accuracy only under substantial color and rotation modifications. These findings offer new insights into the distinct mechanisms underlying human and machine visual recognition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that training machines on diverse extreme transformations enhances their ability to generalize to novel extremes, a property that, to our knowledge, prior models lack. Finally, we explore the implications of these extreme transformations for visual recognition in both humans and machines. We investigate the thermodynamic characteristics of two-dimensional frustrated trimer antiferromagnets by modeling them as arrays of triangular units linked via interunit interactions. These systems are characterized by strong intraunit correlations and correlations extending across multiple units, presenting significant challenges for conventional Monte Carlo techniques. To address this, we introduce a novel cluster Monte Carlo algorithm that effectively decimates intraunit correlations while simultaneously accounting for the influence of surrounding clusters. Our analysis reveals distinct regimes of long-range order and short-range order within the systems. Specifically, we demonstrate that long-range order emerges when the temperature is sufficiently low and the probability of strong internal bond fluctuations is negligible. Conversely, at high temperatures or with weak interunit interactions, long-range order is absent, and the systems exhibit short-range order. Furthermore, we identify a series of weakly first-order phase transitions in the weak-interaction regime, where the order parameter undergoes a sharp, nonanalytic change. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this cluster Monte Carlo method to systems with even more intricate internal structures. This approach offers a versatile framework for studying complex quantum and classical systems that are otherwise difficult to analyze using traditional Monte Carlo methods. Our findings are supported by numerical results from extensive cluster Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we provide a detailed description of the cluster Monte Carlo technique, including a discussion of the necessary mathematical and physical concepts. This work is designed to be accessible to graduate students and researchers in physics and related disciplines, serving as a valuable resource for those interested in the field. The paper includes detailed explanations of the method, examples, and exercises to aid in understanding and implementation. We also provide a comprehensive bibliography of relevant literature for further reading and research. Our study represents a significant advancement in the field of cluster Monte Carlo methods, offering a robust foundation for future research and development. We believe this work will be highly valuable to graduate students and researchers in physics and related fields, providing a solid basis for advancing the field. We have also made every effort to ensure that the writing is clear and concise, and that the content is as accessible as possible to a broad audience. Although pre-trained language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in vision tasks when equipped with appropriate prompt modules, they often struggle in the few-shot and zero-shot regimes. To address this, we introduce a straightforward yet effective framework that enables language models to perform zero-shot learning on image tasks by explicitly mapping visual features to text features within a multimodal space. This approach involves pre-training on a diverse collection of natural image datasets and then fine-tuning on a set of synthetic tasks designed to mirror the characteristics of target tasks. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of fine-tuning on two distinct types of prompt collections: dataset collections and prompt collections. Experimental results indicate that our method surpasses previous zero-shot techniques, particularly in zero-shot object recognition. This study examines the nature and characteristics of the Electroweak Phase Transition (EWPT) within a specific extension of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM), where the tree-level scalar potential remains invariant under a discrete $Z_3$ symmetry. In this framework, the non-zero vacuum expectation value of the additional singlet scalar field breaks a $U(1)_Y$ gauge symmetry, resulting in a mass for the neutral $Z$ boson. The analysis focuses on a scenario where the singlet scalar acquires a vacuum expectation value at a high energy scale, driving a first-order EWPT. We investigate how this transition influences the production and detection of dark matter candidates, specifically a singlet fermion that remains stable due to a residual $Z_3$ symmetry. Furthermore, we assess the potential for detecting a stochastic gravitational wave background generated by this transition, with a particular emphasis on observations by the LISA observatory. Finally, we analyze the impact of recent LHC findings on this specific NMSSM variant and its implications for dark matter detection. Our findings indicate that LHC results impose significant constraints on the model's parameter space, particularly when attempting to align with the direct detection limits established by LUX and XENON1T. Additionally, we demonstrate that a first-order phase transition, capable of generating a detectable gravitational wave signal, can only occur within a very narrow region of the parameter space. Consequently, we conclude that the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM is not a viable dark matter candidate, as viable parameter spaces are severely restricted by LHC data and direct dark matter search constraints. However, the model remains a promising candidate for explaining the LHC excess observed in the dimuon channel. Finally, we show that a first-order EWPT in this model can produce a gravitational wave signal detectable by LISA, with parameter space ranges compatible with LHC findings. This scenario involves a light Higgs boson with a mass of approximately 120 GeV, a dark matter candidate with a mass near 10 GeV, and a singlet scalar mass around 1 TeV. In this configuration, the dark matter relic density aligns with Planck constraints, and the dark matter particle remains undetected by LUX and XENON1T. We introduce a novel diagnostic method for determining redshifts of (sub)millimeter sources, leveraging the inherent grid structure of the spectral energy distribution (SED) to establish robust redshift limits. By applying this technique to a sample of 120 sources with known redshifts from the COSMOS-Web Legacy Survey, we successfully identified 90 objects with redshifts exceeding 2, achieving a median redshift determination accuracy of 0.18. This approach is now integrated into the MIRIAM pipeline, which utilizes MIRI and BLAST-1000 (or similar) photometry to efficiently derive redshifts for (sub)millimeter sources. We demonstrate the method's efficacy on the COSMOS-Web Legacy Survey sub-mm sample and a newly observed 1.5 deg² region of the COSMOS field, which yielded 120 MIRI 21$\mu$m selected sources with redshifts above 2. The technique is highly effective for sources with redshifts greater than 2, provided they are detected at least two bands in the MIRI 5--21$\mu$m range and detected at all four bands in BLAST-1000 (or similar) photometry. Furthermore, we show that this method can be adapted for other (sub)millimeter surveys, such as the COSMOS-Web Legacy Survey, by adjusting the MIRI and BLAST-1000 (or equivalent) flux limits. We conclude that MIRI 21$\mu$m selected sources represent a valuable resource for (sub)millimeter astronomers, offering a straightforward means to isolate a sample with redshifts greater than 2. This strategy is particularly advantageous for small to medium-sized surveys, such as the COSMOS field, where it enables the selection of a high-purity sample of (sub)millimeter sources with redshifts exceeding 2. Additionally, we highlight that this technique is well-suited for identifying rare (z>2) sources, such as AGN and starbursts, which are expected to exhibit strong emission lines in the 21$\mu$m range. Finally, we demonstrate that MIRI 21$\mu$m selected sources can serve as a robust tracer for (sub)millimeter emission, as evidenced by the strong correlation between MIRI 21$\mu$m flux density and BLAST-1000 1.4 mm flux density. We investigate the thermodynamic properties of the $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice using infinite density matrix renormalization group (iDMRG) applied to an infinite two-dimensional square-lattice cylinder with large girth. By analyzing the behavior of specific thermodynamic quantities, we clearly distinguish the 120-degree ordered state at strong coupling from the spin liquid state in the presence of weak fourth-order anisotropy. Furthermore, we examine the dynamical spin structure factor $S(\mathbf{k},\omega)$, which exhibits a gapless continuum in both phases, though with distinct characteristics. Notably, the peak position at $\mathbf{k}=(2\pi/3,0)$ shifts from $1.04(1)$ to $1.07(1)$ as the system transitions from the 120-degree phase to the spin liquid phase. Finally, we compare our iDMRG findings with recent density-matrix-assisted quantum Monte Carlo (DM-AQMC) results for the spin-liquid phase. Our data align well with DM-AQMC at low energies, while discrepancies emerge at higher energies. We attribute these differences to the distinct fourth-order anisotropy parameters utilized in each method. Overall, this study demonstrates that iDMRG serves as a valuable complement to DM-AQMC for investigating thermodynamic and dynamical properties in weakly anisotropic 3D $S=1/2$ $Z$-spin ice models. Furthermore, we show that iDMRG can effectively capture the qualitative features of dynamical properties within the spin-liquid phase. These findings suggest that iDMRG offers a promising avenue for exploring the thermodynamics and dynamics of frustrated quantum magnets in three dimensions. Finally, we outline the limitations of the iDMRG approach in this context. Specifically, we observe that the girth required to achieve a spin-liquid ground state increases with system size, a phenomenon that may also affect dynamical properties. Consequently, the iDMRG method is likely restricted to studying dynamics only in the lowest energy regime of these models. We conclude by discussing potential strategies to extend iDMRG to investigate dynamical properties beyond this limited energy range. These strategies include employing more sophisticated entanglement truncation schemes and utilizing alternative wave function ansätze. Additionally, we propose that the Gutzwiller variational method could be a viable approach for this purpose. We anticipate that these findings will inspire further research into the variational study

This study examines the confinement-deconfinement transition within $3+1$ dimensional $SU(3)$-Higgs theory, which models a non-Abelian monopole plasma. Utilizing the strong-coupling limit of the theory, we determine the critical Higgs self-interaction coupling where the deconfinement transition occurs. Furthermore, we conduct a renormalization group analysis of the relevant Higgs field couplings and, based on these findings, discuss the potential for a second renormalization group fixed point. Finally, we present a discussion regarding the possibility of a second phase transition. These results are derived using the Monte-Carlo renormalization group method. Additionally, we compare our findings with those obtained from renormalization group equations and perturbation theory. Our analysis indicates that the Higgs field is asymptotically free in the strong-coupling limit, a conclusion that aligns with results from perturbation theory. However, this statement remains valid only up to a specific critical value of the Higgs self-interaction coupling, beyond which perturbative methods are no longer applicable. Finally, we address the implications of these findings for QCD. Specifically, we demonstrate that the confinement-deconfinement transition in QCD cannot be investigated using strong-coupling theory, as the relevant critical parameters fall outside the perturbative regime. Consequently, we suggest that a more intricate phase diagram exists for QCD than previously anticipated. This expanded diagram includes not only the well-known deconfinement transition but also a second transition line that terminates at a second fixed point, a feature that may be relevant to the QCD critical point. To explore this, we also examine the critical exponents associated with this second transition. These conclusions are reached by comparing critical exponents derived from strong-coupling theory, perturbative renormalization group equations, and perturbative quantum chromodynamics. We also provide a discussion on the implications of these results for the QCD phase diagram. Specifically, we show that the critical exponents for the second transition differ from those of the deconfinement transition, implying that the QCD critical point exhibits distinct characteristics from the deconfinement transition point. This conclusion is supported by the observation that the confinement-deconfinement transition line and the critical point are not necessarily identical. These results are consistent with those obtained from renormalization group equations and perturbative quantum chromodynamics. Finally, we demonstrate that the strong-coupling theory accurately reproduces the critical exponents of the deconfinement transition,

Cr$_2$Al crystallizes in the AlB$_2$ structure and serves as a representative material for the class of high-temperature antiferromagnets characterized by the ordering vector $(1/2, 1/2, 1/2)$. This study investigates the magnetic properties of Cr$_2$Al using a combination of first-principles calculations and neutron powder diffraction experiments. First-principles results indicate that the antiferromagnetic state is energetically favored over the nonmagnetic state by approximately $120$ meV per formula unit. The experimental neutron diffraction data confirm the presence of the $(1/2, 1/2, 1/2)$ ordering vector in Cr$_2$Al, with magnetic moments of $0.8(1)$ $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}$/atom at 2 K. First-principles calculations predict an in-plane easy-axis anisotropy, a finding corroborated by the ratio of the antiferromagnetic energy for the $(1/2, 1/2, 1/2)$ vector to that of the $(1/1, 0, 0)$ vector, which is $-1.0(1)$. Furthermore, the calculated nearest-neighbor exchange interaction is antiferromagnetic, whereas the next-nearest-neighbor interaction is ferromagnetic. These results are consistent with the observed magnetic structure, which features in-plane ferromagnetic chains along the $c$-axis and antiferromagnetic coupling between adjacent planes. Additionally, the calculated magnetic structure aligns with the experimentally determined magnetic moment at the $(1/2, 1/2, 1/2)$ position. Finally, the analysis of the pair correlation function of the magnetic structure factor reveals that the antiferromagnetic ordering of Cr atoms along the $c$-axis is primarily driven by the third nearest neighbor. These findings are compared with other materials that share the same ordering vector to provide a broader context. Overall, this work establishes a foundation for future investigations into the origin of the relatively high Néel temperature in Cr$_2$Al. (Note: The original text contained a typo stating "Cr$_2$B"; this has been corrected to "Cr$_2$Al" for consistency.)

This study introduces a kinetic model utilizing a velocity-dependent collision frequency to analyze how the intermolecular potential shapes rarefied gas flows. Specifically, the collision frequency is set proportional to an inverse power of molecular speed, denoted as $U^{-\gamma}$. The model's validity is confirmed by comparing its results against the full Boltzmann equation for hard spheres ($\gamma=0$) and hard cubes ($\gamma=1/3$). Furthermore, the model is applied to two representative scenarios: free molecular flow around a sphere within a uniform shear flow. Finally, the impact of $\gamma$ on these representative flows is examined, with additional flows included to elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms. The model is shown to capture the physical effects of the intermolecular potential, offering a viable alternative to the more complex Boltzmann equation for investigating how molecular potential influences rarefied gas flows. Additionally, the model is extended to a mixture of molecular species, where the collision frequency is defined as a weighted average of the exponents $\gamma$ for each species. This extension is applied to a slip flow scenario to explore the influence of $\gamma$ on slip boundary conditions. The proposed model is noted for its simplicity, computational efficiency, and ease of extension to other relevant physical effects. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/VEL-GAS-KINEMATIC-MODEL}. The model is also available in the open-source software package \texttt{PyBoltz}, which implements the Boltzmann equation for hard spheres and the current velocity-dependent collision frequency model for various flows; PyBoltz can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/PyBoltz/PyBoltz}. Semantic parsing involves learning a mapping from natural language text to formal queries within a specific domain vocabulary. Although recent years have seen significant advancements in this field, existing methods often depend on laborious, manual efforts to define mappings between natural language and domain vocabulary items. This paper introduces Data-driven Grounding, a framework that utilizes minimal training data while eliminating the need for these hand-crafted mappings. We evaluate this approach on two newly created, manually annotated datasets and one publicly available dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across all datasets. Furthermore, we assess the naturalness of the generated sentences on both datasets and conduct an analysis of the model's internal behavior. The code and datasets will be made publicly available. Our findings indicate that mapping-free training yields superior performance and more diverse sentence variations, suggesting that manual ground-truth mappings may hinder the training of robust semantic parsers. We also observe that the model learns to generate sentences containing fewer than three words, a phenomenon we investigate in detail. Finally, we discuss the potential of mapping-free training for applications involving few-shot learning.
