This work examines random field manifolds characterized by Gaussian-distributed metrics. We demonstrate that the statistical properties of their geodesic distances can be computed analytically to any desired order. The first and second moments correspond to the expectations of the metric components and their gradients, respectively. Furthermore, we show that higher-order moments depend on these previously defined expectations, enabling the construction of geodesic distance statistics for random field manifolds. These findings are validated through simulations of geodesic distances within random metrics featuring Gaussian, power-law, and log-normal distributions. Additionally, we derive a relationship between geodesic distances and the correlation function, specifically for the power-law distribution scenario. Finally, we discuss potential applications of these results in the context of large-scale structure. Our methodology is also applicable to random field manifolds where the metric is defined as a power of a power-law function. Given that current cosmological simulations increasingly employ such functions, this approach holds significant relevance. We anticipate that these results will facilitate advancements in understanding the large-scale structure of the Universe. The Python code utilized in this study is publicly accessible. We conduct Rayleigh-Taylor Instability experiments by employing magnetic levitation to induce a controlled initial perturbation. Our findings indicate that the resulting growth rate depends on the length of the instabilities. These results are interpreted through the lens of the Zel'dovich-van der Kooij model, which incorporates the fluid's compressibility. This explanation successfully accounts for the observed growth rates and the identified length scale effect. A detailed counterpart to this explanation, which utilizes a more rigorous theoretical framework, will be released separately. This work serves as a pedagogically simplified introduction designed to provide students with a preliminary understanding of the complex underlying mechanisms. The associated theoretical background is tailored for an upper-level undergraduate or introductory graduate-level course. Let $F$ be a cuspidal Hecke eigenform of weight $k\ge2$ on $\Gamma_0(N)$ with coefficients in a number field $K$. For each $n$, let $a_n\in K$ represent the $n$-th Hecke eigenvalue associated with $F$. We propose the following conjecture:

Conjecture. There exists a constant $C>0$, dependent solely on $F$, such that $|\mathcal{D}_L(n)|\le Cn^k$ holds for all $n$ coprime to $N$, where $\mathcal{D}_L(n)$ denotes the denominator of the $L_n$-adic valuation of $L(F,n)$.

In this work, we demonstrate that this conjecture is valid when $K=\mathbb{Q}$. Furthermore, we provide several examples of cases where $K\neq\mathbb{Q}$ that support the conjecture. Additionally, we present an example illustrating how the conjecture can fail if the conditions are not met. Our approach leverages the $p$-adic theory of automorphic forms, building upon the frameworks established by Blasius and Skinner. We also offer an alternative proof of a theorem by Kim and Shahidi. Our findings suggest that this conjecture may be essential for addressing various open questions in the field. We conclude by outlining potential strategies to resolve this conjecture. This study investigates spin-dependent transport in armchair graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) by integrating spin-orbit coupling (SOC) with Zeeman splitting. We analyze how GNR width, Zeeman effects, and SOC influence transmission and conductance. Our findings indicate that Zeeman splitting creates spin-splitting in both transmission and conductance, while SOC generates finite bias-dependent current asymmetry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that adjusting the Zeeman splitting can manipulate the width of the current plateau at zero bias, enabling spin-polarized transport within narrow-width GNRs. These results suggest that GNRs are promising candidates for developing efficient spintronic devices. Additionally, we find that both SOC and Zeeman splitting can be tuned via electric fields, offering a pathway to design GNRs with optimized properties for specific applications. Finally, we propose that these systems could serve as a platform for exploring Majorana fermions. These conclusions are supported by comprehensive numerical analyses of transmission, quantum Hall effects, and current characteristics. Our findings may also be relevant to other low-dimensional systems exhibiting strong spin-orbit interactions. This study establishes analogues of Korovkin's theorem for weakly nonlinear and monotone operators acting on Banach lattices of multivariate functions. The findings address convergence over entire domains, as well as convergence on closed subdomains characterized by partial continuity or partial differentiability. These results extend the classical Korovki and Bohman-Korovki theorems, which specifically apply to linear positive operators on spaces of real-valued functions. Additionally, the work provides analogues of the "smoothing property" and an Erdős-type theorem within this framework. The authors illustrate the applicability of these theoretical results with examples from standard approximation theory, including linear combinations of B-splines, linear combinations of trigonometric polynomials, linear splines, and linear interpolation. Finally, the paper offers a generalization of a result by R. M. Gatto and A. R. Mola regarding weakly nonlinear positive operators defined on $[0,1]$.

A graph with $n$ vertices is defined as pancyclic if it includes cycles of every length from 2 to $n$. In 1972, Dirac established that any simple, connected, and 2-connected graph is pancyclic. Building on this, Pósa demonstrated that for a sufficiently large $n$, a simple graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and a degree sequence $d_1 \leq d_2 \leq \cdots \leq d_n$ is pancyclic provided that either $d_k > k-2$ and $d_{k+1} + d_{k+2} > n + k + 1$ for some $k < n/2$, or if $G$ is strongly Pósa (meaning $d_k + d_{k+1} > n + k$ for all $k < n/2$). This study presents a novel characterization of pancyclicity based on the independence number. Specifically, if $G$ is a simple, connected, and 2-connected graph with an independence number $\alpha(G) = k$, then $G$ is pancyclic if and only if its minimum degree satisfies $\delta(G) > k$. This finding resolves a longstanding question posed by Pósa. Furthermore, the paper establishes that the strong Pósa condition is both necessary and sufficient for pancyclicity when $\alpha(G) = n/2$. Additionally, the paper offers a new characterization of Hamiltonian graphs using the independence number. These results are complemented by a novel algorithm for determining the independence number of a graph. Finally, the work introduces a new characterization of bipartite graphs and provides a straightforward proof of Dirac's theorem on pancyclicity. The paper concludes with several open problems. Keywords: pancyclic graph, strong Pósa condition, Hamiltonian graph, bipartite graph. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05C35, 05C45. This study introduces a new approach to modeling and controlling dynamical systems by integrating adaptive sparse spectral grids with the sparse-keyed functional approximation ansatz (SFAP) within the Koopman framework. The algorithm employs a combination of recursive and re-sampling techniques to enhance computational efficiency. Its primary advantage lies in its ability to estimate the spectral representation of the Koopman operator for systems with high-dimensional state spaces, thereby overcoming the curse of dimensionality inherent in traditional methods. This capability enables the application of spectral techniques, such as spectral control, to more complex systems. The proposed method's performance is evaluated through numerical experiments, including the control of a 20-link robotic arm and the prediction of the California Current System. Additionally, a biological case study examines the dynamics of the yeast cell cycle, demonstrating how the model can identify key regulatory proteins and their interactions. The results indicate that the Koopman model derived from this approach is effective for both system prediction and control. Finally, the paper discusses the method's potential for control applications and outlines future research directions. Keywords: Koopman operator, functional approximation, dimensionality reduction, adaptive sparse grid. This study investigates the ionization of atoms and molecules subjected to strong direct-current (DC) electric fields using the time-independent Schrödinger equation. By incorporating exterior complex scaling, the research examines ionization rates across a broad spectrum of DC fields, offering fresh insights into phenomena such as electron capture, over-the-barrier ionization, and tunnel ionization. Furthermore, the study analyzes molecular alignment dynamics, revealing a correlation between ionization rates and alignment behavior. Additionally, to facilitate comparisons with experimental data, the work provides ionization rates for argon and deuterium. Finally, the study explores the impact of static electric fields on bound states, demonstrating how these fields influence autoionization rates in two-electron atoms. These findings are achieved through extensive calculations utilizing a basis set of Gauss-type orbitals. The study concludes by discussing potential extensions of this approach to more complex atomic and molecular systems. Overall, this work establishes a foundation for future research into the ionization of atoms and molecules under strong DC fields. Key words: exterior complex scaling, DC fields, ionization, electron capture, molecular alignment. PACS numbers: 31.15.-p, 32.80.-t, 52.20.-h.

The Sinkhorn algorithm is a widely used iterative method for solving the Schrödinger system linked to the optimal transport problem with quadratic costs in $\mathbb{R}^2$. This study examines the algorithm's convergence behavior when the existence of a solution to the Schrödinger problem is not guaranteed. We demonstrate that the Sinkhorn iterates converge to a pair of measures satisfying the necessary marginal conditions, though these limits fail to achieve the infimum within the Schrödinger problem. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of a specific sequence derived from the iterates when the Sinkhorn algorithm diverges. Finally, we illustrate the algorithm's performance through various examples, including cases involving discrete measures and functions with compact support, as well as scenarios involving measures without compact support. These outcomes highlight the limitations of Sinkhorn convergence, suggesting the need for alternative approaches to address the non-existence of a solution in the optimal transport problem with quadratic costs. Additionally, we explore a novel approach to the classical Monge problem for quadratic costs, which yields a positive convergence result for a modified Sinkhorn-type algorithm. This new method utilizes a specific family of approximations to the infimum, where a specific approximation sequence yields the necessary necessary conditions for Monge's optimal transport problem. The paper concludes with a discussion on further research directions. This work extends the findings of [10] regarding the Sinkhorn convergence in the context of the Monge problem.

Keywords: Optimal transport, Monge problem, Schrödinger problem, KMT problem, discretization, iterative methods.

This study presents a measurement of the top-quark pair ($t\bar{t}$) production cross-section in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis relies on events where both W bosons from the top quarks decay leptonically. Data were gathered over an integrated luminosity of 32.6 fb$^{-1}$ during the LHC Run 2 period. The measured cross-section is $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 820 \pm 10 \text{(stat)} \pm 14 \text{(syst)}$ pb, which aligns with Standard Model predictions. Additionally, differential cross-sections are reported as functions of the transverse momentum of the $t\bar{t}$ system, the rapidity of the individual top quarks, and the transverse momentum and rapidity of the charged leptons. Differential measurements for the invariant mass and rapidity of the $t\bar{t}$ system are also provided. All observed differential cross-sections are consistent with Standard Model expectations. This work represents the first differential cross-section measurements for $t\bar{t}$ production at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV. Furthermore, the ATLAS collaboration has conducted similar measurements at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, which are currently the most precise available. Comparing these two energy levels offers valuable insights for Standard Model predictions and theoretical models involving new particles. The comparison yields a relative uncertainty of 3.5% for the $t\bar{t}$ cross-section at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, compared to 2.1% at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. Additionally, the paper includes a study on the impact of the charged-particle rapidity gap between the primary and secondary interaction vertices on the precision of the $t\bar{t}$ cross-section measurement. This effect is found to be negligible in events where both top quarks decay leptonically. Overall, this work demonstrates the ATLAS detector's capability for high-precision cross-section measurements in the $t\bar{t}$ channel. The results provide a benchmark for future studies of the $t\bar{t}$ process at higher energies, such as those planned for the High-Luminosity LHC. Although localized thermal equilibrium is generally prohibited by the equipartition theorem, it can emerge in both equilibrium and non-equilibrium scenarios when systems are sufficiently far from equilibrium. This study examines a non-equilibrium central unit coupled to an extensive array of harmonic oscillators that are themselves at thermal equilibrium. We demonstrate that the system exhibits relaxation toward a non-equilibrium steady state, where the central mode displays localized behavior by settling into a specific frequency and amplitude. Furthermore, we establish that this localized dynamics is universal, as it occurs across a wide range of temperatures, driving forces, and natural frequencies. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings using both classical and quantum mechanical frameworks. Notably, in the quantum regime, we observe that the center of the position distribution for the driven-damped mode equilibrates with the rest of the system, whereas its amplitude remains distinct. This result indicates that quantum systems can achieve a form of partial equilibrium, where the position wave function is localized while the amplitude wave function maintains a steady-state distribution. These findings offer a pathway to experimentally verify the existence of localized thermal equilibrium. Additionally, this setup may facilitate the creation of a localized, non-equilibrium central mode within an otherwise equilibrated environment, a critical requirement for investigating energy transfer mechanisms in biological systems. Specifically, our model provides a theoretical basis for the controversial debate regarding whether vibrational energy transfer in the Fenna-Matthews-Ohlson complex proceeds via a localized or delocalized mechanism. By comparing our predictions with experimental data, we can determine which model accurately describes the underlying energy transfer process. This approach underscores the broader significance of our work in addressing a fundamental question in both theoretical and experimental physics. Finally, our model holds potential for diverse applications in both biological and non-biological systems. For instance, it could explain how a single, localized vibrational mode is generated in a carbon nanotube following an impact, thereby triggering a specific mechanical response. Moreover, our approach can be extended to investigate the localized dynamics of driven-dissipative two-level systems, which are essential for quantum information processing. By coupling a central two-level system to an otherwise equilibrated environment, we can investigate the universal characteristics of its steady-state behavior. Ultimately, our findings suggest that quantum systems can reach a type of "partial" equilibrium, where the position wave function becomes localized while the amplitude wave function retains a unique, non-equilibrium distribution. This concept of "partial" equilibrium is expected to be relevant in various contexts, including quantum information processing and the study of localized vibrational energy transfer

Urban environments are renowned for generating a wide array of social interactions, which are vital for fostering economic growth and social equity. These interactions are closely tied to the diversity of urban encounters. This study examines how altered human behavior during the COVID-19 pandemic influenced the diversity of encounters in New York City. We developed a framework that links encounter diversity to city-wide social distancing efforts and the adoption of remote work. Our analysis of nearly 10 million geolocation records from 2019 and 2020 reveals a significant decline in income diversity during the pandemic, despite remote work remaining stable. We attribute this drop to increased segregation in work locations, which reduced opportunities for diverse face-to-face interactions. These results underscore the critical role of urban spaces in providing varied face-to-face encounters and the necessity of maintaining them even during public health crises. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the diversity of face-to-face interactions serves as a valuable metric for assessing the broader societal and economic impacts of pandemic-related behavioral shifts. Finally, we explore how this framework can be applied to other pandemic-related phenomena, such as social isolation and the spread of misinformation. Our research underscores the value of large-scale, high-resolution human mobility data for comprehending the intricate effects of the pandemic on urban life. Additionally, it demonstrates the potential of such data to inform the design of behavior-modifying interventions aimed at mitigating the pandemic's socioeconomic consequences. The dataset and code used in this research are accessible at https://github.com/urbananalytics/encounter-diversity. This study evaluates various nonlinear field-splitting (FS) preconditioners designed for two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media, utilizing the open-source TOUGH-SEW code. We introduce and assess a new nonlinear FS preconditioner based on the locally adaptive geometric multigrid (LMG) method, which is integrated with a new multipoint flux approximation (MPFA-O) scheme. Additionally, we compare it against two other nonlinear FS preconditioners employing the standard multigrid (MG) method paired with either the standard or optimized finite volume (OFV) schemes. Our findings indicate that the proposed preconditioner offers superior performance compared to the two MFV-based alternatives. Furthermore, when contrasting LMG-based versus MG-based approaches using the optimized PV scheme, LMG-based preconditioners demonstrate better performance, provided that the LMG method is applied to both the wet and nonwetting phases. Finally, we observe that the LMG method enhances the convergence of two-phase flow problems by mitigating the impact of permeability contrasts between adjacent grid cells. However, in scenarios involving highly heterogeneous permeability, LMG-based preconditioners may still encounter convergence difficulties. To address this, we propose a strategy that restricts the application of the LMG method to grid cells with moderate permeability variations, which effectively resolves the convergence issues associated with highly heterogeneous permeability. Our results confirm that this approach significantly improves the performance of LMG-based preconditioners in such cases. The paper also includes a detailed discussion on the implementation of LMG-based preconditioners for two-phase flow. Our analysis demonstrates that the LMG method is a viable alternative to traditional MFV-based multigrid techniques for two-phase flow problems in heterogeneous porous media. Additionally, we note that the LMG method is highly adaptable to diverse grid types and can be readily extended to other multiphase flow problems. Finally, we highlight that the proposed LMG-based preconditioner for two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media is highly efficient, as it requires only a single multigrid hierarchy. This efficiency is particularly advantageous for problems with moderate permeability contrasts, where it substantially reduces the number of outer iterations needed for convergence. However, for problems with high permeability contrasts, such as those found in shale formations, we recommend applying the LMG method only to grid cells with moderate permeability variations. This strategy is highly effective in resolving convergence issues in highly heterogeneous permeability problems, such as those involving shale formations, while maintaining the computational efficiency of a single multigrid hierarchy. We introduce an optical cavity featuring a single-handedness (chiral) structure, in which left-handed and right-handed configurations produce distinct resonant modes. This design is implemented using a one-dimensional array of plasmonic oligomers, where the inter-particle spacing is calibrated to generate two separate resonance peaks corresponding to each handedness. Given its potential for asymmetric light-matter interactions, this cavity is a crucial component for next-generation chiral photonic devices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that injecting chiral molecules into the cavity enhances their chiral sensitivity. Our proposed designs achieve both high-asymmetry and high-peak-quality factors, establishing a foundation for the development of advanced chiral devices. Additionally, we show that this cavity structure can effectively separate circularly polarized light. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this one-dimensional plasmonic system in optical switching and signal processing. The Alcubierre metric represents a solution to Einstein's field equations enabling superluminal travel. Originally derived as a vacuum solution with zero cosmological constant ($\Lambda$) driven by the Alcubierre stress-energy tensor, this work presents a novel warped spacetime solution for a cosmological constant ($\Lambda$) within a perfect fluid framework. We derive a new warp drive metric for a general cosmological constant $\Lambda$ in four-dimensional spacetime, expressed via a time-dependent function $f(t)$. This new metric adheres to the weak energy condition, thereby providing a physically viable warp drive model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a superluminal warp drive is achievable in a universe containing a cosmological constant. The study concludes with an analysis of the physical implications of these findings. A comprehensive discussion of the warp drive concept is reserved for future research. This paper is dedicated to Miguel Alcubierre on the occasion of his 70th birthday. Keywords: Alcubierre metric, warp drive, cosmological constant, perfect fluid. PACS: 04.20.Jb, 04.50.+h, 98.80.Hk.

We experimentally investigate spin-dependent dephasing of qubits in a two-dimensional Paul trap by modulating the secular modes. This dephasing serves as a probe for motional state distributions and mode temperatures, offering a dephasing metric that correlates with secular heating rates. Our findings reveal that spin-dependent dephasing relies on both the amplitudes and temperatures of thermalized collective excitations and on non-thermal, incoherent excitations. These results demonstrate that dephasing can arise from a broad spectrum of motional state distributions, facilitating the calibration of techniques designed to prepare specific target distributions. Furthermore, we determine that heating rates are highest for modes that most effectively drive dephasing. These insights into dephasing and motional states are applicable to future experiments utilizing trapped ions. Additionally, we present a method for preparing arbitrary mode temperature distributions, which is essential for quantum-enhanced sensing and metrology. This approach leverages the dephasing mechanism to precisely control mode temperatures. We validate this method by successfully preparing mode temperatures with minimal uncertainties. Finally, we outline a protocol for preparing multimode ion crystals in Gaussian Wigner-Dalembert states. These findings regarding dephasing and motional state preparation are expected to be valuable for future applications in quantum-enhanced sensing and metrology. Specifically, we demonstrate that this Gaussian Wigner-Dalembert state produces a dephasing curve that is nearly identical to the dephasing observed with a Gaussian coherent state. This indicates that the dephasing mechanism is insensitive to the relative weights of the Wigner and Dalembert components, a property that can be exploited to mitigate spin-dependent dephasing. Our proposed dephasing mitigation strategy is expected to be broadly applicable to future quantum-enhanced sensing and metrology. We illustrate this by showing that the dephasing curve for the Wigner-Dalembert state is significantly lower than that of the Schrodinger cat state, which is a leading candidate for quantum-enhanced metrology. This demonstrates that dephasing can be tailored to the specific requirements of a given metrological task. Overall, these results provide a comprehensive understanding of dephasing as a tool for motional state characterization and establish a foundation for developing quantum-enhanced sensing and metrology. Terahertz radiation (0.3–10 THz) offers resonant excitation of molecular vibrations and long wavelengths capable of penetrating biological tissues. However, its weak interaction with matter results in low signal-to-noise ratios. To address this, we investigate quantum-enhanced detection via tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS), which amplifies both electric and magnetic fields at the tip apex. This study compares the two magnetic components: magnetic dipole (MD) coupling and the electric field-induced current loop (ICL) contribution. To accurately model these effects, a fully quantum mechanical approach is employed that includes both the quantum nature of light and the induced electronic response of molecules. The research specifically examines the terahertz resonant excitation of vibrational modes in water molecules near a silver tip. Results indicate that magnetic resonance detection via TERS is feasible, with the ICL contribution being more than an order of magnitude stronger than the MD one. This finding underscores the necessity of accounting for magnetic responses in quantum-enhanced TERS and highlights its potential for terahertz spectroscopy. Additionally, the study explores the impact of tip geometry on magnetic coupling, demonstrating that a bullet-shaped tip yields a higher magnetic cross-section than a sphere-sphere tip. Finally, the influence of molecular orientation on magnetic coupling is analyzed, revealing that the ICL contribution is approximately three times greater for water molecules oriented along the tip axis compared to those perpendicular to it. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of magnetic coupling in TERS, offering a pathway to quantum-enhanced magnetic detection. Furthermore, the methodology is applicable to other scenarios, such as sensing chiral molecules or detecting magnetic materials. The accompanying open-source Python code enables the calculation of both electric and magnetic contributions to TERS. This work establishes a foundation for developing quantum-enhanced magnetic detection techniques, which could lead to new applications in nanoscale sensing. We conducted observations of 11 nearby galaxies to detect Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) in the K-band (21.5 GHz) using the Sardinia Radio Telescope. Our findings reveal a correlation between K-band flux densities and Amplitude of Microwave Emission (AME) values, with a best-fit linear relation of $AME = 1.1 \pm 0.2 \times 10^3 \frac{S_K}{S_K^{\odot}} - 0.5 \pm 0.1 \times 10^3$, where $S_K^{\odot} = 1.5 \times 10^{-4}$ Jy. This result supports the hypothesis that dust emission is the primary driver of AME. Additionally, we determined the spectral index $\alpha$ for six galaxies, finding values ranging from 1.9 to 3.2, which aligns with expectations for AME. For the remaining five galaxies, we established upper limits on $\alpha$ between 2.0 and 4.0. Furthermore, we derived upper limits on K-band flux densities for three galaxies lacking prior measurements, which are lower than previously reported values. These outcomes represent the first comprehensive study of AME across a sample of nearby galaxies. The data will be accessible at http://www.astro.srt.astro.it/AME. Ammonium sulfate ($\mathrm{(NH_4)_2SO_4}$) exhibits a ferroelectric-to-paraelectric phase transition accompanied by a significant entropy shift, making it a promising candidate for molecular caloric applications. This study investigates the origin of this large entropy variation by integrating first-principles calculations with experimental data. Our analysis reveals that the entropy change stems from the complex interplay between the vibrational entropy of the $\mathrm{(NH_4)^+}$ ion and that of the remainder of the crystal lattice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this coupled vibrational entropy is intrinsically linked to the structural instability of the $\mathrm{(NH_4)^+}$ ion within the high-symmetry phase. These findings offer a comprehensive explanation for the entropy phenomenon and a framework for identifying new materials with superior caloric performance. Additionally, our results indicate that $\mathrm{(NH_4)_2SO_4}$ could serve as an effective model system for examining the connection between ion rotational entropy and ferroelectricity. Finally, we propose a potential strategy for enhancing the caloric effect in this material by substituting a portion of the $\mathrm{(NH_4)^+}$ ions with methylammonium ions. This approach would increase the rotational entropy of the ion, thereby boosting the entropy change during the phase transition. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted a preliminary first-principles study on a mixed crystal of $\mathrm{(NH_4)_2SO_4}$ and $\mathrm{CH_3NH_3SO_4}$, which yielded promising outcomes. These results suggest that this specific compositional modification could lead to a material with a ferroelectric Curie temperature near room temperature and a ferroelectric polarization exceeding $100~\mu\mathrm{C/cm^2}$. Our methodology is broadly applicable to other materials, such as lead halide perovskites, which are widely investigated for their potential in optoelectronic and energy technologies. By analyzing the entropy change associated with their ferroelectric-to-paraelectric transitions, we can gain a deeper understanding of their intrinsic properties and identify promising candidates for future device applications. Ultimately, this research underscores the critical role of entropy analysis in materials science. A thorough examination of entropy can elucidate the origin of entropy changes, which is essential for understanding the underlying mechanisms of phase transitions and for designing new materials with enhanced caloric properties. Although numerous studies have identified various neurochemical signals associated with learning, few have examined the relationship between these markers and the behavioral strategies they indicate. We investigated the correlation between dopamine release—measured via fast-scan cyclic voltammetry—and the learning strategies derived from monkey behavior during a probabilistic reward task. Our results show that suboptimal learning strategies are linked to dopamine signals that align with both outcome prediction errors and the change in value following an event. Furthermore, when participants were informed of the task rules, suboptimal strategies correlated with dopamine responses to prediction errors, whereas optimal strategies were linked to responses regarding the new expected value. These findings demonstrate that neurochemical signals of prediction errors, generated during learning, correlate with suboptimal strategies, suggesting that dopamine may not be essential for optimal learning. These insights offer a potential explanation for the diverse behavioral effects observed in animal studies involving dopamine manipulation. This study addresses the Approximate Near Neighbor Search (ANN) problem under the Fréchet distance for a set $\mathcal{P}$ of $n$ polygonal curves, each with $m$ vertices. The objective is to efficiently identify all query points $q \in Q$ that admit a near neighbor in $\mathcal{P}$ within an approximation factor of $\tau > 1$. We establish a baseline algorithm achieving a worst-case query time of $\tilde{O}(|Q| m^{2+\epsilon})$ and construction time of $\tilde{O}(n m)$ for any $\epsilon > 0$. Leveraging a grid-based approach, we demonstrate that when the data is well-separated with a $\tau$-separation ratio, the algorithm can be optimized to run in $\tilde{O}(|Q| m)$ query time and $\tilde{O}(n m)$ construction time. Furthermore, we prove that these bounds are nearly tight by deriving a lower bound of $\Omega(m^{1 + 1/(\lfloor 2^\tau \rfloor + 1)})$ for the best possible worst-case query time. Additionally, we show that the algorithm's performance degrades to $\tilde{O}(|Q| m^{3 + \epsilon})$ query time and $\tilde{O}(n m)$ construction time when the separation ratio is defined as the maximum separation across all scales. Finally, by integrating our proposed techniques with the recent near-tight bounds for Fréchet ANN presented by Bortolot et al. (2022), we derive a worst-case query time of $\tilde{O}(|Q| m^{2 + 2/(\lfloor 2^\tau \rfloor + 1)})$ and a construction time of $\tilde{O}(n m^{1 + 1/(\lfloor 2^\tau \rfloor + 1)})$. These results are supported by a detailed analysis of the algorithm's behavior on real-world datasets. To our knowledge, this represents the first ANN algorithm for time series under the Fréchet distance that operates within nearly tight bounds. Our findings also yield the first subquadratic-time construction algorithm for Fréchet ANN in the Euclidean plane. Moreover, we extend our approach to solve ANN for polygonal curves under the Fréchet distance with respect to a fixed obstacle, a problem with significant applications in Geographic Information Systems. Measurement error mitigation (MEM) is a technique designed to enhance the fidelity of quantum computing results by correcting systematic readout errors. This work introduces a scalable MEM approach that leverages the high-dimensional data capacity of quantum processors to boost measurement fidelity. The proposed method, Iterative Bayesian Unfolding (IBU), utilizes a quantum error mitigation protocol to refine initial raw data through multiple iterations. IBU is compatible with a wide range of existing protocols, including basis adjustment, and can be seamlessly integrated with them. Experimental results demonstrate that combining IBU with basis adjustment achieves a final fidelity of 99.6%, surpassing the physical limit of standard readout capabilities. Furthermore, IBU exhibits robustness against both systematic and random noise. These findings indicate that IBU holds significant potential for improving the fidelity of quantum computing outcomes. This study examines how shared autonomy can facilitate communication with human operators. By delegating specific tasks to an autonomous robot, operators are meant to reduce their workload; however, such autonomy also establishes a convention that allows an operator to request task handovers without explicitly stating the underlying reason. This paper investigates whether these conventions can serve as a channel for the operator and robot to negotiate and align on the reasons for delegation requests. The experiment involved a human participant and a simulated partner operating a vehicle to navigate a dynamic, two-lane road. The simulation featured two distinct modes: shared, where the vehicle was controlled by both the human and a computer agent, and autonomous, where the computer agent controlled the vehicle independently. In this setup, the computer agent acted based on a specific purpose, such as yielding to oncoming traffic or clearing the path for a vehicle behind, and proposed delegation times accordingly. The study gathered data from 20 participants across 40 trials. Results indicated that participants could infer the agent's purpose from their delegation timing, though they tended to yield later than optimal. Furthermore, participants expressed a desire to communicate the reason for delegation to the agent. Although the current system does not support such communication, the findings suggest that refining the purpose of delegations could enable agents to better understand human intentions. Consequently, this research demonstrates that robot-convention-based shared autonomy can facilitate the study of human-agent communication, thereby laying the groundwork for developing communication-enhancing systems. Future work will explore how to implement such systems. The code and data are accessible at: https://github.com/robertkay/understanding-purposes-in-shared-autonomy. Keywords: Shared Autonomy, Human-Robot Interaction, Human-Agent Teamwork, Purpose, Negotiation.

Autonomous navigation within unfamiliar settings is a critical ability for mobile robots. While Topological Maps (TM) are widely used for path planning in large, unknown areas, they often fail to capture sufficient detail for precise localization and obstacle avoidance. Conversely, Metric Maps (MM) excel at representing the geometry of known areas but struggle with path planning in unknown territories. This paper introduces HiTMap, a novel hybrid representation that merges the strengths of TMs and MMs to achieve robust navigation in unknown environments. Specifically, HiTMap, as its name implies, constructs a hierarchical map by integrating topological and metric data. For path planning, it utilizes topological nodes to navigate between key map locations, switching to metric maps for precise movement and obstacle avoidance upon approaching these nodes. Experimental results demonstrate that HiTMap surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in terms of path optimality, traversal speed, and success rate. Furthermore, we evaluated HiTMap in both simulated and real-world scenarios, confirming its superior performance over existing approaches. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/hiitlab/HiTMap.

The IGCC is developed by selecting multivariable functions within a finite field, yielding an expansion factor of $p^2$, where $p$ represents the prime or power of a prime used in the finite field size. The 2D-ZCAC is built using multivariable functions and array techniques, achieving an expansion factor of $(r+1)^2$ with a variable range of $0\leq k\leq r-1$. Both schemes offer zero inter-group or 2D-correlation, a significantly larger expansion factor compared to existing techniques, and support flexible parameter selection. Additionally, algebraic properties of multivariable functions are utilized to enable efficient generation algorithms for the IGCC and 2D-ZCAC. Numerical simulations confirm the validity of these proposed coding sets. These results demonstrate that multivariable functions are a promising tool for constructing low-distortion sequences and arrays, with the IGCC and 2D-ZCAC offering substantial potential for wireless communication applications. Furthermore, multivariable functions hold promise for future coding set constructions that require higher expansion factors and greater flexibility. Finally, the inter-group correlation of the IGCC and the 2D-intercorrelation of the 2D-ZCAC are analyzed. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the correlation properties of these sets using multivariable functions. These findings provide a foundation for future research into coding sets designed for wireless communication systems. Computed Tomography (CT) is a critical imaging technique widely used in both medical and industrial applications. However, acquiring data via CT is time-intensive and demands substantial computational resources. Consequently, there is a pressing need to develop models that are both fast and precise. This paper introduces a new variational framework for simultaneously reconstructing images, denoising sensor data, and performing material decomposition, specifically tailored for polyenergetic X-ray CT. The proposed approach utilizes a non-convex model designed to enhance sharp edges and denoise the ct-sensor signal. We demonstrate the convergence of the algorithm through a proof of boundedness and utilize the primal-dual proof technique to establish the global convergence of the minimizer sequence. Numerical experiments conducted on synthetic and real-world data confirm the method's effectiveness and superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the study presents a fast implementation leveraging the primal-dual approach, which is highly suitable for real-time CT applications. This paper introduces a novel contextual Named Entity Retrieval (NER) task designed to evaluate a retriever's capacity to identify contextually relevant entities within a specific query context. We define this challenge as a top-k search problem utilizing a term relevance feedback approach. To assess the task's difficulty, we developed a new dataset, CTEC, which comprises over 100,000 real-world examples derived from conversations on the Reddit platform. Electronic Health Records (EHRs) are extensively utilized in healthcare, yet their vast size hinders efficient data mining. While recent research has leveraged knowledge graphs to model EHRs, these approaches often overlook the temporal dimensions inherent in patient histories. This study introduces a novel heterogeneous similarity graph neural network designed to integrate temporal information into EHR modeling. The proposed method employs a heterogeneous graph where nodes represent entities and edges denote relationships. A similarity graph is constructed using a patient history as input, with nodes corresponding to EHR elements and weighted edges reflecting edge features. The model utilizes a heterogeneous graph neural network to aggregate features from both elements and edges, generating embeddings for each element. These embeddings are then applied to predict comorbidities and mortality. Experimental results demonstrate that the model achieves an AUC of 0.81 in predicting comorbidities and 0.74 in predicting mortality. Furthermore, the model exhibits robustness in handling missing features. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/EHR-Embedding. This study employs the Poisson-Boltzmann framework to examine how solvent polarization influences the electric double layer forming near a uniformly charged soft surface within an electrolyte solution. Our findings indicate that accounting for solvent polarization leads to a reduction in net charge density at the interface between the brush and the surrounding solution, alongside an increase in the Gouy-Chapman charge at the electric maximum. These results are attributed to the polarization-induced electric dipole moment of the solvent. Additionally, we investigated the impact of the glass dielectric constant on the size of the electrically active layer within a polyelectrolyte brush. We determined that when the dielectric constant of the polarized solvent approaches that of the polymer brush, the electrically active layer thins. However, if the polarized solvent's dielectric constant is significantly lower than that of the brush, the electrically active layer expands. These observations are also explained by the phenomenon of solvent polarization. Finally, we conclude that incorporating solvent polarization into the Poisson-Boltzmann model is essential for accurately describing the electric double layer at a charged soft surface in a polar solvent. This conclusion is supported by experimental data from polyacrylic acid brushes in water, which demonstrate that neglecting solvent polarization in the Poisson-Boltzmann model fails to accurately predict the electric double layer at a charged soft surface. Furthermore, we note that this model is applicable to both symmetric and asymmetric electrolytes. Our analysis reveals that while solvent polarization affects the brush's net charge density, electrically active layer size, and the distribution of counterions and coions, it does not alter the potential of zero charge. Finally, we emphasize that solvent polarization is more pronounced in polyelectrolyte brushes composed of weak polyelectrolytes. These conclusions are also corroborated by experimental data regarding poly(N-isopropylacrylamide-co-methacrylic acid) brushes. In this specific case, we observed that the electrically active layer in weak polyelectrolyte brushes is thinner than in strong polyelectrolyte brushes, a result also consistent with predictions from the Poisson-Boltzmann model that includes solvent polarization. Additionally, we found that the electrically active layer in a weak polyelectrolyte brush diminishes as the dielectric constant of the polarized solvent increases. Automating the identification of software requirements from text is a laborious and error-prone process. While numerous studies have addressed this, most depend on structured inputs like JSON or XML to locate requirement sentences. However, in real-world scenarios, engineers often face unstructured documents such as emails, meeting notes, and news articles. This paper introduces a novel dataset comprising 1,000 unlabeled English documents containing 4,090 unstructured request sentences, annotated by domain experts with both unlabeled and labeled data. We present a new neural network architecture that utilizes a transformer-based language model to predict requirement labels for individual sentences. Furthermore, we propose a new algorithm designed to efficiently select the most relevant unstructured request sentences from an input document. Our model achieves an F1 score of 0.72 on the new dataset and surpasses state-of-the-art approaches on existing datasets. Additionally, our selection algorithm outperforms existing methods, yielding an average precision improvement of 10% across three datasets. Finally, we explore how unstructured data can enhance the quality of software requirement models. The dataset and associated code are accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta123456789/experts_reqs. This work was presented at the 44th International Conference on Software Engineering. This study investigates the energy efficiency of a wireless network employing network coding, where two source nodes transmit to their respective destinations through a cooperative relay. We formulate an optimization problem aimed at maximizing energy efficiency, subject to the constraint that every destination must be reached by at least a minimum proportion of sources. This constraint ensures that no destination is overwhelmed by a disproportionate number of coding requests. The proposed solution is a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves an optimal solution within a specified error margin. This study presents a first-principles theoretical investigation into the spin-polarized Kondo effect, specifically Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states within a half-metallic body-centered-cubic (bcc) niobium (Nb) surface. The research employs a fully relativistic method, incorporating spin-orbit coupling, to examine an Mn adatom and two configurations of Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface. For the adatom, YSR states are observed at the surface Fermi level, with spin-orbit coupling significantly altering their spin texture. In the case of dimers, splitting of the YSR states is detected, a phenomenon that cannot be explained by non-relativistic calculations. These findings offer valuable insights for interpreting recent scanning tunneling microscopy experiments on this system. Additionally, the study provides a comprehensive analysis of the Kondo effect in a half-metallic environment. The developed theoretical framework is broadly applicable to investigating YSR states in other transition metal impurities on Nb and in graphene on topological superconductors. Furthermore, it holds general relevance for exploring the Kondo effect in spin-polarized systems. All employed techniques are implemented in the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method, which is fully relativistic and spin-polarized, utilizing the exact Green's function for surface systems. This approach enables the calculation of complete spectral functions, spin textures, and spin-orbit-induced splittings of YSR states. The theory is also capable of addressing the Kondo effect in bulk systems, including the spin-split Kondo resonance in topological superconductors. All methods are fully non-perturbative and can be extended to fully spin-orbit-coupled systems. The approach is versatile, applicable to both finite and infinite systems, and valid for both non-polarized and spin-polarized settings. It is fully non-empirical, relying solely on the local density approximation for exchange-correlation interactions. The theory is sufficiently general to be adapted for other electronic structure methods, such as the GW approximation, and can be extended to fully relativistic systems, including those with spin-orbit coupling. Finally, the method is fully non-perturbative, allowing for the systematic inclusion of higher-order effects in the Kondo interaction. The code is publicly available. Distribution-to-distribution (D2D) registration is a critical step in point cloud processing, which is widely utilized in applications like autonomous driving and 3D mapping. However, these scenarios often introduce non-rigid deformations and noise, leading to significant drift in the resulting point cloud distribution. This paper introduces a D2D scan matching technique that employs distribution warping to mitigate registration bias. The proposed method, which relies on D2D registration, effectively reduces drift by accounting for non-rigid deformations, noise, and other errors. Experimental results demonstrate that the method achieves state-of-the-art performance, reducing drift by 50% compared to other D2D scan matching approaches. Additionally, the method exhibits robustness in real-world applications, successfully handling non-rigid deformations, varying lighting conditions, and occlusions. Satellite imagery is extensively utilized for various applications, including land cover mapping, object detection, and change detection. While deep learning methods have significantly enhanced the quality of outcomes in these areas, they are often computationally intensive and necessitate large volumes of labeled training data. This paper introduces a deep learning-free approach for detecting objects in satellite images. We develop a semi-unsupervised edge detection technique that requires only a single labeled image to generate a segmentation map. This technique is evaluated against both traditional edge detection algorithms and deep learning models. The results demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses conventional techniques and performs comparably to deep learning approaches while being far less dependent on annotated data. Furthermore, the method is highly efficient, capable of detecting edges in an entire Sentinel-2 satellite strip within approximately 10 seconds on a standard laptop. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of semi-unsupervised learning to edge detection in satellite imagery. Detecting and segmenting brain lesions is essential for diagnosing and managing Multiple Sclerosis (MS). However, deep learning models often struggle to generalize across different institutions due to variations in MRI scanners and protocols. This study investigates the impact of domain shift on MS lesion segmentation and evaluates a continuous training approach that addresses domain gap issues. We introduce a new, large-scale dataset comprising 10,000 manually segmented MS lesions from four distinct hospitals, with 7,000 images reserved for testing. Our experiments demonstrate that training a segmentation model on this diverse data yields significant performance gains compared to models trained on single-hospital data. Furthermore, we find that continuously training a model across these domains is more effective than retraining from scratch, as it better mitigates domain shift. Finally, we assess how varying proportions of source and target domain images affect model generalization in cross-hospital settings. Dynamical systems are defined by equations that evolve over time, with fluid dynamics serving as a primary example. These models are typically imperfect, stemming from incomplete data, simplifying assumptions, or unmodeled physical effects. Consequently, the resulting errors can be substantial and significantly influence the systems' evolution. This study introduces a framework utilizing data-driven methods to learn model errors within dynamical systems. The approach employs model error as a latent variable within a variational formulation, which is solved via an augmented Lagrangian technique. We apply this method to a straightforward fluid dynamics model, demonstrating that it can accurately replicate the complex behavior of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations using only two-dimensional data. Furthermore, the learned error can be transferred to a reduced-order model, thereby enhancing its predictive accuracy. This methodology is versatile and can be extended to other scenarios, including nonlinear dimensionality reduction, discovery of partial differential equation terms, and the correction of other imperfect models. Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for applying machine learning to improve imperfect models in dynamical systems. We present findings from a study of the Dragon IRDC (G033.00+00.3), a nearby molecular cloud hosting the massive star-forming region G033.00+00.3A. Utilizing the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array, we conducted a survey of the 1.3 mm continuum emission across a 1.5 pc scale, revealing a filamentary structure with a characteristic width of approximately 0.1 pc. This study identifies 15 dense cores within G033.00+00.3A, with the most prominent being G033.00+00.3A-1, a massive core roughly 0.05 pc in size and 10^4 solar masses. Our analysis indicates that the Dragon IRDC consists of a network of filaments, where the Dragon SC005 filament is the most massive, containing about 10^4 solar masses. Furthermore, the Dragon IRDC exhibits a core density profile that aligns with the core growth model proposed by Klessen et al. (2012). This observation suggests that the core's mass increases as the star-forming region G033.00+00.3A evolves. Additionally, we identified a large-scale outflow originating from G033.00+00.3A, which may offer insights into the early stages of massive star formation. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results regarding the core growth model and the formation mechanisms of massive star-forming regions. These findings underscore the necessity of high-resolution observations to investigate the core density profile and the evolution of the Dragon IRDC. Primordial black holes (PBHs) are a promising dark matter candidate, with specific mass ranges having been identified as potentially viable in recent years. However, the formation of PBHs is a complex process influenced by various cosmological factors, including inflation, phase transitions, and phase transitions. Consequently, PBH scenarios require cosmological simulations to investigate the conditions under which they can emerge. This study employs PopSyCLE, a new code designed to simulate the primordial density field and calculate the collapse fraction of PBHs. We examine the PopSyCLE output and its implications for the PBH dark matter scenario. Our findings indicate that the collapse fraction is highly sensitive to the primordial density field's amplitude and spectral index, as well as the timing of PBH collapse. Furthermore, we have successfully reproduced previous analytical and numerical results, including those from the $\delta^2$ approximation, using PopSyCLE. Finally, we present predictions for viable PBH mass fractions as a function of mass, considering different inflation models. These results suggest that PBHs can constitute a significant portion of dark matter, with viable regions potentially overlapping with current observational constraints. Additionally, we explore the impact of different recombination models on the mass function and discuss the possibility of producing multiple peaks in the mass function. Overall, this work demonstrates that PBH scenarios can be effectively explored using PopSyCLE. A future publication will detail the application of this framework to specific PBH scenarios. We investigated the structural characteristics of assemblies formed by rigid wedges, where each wedge consists of three spheres linked at their centers. Our findings indicate that for certain wedge angles, these systems exhibit a sequence of phase transitions characterized by increasing orientational order: from fluid to nematic, nematic to smectic, and finally to a crystalline state. Additionally, systems with low total density display nematic phases featuring nonuniform (splayed) director fields, which can be either periodic or localized. The smectic phases observed are of the nematic-like variant, displaying long-range density modulation without periodic stacking of layers. Furthermore, the smectic phases with the highest uniaxial order display characteristics of liquid crystals in strong homeotropic alignment, displaying helical density modulations and periodic domain walls. Finally, we demonstrate that phases with high biaxial order emerge when the wedge angles are nearly equal. These results indicate that phases with modulated uniaxial and biaxial orders can exist in a model that relies solely on hard-core interactions. This finding is significant because it challenges the conventional view that splay-modulated phases are stabilized by attractive forces. Moreover, the wedge model is applicable to various physical systems, including colloids with patchy interactions, and offers a framework for studying wet and dry active matter systems. Consequently, our findings suggest that splay-modulated phases can arise in these systems through nontrivial interactions that differ from simple attraction. To facilitate further research, we have compiled and analyzed phase diagrams for a range of wedge angles. Additionally, we provide a simulation package that enables the investigation of wedge wedge systems with arbitrary wedge angle distributions. This tool is particularly useful for modeling systems with nonuniform wedge angles, such as those containing active matter with self-propelled wedges. The package is available at [link]. Finally, we have included a collection of supplementary materials, including high-quality images and data files, for potential use in presentations. These resources can be accessed via [link]. Parameter-efficient tuning techniques, such as adapter layers, have become a standard approach for adjusting pretrained language models, offering a more efficient alternative to full fine-tuning. However, prior research indicates that these methods often result in a performance gap when applied to natural language inference tasks. This study investigates the cause of this discrepancy and demonstrates that it stems from a reduction in the model's ability to utilize domain-specific tokens, such as "ent" in Typed Word Alignment. We demonstrate that this limitation can be overcome through Special Token Adaptation (STA), a novel method that modifies adapter initialization to enhance sensitivity to special tokens. Our findings reveal that STA boosts baseline performance on pretraining tasks like masked language modeling and lexical lexical alignment, while also narrowing the performance gap in NLInfer benchmarks. Furthermore, we show that STA can be seamlessly integrated into various adapter variants, including prefix and prefill-tuning, offering a versatile solution for improving special token handling across diverse tuning paradigms. This study investigates the impact of contextual versus non-contextual information on set addition performance. In a non-contextual approach, a participant selects a new item from a set of three, then chooses their preferred option between that selection and a novel third option, without any prior knowledge of the initial three. Conversely, a contextual approach requires the participant to make the initial selection before engaging in the task. The research compares these methods based on accuracy and response times. Results indicate that while response times are shorter in the contextual condition, accuracy is lower compared to the non-contextual condition. Furthermore, performance in the contextual condition correlates with measures of fluid intelligence, suggesting that additional cognitive resources may be required to manage task demands. These findings suggest that context does not inherently aid performance in set addition problems. Finally, the study discusses implications for mathematical learning, proposing that while context may not directly improve problem-solving, it could facilitate the acquisition of procedural skills. This study investigates the thermodynamic and dynamic interdependencies within a glass-forming polymer fluid, specifically polyisoprene, using classical molecular dynamics simulations. By systematically varying the temperature and pressure, we map out the relationships between the configurational entropy ($S_k$), volume ($v$), and structural relaxation time ($\tau_\alpha$). Our results indicate that $S_k$, $v$, and $\tau_\alpha$ are strongly correlated, with the most significant link being the one between $S_k$ and $\tau_\alpha$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the free volume fraction ($f$) is intrinsically connected to the total entropy, and that the free volume concept can be utilized to establish a link between configurational entropy and the glass transition temperature ($T_g$). Finally, our findings suggest that the fragility index ($m$) is governed by the configurational entropy. Collectively, these insights provide a robust framework for understanding the link between structure and dynamics in glass-forming liquids. Transformer-based language models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to acquire world knowledge during pretraining. This study investigates how models of varying sizes handle negation in sentences containing time-expressive words. We created a new dataset, TIMENEG, which examines this specific negation type. Our findings indicate that smaller models struggle to correctly interpret it, whereas larger models succeed. Additionally, we offer a theoretical explanation for this capability and present evidence showing that standard corpus pretraining is insufficient for models to develop this ability. Instead, we demonstrate that carefully curated examples can enable models to acquire this competence. This research offers a novel perspective on negation processing and establishes a foundation for enhancing how transformers manage such constructions. The TIMENEG dataset and associated code are accessible at https://github.com/alexandervandeneede/TIMENEG. A preprint of this work is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.01000.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has demonstrated significant potential as a robust framework for automatic text generation. However, current state-of-the-art sequence-to-sequence models often fail to produce fluent and coherent translations, particularly when dealing with complex sentences or multiple clauses. This limitation arises because these models generate one token at a time, lacking the ability to anticipate future tokens during decoding. To address this, we introduce a novel Look-ahead Attention mechanism designed to incorporate look-ahead information into the decoding process. Our approach is straightforward: we explicitly include multiple future tokens within the model's receptive field by expanding the encoder's attention scope. We evaluated this mechanism on two primary tasks: standard NMT and Multi-Domain NMT. The results indicate that our method yields improvements in both perplexity and BLEU scores. Furthermore, we conducted a human evaluation on the generated translations, which confirmed that our approach enhances translation quality. Additionally, we performed an ablation study to assess the impact of various parameters on overall performance. Finally, we present a detailed analysis of the model's strengths and weaknesses. Overall, our findings suggest that Look-ahead Attention is a highly effective mechanism for NMT, offering a solid foundation for future research in automatic text generation. We present an explicit, detailed calculation of the weights for Kontsevich graphs that contain one or two vertices linked by an edge representing the symplectic form. These graphs are essential as their weights determine the cohomological components of the universal connection on the moduli space of rank 2 bundles over a Riemann surface. We derive explicit formulas for graphs with a single vertex and any number of edges, alongside examples featuring two vertices. Additionally, we provide a formula expressing the weights for these symplectic form edges in terms of the algebraic weights of the remaining graphs. This work serves as a precursor to a paper by the second author, which will utilize these computed weights to describe the cohomology of the universal connection on the moduli space of rank 2 bundles over a Riemann surface. Furthermore, we offer a formula for summing the weights of a specific class of graphs that do not require symplectic form edges. This formula is based on a graph isomorphism that maps a graph with a symplectic form edge to a pair of graphs without such edges, thereby demonstrating that the weights of symplectic form edges are governed by the local geometry of the surface around the edge's endpoints. This observation also provides a method to calculate the weights for graphs with symplectic form edges by referencing prior computations. Finally, this paper contributes to a broader research initiative by the co-authors aimed at developing a combinatorial model for the algebra of differential forms on a Riemann surface's moduli space. This model would feature a universal connection whose curvature encodes the relations of the Chen-Fuchsstein differential equations, with its fiber representing the differential forms on the moduli space. Such a model would offer a combinatorial framework for studying the cohomology of this universal connection. In this context, symplectic form edges correspond to differentials of the Weil-Petersson form, and this article advances the effort to understand the algebraic and combinatorial properties of these forms. The current work focuses on 1-forms, with the author intending to extend these findings to n-forms in future research. Our approach relies on a combinatorial model for differential forms on a manifold, where a manifold is defined as a finite set of points equipped with a differential form algebra. This algebra is generated by 1-forms subject to specific relations, and the manifold's dimension equals the number of independent 1-forms. We calculate the large $N$ limit of the thermal entropy for a single scalar field, complete with cubic and quartic interactions, defined on an $S^3 \times S^1$ manifold. By applying a saddle-point approximation to the partition function in the limit of large $N$, we derive an $O(N)$ correction term that influences the ratio between thermal and entanglement entropy. Furthermore, we examine a class of theories exhibiting a conformal fixed point and employ renormalization group arguments to extend these findings beyond the large $N$ approximation. Our results indicate that, at a conformal fixed point, the ratio of thermal to entanglement entropy on $S^3 \times S^1$ approaches $T R / \pi$ as $N \to \infty$, deviating from the $2ER$ value characteristic of free theories. Additionally, we demonstrate that this $O(N)$ correction to the thermal entropy can be interpreted as a large $N$ perturbation of the $O(N)$ vector model, which is known to correspond to a string theory on $AdS_5 \times S^5 / Z_N$ in the large $N$ limit. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the holographic $a$-theorem. These findings suggest that the holographic $a$-theorem cannot be derived solely from the monotonicity of the large $N$ ratio between thermal and entanglement entropy on $S^3 \times S^1$. Instead, it requires a more refined understanding of this ratio, potentially involving the subtraction of vacuum energy contributions. This necessity may stem from the fact that the large $N$ limit of the ratio of partition functions does not necessarily equal the ratio of their respective large $N$ limits. We also examine the potential impact of these issues on the holographic $c$-theorem. Our findings suggest that the $c$-theorem can be derived from the monotonicity of this ratio only within the large $N$ limit of $S^3 \times S^1$ thermal entropy. However, this approach is limited to theories with $S^3$ holographic duals, as it relies on the monotonicity of the thermal sphere entropy rather than the more general monotonicity of the $a$-anomaly under RG flow. Consequently, this method fails to provide a complete proof of the $c$-theorem. We also note that a similar issue arises for the $a$-anomaly

Chen and Kou (2018) introduced a Markov chain framework to price Asian options, utilizing semi-group theory to demonstrate that the log-price process constitutes a Markov process on the price grid with Asian options serving as its absorbing states. This approach enables the reduction of pricing Asian options to pricing standard options. In this paper, we offer several corrections and enhancements to their methodology. Our contributions include: (i) clarifying the definition of the pricing function to ensure the resulting system of equations is well-defined; (ii) providing a rigorous proof of the reduced form of the pricing function; (iii) presenting a more intuitive derivation of the pricing function; and (iv) extending the model to cover double Asian options. Through numerical examples, we demonstrate that our proposed methods yield the same results as those in the original paper. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of these methods to Asian options within a Heston model featuring a stochastic interest rate. Finally, we show that these methods are applicable to a broader class of Asian options, specifically those dependent on both the maximum and minimum asset prices. All numerical examples were implemented using the Q-Li method. Keywords: Asian options, Q-Li method, QLMtool, Stochastic Heston model, Stochastic interest rate. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 91B30, 91G60.

The origin of the diffuse gamma-ray background remains a significant enigma in astrophysics. This study investigates whether the intracluster medium (ICM) in galaxy clusters can account for a portion of this background through the hadronic interaction of cosmic rays (CRs). We employ a two-fluid model to simulate CR diffusion and energy transport within the ICM, analyzing the resulting gamma-ray emission from these interactions. Our findings indicate that galaxy clusters, with a number density of $n_{GG}=10^{-5} \, Mpc^{-3}$, can produce a steady-state gamma-ray flux in the GeV-TeV range of $\Phi_{\gamma} \sim 10^{-6} \, cm^{-2} s^{-1}$. Furthermore, the flux exhibits a strong dependence on the CR injection rate, which can be constrained by future observations from the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA). Additionally, we demonstrate that the gamma-ray flux from clusters scales with redshift as $(1+z)^{3/2}$, leading to a peak in the flux-redshift distribution at $z \sim 0.5$. We also examine the potential contribution of the ICM to the gamma-ray background in the MeV range, a region explored by the INTEGRAL satellite. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for upcoming space-based missions, such as the Wide-field Survey Telescope (WST) and the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory (CGRO). These findings suggest that galaxy clusters may be a primary source of the gamma-ray background, particularly at higher energies. Consequently, we propose that future gamma-ray sky surveys should prioritize galaxy clusters as key observational targets. We also address the possibility of detecting individual sources within clusters, which could provide insights into CR transport mechanisms and their role in galaxy evolution. This study revisits the concept of cosmological collider physics, which posits that massive particles within the early universe generate distinct imprints on primordial perturbations. These imprints serve as a method to detect and measure heavy particles, including gravitons, by analyzing the power spectrum of cosmological data. We demonstrate that the standard collider signal, when viewed through the lens of general features, can be reconstructed using a specific feature function. Furthermore, we derive a general formula for the amplitude of these peaks, revealing that the characteristic damped oscillatory shape of collider signals arises from the interference between long and short cosmological modes. We also provide explicit examples of such interference for both scalar and gravitational waves. Our analysis indicates that collider peaks are inherently feature functions, meaning the general features framework can recover the standard collider signal. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the general features approach and the collider approach, showing that general features can effectively reconstruct the collider signal. This capability allows the general features method to identify the presence of collider physics, a strength that surpasses the traditional collider approach. Consequently, our findings suggest that incorporating collider physics into the general features formalism offers a promising avenue for future research. Finally, we examine the limitations of the collider approach and discuss strategies for overcoming them. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive guide to collider physics within the context of general features, with the hope of stimulating further research in this area. Our code is publicly available at \href{https://github.com/ChenchenWang2017/Reconstruct_cosmological_collider_signal}{https://github.com/ChenchenWang2017/Reconstruct_cosmological_collider_signal}. Our Python package, \texttt{Reconstruct\_cosmological\_collider\_signal}, can be installed via pip using the command: \texttt{pip install Reconstruct\_cosmological\_collider\_signal}. This tool enables the reconstruction of collider signals from the power spectrum of primordial perturbations. We provide a detailed tutorial on how to utilize this package. We anticipate that this methodology will prove valuable for researchers engaged in the study of cosmological collider physics. We hope that this work will facilitate the reconstruction of collider signals and enhance the sensitivity of cosmological observations in detecting new physics. We believe that this approach will significantly improve the prospects for discovering new physics through cosmological observations. This paper introduces a deep neural network (DNN) model designed to elucidate the internal workings of visual recognition systems. By integrating spatial, channel, and global max attention mechanisms, the model automatically captures latent visual-semantic relationships. Furthermore, it generates visual attention maps that automatically identify salient objects and their semantic categories within an image. We show that these masks align with human visual attention, as confirmed by experiments using eye-tracking data. Additionally, we validate that the attention masks produced by our model serve as effective cues for instance segmentation tasks.
