We demonstrate that the one-dimensional repulsion between adjacent copper and oxygen ions can be transformed into a long-range attractive force mediated by acoustic phonons. This phenomenon is illustrated through the specific case of the $e_g$ band in cuprates. Our findings indicate that the minimum energy cost required to establish this attraction corresponds to a bound state of two holes within a $s$-$d$ orbital hybrid. This mechanism offers a quantitative explanation for the exceptionally strong orbital degeneracy lifting observed in the $1/T_1(0)$ data of $\mathrm{La}_{2-x}\mathrm{Sr}_x\mathrm{CuO}_4$. Furthermore, we show that this phonon-mediated attraction is also operative in other materials featuring narrow $p$- and $d$-bands, such as $\mathrm{SrTiO}_3$. A key implication of this discovery is that it provides a pathway to engineer effective attractive interactions, a crucial element for forming Cooper pairs and facilitating superconductivity. Additionally, this process may contribute to the generation of a significant orbital gap in high-$T_c$ cuprates. Finally, we propose that this phonon-mediated attraction could play a pivotal role in understanding the physics of acoustic soft modes near charge density wave transitions. Our results underscore the necessity of incorporating orbital degrees of freedom into both theoretical models and experimental investigations. To achieve this, we have developed a user-friendly computational tool designed to calculate the effective interaction between holes in various $p$- and $d$-bands. This tool is available as a free download at \url{https://github.com/akuzmenko/Phonon-mediated-interaction}. A detailed description of the code can be found in our recent publication: A. Kuzmenko, A. V. Chubukov, and S. V. I. A. Popov, \textit{Phys. Rev. B} \textbf{104}, 024508 (2021). The source code itself is accessible at \url{https://github.com/akuzmenko/Phonon-mediated-interaction}. Our hope is that this tool will facilitate a deeper understanding of the physics governing orbital degrees of freedom in cuprates and other relevant materials. We anticipate that this understanding will be essential for unraveling the mystery of high-$T_c$ superconductivity. We are confident that this work will inspire further research into the fascinating physics of orbital degrees of freedom. We extend our gratitude to A. K. Ge

This paper introduces a novel structural causal model learning algorithm designed for continuous variables, specifically targeting linear structural causal models (SCMs) with exogenous noise following a multivariate normal distribution. The proposed method is a modification of the continuous version of PC algorithm by Spirtes et al. (2001), utilizing a graph score combined with a stepwise regression approach to estimate coefficients for independence tests within the algorithm. We evaluated this method against two existing techniques, including a recent noise-adjacency-based score by Hauser and Maathuis (2017). Using data from the MPHIA study, we applied both methods to a subset of individuals to investigate the causal link between alcohol consumption and liver disease. The resulting causal graphs from both approaches yielded similar probabilities for alcohol intake being a cause of liver disease, with the proposed method demonstrating superior performance in terms of search speed and the quality of the final causal graph. These findings support the method's utility for large-scale data analysis. Additionally, we have made the MPHIA dataset available for researchers to apply and evaluate their own causal structure learning methods. In the magnetic inverse perovskite Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, a metastable skyrmion lattice (SkL) forms within a narrow temperature and field range. This study investigates how the density of these skyrmions changes in response to an out-of-plane magnetic field and an applied strain. By employing x-ray magnetic resonance and topological magnetometry, we observed that both factors induce topological melting of the SkL. Specifically, increasing the applied strain causes the skyrmion density to decrease in a stepwise pattern, which aligns with theoretical predictions regarding strain-induced lattice distortions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the metastable SkL in this material is highly sensitive to strain, a characteristic that makes it a promising candidate for strain-based topological memory devices. These findings also offer insights into the stability of skyrmion lattices in other magnetic inverse perovskites, such as the room-temperature variant Co$_8$CuMn$_2$O$_{20}$. Finally, our results indicate that the SkL in Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ can be stabilized at ambient conditions by introducing a small amount of disorder, such as that caused by deuterium implantation. This suggests that introducing controlled disorder is a viable strategy for enhancing the stability of metastable skyrmion lattices. The topological melting of the SkL in Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ is attributed to the field- and strain-induced annihilation of the local Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI). Consequently, our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the DMI's stability in this system. Ultimately, these results underscore the critical role of the DMI in stabilizing skyrmion lattices. The SkL in Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ is stabilized by a combination of weak dipolar interactions, local DMI, and disorder. Our findings suggest that the SkL is particularly sensitive to perturbations affecting the DMI, which can be mitigated by introducing a small amount of disorder. These insights are essential for advancing the development of topological spintronic technologies. This paper offers a detailed examination of High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models, covering their theoretical foundations, estimation techniques, and inferential methods. Additionally, it highlights future research directions and emerging applications within this rapidly evolving field. Our discussion emphasizes extensions to nonlinear, nonstationary, and heterogeneous contexts, as well as models featuring complex data structures such as network graphs, panel data, and time-series cross-sections. Furthermore, we explore advances in estimation and inference for large-scale nonlinear dynamic factor models, along with the integration of machine learning approaches. The latter part of the survey addresses the application of these models to financial markets, including their use in asset allocation and risk management. We also present potential future applications across diverse domains, such as epidemiology, environmental science, and neuroscience. Finally, we suggest extending current models to incorporate additional features like network structures, panel data structures, and heterogeneity. Additionally, we propose investigating the application of machine learning techniques to enhance both estimation and inference within this framework. These suggested extensions and applications underscore the broad relevance and the exciting prospects for future research in high-dimensional dynamic factor modeling. Keywords: High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models, Factor Models, Dimensionality Reduction, Estimation, Inference, Financial Markets. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 62F10, 62P12, 62P15.

The Nikaidō-Isoda-Fan inequality defines an equilibrium problem that encompasses several well-known problems—including optimization, variational inequalities, Kakutani fixed points, and Nash equilibria—as specific instances. This paper presents fixed point theorems related to this equivalence. Let $(X,d)$ be a complete metric space and let $T: X \to 2^X$ be a set-valued mapping. We establish conditions under which, for any $x \in X$, there exists a $y \in Tx$ satisfying $d(x,y) \le k[d(x,u)+d(y,u)]$ for all $u \in Tx$, where $k \in [0,1)$. This result generalizes the Edelman-Kirk theorem for single-valued mappings and the Browder-Haruki theorem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if $T$ is a multi-valued contraction, then $T$ possesses a closed graph, and its Hausdorff and Hausdorff-existence correspondences are both upper semi-continuous. These findings enable the derivation of multiple fixed point theorems for set-valued mappings. Finally, we apply these outcomes to address the equilibrium problem. Equilibrium problems were first formulated by Blum and Kirk in 2004; since then, they have been utilized to model various practical scenarios, including optimization, economics, game theory, and transportation. Additionally, they serve as a method for bypassing the computational difficulties associated with calculating the projection onto convex sets. In this work, we provide existence theorems for the equilibrium problem and derive related fixed point theorems as corollaries. Recent advancements in Bayesian neural networks have enabled the analysis of complex data distributions, a capability leveraged in this study for reversible steganography. This approach allows secret data to be embedded and subsequently extracted without altering the original host image. We trained a Bayesian neural network on natural images, utilizing its predicted distribution to identify compression artifacts in compressed JPEGs. By exploiting these artifacts, we can hide information within compressed images while ensuring the original host image remains perfectly intact after extraction. Our findings demonstrate that Bayesian networks are highly effective at locating reversible capacity within images, and experimental results indicate that Bayesian models outperform both standard neural networks and support vector machines in this context. Furthermore, we achieved a hidden capacity of 1.5 bits per pixel in synthetic images and 0.25 bits per pixel in real images. These results confirm the potential of Bayesian networks for reversible steganography and offer a promising pathway for future research in the field. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Reversible-Steganography.

We examine the mean-field modeling of convective turbulence within rotating stars and giant planets, specifically analyzing the impact of key turbulent effects on the generation of global magnetic fields. By employing a standard $\alpha-\Omega$ dynamo framework, we demonstrate that turbulent diffusion, viscosity, and the $\alpha$-effect must be modeled as functions of radius, pressure, and density to achieve a self-consistent description of magnetic field generation in these astrophysical objects. Our findings indicate that this approach yields a magnetic Reynolds number ($Rm$) several orders of magnitude higher than when using constant turbulent coefficients, resulting in the sustained generation of a global magnetic field. Consequently, this methodology offers a viable pathway for simulating the magnetic fields of stars and giant planets using computational resources currently accessible. Finally, we highlight that this technique can be applied to study the internal magnetic fields of brown dwarfs and gas giants within our solar system. To advance this understanding, we recommend future missions dedicated to measuring the magnetic fields of Jupiter and Saturn. These measurements would provide constraints on the internal dynamo models we propose, thereby advancing our knowledge of the internal structure of giant planets. (Abridged)

We present ALMA observations of a molecular outflow in the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 4945, utilizing CO isotopologues (13CO and C18O) alongside a high-J transition (3-2) of the primary outflow tracer (12CO). The data reveal a large-scale outflow extending 1.5 kpc along the galaxy's minor axis, driven by central star formation. This structure exhibits a symmetric, butterfly-like morphology, with a 13CO-emitting region spanning 1.2 kpc and a 12CO region spanning 1.5 kpc. The outflow's kinematics indicate a transverse expansion velocity of 100 km/s, a mass of 10^5 solar masses, and a mass loss rate of 0.01 solar masses per year. The 13CO emission is confined to the outflow's center, whereas 12CO extends further outward. The 12CO data also expose a molecular cloud complex in the galaxy's disk, which is obscured in 13CO. This cloud contains a 100 km/s molecular cloud moving at 100 km/s relative to the disk, showing a CO velocity gradient that suggests rotation. We propose that the outflow was launched by the galaxy's central starburst, which compressed the disk's molecular gas and generated the CO velocity gradient. The 13CO-emitting outflow originates from the disk's midplane, while the 12CO emission extends to larger heights. This spatial distribution aligns with theoretical models of outflow launching, where high-J emission traces outflow material at greater distances from the midplane. Our findings support the hypothesis that high-J emission is more effective than low-J emission for tracing the large-scale structure of molecular outflows. The 12CO mass within the outflow is 10^5 solar masses, and the star formation rate required to sustain the outflow is 0.01 solar masses per year. The outflow's lifetime is approximately 10 million years, and its momentum is 10^50 dyne seconds. The momentum flux of the outflow is 10^39 erg/s, which is comparable to the momentum flux of the star formation. The outflow's momentum flux is roughly 100 times lower than that of a starburst-driven wind, suggesting that the wind is launched from the starburst core and propagates outward

Magnetized plasmas are susceptible to a wide range of instabilities, which can be analyzed using the diffusion approximation. This study introduces a conservative Galerkin finite element method for quasilinear diffusion models, where the diffusion coefficient's dependence on the underlying distribution function is handled via a semi-discrete approximation. The spatially discrete formulation is designed to ensure positivity and $L^1$-norm conservation. For time integration, a Runge-Kutta scheme is employed to maintain particle conservation in the fully discrete solution. The proposed algorithm is implemented in C++ and validated through various test cases, including a Riemann problem, a growing mode instability, and a beam-plasma instability scenario. These applications demonstrate the method's robustness and its ability to preserve conservation properties in the discrete solution. Additionally, the range of applicability is explored by applying the algorithm to a new emerging instability known as the kinetic Alfvén wave beam instability. Finally, the scheme's capacity to resolve fine-scale features is highlighted by examining the formation of sharp gradients in beam-plasma instabilities. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchroeder19/QLDiff_FE. Variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods (SGLMs) are typically designed for first-order Initial Value Problems (IVPs) solved with numerical methods featuring variable step sizes. This article extends SDIMSIMs, a class of SGLMs, to accommodate variable step sizes specifically for IVPs involving second-order Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs). The approach employs a general framework utilizing two-stage, two-step, self-starting SDIMSIMs alongside a general error estimator. Numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed Variable Step Size (VSS) SDIMSIMs. These examples illustrate that the new VSS methods are competitive with existing VSS GLMs and capable of achieving higher orders of accuracy. Furthermore, the paper introduces VSS GLMs based on variable stepsize second derivative Runge-Kutta methods and tests them against the new VSS SDIMSIMs. The results indicate that the VSS SDIMSIMs perform comparably to the VSS GLMs. Finally, it is concluded that VSS SDIMSIMs offer a viable alternative for solving ODEs that require the use of second derivatives. Additionally, the study demonstrates the potential of these VSS SDIMSIMs to enhance the efficiency of solving systems of ODEs through the parallel execution of stage evaluations. We introduce MuMuPy, a computational framework designed to evaluate experimental signatures of dimuonium ($\psi_{\mu\mu}$) within various matter-based tests. The system is now accessible for practical use, with a detailed description of its capabilities and capabilities demonstrated through examples. MuMuPy is implemented in Python and relies on PyRant, a Python module for calculating quantum electrodynamics amplitudes. Its core functionality includes estimating the dimuonium production rate required by experiments to set or refine limits on $\psi_{\mu\mu}$-matter interaction strengths. The framework supports multiple scenarios: production via two-photon fusion in $e^+e^-$ collisions, in the nucleus of a dimuonium beam interacting with a target, and within a dimuonium beam interacting with an electron. Additionally, MuMuPy can determine the ratio of dimuonium to muon pair production in two-photon collisions and the ratio of dimuonium to four-muon production in dimuonium-matter interactions. These capabilities are essential for deriving constraints on $\psi_{\mu\mu}$-matter interaction parameters from upcoming experimental results. Furthermore, MuMuPy can predict the screening radius of dimuonium within a plasma, a value that may influence signatures detected in certain dimension-8 dimension-6 operator experiments. The project's source code and a user manual are available at https://github.com/andrews1/MuMuPy. This study investigates the optimal investment portfolio under power utility, which incorporates both absolute and relative (CFA index) wealth. We begin by deriving the necessary and sufficient first-order conditions for an optimal solution within a multi-period framework featuring multiple assets. Subsequently, in a single-period model with a single period, we establish sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the utility maximizer using a complete stochastic asset system. Finally, we numerically illustrate the implications of these sufficient conditions. Additionally, we extend our analysis to a single-period model with a single asset by providing numerical examples that demonstrate the existence of the utility maximizer. Our numerical results show that accounting for relative wealth leads to a more conservative investment strategy. Dwarf galaxies are the most abundant type of galaxy in the universe, yet our understanding of their interstellar medium (ISM) remains limited. This review examines the current state of knowledge regarding the ISM in these systems, focusing on their physical characteristics, chemical abundances, and the observational and theoretical methods used to study them. We outline the primary uncertainties and propose several key areas for future investigation. Specifically, we address the need to determine the true number of dwarfs, establish a robust framework for analyzing their ISM, and investigate the relationship between their ISM and star formation. Additionally, we stress the importance of developing a comprehensive model for the evolution of the ISM in dwarfs, which is essential for understanding their evolution as dark matter halos. Finally, we emphasize the necessity of a unified theoretical and observational approach to fully understand these ubiquitous galactic systems. The stability of fermionic quasiparticles is ensured by their interaction with an effective bosonic bath, which imposes a minimum energy threshold on excitations. This study demonstrates that in certain configurations, the rate at which bosons are consumed during the collapse of fermionic excitations can be significant, resulting in the suppression of quasiparticle coherence. Consequently, a regime of rare quasiparticle formation emerges, where the probability of collapse is negligibly small. These findings are illustrated using a model where electrons couple to local vibrational bosons, mediated by either direct electron-electron scattering or electron hopping between sites. Furthermore, we show that in the presence of a finite bias, boson-assisted tunneling of rare electrons exhibits a step-like structure, where current is carried by a limited number of tunneling electrons. Finally, our results indicate that quasiparticle rarefaction can be observed through shot noise measurements. Our findings are broadly applicable to systems where quasiparticles are fragile, such as those existing near quantum critical points. Additionally, the proposed rare electron tunneling mechanism may be relevant for understanding the weak tunneling currents detected in recent experiments. This study evaluates the challenges of recruiting and training workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) to generate high-quality summaries. We introduce a qualification test designed to screen for workers capable of producing summaries that match human-level quality. By deploying this test across 1,035 workers over 12 months, we observed that 20% passed, yet their outputs still fell short of the best summarization models. To enhance their performance, we implemented various teaching strategies, including providing sample outputs, detailed instructions, and feedback. Our findings indicate that sample outputs were the most effective, improving summary quality by 10% to 30%. We also found that our top-performing workers were naturally inclined toward text summarization, suggesting that targeting specific subgroups may be more effective than attempting to train the general population. Finally, we demonstrate that the workers who achieved the highest scores were the most adaptable, successfully applying new skills to tasks they had never encountered before. These insights offer valuable guidance for future MTurk campaigns aimed at generating qualitative content. Text-video retrieval (TVMR) is a critical yet difficult task that demands a robust understanding of complex video content and semantic alignment. However, current methods often fail to effectively capture fine-grained details and global context, leading to suboptimal retrieval performance. To address these limitations, we introduce the Token Shift and Selection Network (TS2-Net), which leverages transformer architectures to enhance both global and local interactions. Our approach comprises two core components: the Token Shift Module (TSM) and the Token Selection Module (TSM). The first component iteratively aggregates information from both token levels and head levels to strengthen global interactions, while the second identifies and amplifies tokens containing key retrieval cues to refine local interactions. Extensive experiments across two public benchmarks demonstrate that TS2-Net significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, evaluations on a custom dataset highlight the model's ability to extract granular details and establish accurate semantic connections, confirming its effectiveness. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1998/TS2-Net.

We establish that flavour-changing neutral currents (FCNCs) are inevitable within any framework where the top quark acquires its mass through non-linear sigma model interactions. These top FCNCs can be accurately modeled using a non-universal flavour-violating Z boson coupling to top quarks. By integrating current experimental constraints, we derive the most stringent limits on these Z-top FCNC couplings, which are essential for comprehending the top quark's flavor structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these top FCNC limits are incompatible with the standard minimal non-linear sigma model featuring a global $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R$ chiral symmetry. Finally, we investigate various top FCNC scenarios, including their implications for the Higgs boson, and show that the Z-top FCNC limits are mutually consistent with other established experimental bounds. Additionally, we establish that Z boson-mediated FCNCs can violate the unitarity of the CKM matrix without necessitating a fourth generation of quarks. Finally, we outline the necessary conditions for Z FCNs to be accommodated within a low-scale effective Z boson model. This work serves as a foundation for future experimental investigations into top FCN couplings. We anticipate that the upcoming LHC Run 3 will significantly enhance the sensitivity to these interactions, thereby enabling a more precise characterization of the top quark's flavor profile. We investigate the structural characteristics of directed hybrid random networks formed by combining the preferential attachment and uniform attachment mechanisms. In a network of size $n$, a new vertex joins an existing one with probability $1/2$; upon doing so, it selects an incoming or outgoing edge based on the degree of the target vertex with probability $p$, or chooses the target uniformly at random with probability $1-p$. Our primary contribution establishes both asymptotically almost sure (a.a.a.) and probabilistic bounds. Specifically, we demonstrate that the in-degree and out-degree distributions converge to a power law with exponent $\gamma=3$ (a.a.a.), whereas the average path length follows a logarithmic normal distribution. Additionally, we prove that the network exhibits small-world properties and contains a giant strongly connected component comprising $\Omega(n)$ vertices. We also provide a detailed analysis of the degree distribution for the largest strong component. All findings are supported by numerical simulations. Finally, we discuss how hybrid attachment models can be integrated with detachment mechanisms. Identifying concurrent wireless interference is a critical challenge for engineers and researchers. This study introduces a convolutional neural network (CNN) capable of simultaneously detecting and classifying multiple interference signals. The proposed method was evaluated using a synthetic dataset generated from a wireless channel model, comprising 802.11b, 802.11n, and frequency-modulated (FM) signals. Experimental results indicate that the CNN achieves an average accuracy of 96.5% and a mean response time of 10.5 ms. Furthermore, the paper discusses the algorithm's performance in terms of accuracy, response time, and computational complexity. Finally, the work explores potential applications for this CNN within smart home and industrial automation environments. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ahmedhassan1234567890/wii-cnn}. The study was conducted while the author was a visiting researcher at the University of Oulu, Finland. This study examines the dynamics of spin-0 particles within the Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime, representing a cosmic spacetime with a twist or dislocation. The resulting Klein-Gordon equation incorporates time-dependent potentials to model interactions between Klein-Gordon particles and the cosmic string's dislocation, alongside various electromagnetic fields. These potentials serve as sources of energy and charge, enabling the analysis of correlations between a particle's energy and its charge in this spacetime. The cosmic string exerts influence over the system through multiple electromagnetic fields and the time-dependent dislocation potential, driving the associated correlations. Furthermore, the equation includes a quantum correction term that accounts for the quantum nature of particles, thereby affecting their dynamics. The study demonstrates that this quantum correction term can be interpreted as a signature of the Klein-Gordon particles. Additionally, it is noted that the signature is more pronounced when the dislocation is significant, as the quantum correction term scales with the dislocation. Consequently, the research concludes that signatures arise from the interplay between the cosmic string and the charge of a specific particle, rather than from the quantum correction term acting in isolation. Finally, the paper establishes that signatures can be observed in the Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime, a finding that may have implications for the detection of cosmic strings. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the signature remains independent of the electromagnetic field, as the quantum correction term does not depend on any specific electromagnetic field. The paper also highlights that signatures can be detected through correlations between a particle's energy and its charge within the Klein-Gordon framework. Finally, it is emphasized that signatures are detectable in this spacetime because the cosmic string's dislocation is space-like; if the dislocation were time-like, the signature would vanish. The paper also addresses the issue of singularities, showing that they occur only at the string's location, where the metric determinant becomes zero. The study further investigates the geodesics of free-falling particles in this spacetime, revealing that these trajectories are helical and share a common axis with the cosmic string. This characteristic is attributed to the vorticity of the free-falling particles, which is induced by the twist in the spacetime geometry. The paper also examines the energy-momentum of free-falling particles, demonstrating that the dislocation of the cosmic string affects this energy-momentum. Additionally, it is noted that the twist causes the linear momentum of free-falling particles to be zero, resulting in their total momentum from all directions also being zero. Countable locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair consisting of a Steinitz number and a real number that is at least 1. This result serves as an analogue to the theorems established by J. Dixmier and A. A. Beurling regarding Borel spaces and chains of cardinality $\omega$. Furthermore, this finding extends the work conducted by R. E. Johnson and the author concerning the scenario where the underlying $\sigma$-ideal possesses a countable generating sequence. Additionally, our research demonstrates that the specific findings by J. Dixmier and A. A. Beurling do not hold in locally standard settings that lack the $\omega$-chain property. Our work also introduces several novel concepts, including the order dimension, dimension spectrum, and dimension index of a measure algebra. The dimension of such algebras is not invariably one, even when the associated $\sigma$-ideal is both $\omega_1$-generable and a $G_\delta$ set within the power set of natural numbers. The text concludes by examining various problems and questions pertinent to this field. Finally, the paper presents a survey of the history of locally standard measure algebras, tracing key developments from the 1940s through to the present day. This survey highlights the field's rich historical depth and significant unresolved issues. The authors express their gratitude to A. A. Beurling, J. Dixmier, and R. E. This study investigates the proton recoil polarization observable in Deep Virtual Compton Scattering (DVCS), examining its sensitivity to individual Generalized Parton Distributions (GPDs). Utilizing the framework established by Kumericki et al. [arXiv:0809.1551], we analyze this observable across the kinematic range of JLab's 12 GeV program, which extends to $Q^2 \leq 11$ (GeV/$c)^2$. Our findings indicate that the polarization asymmetry is primarily driven by the product $H-E$, making it a valuable complementary observable to the unpolarized cross section. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the asymmetry can be enhanced by incorporating a transverse photon polarization component. These results establish a foundation for future DVCS experiments at the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC). Our analysis code is accessible at https://github.com/andrews10/DVCS_GPDs. Although Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into daily human activities, it is often depicted as an autonomous system operating independently of human influence. This paper introduces the newly coined term "Augmented Artificial Intelligence" (AAI) to describe a framework where intelligent systems are enhanced by human traits and characteristics. We provide a comprehensive overview of this emerging concept and demonstrate its applicability to various AI subfields, including machine learning, natural language processing, and computer vision. Furthermore, the paper outlines the benefits of this approach and proposes future research directions. The study is supported by illustrative examples and case studies. Ultimately, this work serves as a foundational piece of research that paves the way for further investigation into the broader concept of Augmented Artificial Intelligence. Additionally, it offers a valuable resource for researchers and scholars interested in the convergence between AI and human cognition. Our aim is to inspire future research that explores the synergy between artificial intelligence and human cognition. The paper is accessible at the following link: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/341601800_Augmented_Artificial_Intelligence_A_Conceptual_Framework. The corresponding author can be contacted at: email: srikanth@iitkgp.ac.in. Keywords: Augmented Artificial Intelligence, Human Cognition, Artificial and Human Intelligence Convergence.

We present findings from a numerical finite-temperature study of homogeneous, spin-orbit-coupled, interacting bosons within the mean-field framework. This system exhibits a rich landscape of phases, including paramagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and superfluid states. In the superfluid phase, a modulated gapless excitation spectrum emerges at a finite momentum. This modulation arises from the competition between the linear Rabi coupling and the nonlinear Rabi oscillation of the mean-field spin-orbit coupling, which is induced by the non-diagonal elements of the two-spin density matrix. These effects are particularly pronounced in the quantum-correlated Bose-Einstein condensate regime. We demonstrate that the modulation wavelength increases as the linear Rabi coupling strength rises. Furthermore, we investigate the thermal evolution of these modulations and their associated lifetime. At elevated temperatures, the modulation is damped, and its lifetime diminishes. However, at the critical temperature marking the transition to the paramagnetic phase, the modulation reappears. This phenomenon is attributed to a divergence in the two-spin density matrix elements at this critical point. We also examine the thermal behavior of the antiferromagnetic phase, noting that it is damped at lower temperatures compared to the superfluid phase. Finally, we analyze the thermal transitions between these distinct phases. Our results indicate that the modulated superfluid phase is thermally stable, existing within a finite temperature range bounded by the transitions to both the paramagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases. Additionally, we explore the possibility of first-order phase transitions between the superfluid and paramagnetic phases, as well as between the superfluid and antiferromagnetic phases. These transitions are governed by the linear Rabi coupling, linear Rabi frequency, and inter-species interaction strength. Finally, we discuss the potential experimental observability of these phenomena in ultracold atomic experiments. We conclude that modulated superfluids can be observed via the momentum distribution of the Bose-Einstein condensate, while the modulations themselves can be detected through the two-spin density matrix. Furthermore, the first-order transitions can be identified through the specific heat of the system. These predictions are based on the mean-field results we have derived. Finally, we suggest that these phenomena could be experimentally realized using two-component ultracold atomic gases in optical lattices, where linear Rabi coupling is achievable via radio-frequency fields, and Rabi oscillations can be readily observed. The necessary theoretical tools for such experiments are also available. We anticipate that our findings will stimulate further experimental investigations

We demonstrate that every connected graph with a realization by a finite abelian group degenerates to one realized by a regular group via an $S$-equivalence of rank 1. Furthermore, we provide a combinatorial characterization of the order of elements in finite abelian groups based on their regular neighbors within the group realization space, derived from the minimal relations defining the group realization space. The proof relies on a new normal form for graphs realized by finite abelian groups, which generalizes the canonical form established by Gonzalez and Gonzalez. Additionally, we present a complete classification of all rank 1 $S$-equivalence classes containing connected graphs realized by finite abelian groups. These findings are applied to characterize graphs realizable by regular groups and to classify such graphs up to isomorphism within finite abelian groups. Specifically, regarding the characterization, we identify that graphs realized by elementary groups are precisely those possessing a realization by a regular group that cannot be obtained through degenerations from other regular group realizations. Regarding classification, we determine that any two realizing homomorphisms from graph $G$ to finite abelian groups $A$ and $B$ differ by an automorphism of $G$ and an element of $B$, provided the realization space is non-empty. Finally, we establish that the number of realizations of graph $G$ in finite abelian groups is either zero or equal to $|G|$. This work extends the results of Gonzalez and Gonzalez to all connected graphs realized by finite abelian groups. The paper also includes several illustrative examples and open problems. Notably, we confirm that every connected graph realized by finite abelian groups degenerates to a realization by a regular group, even when the target groups are not necessarily abelian. Additionally, we characterize graphs possessing a unique realization within finite abelian groups and identify those whose realizations in finite abelian groups constitute an isomorphism class. These results extend the findings of Gonzalez and Gonzalez to all connected graphs. The paper also features several examples and instances of graphs with multiple realizations in finite abelian groups. Finally, we present a characterization of graphs that admit realizations in finite abelian groups but not in elementary abelian $p$-groups, and we provide a characterization of graphs that realize every finite abelian group of a specific order. Both of these results also extend the findings of Gonzalez and Gonzalez. This paper examines how low-dimensional gauge theories are dual to low-dimensional supergravity theories, specifically within the context of AdS/CMT, by analyzing various flux backgrounds derived from massive Type IIA string theory. We explore the low-energy limits of these backgrounds, which yield three-dimensional CFTs and 2d CFTs. In the three-dimensional case, we demonstrate that the dual supergravity theories are massive three-dimensional super-AdS$_3$ CS theories, with the specific theories and fluxes determined by the background's parameters. Furthermore, we show that chiral primary operators in the 3d CFTs can be identified with Kaluza-Klein modes in the supergravity sector. Turning to the two-dimensional case, we find that the dual supergravity theories consist of a two-dimensional superconformal algebra coupled with a super-Kac-Moody algebra. Additionally, we establish that the 2d central charges are fixed by the Kaluza-Klein spectrum. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the low-energy behavior of the 3d and 2d CFTs. These results are supported by numerical computations. The paper concludes by outlining potential extensions of this work to other flux backgrounds. Throughout this study, we employ a systematic method for reducing fluxes and establishing the link between the low-energy limit and the supergravity theory. This approach is encapsulated in a Python package named `FluxToAction`, available on GitHub. We also outline the method and illustrate its application through explicit examples. The paper begins with an introduction, followed by a detailed presentation of the method, its applications, and their implications. Finally, we provide an appendix containing the explicit form of the reduced action. This work is based on the doctoral thesis of the second author. A kernel's choice is pivotal in Gaussian Process (GP) modeling, as it encodes prior knowledge regarding the target function's characteristics. However, selecting an appropriate kernel can be difficult, and existing literature offers limited guidance on the effects of altering kernel components or combining them. This paper introduces a Bayesian optimization framework that automatically discovers GP kernels by evolving mathematical expressions. We evaluate this method across various regression tasks, demonstrating that the optimal expression frequently corresponds to a practical kernel. The resulting generated kernels enhance model performance and robustness, particularly in scenarios involving limited data. Furthermore, we illustrate how this approach facilitates the novel kernel selection for image classification, highlighting its versatility. The code is accessible at https://github.com/brunofreitas/ELEMENTAL. This work serves as a step toward developing automated tools for GP hyperparameter optimization. Our findings indicate that simultaneously optimizing hyperparameters and mathematical expressions yields superior results compared to optimizing the kernel structure first and then its hyperparameters. Additionally, we show that a recent method for function composition, which was originally designed for hyperparameter optimization, can also be applied to generate mathematical expressions. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's performance, revealing that it scales effectively to high-dimensional problems. In summary, this work represents a significant step toward automating tools for GP hyperparameter optimization. The presented algorithm is versatile, enabling the discovery of both known and novel kernels, as well as other mathematical expressions. This represents a substantial advancement in hyperparameter optimization, as it allows for the search of a space of continuous, discrete, and structural variables within a unified framework. The method is versatile, generating kernels for both RBF and Matern families, and can be extended to other machine learning tasks, such as function composition. Future muon collider detectors will face significant challenges from beam-induced background, which includes beam halo and beam loss, posing a serious threat to detector functionality and data acquisition systems. This paper reviews various beam-induced mitigation strategies, incorporating recent advancements and simulations. It demonstrates that a multi-faceted approach is essential to minimize beam-induced background to acceptable levels. Additionally, the acquisition and processing of data from these detectors will require specialized techniques. We illustrate that combining multiple mitigation methods can reduce beam-induced hits by several orders of magnitude, thereby substantially lowering the computational burden for data acquisition and processing. Furthermore, we present a method to mitigate the impact of beam-induced data by leveraging the high-momentum and low-vertex multiplicity characteristics of signal events. This technique is expected to be highly effective for both tracking and calorimetry systems. Overall, implementing several mitigation methods together will significantly reduce beam-induced backgrounds, ensuring that signal data acquisition and processing remain feasible. These findings will support the design of next-generation collider detectors. Finally, we conclude that further research into beam dynamics and beam loss mechanisms is necessary to achieve the necessary reductions in beam-induced backgrounds. Such studies are crucial for the development of advanced mitigation methods and will aid in the design of future muon colliders. These investigations should be conducted in close collaboration with detector designers and operators. Additionally, it is recommended that detector designers and operators incorporate beam-induced effects into their simulations and studies to better understand the problem and prepare for its mitigation. This will facilitate the development of effective mitigation methods and ensure the success of the muon collider. To achieve this, a framework for simulating beam loss and beam halo effects on detectors is being developed and will be made available to the community. This will enable the study of mitigation methods and the evaluation of their effectiveness. The paper is intended for a broad audience, including accelerator physicists, beam dynamics experts, and detector designers. It aims to provide a comprehensive overview of beam-induced effects and their mitigation, while also highlighting recent progress in this field. The paper is structured to be accessible to both accelerator and detector physicists, with a focus on the implications of beam-induced effects for detector design and data processing. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of beam-induced effects, while Section 3 discusses mitigation methods for the general case. Section 4 presents a detailed study of mitigation methods for the detector tracking system, and Section 5 examines the impact of beam-induced effects on the calorimeter system. This paper presents Spartan, a framework designed to produce sparsity in both weights and activations through a convex, differentiable objective function. Spartan integrates the strengths of prior approaches by merging the differentiable weight sparsity capability of DropNet with the differentiable joint sparsity of Structured Pruning. To achieve this, we apply regularized optimal transport to enforce sparsity on activations while simultaneously managing dispersion to ensure the resulting tensors possess an arbitrary, specified rank. We demonstrate that Spartan offers superior sparsity models compared to existing methods across various architectures and tasks. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the relationship between the Lp norm and rank, demonstrating how this relationship enables Spartan to create smooth, differentiable sparsity objectives. Finally, we illustrate that these smooth objectives can enhance model performance and simplify the learning process. The code is accessible at https://github.com/robertkatzman/Spartan.

The phenomenon of Pauli blocking, which restricts momentum exchange in gas atoms, is typically observed only at ultra-low temperatures. However, this study demonstrates that Pauli blocking can emerge at significantly higher temperatures within a trapped Bose gas, even without altering the interparticle potential. These findings are supported by both kinetic theory calculations and quantum Monte Carlo simulations. The resulting suppression of thermalization accelerates gas cooling, enabling the creation of a non-equilibrium Bose-Einstein distribution at temperatures substantially above the condensation point. This represents a significant advancement in the field of non-thermal statistical mechanics. Furthermore, the research investigates the impact of Pauli blocking on the formation and stability of a Bose-Einstein condensate, revealing a novel mechanism for the sudden appearance of condensation. These results are directly applicable to experiments involving trapped Bose gases at temperatures far higher than the critical threshold. Additionally, the proposed method for preparing non-thermal distributions is relevant to cold atomic gases confined in optical lattices. Finally, these insights may prove valuable for investigating non-thermal effects in other quantum many-body systems. Unit testing serves as a critical element of the software development lifecycle, enabling the early detection of design flaws and bugs. However, the presence of unit tests "smells"—indicators of poorly written tests—can significantly hinder the efficiency of both tests and developers. While prior research has established that test smells are more prevalent in software than code defects, there is a notable lack of data regarding developers' perceptions of their severity. This study addresses that gap through a survey of 100 developers. The findings indicate that developers view test smells as being more severe than corresponding code smells. Furthermore, severity varies by smell type; for instance, developers consider "Duplicate Test" to be more severe than "Too Broad Test." These insights can inform the creation of automated test quality tools, such as detectors and fixers. Additionally, the study reveals that developers' severity ratings correlate with their experience levels, suggesting that less experienced developers tend to rate the severity of test smells higher than those with more experience. This relationship is particularly strong for "Duplicate Test," which is perceived as more severe by developers with fewer than 10 years of experience. These results may assist developers in managing expectations and allocating resources more effectively. Finally, developers with over 10 years of experience are more likely to agree that test smells are more severe than code smells, whereas those with 1–10 years of experience are more likely to hold the opposite view. This paper contributes to the literature by offering the first empirical evidence on developers' perceptions of test smell severity, a dimension that has been largely overlooked in previous research. These insights can assist developers in test activities, such as refactoring, by helping them prioritize which smells to address. The study also highlights that experience influences how developers evaluate test smells, a factor that should be considered when designing tools to support them. Finally, this research advances the broader understanding of developer perceptions, preferences, and experiences. To support future investigations, the authors have made the survey questionnaire available for reuse. The data and analysis presented herein can facilitate further research into the relationship between developer experience and perceptions of test smells. Additionally, these findings can aid in the design of tool support for test activities, such as refactoring, and inform the development of tools to assist developers in understanding the impact of test smells. The study also contributes to the wider context of developer perceptions, preferences, and experiences. The authors intend to explore the link between developer experience and perceptions of test smells in future work. This paper investigates and explores a novel nonconvex integro-differential sweeping process within the context of variational and dynamical optimization. We first establish the existence of solutions by transforming the problem into a differential inclusion that leverages recent findings by sublevel compactness. Subsequently, we propose two algorithms to demonstrate the practical applicability of our results. The first is a general proximal point method, while the second is a specific scheme designed for a nonconvex sweeping process featuring an integral term dependent on past trajectories. Our analysis confirms that this scheme converges to a solution, thereby validating the application of proximal point algorithms in solving sweeping process problems. Furthermore, we illustrate the relevance of integro-differential sweeping process models through two examples: a dynamical method for minimizing nonconvex energy functionals and a model describing the evolution of a rigid particle within a viscoelastic medium. Finally, we note that the recent advancements in set-valued analysis utilized in this study are also applicable to other significant problems in set-valued analysis, such as sweeping process and differential inclusion models. These findings pave the way for future research into dynamical algorithms for such problems. Additionally, our approach may offer a new perspective for addressing other pertinent issues in variational analysis, including generalized sweeping process problems. This line of inquiry could also inform the development of dynamical optimization methods. In this context, we have already initiated the study of gradient flows associated with nonconvex sweeping process problems in a recent publication. These topics will be explored in detail in upcoming papers. Finally, it is worth mentioning that the techniques employed in this work can be extended to various other problems, such as generalized sweeping process problems. We introduce {\sc KKMCee} ({\sc Monte Carlo} for Kirchhoff--{\sc K}inoshita for lepton pair prOduction in eee colliders), a versatile tool designed for high-energy electron-positron collisions. We introduce a randomized algorithm for computing the singular value decomposition (SVD) of a tensor through random sampling. This method iterates a specific subiteration a predetermined number of times, where each subiteration involves sketching tensor modes via random sampling and reconstructing these modes from the sketches. The primary application of this approach is calculating approximate tensor singular vectors. The proposed algorithm operates within $O(r^2\log^3(n_1n_2\dots n_d))$ time, requiring $O(r\log^2(n_1n_2\dots n_d))$ storage, where $n_1, n_2, \dots, n_d$ represent the tensor's dimensions and $r$ denotes the desired rank. Additionally, we establish a lower bound on the passes necessary to achieve a relative error of $\epsilon$ for the singular vectors with high probability. Specifically, at least $k = \Omega(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2}\log(1/\delta))$ passes are needed to construct an approximation $\hat{v}$ of a singular vector $v$ such that $\frac{\|\hat{v}-v\|_2}{\|v\|_2} \leq \epsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. This lower bound demonstrates that a constant number of passes are sufficient to obtain a constant-approximation singular vector with constant probability. Furthermore, we prove that our upper bound is nearly tight with respect to the number of passes. Finally, we examine the application of this method in recommendation systems. Empirical results indicate that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art single-pass Subspace Iteration algorithm. To our knowledge, this work presents the first algorithm addressing the passes complexity of tensor singular vector approximation. Our findings underscore the significance of passes complexity in tensor computations and suggest that future research should prioritize developing efficient passes complexity for tensor operations. Additionally, we outline several promising future directions for applying our algorithm to various tensor computation tasks. Graph embedding aims to map nodes in a graph to low-dimensional vectors that capture the graph's structural and functional characteristics. While most existing methods focus on static graphs, many real-world networks are inherently dynamic, evolving over time. Directly applying static graph embedding techniques to dynamic networks often fails to fully leverage their temporal structure, resulting in suboptimal representations. Consequently, a growing body of research has been dedicated to developing embedding methods specifically for dynamic graphs. This survey reviews and categorizes these approaches, with a primary emphasis on unsupervised methods, while also briefly touching upon supervised paradigms. The paper begins by outlining fundamental concepts and definitions, followed by an analysis of dynamic graph embedding methods based on their core techniques. Finally, we discuss current research challenges and potential future directions. We anticipate that this survey will assist researchers in efficiently navigating the field of dynamic graph embedding. We present a Sinkhorn Divergence, which functions as a pseudo-entropy regularized optimal transport cost applicable to any $n$-dimensional probability distributions. Unlike the standard Sinkhorn divergence limited to 2-dimensional distributions, our approach offers significant flexibility, enabling the matching of an arbitrary number of distributions. This capability facilitates the training of deep optimal transport networks capable of embedding any number of distributions into a shared metric space. Furthermore, our framework supports the training of these networks to preserve multiple distributions simultaneously. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms current approaches in both theoretical and empirical aspects. Specifically, our proposed deep OT network successfully learns embeddings that capture the characteristics of multiple distributions, thereby enabling downstream tasks such as multi-distribution anomaly detection. Additionally, we show that our network can be trained to learn a metric space consistent with multiple distributions simultaneously. Finally, we validate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in various downstream tasks, including multi-distribution anomaly detection and anomaly detection on imbalanced datasets. These outcomes highlight the potential of our method for learning rich metric spaces that retain diverse distributional properties. To evaluate how local tracing partnerships influence the efficiency of England's COVID-19 contact tracing system, we developed a simulation model. This model incorporates key factors such as partnership size, the proportion of infected individuals within each partnership, and the rate at which new infections occur. Our modeling process involved analyzing data from the first 10,000 daily reports submitted by partnerships, followed by the construction and execution of a simulation using these parameters. Results indicate that smaller partnerships are more effective at tracing a higher volume of cases. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that when a partnership consists of 50 or more members, its ability to trace cases remains stable even as the overall infection rate rises. These findings hold true regardless of whether the partnership structure is small or large. The simulation was executed using Python version 3.8.2. Utilizing the second Gaia Data Release (Gaia DR2), we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the photometric and astrometric characteristics of the open cluster Melotte 72 (M72). We identified 1,003 member stars by applying a stringent selection process that incorporates proper motion, parallax, and photometric criteria. Our investigation yielded a cluster age of 1.05 billion years, a distance of 1.79 kiloparsecs, and a line-of-sight velocity of 130.2 km/s. Additionally, we determined the cluster's physical dimensions to be 1.71 parsecs in length and 1.1 parsecs in width. By constructing a Color-Magnitude Diagram (CMD) and comparing it with theoretical isochrones, we derived the aforementioned age and distance parameters. Furthermore, we identified a blue straggler within M72 and examined the CMDs of both the cluster and the surrounding field stars. Finally, we analyzed the cluster's density profile and color distribution to assess the influence of the Galactic tidal field. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of M72's physical properties and its evolutionary history. This study examines a Gaussian random field under the assumption of sparsity, focusing on the behavior of its excursion sets as a threshold approaches infinity. We demonstrate that, within a specific range of scales where the field adheres to the sparsity condition, all Betti numbers of the excursion set converge in distribution to independent Poisson random variables. The parameters governing these Poisson distributions are expressed as functions of the field's local geometry. This theoretical framework is validated through simulations of stationary elliptically correlated Gaussian processes and an analysis of magnetic data. Additionally, we establish concentration results for the Betti numbers of superlevel sets in Gaussian fields that satisfy sparsity criteria. A key contribution of this work is the derivation of a data-driven method to identify parameter regimes that satisfy sparsity requirements, based solely on global statistical characteristics of the field. This approach is applied to analyze both synthetic and real-world data. Finally, we derive asymptotic results for the total Betti number within arbitrary bounded regions, extending prior findings that were limited to toroidal domains. These results are illustrated using data from the CMB and a real volcano. The paper concludes with a discussion on the volcano case study, which highlights the limitations of current theoretical results. Furthermore, we address the challenge of determining whether an excursion set is empty, a problem that is NP-hard for general sparsity kernels but becomes tractable in certain special cases. We also discuss strategies for selecting parameters in data applications and present a variety of examples. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments, and we conclude with an outline of several promising directions for future research. This work extends the authors' prior research, specifically \cite{Chen2020, Chen2021}. The current manuscript incorporates several new results, including the characterization of empty excursion sets, concentration results for Betti numbers, and an analysis of Betti numbers within arbitrary bounded sets. Additionally, the text has been expanded to better align with applications, featuring an application to a real volcanic eruption and a more thorough discussion of parameter selection. The number of figures has been increased to aid in illustrating key results. Finally, the length of the introduction has been extended to provide greater context for readers. Eye-in-hand camera calibration is a critical process for integrating vision systems with robotic manipulators, enabling tasks such as 3D localization and visual servoing. Although numerous analytical and non-analytical methods exist, they typically demand extensive data collection via a manipulator, demanding time and resources. This paper introduces a novel learning-based approach that achieves accurate calibration using only a single image captured while the camera is positioned at eight pre-defined poses. By leveraging the perspective-n-point problem within a deep learning framework, the method localizes known 3D object points within the camera frame. Unlike traditional techniques, this approach eliminates the need for additional fiducial markers. The proposed method was validated using the OpenCV library and the VisionEye-to-Hand Manipulator (ViHaM) at the Robotics and Vision Laboratory (LAV) of the Universidad Polit{\`e}cnica de Valencia. Experimental results demonstrate an average Euclidean error of 1.1 cm against ground truth data, with a maximum error of 2.5 cm. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness, tolerating up to 20% of incorrect 3D point locations without significant performance degradation. Recent advancements in inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) have enabled the recovery of reward functions from observed state-action data. However, practical applications often require prior knowledge of certain constraints within the reward, a capability that current IRL methods lack. To address this, we introduce ICIRL (Inverse constrained IRL), a novel framework that learns a reward function consistent with observed data while incorporating a prior constraint on specific prior-known action features within the feature space. We provide a theoretical analysis of ICIRL, demonstrating that it can accurately recover the true reward function when provided with enough informative trajectories. Furthermore, experimental results confirm that ICIRL outperforms existing IRL approaches in terms of both sample efficiency and the accuracy of the learned reward function. Combined with an existing linear-time decomposition algorithm, our technique yields the most efficient known linear-space algorithm for identifying linear treewidth. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can be implemented to generate separators with minimum size. Finally, we establish that no algorithm utilizing vertex separators can achieve linear time complexity for decomposing general graphs into treewidth components without also achieving linear space complexity. These findings rely on a lower bound from Berman et al. (2019) regarding the space requirements for computing vertex separators. Furthermore, we prove that the space complexity of vertex-decomposition algorithms is inherently tied to the space complexity of graph minor operations. Consequently, the space-limited nature of minor operations, as described by Marx and Saurabh (2019), directly imposes space limitations on vertex-decomposition algorithms. Clustering, or community detection, is a widely used method for analyzing networks, which are increasingly employed to represent relationships across diverse domains. This study investigates the clustering of heterogeneous networks, characterized by multiple distinct types of connections between a set of entities. We introduce a weighted directed clustering approach that extends existing heuristics to accommodate multi-relational data and integrate multiple scoring mechanisms. Furthermore, we propose a general framework for clustering within potentially inferred networks that may contain structural errors. This framework enables the combination of both measured and inferred network data, addressing a critical challenge in network analysis. We demonstrate this approach through its application to a specific case study. Additionally, various clustering methods are evaluated based on their adherence to a set of desirable properties when applied to weighted directed networks. The paper concludes by discussing the strengths and limitations of current methods and offering recommendations for future research. Given that no single method excels across all network types, method selection should be guided by an understanding of the target properties and the specific attributes of the networks under analysis. This work aims to provide a comprehensive guide for navigating the available methodological options. Finally, the theoretical and computational findings are supported by extensive experiments conducted on both real-world and synthetic networks. Specifically, the study examines the impact of adding noise to network data on clustering results and explores the relationship between network density and the number of network types. These experiments were conducted across a broad spectrum of networks featuring varying numbers of entities, types, and relationships. The code used for all experiments is publicly available. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a hybrid approach integrating the advantages of both data-driven learning and established physics-based modeling techniques. This study introduces a novel a posteriori error estimation framework for PINNs, specifically tailored for surrogate models within the computational mechanics domain. The proposed method calculates the discrepancy between predicted outputs and the underlying partial differential equation (PDE) constraints across a finite set of points. Leveraging the inherent smoothness of PINN solutions, this pointwise residual error is extrapolated to a broader region via a parametric bootstrap procedure. The resulting confidence intervals for PINN predictions enable the differentiation and ranking of samples based on their reliability, thereby facilitating the optimization of data collection strategies. We validate this methodology on a surrogate model designed for a shell structure subjected to impact loading. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed a posteriori error estimation technique yields more precise confidence intervals for PINN predictions compared to conventional uncertainty quantification methods. Furthermore, we illustrate how incorporating this a posteriori error information can direct the optimization of sampling protocols. Ultimately, this research establishes a foundation for the certified machine learning of complex physical phenomena. The code implementing this work is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchwab1997/a-priori-PINNs. Keywords: a posteriori error estimation, uncertainty quantification, physics-informed neural networks, certified machine learning, computational mechanics. Air pollution epidemiology relies on statistical models that integrate data from various sources, including long-term monitoring networks, short-term instruments, ground-based sensors, and satellite observations. This article examines the statistical and machine learning techniques employed to synthesize these diverse data streams into reliable air pollution exposure estimates for use in epidemiological research. It begins by outlining foundational concepts in geostatistics and machine learning before detailing specific methodologies. The discussion covers geostatistical approaches like kriging and co-kriging, as well as advanced machine learning techniques such as Gaussian process regression and neural networks. Additionally, the text introduces emerging machine learning applications in air pollution epidemiology, including the use of natural language processing to derive exposure metrics from news reports. The article concludes by addressing current challenges and future directions within this rapidly evolving field. Keywords: air pollution, epidemiology, geostatistics, machine learning.

We introduce a method to differentiate between peaks arising from Majorana bound states and other non-superconducting topological phases through tunneling spectroscopy, specifically examining how Ohmic dissipation influences conductance. This dissipation is governed by the resistance of tunneling electrodes. Our theoretical framework utilizes a Hamiltonian that incorporates a tunneling Hamiltonian alongside a quantum field representation of the Ohmic environment. We demonstrate that the Majorana peak exhibits unique conductance characteristics: at low temperatures, its conductance rises with temperature before falling at higher temperatures, whereas the conductance of other peaks consistently decreases as temperature increases. Furthermore, the Majorana peak's conductance is highly sensitive to variations in tunneling resistance, a factor that must be accounted for when analyzing experimental data. These predictions offer a viable pathway for confirming the existence of Majorana bound states in topological superconductors. Finally, we compare our findings with prior theoretical studies and discuss the experimental requirements necessary to observe these specific conductance features. We examine the classical problem of exploration in linear bandits featuring a vast action space, where the goal is to identify the optimal action that maximizes expected reward. Our primary contribution is a new algorithm that achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(d \log(N^*) K \log(K))$, where $N^*$ represents the count of arms situated near the set of optimal arms, $K$ is the total number of available arms, and $d$ denotes the dimensionality of the reward vector. This bound surpasses the previous best result of $\tilde{O}(d N^* K \log(K))$ established by Li et al. (2027). Furthermore, our method improves upon the prior best bound of $\tilde{O}(d \sqrt{T K} )$ found in works by Li et al. (2017) and Li et al. (2019). Additionally, we demonstrate that our regret is sensitive to the value of $N^*$, a trait that recent deep learning-based approaches fail to exhibit. We also explore how this exploration-based framework can be utilized to derive high-probability confidence intervals for estimating unknown parameters, thereby broadening the application of linear bandits to other critical decision-making contexts. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of experiments. (Note: This work appears in Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning, 2023). Gapped graphene has been suggested as an ideal system for observing the valley Hall effect. However, we demonstrate that this effect is fundamentally distinct from the orbital Hall effect. Specifically, while the orbital Hall effect is a drift phenomenon, the effect previously attributed to orbital Hall is actually a migration of valley Hall solitons. Our findings indicate that the orbital Hall effect is an intrinsic property of gapped graphene, potentially realizable in existing experiments. Furthermore, we show that the orbital Hall effect can be enhanced by introducing a second term to the Hamiltonian, which is a common characteristic of most graphene models. This term can be incorporated into the tight-binding Hamiltonian through a specific spin-orbit coupling mechanism. Consequently, we propose a viable experimental setup to realize this effect. Finally, our results offer a crucial distinction between orbital Hall effect-driven drift and valley Hall soliton migration, a differentiation that is essential for developing orbital Hall devices. Additionally, we provide the first comprehensive analysis of valley Hall solitons in gapped graphene. These solitons possess a finite velocity and can be manipulated via an external electric field, a feature that sets them apart from topological edge states. This capability enables the construction of valley Hall devices, such as valley Hall transistors, using graphene. We have already proposed a viable configuration for such a device. Notably, the valley Hall effect is not limited to graphene; it can be induced in any two-band model. We also discuss the orbital Hall effect in various other materials. Overall, our findings establish a new framework for investigating the orbital Hall effect and its associated phenomena. Specifically, we demonstrate that orbital Hall currents can be interpreted as a manifestation of orbital Hall instability. This insight is expected to significantly advance the field of orbital Hall physics. Finally, we anticipate that our work will facilitate the realization of orbital Hall devices, thereby expanding the scope of electronic technologies based on orbital Hall effects. In this context, graphene is expected to play a pivotal role. Furthermore, our findings may contribute to the development of orbital magnetic memory and logic technologies. We have also shown that the orbital magnetization of graphene can be manipulated using an external electric field. This capability is expected to be valuable for advancing orbital magnetism research. Additionally, our findings may aid in the creation of orbital magnetic memory devices. We have also demonstrated that the orbital magnetization in graphene exhibits non-topological behavior. Adversarial attacks have become a significant concern in machine learning, particularly in computer vision, where they involve introducing subtle perturbations to input data to deceive models. In contrast, data poisoning attacks compromise training data to induce models to produce incorrect predictions for specific inputs. While graph classification is a prevalent application of machine learning, graph-level attacks remain underexplored. This paper investigates data poisoning on graphs, aiming to introduce new, challenging attack scenarios and establish a comprehensive evaluation framework. We demonstrate that our proposed attacks are effective and difficult to detect, and we show that the current state-of-the-art method for poisoning graph training data can be surpassed through the use of reinforcement learning. Additionally, we highlight that reinforcement learning enables more efficient attacks, facilitating the exploration of more complex attack strategies. Our code is accessible at: https://github.com/SebastianSchroeder1997/DataPoisoning. The source code for all methods can be found at: https://github.com/SebastianSchroeder1997/DataPoisoning/tree/master/poisoning_code.

Catalogue matching is a critical step in the data reduction process for modern time-domain surveys. This study introduces a novel approach to enhance the matching of new observations with existing catalogues by incorporating supplementary data. By utilizing photometric information from neighboring sources, the method models the new light curve of a potential source to facilitate identification. We demonstrate that this technique surpasses traditional matched-filter methods when applied to crowded fields, as verified through tests on both simulated and real data. Furthermore, we illustrate the method's effectiveness in identifying real sources that were previously missed by conventional approaches. Given its utility in improving source recovery rates, this approach is particularly valuable for crowded regions and short-cadence surveys, thereby enhancing the data reduction workflow for future time-domain initiatives. The source recovery rate achieved by this method is detailed in our companion paper (Kraus et al. 2022, arXiv:2201.01000). The algorithm is publicly accessible via a Jupyter notebook at https://github.com/brandonkraus123/catalog_match. Additionally, we have developed a Python package, `catmatch`, which implements the algorithm and is available at https://github.com/brandonkraus123/catalog_match. We outline a recommended workflow for applying this method in a separate paper (Kraus et al. 2022, arXiv:2201.01001). Future enhancements to the `catmatch` package will be detailed in another paper (Kraus et al. 2022, arXiv:2201.01002). This paper addresses the infinite analog of a longstanding open problem in finite hypergraph theory: determining the maximum possible size of a minimal vertex cover in a hypergraph where every vertex cover has a size of at least $k$. We demonstrate that this bound is asymptotically $(1-\frac{1}{k})|V|$. Furthermore, we present an alternative formulation of the problem using filters and present it as an open question within the framework of Prikry filters. Finally, we examine several related problems concerning family sizes and the maximum cardinality of a hypergraph containing no vertex cover of size at most $k$. One such problem serves as the hypergraph equivalent of the classical Erdős-Gallai problem regarding the maximum number of edges in a graph with no cycle of length at most $k$. We establish the correct asymptotic bound for this problem and provide a characterization of the extremal hypergraphs. Additionally, we offer a characterization of extremal families for a related problem using a novel game-theoretic approach. Our primary tool is a new generalization of the Erdős-Stone theorem tailored for hypergraphs with specified vertex cover properties. We also explore connections between this result and the Erdős-Hajnal problem concerning large cliques within hypergraphs that avoid a specific subhypergraph. Finally, we consider the natural extension of this problem to $d$-wise independent events and outline an approach to deriving the optimal upper bound for this scenario.
