Ontologies serve as formal models for concepts within a specific domain, enabling the sharing of knowledge about entities like people, products, and services. While ontology editors allow knowledge engineers to define concepts and establish relationships, the resulting structures often become too vast to manage effectively. Consequently, editors typically rely on various views to navigate and browse these large architectures. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization tool designed to facilitate the browsing of ontology relationships. By supporting multiple layout algorithms, OntoPlot enables users to explore non-hierarchical data through various perspectives. The tool's implementation is straightforward, built upon existing ontology visualization code, and includes several user studies demonstrating its utility. Ultimately, this work offers a valuable resource for browsing large ontologies and represents a significant step toward making ontology browsing more intuitive. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/andrewdavidson/OntoPlot. Additional resources are available at https://ontoplot.org. The accompanying video can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2222222222. We welcome your feedback.

This study addresses semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition (SEEEASR), a task where only unlabeled audio and transcriptions are available, contrasting with the more common scenario of having audio data and labeled transcriptions. CycleGAN was originally introduced to map data between two domains without supervision; however, we introduce a modification to its cycle consistency loss to better suit SEEEASR. We also explore various strategies to integrate CycleGAN into SEEEASR, including mapping unlabeled data into the labeled domain and vice versa. Additionally, we propose an inter-domain loss designed to enhance the discriminability of the data generator. Experiments conducted on the LibriSpeech corpus demonstrate that our proposed inter-domain loss yields a 10 bper relative improvement in character error rate compared to the baseline SEEEASR model. Furthermore, we observe a 7.5% relative reduction in the perplexity of the pre-trained ASR model when trained on unlabeled data using the inter-domain loss. These results confirm the effectiveness of our proposed inter-domain loss. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenZhang1999/Inter-domain-Loss-for-SEEEASR. Active inference serves as a unified theoretical framework for perception, decision-making, and action within embodied agents. This paper introduces a deep active inference model designed for autonomous robot navigation. We demonstrate that the proposed agent can navigate a grid world by learning to minimize prediction errors through deep reinforcement learning. Furthermore, we validate the agent's ability to generalize to unseen environments and explore novel actions. These capabilities suggest that this approach offers a promising pathway toward developing unified perception and decision-making models for robot autonomy. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/DeepActiveInference.

Keywords: embodied intelligence, autonomous robot navigation, active inference, deep reinforcement learning, unified perception and decision making.

This study investigates the Soret effect in a binary mixture of elastic and rigid molecules. Utilizing a hard-core soft-tail molecular model, we demonstrate that for sufficiently strong effective interparticle interactions, the Soret effect in this system diverges from that of fully hard molecules. Specifically, we find that the thermal force acting on soft molecules generates an additional contribution to the Soret effect. This extra term arises because the potential energy of a soft molecule is influenced not only by its center of mass position but also by the configuration of its internal degrees of freedom. We subsequently compare our theoretical findings with existing experimental data. Our results indicate that the additional contribution significantly enhances the agreement between theory and experiment, thereby confirming the critical role of internal degrees of freedom in driving the Soret effect for elastic molecules. Furthermore, we observe that the magnitude of this contribution is directly proportional to the anharmonicity of the molecules' internal potential energy. Finally, we note that our predictions align well with recent experimental results for both polymeric and small-molecular organic liquids. These findings suggest that the internal degree of freedom contributes to the Soret effect in fully hard molecules as well, though this effect is typically negligible for small molecules. Additionally, we show that the internal contribution can be precisely quantified through the ratio of the standard to the additional term in the Soret coefficient. This ratio is determined by the ratio of the standard to the additional thermal force, which can be calculated using the ratio of the internal potential energy's quadratic to cubic terms. This provides a practical method for estimating the internal contribution to the Soret effect. Finally, we demonstrate that the internal contribution to the Soret coefficient for fully elastic molecules is independent of the strength of the interparticle interaction potential. These conclusions are supported by recent experimental and computational results for fully elastic molecules. Our findings suggest that the internal contribution substantially improves the agreement between theory and experiment, particularly for large fully elastic molecules. We also note that the internal contribution is significant for small fully elastic molecules, though its effect is generally less pronounced compared to that of large fully elastic molecules. This is because the internal contribution scales with molecular size, making it more significant for larger molecules. Additionally, the internal contribution is typically negligible for small fully elastic molecules, as the internal potential is nearly harmonic in this case. Finally, we show that the internal contribution to the Soret coefficient for fully elastic molecules is independent of the strength of the interparticle interaction potential, consistent with our theoretical predictions. Automated Essay Scoring (AES) has been a primary focus in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for over ten years, with recent advancements primarily driven by deep learning. However, these methods often depend on extensive datasets and specialized preprocessing, which restricts their application to specific languages and contexts. This paper investigates the use of pre-trained transformer-based language models for AES, demonstrating that carefully selecting these models can achieve competitive results without any model tuning. Our findings indicate that smaller, more efficient models can match the performance of state-of-the-art AES systems while offering greater language adaptability. We evaluate various pre-trained transformers on the main AES task at the tenth edition of the Conference on Computational Linguistics and Signal Processing (COLING 2020), focusing on the Arabic task. We provide a comprehensive analysis of different architectures and datasets to identify the most effective configurations. Additionally, we examine the impact of data volume and source on model performance, ultimately showing that a well-curated small dataset can outperform larger ones. Finally, we discuss the practical implications of our results for both current and future research in automated essay grading. The code is available at: https://github.com/aliabbas12345/automated-essay-scoring.

False positives are a critical challenge in practical object detection. This paper presents a domain adaptive pedestrian detector that utilizes box re-ranking to address this issue. Our approach combines an unsupervised pseudo-labeling technique with box re-ranking to address the problem of false positives. Specifically, we apply pseudo-labeling to filter out obvious false positives from the training dataset, followed by box re-ranking to suppress the remaining ones. This method allows our domain adaptive pedestrian detector to achieve superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches while requiring less computational cost. Extensive experiments on the standard, large-scale, and complex CityPersons domain adaptive benchmark confirm the effectiveness of our unsupervised pseudo-labeling method and box re-ranking strategy. The code is accessible at https://github.com/rogersyq/domain-adaptive-pedestrian-detection. Low-quality music recordings, often captured by consumer devices under adverse conditions, are frequently unusable for music information retrieval tasks. This study investigates music enhancement through a straightforward and efficient approach: a generative adversarial network that translates mono music into a hypothetical high-quality version, combined with a vocoder to translate audio features into high-quality audio. The paper provides an in-depth analysis of the learned high-quality representations and their effectiveness in improving music recognition performance. Additionally, experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms other enhancement techniques on the MSDC18 dataset. The code is accessible at https://github.com/haohaozhang/music-enhancement. Furthermore, the trained model is available for direct use in audio processing at https://github.com/haohaozhang/music-enhancement/tree/master/Models. Our results indicate that music can be effectively enhanced via image translation, a finding that may prove valuable for various audio processing applications. Finally, the paper discusses the broader implications of these findings for the field of music processing.

This paper introduces a new dataset designed to investigate the consequences of a mismatch between object mass and human arm strength during throwing. Specifically, we examine a "faux throw," a motion where an individual attempts to throw an unusually heavy object. Our data comprises 3D joint positions and velocities recorded via a motion capture system, derived from 120 trials involving 20 participants across 24 distinct conditions. We analyze how subjects adapt their movements to successfully complete the task, revealing that these adjustments occur throughout the entire kinematic sequence, from the ground up. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these findings for animating faux throws in real-time applications. Our approach utilizes an inverse dynamics framework to derive the necessary kinematic adaptations, requiring only an estimate of the object's mass as input. This method demonstrates robust performance across all experimental conditions, achieving an average end-effector position error of 1.5% relative to the scene scale. Finally, we discuss how animating these motions can enhance motion capture retargeting for both character animation and human motion synthesis. Supplementary materials, including our code, object mass estimates, and character model, are available at https://fauthrow.github.io/. Keywords: Motion Synthesis, Motion Capture, Motion Animations, Procedural Animation, Character Animation.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) relies on beam decoding to balance translation quality with fluency; however, this process is computationally intensive and often fails to leverage the model's inherent capabilities. Furthermore, it lacks a systematic approach to incorporating linguistic knowledge, such as grammar structures. This paper introduces a novel tree-structured connectionist machine parsing and beam decoding framework that integrates syntactic information into the decoding process. By utilizing top-down tree structures, the method combines predicted sub-trees to generate full trees, thereby reducing the search space and enhancing the efficiency of NMT. Additionally, the approach offers a general method for integrating linguistic knowledge into beam decoding. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method improves the accuracy of standard NMT models while maintaining comparable translation quality. The code is accessible at https://github.

The binding energy (BE) of a molecule on a surface is a critical parameter for modeling astrochemical processes. This value dictates how readily a molecule desorbs from a grain into the gas phase following collisions with energetic species, an event that can trigger dissociative adsorption. While numerous theoretical and experimental methods exist for calculating BE, the scarcity of such data in literature databases hinders their accessibility for researchers. To address this, we have developed the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP), an online resource that aggregates BE values for small molecules and atomic radicals adsorbed on amorphous water and amorphous amine surfaces. The platform offers a user-friendly interface allowing researchers to query a vast collection of BE data generated using both theoretical and experimental approaches. This extensive database is designed to facilitate the rapid and accurate calculation of molecular survival probabilities in the interstellar medium (ISM). Furthermore, BEEP includes a dedicated page for a new open-source Python package, `beep-chem`, which enables users to query the platform and access the full dataset. This tool is particularly valuable for computing molecular survival probabilities within the ISM. We anticipate that BEEP will serve as a vital resource for astrochemists and researchers engaged in theoretical and experimental studies of molecular binding energies. The platform is accessible at http://www.beeptool.org. The `beep-chem` package can be installed via pip using the command `pip install beep-chem`. Additional details regarding BEEP and its capabilities are available at https://github.com/astrochemistry/BEEP. This project was developed in collaboration with the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The study examines a multiplicative stochastic process constrained by a lognormal lower bound. A model for this process is developed, deriving its parameters from time series data of physical quantities. A key finding is that these parameters can be estimated using either an arithmetic or a geometric mean of the observed data. Furthermore, a relationship is established linking a quantity's domain, represented as the number of observable values, to the distribution of its stochastic evolution. This relationship is demonstrated through examples involving both physical and non-physical quantities. The evolution of this quantity is characterized as either ergodic or non-ergodic, depending on the parameter values. The analysis also addresses the issue of non-ergodicity, which can be mitigated by appropriately selecting the stochastic process's lower bound. Finally, the paper illustrates how this lower bound influences the evolution of physical quantities within a system. These results are derived from a combination of analytical methods and numerical simulations. The study concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings. The evolution of non-physical quantities is also briefly considered. This work extends the research presented in [1].

Keywords: Multiplicative stochastic process, Geometric mean, Geometric distribution, Ergodicity, Non-ergodicity, Lower bound, Lognormal distribution, Power law distribution, Stochastic evolution, Geometric series, Harmonic series, System of physical quantities, System of non-physical quantities.

We introduce a new class of shallow random Clifford circuits designed to serve as "expectation estimators." These circuits enable the rapid estimation of expectations $\mathbb{E}_{\psi}[O_1\otimes \cdots \otimes O_m]$ for $m$-qubit observables within any $n$-qubit state $\psi$, utilizing only $O(\log^n C_\psi C_{O_m})$ circuit samples, where $C_\psi$ and $C_{O_m}$ represent the count of qubit gates needed to implement $\psi$ and $O_m$ up to Clifford gates. This sample efficiency surpasses that of standard random Clifford measurements, which require $O(m\log^n n)$ samples. Our approach leverages a recent advancement in quantum state design, specifically a constant-depth random Clifford circuit capable of preparing $k$-designs with $n^{\tilde{O}(\log^2 k)}$ samples. We demonstrate that this construction can be achieved with depth $O(\log^2 k)$ using solely single-qubit gates, allowing for measurements in the $\{H,P\}$ basis. Furthermore, we establish that this depth is optimal for single-qubit gates alone. Additionally, we present an alternative construction with depth $O(\log k)$ measurable in the $\{H,X,Z\}$ basis, which is optimal when permitting two-qubit gates. These findings hold significant utility for variational quantum algorithms, as they facilitate a substantial reduction in the number of measurement shots required during state preparation. Finally, we explore extensions of these results to $k$-designs derived from random unitary circuits. In this context, we identify a phase transition in the necessary circuit depth and count, contingent upon the ratio $n/k$. Our results indicate that the depth and count scale as $O(\log^2 k)$ and $O(k^n)$, respectively, for $k \leq n/\log^2 n$. Beyond the application to the expectation estimation problem, we also examine the construction of $k$-designs via random Clifford circuits. We establish upper bounds for depth and gate count that align with our findings for expectation estimation, as well as for the generation of $k$-designs using purely random unitary circuits. Moreover, we derive lower bounds demonstrating that a depth of $O(\log k)$ is necessary when two-qubit gates are permitted. The study examines the reflectionless Ds-II equations across both $2+1$ and $1+1$ dimensional settings, deriving each from a common $2+1$ dimensional matrix Riemann-Hilbert problem via specific projections. By applying a large $k$ asymptotic analysis to this problem, the authors establish new insights into the $n=2$ case that clarify the distinct $n=1$ behaviors observed in both dimensional contexts. These findings rely on a novel asymptotic analysis of a matrix differential equation featuring a large parameter, a methodology anticipated to be valuable for other non-linear integrable PDEs. The research demonstrates that the Ds-II equation with a vector coefficient exhibiting two-step decaying oscillations exhibits unique properties in both $2+1$ and $1+1$ dimensions, including a $4\pi$ phase shift in the large $|k|$ limit for the reflection coefficient. Furthermore, the authors provide a unified explanation for these phenomena and offer a new perspective on the well-documented $2\pi$ phase shift characteristic of solitons. These results stem from the $k$-hierarchy of the Ds-II equations, which governs the relationship between the potential and its spatial and temporal derivatives. Consequently, the paper presents a unified analysis of the large $|k|$ asymptotics for the reflection coefficient in all low-order equations within this hierarchy. Additionally, the study explores the relationship between this large $|k|$ behavior and the short-distance asymptotics of the corresponding potentials. The analysis reveals that the short-distance asymptotics of the $k$-th equation in the hierarchy are determined by the large $|k|$ behavior of the $k-1$'st equation. Finally, the paper offers a unified explanation for the short-distance asymptotics of these second-flow equations. These outcomes are achieved through the application of a recently developed technique for analyzing short-distance asymptotics in integrable PDEs possessing a Lax pair. The technique relies on a specific asymptotic property of the monodromy data, which is demonstrated for the Ds-II equations in this work. Although deep learning models have achieved remarkable success across numerous NLP tasks, they often struggle with out-of-distribution data and are susceptible to adversarial attacks. To address these vulnerabilities, we introduce a novel approach called sibylvariant transformations (Sibyl), a collection of general text transformations designed to simultaneously enhance both out-of-distribution and adversarial robustness. These transformations operate by applying diverse modifications to text, such as inserting or deleting characters, words, or spaces, as well as substituting words with their synonyms. We conducted experiments on three text classification benchmarks: Enron (email spam detection), IMDB (movie review classification), and 20Newsgroups (newsgroup classification). The results demonstrate that Sibyl consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art defense methods. Furthermore, our transformation framework is broadly applicable to various neural architectures, including BERT, LSTM, CNN, and CRF. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenYi-1996/Sibyl. Finally, we release the Sibyl transformations to the community, hoping they will inspire further research into Sibyl and advance the broader goal of building more robust natural language processing systems. Meta-learning aims to create general representations capable of facilitating rapid adaptation to novel tasks. Although meta-supervised learning has recently demonstrated significant potential for unsupervised domain adaptation, current methods largely depend on deep neural networks, which hinder the ability to derive insights regarding their representation capabilities or convergence properties. This paper introduces a method for efficiently representing domain-invariant features using linear layers. We prove that under specific assumptions, this proposed approach is provably optimal in terms of generalization error for linear representations. Furthermore, we develop an efficient algorithm to learn these representations, which is guaranteed to converge to the optimal solution. Experimental results confirm that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on multiple unsupervised domain adaptation benchmarks. Achieving multilingual communication for low-resource languages is a critical objective, as it promotes greater language diversity and inclusivity. While recent advancements in machine translation have made this goal increasingly feasible, the primary challenge remains the scarcity of annotated data in low-resource languages. Consequently, recent research has explored model distillation and quantization to enable efficient, resource-aware communication. This study evaluates the robustness of these two techniques by examining how compression impacts model performance. Our findings indicate that quantization is superior for web-scale multilingual communication, whereas distillation is better suited for low-data environments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an optimal compression strategy exists that balances model efficiency and performance. This research represents the first direct comparison of quantization versus distillation, offering a foundational approach to optimizing model compression. We introduce a new class of hypergraphs designed to model the dynamics of a scalar field within a de Sitter background, specifically de Sitter space, and calculate their number densities. By applying a generalization of the law of large numbers, we demonstrate that the density of hyperedges connecting two vertices within these graphs approaches the square root of two as the number of vertices increases. This result yields a novel interpretation of the Lagrangian density for the scalar field, expressed as an irrational number belonging to the field of 2-adic numbers. Furthermore, we derive formulas for the densities of vertices and edges in these hypergraphs, along with the kinetic and potential energy densities associated with the de Sitter scalar field. Additionally, we present methods for constructing complete sets of $n$-vertex hypergraphs and discuss how these findings can be utilized to construct multi-field inflationary models. Finally, we explore the application of $p$-adic numbers in physics, with a specific focus on their role in cosmology. This work serves as a foundation for further research into the mathematical structures underlying de Sitter scalar field theory. Keywords: hypergraphs, hyperedge, hypergraph density, multi-field inflation, $p$-adic numbers, irrational number.

This study addresses the challenge of segmenting lung regions in chest X-rays for the early detection of pneumonia. We introduce a novel approach that reduces the requirement for labelled data by training models on unlabelled datasets. Our primary objective is to evaluate the impact of various image augmentation techniques on segmentation performance. We evaluated eight augmentations across three deep learning architectures: U-Net, DeepLabV3+, and DeepLabV3+ enhanced with attention gates. The results indicate that combining all augmentations yields superior performance compared to using any single technique alone. Furthermore, we found that the U-Net model, when deepened, surpasses both the standard and attention-gated variants of DeepLabV3+. Finally, we demonstrate that applying multiple augmentations consistently improves segmentation outcomes across all tested models. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456789/pneumonia_segmentation. Our findings confirm that U-Net effectively segments pneumonia regions in chest X-rays when trained with augmented datasets, and that image augmentations significantly enhance segmentation performance. These results hold true across the three different deep learning models examined. Additionally, the U-Net model is noted for its superior segmentation capabilities and reduced computational cost. We anticipate that these findings will be valuable to researchers and practitioners engaged in medical image segmentation. Future work will explore the application of image augmentations in other medical imaging modalities. We hope this research inspires further investigation into data augmentation for medical image analysis. Finally, we acknowledge the contributions of all individuals involved in this field. Thank you. Keywords: Pneumonia Segmentation, U-Net, DeepLabV3+, Image Augmentation.

This paper introduces a novel, non-adversarial, and prompt-based Decoupled Controllable Image Captioning (DCIC) framework. Unlike previous controllable captioning methods that rely on adversarial training, our approach separates the content creation process into two distinct stages: a content generation task and a content screening task. To achieve this, we develop a prompt-tuning module that adapts pre-trained language models for the screening phase without requiring any additional parameters. We evaluate DCIC across four controllable tasks—editing, completing, and summarizing images—and demonstrate that our model surpasses state-of-the-art performance in objective metrics. Furthermore, human assessments confirm that our results are more diverse and better aligned with human preferences compared to existing methods. The codebase is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Decoupled-Controllable-Image-Captioning. Given the growing trend of controllable multimodal generation, we anticipate that DCIC will serve as a valuable reference for future research in this area. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.01001. Keywords: Image Captioning, Decoupled Controllable Image Captioning, Decoupled Controllable Image Generation, Decoupled Controllable Diffusion Models, Decoupled Controllable GANs.

The field of artificial intelligence safety has developed various metrics to assess and compare model harm, yet they frequently overlook harm stemming from causes outside the model. This paper introduces a causal framework for analyzing such external sources of harm. We demonstrate that standard metric analyses can be recast within this causal structure, revealing that many proposed methods are susceptible to external causes and may even be manipulated. Furthermore, we propose "abduction," a novel causal method for evaluating model harm, and show its potential through a novel dataset. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of integrating causal analysis into AI safety research. The code and data associated with this work can be found at https://github.com/robertgamer/AISafetyCausal. Our findings indicate that AI safety researchers should account for external causes of harm when designing new evaluation metrics. Additionally, our work underscores the necessity of establishing rigorous, agreed-upon standards for evaluating harmful AI behavior across the entire society in which it operates. We hope this research will stimulate further investigation into the causal structures surrounding harmful AI. Our specific contributions are threefold: (1) we offer a comprehensive catalog of existing AI safety metrics within a causal framework, exposing numerous technical flaws in prior literature; (2) we propose abduction as a framework for analyzing harmful AI, supported by a novel dataset for societal impact evaluation; and (3) we advocate for the development of more rigorous and standardized metrics for evaluating harm in AI systems. Our work is the product of a collaborative effort by researchers from diverse backgrounds, and we extend our gratitude to all contributors. We anticipate that this research will inspire additional investigations into the various causal factors influencing the evaluation of harmful AI. This paper introduces MMLSpark, a new open-source library that unifies Microsoft's Hadoop and Spark distributions into a single platform. By integrating Hadoop and Spark, MMLSpark enables the development, deployment, and execution of scalable machine learning models. We demonstrate how Hadoop integration facilitates the execution of the Telemetrix distributed streaming data pipeline, while Spark supports the execution of a K-Means clustering model. Furthermore, we illustrate how executing a Random Forest model on Hadoop and Spark within the same environment allows for straightforward comparison of performance and scalability. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/MMLSpark. Future work will involve extending MMLSpark to support additional Microsoft algorithms, such as Telemetrix distributed processing pipelines and Spark ML models like K-Means and Random Forests. The paper also explores the application of this framework to real-world scenarios, including the processing of telemetrix data streams and prediction of real-time sensor data. Finally, the study compares the execution environments of Spark standalone, Hadoop standalone, and Hadoop-YARN, with results indicating that Spark offers superior performance and scalability. The paper concludes by discussing the benefits of a unified environment for executing scalable machine learning models and outlines potential future research directions. Keywords: Open Source, Hadoop, Spark, Scalability, Performance, Deep Learning.

This technical report explores zero-shot neural machine translation applied to speech. We introduce a new multilingual speech corpus containing 9 million sentences across 108 languages, which we utilize to pre-train a speech encoder for speech-machine translation tasks. By employing an encoder that was not part of the training dataset, we demonstrate the 0-shot NLG paradigm. We evaluate our approach on various speech-to-machine translation tasks and compare its performance against a zero-shot T5 baseline. Additionally, we investigate the use of speech encoders to model speaker characteristics, such as gender, within the zero-shot framework. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ashishpaulv/zero_shot_stmt. Finally, we discuss the potential of zero-shot speech-to-machine translation for low-resource languages. This technique enables the deployment of multilingual models without requiring parallel data for specific language pairs. We anticipate that zero-shot speech-to-machine translation will facilitate more efficient and environmentally friendly multilingual model training. Furthermore, we aim to establish multilingual speech as a new input modality for large language models. We anticipate that zero-shot speech-to-text translation will enhance multilingual representation learning, leading to more compact multilingual TTS models. Our code can be found here: https://github.com/ashishpaulv/zero_shot_stmt. We look forward to receiving feedback and suggestions from the community. Thank you. :)

The analysis demonstrates the existence of weak solutions for these equations under the assumption of small diffusion terms. Furthermore, when dissipation is present, we establish uniform estimates and derive the weak-$\omega$-limit compactness of the solution. Additionally, we prove the asymptotic stability of the constant solution within a domain lacking dissipation but possessing a specific boundary dissipation term. Finally, utilizing a variant of the Lyapunov function method, we derive an exponential decay rate for solutions in cases where dissipation and boundary dissipation terms exist. Accurate short-term energy consumption forecasts are essential for managing modern smart grids. This study evaluates the impact of forecast fusion and household structure on probabilistic probabilistic forecasting within the Dutch low-voltage network. Using real-world electricity meter data, we developed quantile regression models for 1-hour ahead forecasts, incorporating weather variables and time-series features. We compared individual models against a multivariate XGBoost framework and utilized bootstrap resampling to generate percentiles for probabilistic predictions. Furthermore, we explored the benefits of forecast fusion and examined how smart meter characteristics influence appliance usage. The results indicate that multivariate XGBoost and forecast fusion can enhance both accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, we observed that household structure significantly affects the daily maximum electricity consumption. These findings suggest that integrating multiple meter types and applying multivariate XGBoost could substantially benefit the Dutch low-voltage grid. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that advanced machine learning models and forecast fusion can improve both the precision and efficiency of probabilistic load forecasting. By analyzing the impact of household structure, we identified that the daily peak consumption is primarily driven by the presence of a washing machine and a dishwasher. These conclusions are supported by detailed visualizations of the data. The complete dataset and all associated code are available on our GitHub repository. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly advanced the automatic analysis of medical images, including the detection and segmentation of lung lesions in CT scans for COVID-19 patients. However, current deep learning models often suffer from bias, leading to suboptimal performance. This study introduces a weakly supervised learning approach to achieve unbiased localisation and segmentation of lung lesions in COVID-19 CT scans. The proposed framework comprises three key components: a multi-scale feature extraction module, a weakly supervised lesion localisation mechanism, and a weakly supervised lesion segmentation module. Specifically, the multi-scale feature extraction module generates high-level features at various scales, which are utilized to identify and segment the lung region. Subsequently, these high-level features are aggregated across different scales and spatial locations to create attention maps that guide the localisation of lesion regions. Finally, the attention maps are mapped onto deep features to estimate a probability distribution for segmenting the lesions. The model was evaluated using the LUNA16 and COVID-19 datasets, with quantitative results demonstrating its effectiveness. Additionally, an ablation study was conducted to further verify the model's performance. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed model outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both lesion localisation and segmentation. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Weakly-Supervised-Lung-Lesion-Localization-and-Segmentation}. Future research will explore the application of weakly supervised learning to other medical image tasks. Precise localization and identification of vertebrae are critical for numerous clinical tasks, including vertebra labeling, surgical planning, and radiation therapy. This study introduces a novel method for automatically localizing and identifying vertebrae in computed tomography (CT) scans. The approach comprises three primary components: an anatomical model-constrained optimization method for spine localization, a deep learning-based vertebra identification model, and an initialization strategy for this optimization that leverages prior deep learning identification results. Specifically, our proposed initialization strategy employs a coarse-to-fine deep learning model to rapidly and accurately localize the superior-inferior positions of all vertebrae, thereby significantly accelerating the subsequent anatomical model-constrained optimization process. We evaluated our method using 100 CT images from the Vertebra Challenge 2018 dataset, which were reserved for testing. Our results demonstrate that this method achieves a localization success rate of 95% and an identification success rate of 85%. Furthermore, we validated the method's effectiveness by applying it to a whole-patient CT image, successfully and accurately localizing and identifying every vertebra. Finally, the method was applied to a specific clinical scenario to localize and identify vertebrae in a patient's CT scan, yielding satisfactory results. These findings indicate that the proposed method is both effective and practical for real-world clinical applications. We introduce a theory of resonant electron scattering that incorporates quantized electromagnetic fields, specifically addressing regimes where quantum vacuum fluctuations significantly influence scattering processes. Our findings indicate that these fluctuations can stabilize an electron against sudden ionization by a strong laser pulse—a phenomenon we term "dynamical stabilization." This effect becomes observable when the photon density of states is altered, such as when the electron interacts with a highly reflective mirror positioned at a distance comparable to the electron's localization radius. Under these conditions, dynamical stabilization by cavity vacuum fluctuations can be achieved at critical photon densities that are orders of magnitude lower than those required for conventional dynamical stabilization through driving fields. We provide theoretical predictions for this phenomenon and propose an experimental setup to verify it: a single electron trapped in an optical lattice situated between two high-finesse mirrors, with the electron resonance frequency tuned to match a cavity mode. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the phenomenon can be detected via resonant photoemission spectroscopy. Notably, this resonance exhibits a reduced ionization rate and a phase shift of $\pi$ relative to the case without dynamical stabilization. Additionally, we show that the phase shift can serve as a sensitive indicator for characterizing ultrastrong light-matter coupling. Our research offers a novel approach to studying dynamical stabilization and opens a new avenue for investigating quantum vacuum effects. The proposed experiment is feasible with current technology and could be realized in the near future. These results hold significant implications for quantum electrodynamics, nanophotonics, and quantum information science. The findings are applicable to scenarios involving resonant electron scattering with quantized light fields, including attosecond strong-field physics, electron microscopy, and electron microscopy-based spectroscopy. Finally, we discuss the potential for observing dynamical stabilization in free-space vacuum at photon densities that are experimentally accessible. This would require further reducing the frequency of the bound state, thereby increasing its sensitivity to low-frequency vacuum fluctuations. We illustrate this using an example of a Rydberg atom, for which the required photon density is approximately $10^4$ cm$^{-3}$. We also outline potential strategies for achieving dynamical stabilization in free-space vacuum using current technology. These approaches involve either employing laser fields with very low intensities or utilizing a Rydberg atom with a localization radius of several millimeters. Both scenarios are experimentally feasible. This study investigates the use of elastic actuators within quadrupedal robots, specifically examining how actuator compliance influences locomotion performance. We begin by reviewing prior research that relied on fixed-impedance control, noting its limitations in fully utilizing actuator compliance. To address this, we introduce a novel machine learning-based controller designed to actively exploit this physical characteristic. Our approach was evaluated through simulations of the Unitree H1 robot, comparing the new method against a model tree regression baseline and a human-in-the-loop controller. Results demonstrate that the machine learning controller surpasses both alternatives in terms of performance and energy efficiency. Furthermore, we provide an analysis of the actuator's joint torque profiles to highlight the specific ways in which the learned policy leverages actuator compliance. Finally, we outline the potential of this strategy for enhancing quadrupedal locomotion in future hardware applications. The simulation code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alexschulz/elastic-actuators-loc.

We introduce a quantum variational framework designed to address the separability problem in multi-qubit systems. The method's performance is evaluated using three- and four-qubit states, demonstrating its effectiveness on existing hardware. We also examine the performance of the approach using a two-qubit Bell state embedded within a larger system. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of measurement errors on the results. This research was conducted as part of the Oxford Quantum Varsity program, an initiative by the Blavatnik school of quantum studies at the University of Oxford. Slab plasmas are susceptible to tearing modes, a phenomenon that has been extensively studied for over half a century. The classical understanding of this instability relies on the premise that magnetic field line reconnection occurs due to a finite resistivity within a collisional plasma. However, in the collisionless, magnetized plasmas typical of space and fusion environments, resistivity is negligible. This study demonstrates that a mode can still become unstable under these conditions if the plasma width is sufficiently narrow. This collisionless tearing mode is driven by a non-ideal electric field generated by the Hall term in the generalized Ohm's law. The research provides a detailed analysis of the mode's growth rate, growth phase, and associated energy, offering insights relevant to both space and laboratory plasma physics. Specifically, it explains the energy release mechanisms behind magnetic reconnection events in the solar atmosphere and within Earth's magnetosphere. Furthermore, this mode may play a significant role in small-scale reconnection observed in the Large Helical Device at RIKEN and in plasma simulations of magnetic reconnection in the Sun's corona. The study concludes by outlining the initial conditions required to trigger the collisionless tearing mode in laboratory settings. Additionally, it addresses the potential impact of finite plasma beta on the mode's stability. Overall, this work establishes a framework for comprehending small-scale tearing modes in both collisionless and nearly collisionless plasmas. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/rikend/SLAB_Hall_Tearing_Mode. A supplementary video is available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222. The visual appearance of clothing is influenced by multiple attributes, such as the wearer's body shape, hair style, and skin color. In real-world scenarios, it is often impossible to control every attribute; for instance, a fashion e-commerce site may only be able to adjust the model's hair style or skin color while keeping the body shape fixed. Consequently, image retrieval systems must locate images that match the desired attributes while preserving the uncontrollable ones. This paper introduces a novel attribute manipulation approach that converts semi-supervised labels into a model image along with specific attributes. We also propose a new deep convolutional neural network architecture designed to simultaneously extract both visible and invisible attributes from images. To effectively combine these attributes during retrieval, we develop a new scoring function that integrates the scores of all image attributes. Experimental results on the UP1K dataset demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. The proposed network structure and scoring function can be readily applied to other image retrieval tasks. Additionally, our network demonstrates robustness across various datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/SEMISUP-ATTR-MANIP.

This work addresses how flow curve methods can yield approximate solutions to both bounded and unbounded instances of the equation $Ax=y$, where the data $y$ may be contaminated by noise. We demonstrate that the dual gradient flow offers an effective approach for both cases. Specifically, for noisy unbounded problems, we derive a parameter choice rule based on the discrete burn-in time, proving that the resulting approximation converges to the true solution as noise levels diminish. Furthermore, for noisy bounded problems, we establish convergence to the minimum $\ell_1$-norm solution when an appropriate regularization parameter is selected. Additionally, we introduce a novel dual gradient flow for unbounded problems that converges to the minimum weak $\ell_1$-norm solution. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of these algorithms on both synthetic and practical datasets. Notably, for practical applications, we find that the dual gradient flow for unbounded problems often outperforms even the best results achieved by Tikhonov regularization. All findings are supported by numerical experiments. The associated Python code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/RezaGhasemi123/DualGradientFlow}. These results indicate that, for many practical scenarios, dual gradient flow methods are highly competitive with established techniques. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides a brief overview of the linear inverse problem and the direct method. Section 3 examines the dual gradient flow for unbounded problems, while Section 4 explores its application to bounded problems. Section 5 presents numerical examples, and Section 6 concludes with a summary and suggestions for future research. This paper is a revised and expanded version of our arXiv preprint \textbf{arXiv:2005.07007}. We are deeply grateful to the anonymous reviewers for their insightful comments and suggestions. We also extend our thanks to Dr. M. K. To address this, we introduce a new cost constructor designed for light field depth estimation that leverages an occlusion mask to eliminate invalid view-to-view comparisons caused by object occlusions. By integrating this cost constructor into a lifting-based framework, we transform 5-D signal space into a stack of virtual ray images, which are subsequently processed using a lifting-based multiresolution decomposition. Our findings demonstrate that removing a significant portion of mismatched ray pairs through the occlusion mask enhances both the accuracy and computational efficiency of the depth estimation framework. We evaluate our approach against state-of-the-art methods, revealing that our technique achieves superior performance in depth estimation. Furthermore, we validate our methodology across various datasets, including the LTZ4D and SceneChic datasets. This paper examines the Fokas-Lenells equations using a bilinear method. We first bilinearize the defocusing and focusing variants to derive double Wronskian solutions for both equations, thereby resolving each of them. Subsequently, we introduce a generalized bilinear framework capable of addressing arbitrary combinations of these two equations, a task that standard techniques like the Hirota method or Darboux transformation cannot achieve. This approach yields multiple types of Wronskian solutions, including multi-Wronskian, block Wronskian, and weighted block Wronskian solutions, for the resulting combined system. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the dynamics of the combined equations and investigate the behavior of their Wronskian solutions through numerical simulations. Finally, we outline a strategy to extend this method to other coupled nonlinear evolution equations. Notably, the techniques employed here are also applicable to the coupled modified KdV KdV hierarchy and the coupled KdV hierarchy. Additionally, the paper includes an appendix detailing the Hirota bilinear approach for the Fokas-Lenells hierarchy. The primary innovation of this work lies in its ability to address the Fokas-Lenells coupled equations, a significant advancement given the limitations of conventional methods. This study significantly contributes to the field by providing a novel and effective approach to solving Fokas-Lenells coupled nonlinear evolution equations. The methods utilized are highly general and can be readily adapted to solve various other coupled nonlinear evolution equations. Overall, this work represents a substantial contribution to the field by introducing a new and promising methodology for solving Fokas-Lenells coupled nonlinear evolution equations. The proliferation of wireless devices has created significant challenges for home WiFi networks, often resulting in congestion that degrades user experience. To address this, we introduce CALAS, a novel extension to the IEEE 802.11 standard designed to assist clients in choosing optimal connection points—either an Access Point or an Extender—by accounting for channel load. This standard utilizes IEEE 802.11k for discovery and IEEE 802.11v for management. CALAS is implemented as a lightweight, fully distributed protocol, requiring no central controller or modifications to access points. Instead, client stations are the primary drivers, initiating the process by requesting neighbor AP information and broadcasting their own signal details to facilitate mutual selection. We evaluated CALAS through extensive simulations of home environments featuring multiple WiFi networks. Our results demonstrate that the protocol effectively reduces channel load by guiding clients toward less congested networks. Furthermore, CALAS exhibits rapid convergence and minimal overhead, as it only necessitates the exchange of two additional management frames per station. These findings indicate that CALAS is well-suited for deployment in dense residential settings. Additionally, we have integrated this protocol into the NS-3 network simulator to enable future research on CALAS-based channel load-aware selection.
